explain.title: Scalars and vectors
explain.body: A scalar has magnitude only. A vector has both magnitude and direction. Distance and speed are scalars; displacement, velocity and acceleration are vectors.

explain.title: Distance and displacement
explain.body: Distance is the total path travelled. Displacement is the change in position in a specified direction. Displacement magnitude cannot be greater than distance.

explain.title: Speed, velocity and acceleration
explain.body: Speed is distance per unit time. Velocity is displacement per unit time. Acceleration is the change in velocity per unit time.

explain.title: Motion graphs
explain.body: The gradient of a distance–time graph gives speed; the gradient of a displacement–time graph gives velocity. The gradient of a speed–time graph gives acceleration, and its area gives distance.

explain.title: Equations of motion
explain.body: For constant acceleration, use v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², or v² = u² + 2as. For motion under gravity, use g as the acceleration and keep the chosen direction and signs consistent.

mistakes: Treating distance and displacement as identical even when direction changes.
Calling velocity uniform just because speed is constant; direction must also stay constant.
Reading the gradient of a speed–time graph as distance; distance is the area under that graph.
Forgetting to convert km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹ before using SI units in an equation.
Using the wrong sign for gravity or braking acceleration.
Leaving units out of a numerical answer or omitting the direction when it matters.

recap.question: A stone is dropped from rest. What is its initial velocity, and which way is g positive?
recap.answer: For a body dropped from rest, vᵢ = 0 and g = 10 m s⁻² downward.

recap.question: A stone is dropped from rest. How far does it fall in the first second? Take g = 10 m s⁻².
recap.answer: 5 m

solutions.question: Define scalar and vector quantities.
steps: A scalar quantity is a physical quantity which has magnitude only and no direction.
A vector quantity is a physical quantity which has both magnitude and direction.
solutions.answer: A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has magnitude and direction.

solutions.question: Give 5 examples each for scalar and vector quantities.
steps: Examples of scalar quantities: distance, speed, time, mass and temperature.
Examples of vector quantities: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and weight.
solutions.answer: Scalars: distance, speed, time, mass and temperature. Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and weight.

solutions.question: State head-to-tail rule for addition of vectors.
steps: To add vectors by the head-to-tail rule, place the tail of the second vector at the head of the first vector.
The resultant vector is drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector.
solutions.answer: Join the vectors head to tail; the resultant extends from the first tail to the last head.

solutions.question: What are distance- time graph and speed-time graph?
steps: A distance-time graph represents the distance covered by a body with respect to time.
A speed-time graph represents the speed of a body with respect to time.
solutions.answer: A distance-time graph shows distance against time; a speed-time graph shows speed against time.

solutions.question: Falling objects near the Earth have the same constant acceleration. Does this imply that a heavier object will fall faster than a lighter object?
steps: No. The same constant acceleration of falling objects does not mean that a heavier object falls faster than a lighter object.
In the absence of air resistance, all objects near the Earth fall with the same acceleration, regardless of their masses.
solutions.answer: No. Without air resistance, heavy and light objects fall with the same acceleration.

solutions.question: The vector quantities are sometimes written in scalar notation (not bold face). How is the direction indicated?
steps: When a vector is written in scalar notation, its direction is indicated by a plus (+) or minus (−) sign with respect to a chosen reference direction.
solutions.answer: Its direction is indicated by a plus or minus sign relative to a chosen reference direction.

solutions.question: A body is moving with uniform speed. Will its velocity be uniform? Give reason.
steps: No, not necessarily.
Velocity is uniform only when both speed and direction remain constant.
A body moving with uniform speed may change its direction; therefore, its velocity may change.
solutions.answer: Uniform speed does not necessarily mean uniform velocity, because the direction may change.

solutions.question: Is it possible for a body to have acceleration? When moving with: (i) constant velocity (ii) constant speed
steps: (i) A body moving with constant velocity has no acceleration, because its velocity does not change.
(ii) A body moving with constant speed may have acceleration if its direction changes, as in circular motion.
If it moves with constant speed in a straight line without changing direction, its acceleration is zero.
solutions.answer: Constant velocity means zero acceleration; constant speed can have acceleration if direction changes.

solutions.question: Distance and displacement may or may not be equal in magnitude. Explain this statement.
steps: Distance is the total length of the actual path travelled by an object, whereas displacement is the shortest straight-line distance from its initial to its final position in a specified direction.
If an object moves along a straight line in one direction, the magnitude of its distance and displacement are equal.
If an object changes direction or follows a curved path, the magnitude of its distance is greater than the magnitude of its displacement.
solutions.answer: Distance and displacement are equal in magnitude for straight-line motion in one direction; otherwise, distance is greater.

solutions.question: When a bullet is fired, its velocity with which it leaves the barrel is called the muzzle velocity of the gun. The muzzle velocity of one gun with a longer barrel is lesser than that of another gun with a shorter barrel. In which gun is the acceleration of the bullet larger? Explain your answer.
steps: Assume the bullet starts from rest and has uniform acceleration while moving through the barrel.
For motion with uniform acceleration, v² = u² + 2as. Since u = 0, a = v²/(2s).
The gun with the longer barrel produces a lower muzzle velocity, while its barrel length is greater.
Therefore, its value of v²/(2s) is smaller. The bullet's acceleration is larger in the gun with the shorter barrel.
solutions.answer: The bullet's acceleration is larger in the gun with the shorter barrel.

solutions.question: For a complete trip, average velocity was calculated. Its value came out to be positive. Is it possible that its instantaneous velocity at any time during the trip had the negative value? Give justification of your answer.
steps: Yes, it is possible.
A positive average velocity for the complete trip means that the net displacement is in the positive direction.
The object may move in the negative direction during part of the trip and still have a positive net displacement for the complete trip.
Therefore, its instantaneous velocity may be negative at some time during the trip.
solutions.answer: Yes. Instantaneous velocity can be negative during part of a trip even when average velocity for the complete trip is positive.

solutions.question: A ball is thrown vertically upward with velocity v. It returns to the ground in time T. Which of the following graphs correctly represents the motion? Explain your reasoning.
steps: For upward motion, take the upward direction as positive.
The ball has initial velocity +v and constant acceleration −g due to gravity.
Its velocity decreases uniformly with time, becomes zero at the highest point, and then becomes negative as the ball falls.
Thus, the correct velocity–time graph is a straight line with negative slope, starting at +v, crossing the time axis at T/2, and ending at −v at time T.
solutions.answer: The correct velocity–time graph is a straight line from +v at t = 0 to −v at t = T, crossing zero at T/2.

solutions.question: The figure given below shows the distance - time graph for the travel of a cyclist. Find the velocities for the segments a, b and c.
steps: The distance–time graph referred to in the question is not included, so the numerical velocities of segments a, b and c cannot be determined.
The velocity for each segment is found from the slope of that segment of the distance–time graph: velocity = change in distance / change in time.
A steeper segment represents a greater velocity; a horizontal segment represents zero velocity.
solutions.answer: The velocities cannot be calculated without the graph and its scale; each is the slope of its segment.

solutions.question: Is it possible that the velocity of an object is zero at an instant of time, but its acceleration is not zero? If yes, give an example of such a case.
steps: Yes, it is possible for the velocity of an object to be zero at an instant while its acceleration is not zero.
For example, when a ball is thrown vertically upward, its velocity is zero for an instant at the highest point.
At that instant, its acceleration is still g downward due to gravity.
solutions.answer: Yes. At the highest point of a vertically thrown ball, velocity is momentarily zero but acceleration is g downward.

solutions.question: How a vector can be represented graphically? Explain.
steps: A vector is represented graphically by a directed line segment.
The length of the line segment, drawn according to a suitable scale, represents the magnitude of the vector.
The arrowhead shows the direction of the vector.
The vector is labelled with its symbol.
solutions.answer: A vector is shown by a scaled directed line segment: its length represents magnitude and its arrowhead represents direction.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: (a) rest and motion
steps: Rest: An object is at rest if its position does not change with time relative to its surroundings.
Motion: An object is in motion if its position changes with time relative to its surroundings.
Rest and motion are relative terms; an object may be at rest relative to one body and in motion relative to another.
solutions.answer: An object is at rest if its position does not change with time relative to its surroundings, and in motion if it does.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: (b) speed and velocity
steps: Speed is the distance covered by an object in unit time.
Velocity is the displacement of an object in unit time in a specified direction.
Speed is a scalar quantity; it has magnitude only.
Velocity is a vector quantity; it has both magnitude and direction.
solutions.answer: Speed is distance per unit time and a scalar; velocity is displacement per unit time in a specified direction and a vector.

solutions.question: Describe different types of motion. Also give examples.
steps: Motion is of three types: translatory motion, rotatory motion and vibratory motion.
In translatory motion, a body moves from one place to another. Its particles move the same distance in the same direction in a given time.

Translatory motion may be linear, circular or random. A car moving along a straight road shows linear motion; a stone tied to a string and whirled shows circular motion; and the motion of gas molecules shows random motion.
In rotatory motion, a body spins about an axis passing through it. The spinning of a fan is an example.
In vibratory motion, a body moves to and fro about its mean position. The motion of a simple pendulum is an example.
solutions.answer: The three types of motion are translatory, rotatory and vibratory motion; examples include a moving car, a spinning fan and a simple pendulum, respectively.

solutions.question: Explain the difference between distance and displacement.
steps: Distance is the length of the actual path covered by a moving body.
Displacement is the shortest distance between the initial and final positions of a body in a specified direction.
Distance is a scalar quantity, whereas displacement is a vector quantity.
Distance is always positive, while displacement may be positive, negative or zero.
The magnitude of displacement is always less than or equal to the distance travelled.
solutions.answer: Distance is the actual path length; displacement is the shortest directed distance from the initial to the final position.

solutions.question: What do gradients of distance-time graph and speed-time graph represent? Explain it by drawing diagrams.
Prove that the area under speed-time graph is equal to the distance covered by an object.
steps: Consider an object moving with uniform speed v for time t.
Distance covered, s = speed × time = vt.
The area under its speed-time graph is the area of a rectangle.
Area = base × height = t × v = vt.
Therefore, the area under the speed-time graph is equal to the distance covered. For a changing speed, the area under the graph gives the total distance covered.
solutions.answer: The area under a speed-time graph represents the distance covered by the object.

solutions.question: How equations of motion can be applied to the bodies moving under the action of gravity?
steps: For a body moving under gravity, the acceleration a in the equations of motion is replaced by the acceleration due to gravity g.
The equations of motion become: v = u + gt; s = ut + ½gt²; v² = u² + 2gs.
These equations apply when downward is taken as the positive direction.
If upward is taken as positive, the acceleration is −g, so g is replaced by −g in the equations.
solutions.answer: For motion under gravity, use the equations of motion with a = g (or a = −g when upward is positive).

solutions.question: Draw the representative lines of the following vectors: (a) A velocity of 400 m s⁻¹ making an angle of 60° with x-axis.
steps: Choose the scale 1 cm = 100 m s⁻¹.
Draw the positive x-axis as the reference direction.
From the origin, measure 60° anticlockwise from the positive x-axis and draw a 4 cm line in that direction.
Put an arrowhead at the end and label the line 400 m s⁻¹.
solutions.answer: The representative line is 4 cm long at 60° to the positive x-axis, labelled 400 m s⁻¹, using the scale 1 cm = 100 m s⁻¹.

drawn.title: Velocity vector
drawn.description: Draw the representative line 4 cm long, at 60° anticlockwise from the positive x-axis. Scale: 1 cm = 100 m s⁻¹. Add an arrowhead and label it 400 m s⁻¹.

solutions.question: Draw the representative lines of the following vectors: (b) A force of 50 N making an angle of 120° with x-axis.
steps: Choose the scale 1 cm = 10 N.
Draw the positive x-axis as the reference direction.
From the origin, measure 120° anticlockwise from the positive x-axis and draw a 5 cm line in that direction.
Put an arrowhead at the end and label the line 50 N.
solutions.answer: The representative line is 5 cm long at 120° to the positive x-axis, labelled 50 N, using the scale 1 cm = 10 N.

drawn.title: Force vector
drawn.description: Draw the representative line 5 cm long, at 120° anticlockwise from the positive x-axis. Scale: 1 cm = 10 N. Add an arrowhead and label it 50 N.

solutions.question: A car is moving with an average speed of 72 km h⁻¹. How much time will it take to cover a distance of 360 km?
steps: Given: Average speed, v = 72 km h⁻¹ = 20 m s⁻¹; distance, d = 360 km = 360000 m.
Required: Time, t.
Formula: t = d / v.
Substitution: t = 360000 m / 20 m s⁻¹.
Working: t = 18000 s = 5 h.
Result: The car will take 5 h.
solutions.answer: 5 h

solutions.question: A truck starts from rest. It reaches a velocity of 90 km h⁻¹ in 50 seconds. Find its average acceleration.
steps: Given: Initial velocity, u = 0 m s⁻¹; final velocity, v = 90 km h⁻¹ = 25 m s⁻¹; time, t = 50 s.
Required: Average acceleration, a.
Formula: a = (v − u) / t.
Substitution: a = (25 m s⁻¹ − 0 m s⁻¹) / 50 s.
Working: a = 25 / 50 = 0.5 m s⁻².
Result: The average acceleration is 0.5 m s⁻².
solutions.answer: 0.5 m s⁻²

solutions.question: A car passes a green traffic signal while moving with a velocity of 5 m s⁻¹. It then accelerates to 1.5 m s⁻². What is the velocity of car after 5 seconds?
steps: Given: Initial velocity, u = 5 m s⁻¹; acceleration, a = 1.5 m s⁻²; time, t = 5 s.
Required: Final velocity, v.
Formula: v = u + at.
Substitution: v = 5 m s⁻¹ + (1.5 m s⁻² × 5 s).
Working: v = 5 m s⁻¹ + 7.5 m s⁻¹ = 12.5 m s⁻¹.
Result: The velocity of the car after 5 s is 12.5 m s⁻¹.

solutions.question: A motorcycle initially travelling at 18 km h⁻¹ accelerates at constant rate of 2 m s⁻². How far will the motorcycle go in 10 seconds?
steps: Given: Initial velocity, u = 18 km h⁻¹ = 5 m s⁻¹; acceleration, a = 2 m s⁻²; time, t = 10 s.
Required: Distance travelled, s.
Formula: s = ut + ½at².
Substitution: s = (5 m s⁻¹ × 10 s) + ½(2 m s⁻² × (10 s)²).
Working: s = 50 m + 100 m = 150 m.
Result: The motorcycle will travel 150 m.

solutions.question: A wagon is moving on the road with a velocity of 54 km h⁻¹. Brakes are applied suddenly. The wagon covers a distance of 25 m before stopping. Determine the acceleration of the wagon.
steps: Given: Initial velocity, u = 54 km h⁻¹ = 15 m s⁻¹; final velocity, v = 0 m s⁻¹; distance, s = 25 m.
Required: Acceleration, a.
Formula: v² = u² + 2as.
Substitution: (0 m s⁻¹)² = (15 m s⁻¹)² + 2a(25 m).
Working: 0 = 225 + 50a; therefore, a = −225 / 50 = −4.5 m s⁻².
Result: The acceleration of the wagon is −4.5 m s⁻².

solutions.question: A stone is dropped from a height of 45 m. How long will it take to reach the ground? What will be its velocity just before hitting the ground?
steps: Given: Initial velocity, u = 0 m s⁻¹; distance fallen, s = 45 m; acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻².
Required: Time taken, t, and final velocity, v.
Formula: s = ut + ½gt²; v = u + gt.
Substitution: 45 m = (0 m s⁻¹ × t) + ½(10 m s⁻² × t²).
Working: 45 = 5t²; t² = 9; therefore, t = 3 s. Then v = 0 + (10 m s⁻² × 3 s) = 30 m s⁻¹.
Result: The stone takes 3 s to reach the ground and its velocity just before hitting the ground is 30 m s⁻¹.
solutions.answer: 3 s, 30 m s⁻¹

solutions.question: A car travels 10 km with an average velocity of 20 m s⁻¹. Then it travels in the same direction through a diversion at an average velocity of 4 m s⁻¹ for the next 0.8 km. Determine the average velocity of the car for the total journey.
steps: Given: First distance, d₁ = 10 km = 10000 m; first average velocity, v₁ = 20 m s⁻¹; second distance, d₂ = 0.8 km = 800 m; second average velocity, v₂ = 4 m s⁻¹.
Required: Average velocity for the total journey, v̄.
Formula: v̄ = total displacement / total time.
Substitution: t₁ = d₁ / v₁ = 10000 m / 20 m s⁻¹ = 500 s; t₂ = d₂ / v₂ = 800 m / 4 m s⁻¹ = 200 s.
Working: Total displacement = 10000 m + 800 m = 10800 m; total time = 500 s + 200 s = 700 s. Therefore, v̄ = 10800 m / 700 s = 15.4 m s⁻¹.
Result: The average velocity of the car for the total journey is 15.4 m s⁻¹.

solutions.question: A ball is dropped from the top of a tower. The ball reaches the ground in 5 seconds. Find the height of the tower and the velocity of the ball with which it strikes the ground.
steps: Given: Initial velocity, u = 0 m s⁻¹; time, t = 5 s; acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻².
Required: Height of the tower, s, and velocity of the ball when it strikes the ground, v.
Formula: s = ut + ½gt²; v = u + gt.
Substitution: s = (0 m s⁻¹ × 5 s) + ½(10 m s⁻² × (5 s)²).
Working: s = 125 m. Also, v = 0 + (10 m s⁻² × 5 s) = 50 m s⁻¹.
Result: The height of the tower is 125 m and the ball strikes the ground with a velocity of 50 m s⁻¹.

solutions.question: A cricket ball is hit so that it travels straight up in the air. An observer notes that it took 3 seconds to reach the highest point. What was the initial velocity of the ball? If the ball was hit 1 m above the ground, how high did it rise from the ground?
steps: Given: Time to reach highest point, t = 3 s; height above ground at which the ball was hit, h₀ = 1 m; acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻² downward.
Required: Initial velocity, u; maximum height from the ground, H.
At the highest point, final velocity v = 0.
Using v = u − gt: u = v + gt.
Substitution: u = 0 m s⁻¹ + (10 m s⁻²)(3 s).
Working: u = 30 m s⁻¹.
Using s = ut − ½gt², the height risen above the point of launch is: s = (30 m s⁻¹)(3 s) − ½(10 m s⁻²)(3 s)².
Working: s = 90 m − 45 m = 45 m.
Maximum height from the ground: H = h₀ + s = 1 m + 45 m = 46 m.

definitions.text: A scalar is that physical quantity which can be described completely by its magnitude only.
A vector is that physical quantity which needs magnitude as well as direction to describe it completely.

A vector can be represented graphically by drawing a straight line with an arrow head at one end. The length of line represents the magnitude of the vector quantity according to a suitable scale while the direction of arrow indicates the direction of the vector.

To add a number of vectors, redraw their representative lines such that the head of one line coincides with the tail of the other. The resultant vector is given by a single vector which is directed from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector.
If a body does not change its position with respect to its surroundings, it is said to be at rest.
If a body continuously changes its position with respect to its surroundings, it is said to be in motion.
The distance is the length of actual path of the motion.

The displacement of an object is a vector quantity whose magnitude is the shortest distance between the initial and final positions of the motion and its direction is from the initial position to the final position.
For this purpose, we have to find the distance covered in unit time which is known as speed.
It is defined as: Average speed = (Total distance covered)/(Total time taken)
The speed of a vehicle that is shown by its speedometer at any instant is called instantaneous speed.
The net displacement of a body in unit time is called velocity.
The velocity is said to be uniform if the speed and direction of a moving body does not change.
If the speed or direction or both of them change, it is known as variable velocity or non-uniform velocity.
Acceleration is defined as the time rate of change of velocity.
Negative acceleration is also called deceleration or retardation.
If time rate of change of velocity is constant, the acceleration is said to be uniform.
If anyone of the magnitude or direction or both of them changes it is called variable or non-uniform acceleration.
Distance-time graph shows the relation between distance S and time t taken by a moving body.
Suppose we can note the speed of the same car after every one second and record it in the table given below, we can draw the graph between speed v versus time t. This is called speed-time graph.
Gradient of the distance-Time graph is equal to the average speed of the body.
Gradient of the speed-Time graph is equal to the average acceleration of the body.
The area under the speed-time graph up to the time axis is numerically equal to the distance covered by the object.
When a body is falling freely under the action of gravity of the Earth, the acceleration acting on it is the gravitational acceleration and is denoted by g.
Any object with mass cannot achieve speeds equal to or greater than that of light. This is known as universal speed limit.

formulas.use: Speed from distance and time (v in m s⁻¹, S in m, t in s).
Distance at constant speed (S in m, v in m s⁻¹, t in s).
Average speed from total distance and total time (v_av in m s⁻¹, S in m, t in s).
Average velocity from displacement and time (v_av in m s⁻¹, d in m, t in s).
Average acceleration from velocity change and time (a_av in m s⁻², v_f and v_i in m s⁻¹, Δv in m s⁻¹, t in s).
Final velocity for uniform acceleration (v_f and v_i in m s⁻¹, a in m s⁻², t in s).
Distance for straight-line motion with uniform acceleration (S in m, v_i in m s⁻¹, t in s, a in m s⁻²).
Motion with uniform acceleration when time is not given (a in m s⁻², S in m, v_f and v_i in m s⁻¹).

formulas.formula: Gradient of distance-time graph = ΔS ÷ Δt = average speed
formulas.use: Find average speed from the slope (ΔS in m, Δt in s; gradient in m s⁻¹).

formulas.formula: Gradient of speed-time graph = Δv ÷ Δt = average acceleration

fullMarks: For a definition or rule, write the complete statement, including key words such as magnitude, direction, initial position and final position.
For a vector diagram, draw and label the axes, choose and show a suitable scale, mark the angle from the correct axis, and put an arrowhead on the representative line.
For a difference question, compare both quantities clearly on the same points—for example, scalar or vector, and distance or displacement—and include units where useful.
For a numerical, write the given data in SI units first, then the formula, substitution with units, calculation, and final answer with its unit.
For acceleration questions, identify initial and final velocities correctly; convert km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹ before substituting.
For free-fall questions, state the direction sign convention and use g = 10 m s⁻². A dropped object starts with v_i = 0; for an object thrown upward, g is negative when upward is positive.
For a graph answer, label both axes with quantity and unit, use an even scale, and show the plotted points or the slope/area used.

mistakes: Mistake: Treating distance and displacement as the same. Fix: Distance follows the actual path; displacement is the straight-line change from start to finish and has direction.
Mistake: Saying speed and velocity are both scalars. Fix: Speed is scalar; velocity is vector because it includes direction.
Mistake: Adding vectors like ordinary numbers without considering direction. Fix: Use a suitable vector method, such as the head-to-tail rule.
Mistake: Substituting km h⁻¹ directly into formulas that need SI units. Fix: Convert km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹ first by multiplying by 5 ÷ 18.
Mistake: Using v_i as zero for every motion problem. Fix: Use v_i = 0 only when the object starts from rest or is dropped from rest.
Mistake: Giving deceleration as positive when the chosen positive direction is the direction of motion. Fix: Use the sign convention consistently; braking then gives negative acceleration.
Mistake: Mixing up graph slope and graph area. Fix: Distance-time slope gives speed; speed-time slope gives acceleration, while speed-time area gives distance.

shortTheory.question: Short 2.1: Define scalar and vector quantities.
shortTheory.answer: A scalar is that physical quantity which can be described completely by its magnitude only. A vector is that physical quantity which needs magnitude as well as direction to describe it completely.

shortTheory.question: Short 2.3: State head-to-tail rule for addition of vectors.
shortTheory.answer: To add a number of vectors, redraw their representative lines such that the head of one line coincides with the tail of the other. The resultant vector is given by a single vector which is directed from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector.

shortTheory.question: Short 2.4: What are distance- time graph and speed-time graph?
shortTheory.answer: Distance-time graph shows the relation between distance S and time t taken by a moving body. This is called speed-time graph. [A speed-time graph shows the relation between speed v and time t.]

shortTheory.question: Define distance and displacement.
shortTheory.answer: The distance is the length of actual path of the motion. The displacement of an object is a vector quantity whose magnitude is the shortest distance between the initial and final positions of the motion and its direction is from the initial position to the final position.

shortTheory.question: Define speed and velocity.
shortTheory.answer: For this purpose, we have to find the distance covered in unit time which is known as speed. The net displacement of a body in unit time is called velocity.

shortTheory.question: Define acceleration.
shortTheory.answer: Acceleration is defined as the time rate of change of velocity.

explain.title: What a force does
explain.body: A common concept of a force is a push or a pull that starts, stops or changes the magnitude and direction of velocity of a body. For example, a person pushes or pulls a door to open it.

explain.title: Contact forces
explain.body: A contact force is a force that is exerted by one object on the other at the point of contact. Friction, drag, thrust, normal force, air resistance, tension force and elastic force are examples given in your textbook.

explain.title: Friction and drag
explain.body: It is the force that resists motion when the surface of one object comes in contact with the surface of another. This is the textbook definition of friction. The drag force is the resistant force caused by the motion of a body through a fluid. It acts opposite to the relative motion of any object moving with respect to surrounding fluid.

explain.title: Non-contact forces
explain.body: A non-contact force is defined as the force between two objects which are not in physical contact. The non-contact forces can work from a distance. Gravitational, electrostatic and magnetic forces are examples.

explain.title: Examples of non-contact forces
explain.body: Gravitational force is an attractive force that exists among all bodies which have mass. An electrostatic force acts between two charged objects. Magnetic force is a force which a magnet exerts on other magnets and magnetic materials like iron, nickel and cobalt.

mistakes: Do not say that every force needs physical contact; gravitational, electrostatic and magnetic forces can act at a distance.
Do not confuse drag with friction: drag is caused by motion through a fluid and acts opposite to relative motion.
Do not confuse tension with normal force: tension is experienced by a rope when pulled, while normal force is the surface's reaction on an object lying on it.
When listing contact forces, give the number requested and choose forces from the contact-force list.
Use the textbook's stated definitions and examples when answering board questions.

examTips: This section is most naturally tested through short-answer questions asking for the four forces, their effects, or their ranges.

For weak nuclear force, connect it to beta decay and radioactive decay; include its range, about 10⁻¹⁷ m, if asked.
For a comparison, keep the facts distinct: gravity is the weakest and long-range; strong and weak nuclear forces are short-range.
The section gives no worked example or exercise item specifically testing fundamental forces, so there is no section-specific worked calculation to reproduce.

explain.title: Four forces
explain.body:
There are four fundamental forces in nature. These are:

1. Gravitational force
2. Electromagnetic force
3. Strong nuclear force
4. Weak nuclear force

Every force comes under any of these forces. In other words, these four are the basic categories of force.

explain.title: Gravity and electromagnetic force
explain.body:
The gravitational force is the weakest one among all four forces. Being a long range force, it extends to infinite distance although it becomes weaker and weaker.

The electromagnetic force causes the interaction between electrically charged particles. Electrostatic and magnetic forces come under this category. These are long-range forces. Electromagnetic forces are stronger than gravitational and weak nuclear forces. This force causes all chemical reactions and binds together atoms, molecules and crystals.

explain.title: Strong nuclear force
explain.body: It holds the atomic nuclei together by binding the protons and neutrons in the nucleus overcoming repulsive electromagnetic force between positively charged protons. It is also a short-range force with the order of 10⁻¹⁴ m. If the distance between nucleons increases beyond this range, this force ceases to act.

explain.title: Weak nuclear force and unification
explain.body:
Weak nuclear force is responsible for the disintegration of a nucleus. For example, the weak nuclear force executes the β-decay (beta decay) of a neutron, in which a neutron transforms into a proton. In the process, a β-particle (electron) and an uncharged particle called antineutrino are emitted. In other words, we can say that due to weak nuclear force radioactive decay of atoms occurs. It is a short-range force of the order 10⁻¹⁷ m.

The section explains that the weak nuclear force and electromagnetic force can be modelled as two aspects of the same force, called the electroweak force.

mistakes: Do not mix up the roles of the strong and weak nuclear forces: the strong force binds the nucleus, while the weak force is responsible for its disintegration and beta decay.
Do not give the ranges in reverse: the strong nuclear force is of order 10⁻¹⁴ m and the weak nuclear force is of order 10⁻¹⁷ m.
Do not say gravity is the strongest force; the section specifically calls it the weakest of the four.
Do not describe electromagnetic force as acting only in nuclei; it acts between electrically charged particles and is long-range.
Do not omit that the antineutrino emitted in the described beta decay is uncharged.

explain.title: Newton’s first law and inertia
explain.body: Your textbook states: “A body continues its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by some external force.” This means an object does not change its motion by itself. The property of a body to maintain its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line is called inertia. Mass measures inertia: a greater mass means greater inertia.

explain.title: Newton’s second law
explain.body: Your textbook states that if a net external force acts on a body, it accelerates in the direction of the force. Acceleration is directly proportional to force and inversely proportional to mass. The relation is F = ma. One newton produces an acceleration of 1 m s⁻² in a body of mass 1 kg.

explain.title: Force changes velocity
explain.body: A force can produce acceleration or deceleration and so change velocity. Because velocity is a vector, the change may be in its magnitude, direction, or both.

explain.title: Newton’s third law
explain.body: Your textbook states: “For every action, there is always an equal and opposite reaction.” The two forces act on different bodies, so they do not balance each other. For example, when a gun fires a bullet forward, the gun recoils backward.

Force applied = F = 7500 N
Acceleration = a = ?
Initial speed = v_i = 36 km h⁻¹
Final speed = v_f = 72 km h⁻¹ = 72 × 1000 m / (60 × 60 s) = 20 m s⁻¹
Time = t = ?
By Newton's second law, F = ma

explain.title: Mass
explain.body: The simplest definition of mass is that it is a measure of the quantity of matter in a body. Scientifically, mass is a scalar quantity and remains the same everywhere. Its SI unit is kilogram (kg), and an ordinary balance measures mass.

explain.title: Scientific definition of mass
explain.body: The characteristic of a body which determines the magnitude of acceleration produced when a certain force acts upon it is known as mass of the body.

explain.title: Weight
explain.body: Weight is a gravitational force acting on the object. It is a vector quantity directed downward, towards the centre of the Earth. The weight of an object is equal to the force with which the Earth attracts the body towards its centre.

explain.title: Gravitational field and weight
explain.body: The gravitational field is a space around a mass in which another mass experiences a force due to gravitational attraction. The gravitational field strength is defined as the gravitational force acting on unit mass. Weight is given by w = mg, where g is the gravitational field strength. Its value is 10 N kg⁻¹. Since g varies from place to place and with altitude, weight can change; mass stays the same. Weight is measured in newtons (N) using a spring balance.

mistakes: Do not say that an object's weight is measured in kilograms; kilograms are the unit of mass and newtons are the unit of weight.
Do not treat mass and weight as the same quantity: mass is scalar and stays the same, while weight is a vector force that depends on g.
Do not use Earth's value of g when a question gives a different value, such as the Moon's gravitational acceleration.
Do not omit the unit N from a calculated weight.

recap.question: When is relativistic mechanics applicable?
recap.answer: Newton’s laws are a good approximation for everyday motion, but are not exact for very small objects or objects moving close to the speed of light.

solutions.question: A force of 7500 N is applied to move a truck of mass 3000 kg. Find the acceleration produced in the truck. How long will it take to accelerate the truck from 36 km h⁻¹ to 72 km h⁻¹ speed?
steps: Mass of truck = m = 3000 kg
Force applied = F = 7500 N
Acceleration = a = ?
Initial speed = v_i = 36 km h⁻¹
Final speed = v_f = 72 km h⁻¹ = 72 × 1000 m / (60 × 60 s) = 20 m s⁻¹
Time = t = ?
By Newton's second law, F = ma
or a = F/m
Putting the values, a = 7500 N / 3000 kg = 2.5 m s⁻²
Now, using first equation of motion,
v_f = v_i + at
or t = (v_f − v_i)/a
Putting the values, t = (20 m s⁻¹ − 10 m s⁻¹) / 2.5 m s⁻² = 4 s

explain.title: Mechanical balances
explain.body: A mechanical balance consists of a rigid horizontal beam that oscillates on a central knife edge as a fulcrum. It has two end knife edges equidistant from the centre. Two pans are hung from bearings on the end knife edges. Put the object in one pan and standard weights in the other, then adjust the weights until the beam is in equilibrium.

explain.title: Platform balances
explain.body: A mechanical platform balance is used for heavy items such as flour bags, cement bags, and steel bars. Its fulcrum is very near one end of the beam, so smaller weights can balance the load. These smaller weights have already been calibrated to standard weights.

explain.title: Electronic balances
explain.body: An electronic balance does not need standard weights. It must be connected to a power supply, although some models use dry-cell batteries. It displays the mass, and some models can display the total price if the rate per kg is entered.

explain.title: Force meters
explain.body: A force meter is a scientific instrument that measures force. It is also called as a newton meter or a spring balance. It measures force directly in newtons (N), unlike balances, which measure mass in kilograms or its multiples.

explain.title: How an ordinary force meter works
explain.body: An ordinary force meter has a spring, a handle, a hook, a pointer, and a scale in newtons. The pointer coincides with zero when nothing is hung from the hook. Hanging an object makes the spring compress or stretch, and the pointer indicates the object's weight.

mistakes: Do not say that a balance measures force in newtons; balances measure mass.
Do not confuse mass in kilograms with weight in newtons.
Do not forget that an ordinary force meter should read zero when nothing is hung from its hook.
Do not say that all electronic balances must use dry-cell batteries; some models use them, while the balance must be connected to a power supply.
Do not claim that a mechanical platform balance uses no calibrated weights; its smaller weights are calibrated to standard weights.

explain.title: Friction opposes motion and dissipates energy
explain.body: Friction is a dissipative force due to which the energy is wasted in doing work to overcome against friction. The lost energy appears in the form of heat. For example, rubbing hands makes them warm, and friction can heat and wear vehicle tyres.

explain.title: Static and kinetic friction
explain.body: The friction between two solid surfaces is called sliding friction which can be divided into two categories. Static friction acts when a pull tends to move an object but it remains at rest. When the object slides, the friction is known as kinetic friction.

explain.title: Terminal velocity
explain.body: As a falling object gets faster, air resistance increases. When the upward force of air resistance balances the downward force of gravity, the object stops accelerating and keeps falling at a constant velocity. This constant velocity achieved by an object is called its terminal velocity.

explain.title: Rolling friction and reducing friction
explain.body: When an object rolls over a surface, the friction produced is called rolling friction. Rolling friction is about one hundred times smaller than sliding friction. Friction can also be reduced by polishing surfaces, applying oil or grease, using ball bearings and making moving bodies streamlined.

explain.title: Change in momentum

explain.body: The rate of change of momentum of a body is equal to the force acting on it. In symbols, F = Δp/Δt. The direction of change in momentum is that of the force.

explain.title: Why longer impact time helps

writtenQuestions.text: A ball of mass 3 kg moving with a velocity of 5 ms⁻¹ collides with a stationary ball of mass 2 kg and then both of them move together. If the friction is negligible, find out the velocity with which both the balls will move after collision.
modelAnswer: Mass of first ball = m₁ = 3 kg
Velocity of first ball before collision = v₁ = 5 m s⁻¹
Mass of second ball = m₂ = 2 kg
Velocity of second ball before collision = v₂ = 0
Velocity of both the balls after collision = v = ?
Total mass of balls after collision = m₁ + m₂
By law of conservation of momentum,
Total momentum before collision = Total momentum after collision
or
m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v
Putting the values,
3 kg × 5 m s⁻¹ + 0 = (3 kg + 2 kg) v
15 kg m s⁻¹ = 5 kg × v
v = 3 m s⁻¹

rubric.how: Explain that expelled material moves away and the astronaut recoils toward the spaceship.

examTips: This section can appear as a definition or explanation: state the conservation principle and its condition—no external force acts on an isolated system.
Numerical questions often involve recoil or two objects that stick together. Show total momentum before = total momentum after, substitute values, and solve for the unknown.
For opposite directions, choose one direction as positive and use a negative sign for the other. Include units and state the direction when asked.
For a short conceptual question, explain that momentum may transfer between objects, while the total momentum of the isolated system remains the same.
A numerical answer earns clearer method marks when you show the equation, substitution, rearrangement, and final answer rather than only writing the result.

hints: Convert the bullet mass from grams to kilograms.
The gun and bullet start at rest: use 0 = momentum of bullet + momentum of gun, then solve for gun velocity.
yourTurn.question: Q3.4. A 5 g bullet is fired by a gun. The bullet moves with a velocity of 300 m s⁻¹. If the mass of the gun is 10 kg, find the recoil speed of the gun.
solution: Mass of bullet = 5 g = 0.005 kg
Before firing, total momentum = 0
Let the velocity of the gun after firing be v.
By law of conservation of momentum,
0 = m_bullet v_bullet + m_gun v

hints: Both bogies move in the same direction, so add their initial momenta.
Because they couple, use their combined mass and one common final velocity.
yourTurn.question: Q3.6. A 6.5 × 10³ kg bogie of a goods train is moving with a velocity of 0.8 m s⁻¹. Another bogie of mass 9.2 × 10³ kg coming from behind with a velocity of 1.2 m s⁻¹ collides with the first one and couples to it. Find the common velocity of the two bogies after they become coupled.
solution: Mass of first bogie = 6.5 × 10³ kg; velocity = 0.8 m s⁻¹
Mass of second bogie = 9.2 × 10³ kg; velocity = 1.2 m s⁻¹
Let the common velocity after collision be v.
By law of conservation of momentum,
m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v
v = 1.03 m s⁻¹

steps.why: These are the given quantities needed to write the momentum equation.
steps.text: Mass of first ball = m₁ = 3 kg; velocity before collision = v₁ = 5 m s⁻¹.

steps.why: The second ball is stationary before collision.
steps.text: Mass of second ball = m₂ = 2 kg; velocity before collision = v₂ = 0.

steps.why: The two balls move together, so they have the same unknown final velocity.

steps.why: For the collision, total momentum before equals total momentum after.
steps.text: By law of conservation of momentum, m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v.

steps.text: 3 kg × 5 m s⁻¹ + 0 = (3 kg + 2 kg) v.

steps.text: 15 kg m s⁻¹ = 5 kg × v.

steps.text: v = 3 m s⁻¹.

example.question: A ball of mass 3 kg moving with a velocity of 5 ms⁻¹ collides with a stationary ball of mass 2 kg and then both of them move together. If the friction is negligible, find out the velocity with which both the balls will move after collision.
example.answer: v = 3 m s⁻¹

explain.title: What is a system?
explain.body: The collection of objects is known as a ‘system’. If no external force acts on any object of the system, it is known as isolated system.

explain.title: Conservation of momentum
explain.body: If no external force acts on an isolated system, the final total momentum of the system is equal to the initial total momentum of the system. For two objects, m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = m₁v′₁ + m₂v′₂.

explain.title: Momentum can transfer
explain.body: During a collision, one object may lose momentum while another gains momentum. The total momentum of the two-object system remains the same if no external force acts.

explain.title: Recoil
explain.body: When a bullet moves forward after firing, the gun moves backward. The opposite momenta balance because the system's initial total momentum was zero.

explain.title: Impulse and safety
explain.body: Impulse is defined as the product of F × Δt = m × Δv = total change in momentum. Seatbelts prevent passengers from moving forward when a car stops suddenly.

mistakes: Forgetting to say that no external force acts on an isolated system.
Adding momentum magnitudes without using signs for opposite directions.
Using only one object's momentum instead of the total momentum of the system.
For objects that move together after collision, forgetting to use their combined mass for the final momentum.
Leaving out units or failing to interpret a negative velocity as motion in the opposite direction.

recap.question: What happens to the average force if the same change in momentum takes place over a longer time?
recap.answer: Impulse is the total change in momentum of an object when a large force acts on it for a short time.

recap.question: What is the SI unit of momentum?
recap.answer: kg m s⁻¹

solutions.question: A bullet of mass m₁ is fired by a gun of mass m₂. Find the velocity of the gun in terms of velocity of bullet v₁ just after firing.
steps: Before firing, the velocity of bullet as well as that of gun was zero. Therefore, total momentum of bullet and gun was also zero. After firing, the bullet moves forward with velocity v₁ whereas the gun moves with velocity v₂.
According to law of conservation of momentum,
Total momentum before firing = Total momentum after firing
Putting the values,
or
The negative sign in this equation, indicates that the gun moves backward, i.e. opposite to the bullet. It is because of the backward motion of the gun that the shooter gets a jerk on his shoulder.

solutions.question: A ball of mass 3 kg moving with a velocity of 5 ms⁻¹ collides with a stationary ball of mass 2 kg and then both of them move together. If the friction is negligible, find out the velocity with which both the balls will move after collision.
steps: Mass of first ball = m_1 = 3 kg
Velocity of first ball before collision = v_1 = 5 ms⁻¹
Mass of second ball = m_2 = 2 kg
Velocity of second ball before collision = v_2 = 0
Velocity of both the balls after collision = v = ?
Total mass of balls after collision = m_1 + m_2
By law of conversion of momentum,
Total momentum before collision = Total momentum after collision
or
Putting the values,
3 kg × 5 m s⁻¹ + 0 = (3 kg + 2 kg) v
15 kg m s⁻¹ = 5 kg × v
v = 3 m s⁻¹
KEY POINTS
• A force is a push or a pull that starts, stops and changes the magnitude and direction of velocity of a body.
• A contact force is a force that acts at the point of contact between two objects.
• Non-contact force is a force between two objects which are not in physical contact.
• Gravitational force, electromagnetic force, strong nuclear force and weak nuclear force are the four fundamental forces in nature.

• Every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force that is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. This is known as Newton's law of gravitation.
• Newton's first law of motion states that a body continues its state of rest or of uniform motion with the same constant velocity, unless acted upon by some net external force.
• The property of a body to maintain its state of rest or of uniform motion is called inertia.

• The second law of motion states that when a net force acts upon a body, it produces an acceleration in the direction of force and the magnitude of acceleration is directly proportional to the force and is inversely proportional to the mass.
• The third law of motion states that to every action there is an equal but opposite reaction.
• Action and reaction do not act on the same body but act on two different bodies.

• Mass of a body is the quantity of matter in it. It determines the magnitude of acceleration produced when a force acts on it. Mass of a body does not vary. It is a scalar quantity and its unit is kilogram (kg).
• The weight of an object is equal to the force with which the Earth attracts a body towards its centre.
• Force meter is a scientific instrument that measures force in newtons (N).
• Friction is the force that tends to prevent the bodies from sliding over each other.
• The resisting force between the two surfaces before the motion starts is called the static friction. The maximum value of the static friction is called limiting friction.
• The friction during motion is called kinetic friction.
• When a body moves with the help of wheels, the friction in this case is known as rolling friction. Rolling friction is much less as compared to the sliding friction.
• Energy is wasted in doing work against friction that appears in the form of heat.
• When upward air resistance balances the downward force of gravity on a falling object, it falls down with constant (safe) velocity, it is called terminal velocity.
• The product of mass and velocity of a moving body is called momentum.
• The principle of conservation of momentum states that if no external force acts on an isolated system, the final total momentum of the system is equal to the initial total momentum of the system.
• Impulse is defined as the product of F × Δt = m × Δv = total change in momentum.

A force may also change its shape.

Short questions usually earn marks for a precise definition or a brief cause-and-effect explanation.
Constructed and comprehensive answers earn marks for naming the law, explaining the force or momentum change, and applying it to the situation.
For numericals, show the given values, formula, substitution, calculation and final unit. Use signs to show direction in momentum questions.
For multi-stage motion, calculate each stage separately and add the distances.

hints: Find the total mass of the cyclist and bicycle, then calculate acceleration using F = ma.
Find distance in the first 8 s using s = ½at²; then find the distance in the next 8 s at constant speed.
yourTurn.question: A cyclist weighing 55 kg rides a bicycle of mass 5 kg. He starts from rest and applies a force of 90 N for 8 seconds. Then he continues at a constant speed for another 8 seconds. Calculate the total distance travelled by the cyclist.
solution: Total mass = 55 + 5 = 60 kg.
Distance during first 8 s: s₁ = ½at² = ½ × 1.5 × 8² = 48 m.
Speed after 8 s: v = u + at = 0 + 1.5 × 8 = 12 m s⁻¹.
Distance during next 8 s = vt = 12 × 8 = 96 m.
Total distance = 48 + 96 = 144 m.

steps.text: Formula: F = ma, so a = F/m.

steps.why: Substitution with units gives the acceleration in SI units.
The constant-acceleration relation gives the velocity after five seconds.

example.question: A 10 kg block is placed on a smooth horizontal surface. A horizontal force of 5 N is applied to the block. Find (a) the acceleration produced in the block and (b) the velocity of block after 5 seconds.

explain.title: Force and motion
explain.body: A force is a push or pull that can change an object's motion or shape. The resultant force is the combined effect of all forces on the object.

explain.title: Newton's laws
explain.body: The first law describes inertia. The second law relates net force to the rate of change of momentum (and gives F = ma for constant mass). The third law says action and reaction are equal and opposite and act on different bodies.

explain.title: Momentum and impulse
explain.body: Momentum is p = mv. Impulse is force multiplied by the time for which it acts, and equals the change in momentum. Increasing the time of a collision reduces the force for the same momentum change.

explain.title: Conservation of momentum
explain.body: If no external resultant force acts on a system, total momentum remains constant. In a collision, calculate the signed momentum before and after.

explain.title: Friction
explain.body: Friction opposes relative motion or its tendency. Static friction acts before sliding starts; kinetic friction acts during sliding. Rolling friction is less than sliding friction, and tyre-road friction provides grip and braking.

mistakes: Using the mass of only the cyclist or vehicle instead of the combined moving mass.
Forgetting to convert grams to kilograms or minutes to seconds.
Ignoring direction signs in recoil and collision problems.
Confusing impulse with force; impulse is force multiplied by time and equals momentum change.
Writing an answer without units, or using a velocity unit for acceleration.
Treating action and reaction forces as cancelling even though they act on different bodies.
Adding the wrong distances in a motion problem with separate acceleration and constant-speed stages.

recap.question: What stays equal before and after a collision in an isolated system?
recap.answer: The total momentum before and after the collision is equal.

recap.question: In an isolated system, two objects collide. Which statement follows from conservation of momentum?
recap.answer: Momentum before the collision equals momentum after it.

solutions.question: What kind of changes in motion may be produced by a force?
steps: A force may change the speed of an object. It may make a stationary object move, or a moving object stop.
A force may change the direction of motion of an object.
A force may change both the speed and direction of motion of an object.
solutions.answer: A force can change an object’s speed, direction, or both.

solutions.question: Give 5 examples of contact forces.
steps: Examples of contact forces are:
1. Frictional force
2. Tension force
3. Normal force
4. Air resistance
5. Spring force
solutions.answer: Frictional, tension, normal, air-resistance and spring forces are examples of contact forces.

solutions.question: An object moves with constant velocity in free space. How long will the object continue to move with this velocity?
steps: According to Newton’s first law, an object continues moving with constant velocity unless acted upon by an external force.
In free space, if no external force acts on the object, it will continue moving with that velocity indefinitely.
solutions.answer: The object will continue to move with constant velocity indefinitely, as long as no external force acts on it.

solutions.question: Define impulse of force.
steps: The product of a force and the time for which it acts is called the impulse of the force.
Impulse = Force × Time interval
It is equal to the change in momentum of the object: I = FΔt = Δp.
solutions.answer: Impulse is the product of a force and the time interval for which it acts, and equals the change in momentum.

solutions.question: Why has not Newton's first law been proved on the Earth?
steps: Newton’s first law cannot be proved on the Earth because a completely frictionless surface cannot be obtained.
A moving object on the Earth experiences friction and air resistance, which oppose its motion and eventually stop it.
solutions.answer: It cannot be proved on Earth because friction and air resistance act on moving objects.

solutions.question: When sitting in a car which suddenly accelerates from rest, you are pushed back into the seat, why?
steps: When the car accelerates forward, the part of your body in contact with the seat moves forward with the car.
Due to inertia, the rest of your body tends to remain in its initial state of rest.
Therefore, you appear to be pushed backward into the seat.
solutions.answer: Due to inertia, your body tends to remain at rest as the car accelerates forward, so you appear to be pushed back.

solutions.question: The force expressed in Newton's second law is a net force. Why is it so?
steps: Several forces may act on an object at the same time.
The resultant of all the forces acting on an object is called the net force.
Balanced forces cancel one another and do not produce acceleration; only an unbalanced (net) force produces acceleration.
Therefore, Newton’s second law relates acceleration to the net force acting on an object.
solutions.answer: Newton’s second law uses net force because only the resultant, unbalanced force produces acceleration.

solutions.question: How can you show that rolling friction is lesser than the sliding friction?
steps: Place a block on a table and pull it horizontally with a spring balance. Note the force required to keep it moving; this measures sliding friction.
Now place rollers (cylindrical rods) between the block and the table and pull the block with the spring balance again.
The spring-balance reading is smaller when the block rolls on the rollers than when it slides on the table.
Therefore, rolling friction is less than sliding friction.
solutions.answer: A smaller spring-balance reading when the block rolls on rollers shows that rolling friction is less than sliding friction.

solutions.question: Define terminal velocity of an object.
steps: Terminal velocity is the constant maximum velocity attained by a body falling through a fluid.
It is reached when the resistive force of the fluid balances the gravitational force, so the resultant force and acceleration become zero.
solutions.answer: Terminal velocity is the constant velocity attained by a falling body when the fluid’s resistive force balances its weight.

solutions.question: An astronaut walking in space wants to return to his spaceship by firing a hand rocket. In what direction does he fire the rocket?
steps: He should fire the rocket in the direction opposite to the direction in which he wants to move.
The rocket gases move in one direction and, by Newton’s third law, exert an equal and opposite force on the astronaut, pushing him towards the spaceship.
solutions.answer: He should fire the rocket away from the spaceship.

solutions.question: Two ice skaters weighing 60kg and 80 kg push off against each other on a frictionless ice track. The 60 kg skater gains a velocity of 4 ms⁻¹. Considering all the relevant calculations involved, explain how Newton's third law applies to this situation.
steps: Given: Mass of the 60 kg skater, m₁ = 60 kg; mass of the 80 kg skater, m₂ = 80 kg; velocity gained by the 60 kg skater, v₁ = 4 m s⁻¹; initial momentum of the two skaters = 0.
Required: Velocity of the 80 kg skater and an explanation of Newton’s third law.
By Newton’s third law, the skaters exert equal and opposite forces on each other when they push off.
The forces act for the same time, so the impulses and changes in momentum are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
By conservation of momentum: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = 0.
Substitution: (60 kg)(4 m s⁻¹) + (80 kg)v₂ = 0.
Working: 240 kg m s⁻¹ + (80 kg)v₂ = 0; v₂ = −240/80 = −3 m s⁻¹.
The negative sign shows that the 80 kg skater moves in the direction opposite to the 60 kg skater.
solutions.answer: The 80 kg skater moves at 3 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction; their momenta are equal and opposite.

solutions.question: Inflatable airbags are installed in the vehicles as safety equipment. In terms of momentum, what is the advantage of airbags over seatbelts?
steps: When a moving person is brought to rest, the change in momentum is the same whether an airbag or a seatbelt stops the person.
An airbag increases the time over which this change in momentum occurs.
Since force is the rate of change of momentum, increasing the stopping time reduces the force on the person and lowers the chance of injury.
solutions.answer: An airbag increases the time taken to stop the person, reducing the force produced by the change in momentum.

solutions.question: A horse refuses to pull a cart. The horse argues, “according to Newton's third law, whatever force I exert on the cart, the cart will exert an equal and opposite force on me. Since the net force will be zero, therefore, I have no chance of accelerating (pulling) the cart.” What is wrong with this reasoning?
steps: The horse’s reasoning is wrong because the action and reaction forces act on different bodies; they do not cancel each other on one body.
The horse pulls the cart forward, while the cart pulls the horse backward with an equal force.
At the same time, the horse pushes the ground backward, and the ground exerts a forward frictional force on the horse.
This forward force from the ground can move the horse and cart forward if it is greater than the opposing forces.
solutions.answer: The action and reaction forces act on different bodies; the ground’s forward frictional force can accelerate the horse and cart.

solutions.question: When a cricket ball hits high, a fielder tries to catch it. While holding the ball he/she draws hands backward. Why?
steps: The fielder moves his or her hands backward while catching the ball to increase the time taken to bring it to rest.
The change in momentum of the ball is the same, but the rate of change of momentum is reduced when the stopping time is increased.
Therefore, the force exerted on the hands is reduced and the chance of injury is lessened.
solutions.answer: Drawing the hands backward increases the stopping time and reduces the force on the fielder’s hands.

solutions.question: When someone jumps from a small boat onto the river bank, why does the jumper often fall into the water? Explain.
steps: When the jumper pushes off the boat towards the bank, the boat is pushed in the opposite direction by an equal and opposite force.
The boat moves backward, away from the bank.
As a result, the jumper may lose the support of the boat before reaching the bank and fall into the water.
solutions.answer: The boat moves backward as the jumper pushes off, so the jumper may lose support and fall into the water.

solutions.question: Imagine that if friction vanishes suddenly from everything, then what could be the scenario of daily life activities?
steps: Without friction, a person could not walk because the feet would slip on the ground.
Vehicles could not move properly, turn, or stop by applying their brakes.
It would be difficult to hold objects, write with a pencil, or grip things.
Objects and machines would keep sliding, and many everyday activities that depend on grip would become impossible.
solutions.answer: Without friction, walking, gripping, writing, and controlling or stopping vehicles would become difficult or impossible.

solutions.question: Explain the concept of force by practical examples.
steps: Force is a push or a pull acting on an object.
A force can change or tend to change the state of rest or motion of an object, its direction of motion, or its shape.
For example, pushing a stationary door can make it move; kicking a stationary ball makes it move; and squeezing a sponge changes its shape.
solutions.answer: A force is a push or pull that can change an object's state of motion, direction, or shape.

solutions.question: Describe Newton's laws of motion.
steps: Newton’s First Law of Motion: A body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an external force. This is also called the law of inertia.
Newton’s Second Law of Motion: The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of the force. For constant mass, F = ma.
Newton’s Third Law of Motion: To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Action and reaction act on different bodies.
solutions.answer: The three laws describe inertia, the relation between force and change in momentum, and equal and opposite action–reaction forces.

solutions.question: Define momentum and express Newton's 2nd law of motion in terms of change in momentum.
steps: The momentum of a body is the product of its mass and velocity: p = mv.
Momentum is a vector quantity. Its SI unit is kg m s⁻¹.
According to Newton’s Second Law, force is equal to the rate of change of momentum: F = Δp/Δt.
For a body of mass m changing velocity from u to v in time t: F = (mv − mu)/t = m(v − u)/t.
solutions.answer: Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity (p = mv), and force equals the rate of change of momentum (F = Δp/Δt).

solutions.question: State and explain the principle of conservation of momentum.
steps: The principle of conservation of momentum states that if no external force acts on a system, its total momentum remains constant.
When two bodies interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite, so their changes in momentum are equal and opposite.
Therefore, total momentum before interaction equals total momentum after interaction: total initial momentum = total final momentum.
solutions.answer: In the absence of an external force, the total momentum of a system remains constant.

solutions.question: Describe the motion of a block on a table taking into account the friction between the two surfaces. What is the static friction and kinetic friction?
steps: When a horizontal force is applied to a block on a table, friction acts between the surfaces and opposes the tendency of the block to move.
At first, the block remains at rest because static friction adjusts to balance the applied force.
Static friction is the frictional force between surfaces that are not moving relative to each other. It increases with the applied force up to a maximum value.
When the applied force becomes greater than the maximum static friction, the block starts to slide.
Kinetic friction is the frictional force between surfaces sliding over each other. It opposes the motion and is generally less than the maximum static friction.
solutions.answer: Static friction acts between surfaces at rest relative to each other; kinetic friction acts between sliding surfaces, and both oppose motion or its tendency.

solutions.question: Explain the effect of friction on the motion of vehicles in context of tyre surface and braking force.
steps: Friction between a vehicle’s tyres and the road provides grip, enabling the vehicle to move and turn.
Tyre treads improve grip by increasing friction with the road. Worn or smooth tyres provide less grip and may cause skidding, especially on a wet or slippery road.
When brakes are applied, friction in the braking system slows the wheels, and friction between the tyres and road helps bring the vehicle to a stop.
If friction is small, the vehicle takes longer to stop and is more likely to skid.
solutions.answer: Tyre–road friction provides grip for movement and braking; reduced friction makes a vehicle more likely to skid and take longer to stop.

solutions.question: A 10 kg block is placed on a smooth horizontal surface. A horizontal force of 5 N is applied to the block. Find: (a) the acceleration produced in the block.
steps: Given: m = 10 kg, F = 5 N
Required: Acceleration, a
Formula: F = ma; therefore, a = F/m
Substitution: a = 5 N / 10 kg
Working: a = 0.5 m s⁻²
Result: a = 0.5 m s⁻²
solutions.answer: 0.5 m s⁻²

solutions.question: A 10 kg block is placed on a smooth horizontal surface. A horizontal force of 5 N is applied to the block. Find: (b) the velocity of block after 5 seconds.
steps: Given: u = 0 m s⁻¹, a = 0.5 m s⁻², t = 5 s
Required: Velocity, v, after 5 s
Formula: v = u + at
Substitution: v = 0 m s⁻¹ + (0.5 m s⁻²)(5 s)
Working: v = 2.5 m s⁻¹
Result: v = 2.5 m s⁻¹
solutions.answer: 2.5 m s⁻¹

solutions.question: The mass of a person is 80 kg. What will be his weight on the Earth? What will be his weight on the Moon? The value of acceleration due to gravity of Moon is 1.6 m s⁻².
steps: Given: Mass of person, m = 80 kg; acceleration due to gravity on Earth, gₑ = 10 m s⁻²; acceleration due to gravity on Moon, gₘ = 1.6 m s⁻².
Required: Weight on Earth and weight on Moon.
Formula: Weight, W = mg.
On Earth: Wₑ = mgₑ = 80 kg × 10 m s⁻² = 800 N.
On Moon: Wₘ = mgₘ = 80 kg × 1.6 m s⁻² = 128 N.
solutions.answer: Weight on Earth = 800 N; weight on Moon = 128 N.

solutions.question: What force is required to increase the velocity of 800 kg car from 10 m s⁻¹ to 30 m s⁻¹ in 10 seconds?
steps: Given: Mass of car, m = 800 kg; initial velocity, u = 10 m s⁻¹; final velocity, v = 30 m s⁻¹; time, t = 10 s.
Required: Force, F.
Formula: a = (v − u)/t and F = ma.
Substitution: a = (30 m s⁻¹ − 10 m s⁻¹)/10 s = 2 m s⁻².
Working: F = 800 kg × 2 m s⁻² = 1600 N.

solutions.question: A 5 g bullet is fired by a gun. The bullet moves with a velocity of 300 m s⁻¹. If the mass of the gun is 10 kg, find the recoil speed of the gun.
steps: Given: Mass of bullet, m₁ = 5 g = 0.005 kg; velocity of bullet, v₁ = 300 m s⁻¹; mass of gun, m₂ = 10 kg. Initially, both are at rest.
Required: Recoil velocity of the gun, v₂.
Formula: By the law of conservation of momentum, total momentum before firing = total momentum after firing.
Substitution: 0 = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
Working: v₂ = −(m₁v₁)/m₂ = −(0.005 kg × 300 m s⁻¹)/(10 kg) = −0.15 m s⁻¹.
The negative sign shows that the gun moves opposite to the bullet.

solutions.question: An astronaut weighs 70 kg. He throws a wrench of mass 300 g at a speed of 3.5 m s⁻¹. Determine: (a) the speed of astronaut as he recoils away from the wrench.
steps: Given: Mass of astronaut, mₐ = 70 kg; mass of wrench, m𝓌 = 300 g = 0.3 kg; velocity of wrench, v𝓌 = 3.5 m s⁻¹. Initially, both are at rest.
Required: Recoil velocity of the astronaut, vₐ.
Formula: By the law of conservation of momentum, total momentum before throwing = total momentum after throwing.
Substitution: 0 = m𝓌v𝓌 + mₐvₐ.
Working: vₐ = −(m𝓌v𝓌)/mₐ = −(0.3 kg × 3.5 m s⁻¹)/(70 kg) = −0.015 m s⁻¹ = −1.5 × 10⁻² m s⁻¹.
The negative sign shows that the astronaut recoils in the direction opposite to the wrench.

solutions.question: An astronaut weighs 70 kg. He throws a wrench of mass 300 g at a speed of 3.5 m s⁻¹. Determine: (b) the distance covered by the astronaut in 30 minutes.
steps: Given: Recoil speed of the astronaut, v = 1.5 × 10⁻² m s⁻¹; time, t = 30 min = 1800 s.
Required: Distance covered by the astronaut, d.
Formula: d = vt.
Substitution: d = 1.5 × 10⁻² m s⁻¹ × 1800 s.
Working: d = 27 m.

solutions.question: A 6.5 × 10³ kg bogie of a goods train is moving with a velocity of 0.8 m s⁻¹. Another bogie of mass 9.2 × 10³ kg coming from behind with a velocity of 1.2 m s⁻¹ collides with the first one and couples to it. Find the common velocity of the two bogies after they become coupled.
steps: Given: Mass of first bogie, m₁ = 6.5 × 10³ kg; velocity of first bogie, u₁ = 0.8 m s⁻¹; mass of second bogie, m₂ = 9.2 × 10³ kg; velocity of second bogie, u₂ = 1.2 m s⁻¹.
Required: Common velocity, v, after the bogies couple.
Formula: By the law of conservation of momentum, m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v.
Substitution: (6.5 × 10³ kg × 0.8 m s⁻¹) + (9.2 × 10³ kg × 1.2 m s⁻¹) = (6.5 × 10³ kg + 9.2 × 10³ kg)v.

solutions.question: A cyclist weighing 55 kg rides a bicycle of mass 5 kg. He starts from rest and applies a force of 90 N for 8 seconds. Then he continues at a constant speed for another 8 seconds. Calculate the total distance travelled by the cyclist.
steps: Given: Mass of cyclist = 55 kg; mass of bicycle = 5 kg; applied force, F = 90 N; time of acceleration, t₁ = 8 s; time at constant speed, t₂ = 8 s; initial velocity, u = 0 m s⁻¹.
Required: Total distance travelled.
Formula: Total mass, m = mass of cyclist + mass of bicycle; F = ma; s = ut + ½at²; and distance at constant speed = vt.
Substitution: m = 55 kg + 5 kg = 60 kg; a = F/m = 90 N/60 kg = 1.5 m s⁻².
Distance in the first 8 s: s₁ = ut₁ + ½at₁² = 0 + ½ × 1.5 m s⁻² × (8 s)² = 48 m.
Velocity after 8 s: v = u + at₁ = 0 + 1.5 m s⁻² × 8 s = 12 m s⁻¹.
Distance in the next 8 s: s₂ = vt₂ = 12 m s⁻¹ × 8 s = 96 m.
Total distance = s₁ + s₂ = 48 m + 96 m = 144 m.

solutions.question: A ball of mass 0.4 kg is dropped on the floor from a height of 1.8 m. The ball rebounds straight upward to a height of 0.8 m. What is the magnitude and direction of the impulse applied to the ball by the floor?
steps: Given: Mass of ball, m = 0.4 kg; height from which it is dropped, h₁ = 1.8 m; rebound height, h₂ = 0.8 m; acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻².
Required: Magnitude and direction of impulse applied to the ball by the floor.
Take upward as the positive direction.
Formula: v² = u² + 2as; impulse = change in momentum = m(v − u).
Velocity just before hitting the floor: u = −√(2gh₁) = −√(2 × 10 m s⁻² × 1.8 m) = −6 m s⁻¹.
Velocity just after rebounding: v = +√(2gh₂) = +√(2 × 10 m s⁻² × 0.8 m) = +4 m s⁻¹.
Impulse = m(v − u) = 0.4 kg × [4 m s⁻¹ − (−6 m s⁻¹)] = 4 N s.
The positive sign shows that the impulse is upward.
solutions.answer: 4 N s, upward

solutions.question: Two balls of masses 0.2 kg and 0.4 kg are moving towards each other with velocities 20 m s⁻¹ and 5 m s⁻¹ respectively. After collision, the velocity of 0.2 kg ball becomes 6 m s⁻¹. What will be the velocity of 0.4 kg ball?
steps: Given: m₁ = 0.2 kg, m₂ = 0.4 kg, u₁ = 20 m s⁻¹, u₂ = −5 m s⁻¹, v₁ = 6 m s⁻¹. Take the initial direction of the 0.2 kg ball as positive.
Required: Velocity (v₂) of the 0.4 kg ball after collision.
According to the law of conservation of momentum: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂
Substitution: (0.2 kg)(20 m s⁻¹) + (0.4 kg)(−5 m s⁻¹) = (0.2 kg)(6 m s⁻¹) + (0.4 kg)v₂
Working: 4 kg m s⁻¹ − 2 kg m s⁻¹ = 1.2 kg m s⁻¹ + (0.4 kg)v₂
0.8 kg m s⁻¹ = (0.4 kg)v₂
v₂ = (0.8 kg m s⁻¹) ÷ (0.4 kg) = 2 m s⁻¹
The positive sign shows that the 0.4 kg ball moves in the initial direction of the 0.2 kg ball.
solutions.answer: 2 m s⁻¹

definitions.text: A common concept of a force is a push or a pull that starts, stops or changes the magnitude and direction of velocity of a body.
A contact force is a force that is exerted by one object on the other at the point of contact.
It is the force that resists motion when the surface of one object comes in contact with the surface of another.
The drag force is the resistant force caused by the motion of a body through a fluid. It acts opposite to the relative motion of any object moving with respect to surrounding fluid.
It is an upward force exerted by a liquid on an object immersed in it.
It is the force of reaction exerted by the surface on an object lying on it. This force acts outward and perpendicular to the surface. It is also called the support force upon the object.
It is the resistance (opposition) offered by air when an object falls through it.
It is the force experienced by a rope when a person or load pulls it.
It is a force that brings certain materials back to their original shape after being deformed.
A non-contact force is defined as the force between two objects which are not in physical contact.

Every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force that is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. This is known as Newton's law of gravitation.

There are four fundamental forces in nature. These are:

1. Gravitational force
2. Electromagnetic force
3. Strong nuclear force
4. Weak nuclear force
A body continues its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by some external force.
Force is an agency which changes or tends to change the state of rest or of uniform motion of a body.
The property of a body to maintain its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line is called inertia.

If a net external force acts upon a body, it accelerates the body in the direction of force. The magnitude of acceleration is directly proportional to the magnitude of force and is inversely proportional to the mass of the body.
One newton is the force which produces an acceleration of 1 m s⁻² in a body of mass 1 kg.

For every action, there is always
an equal and opposite reaction.

If one body exerts a force on a second body,
the second body also exerts an equal and
opposite force on the first body.
The characteristic of a body which determines the magnitude of acceleration produced when a certain force acts upon it is known as mass of the body.
The weight of an object is equal to the force with which the Earth attracts the body towards its centre.
The gravitational field is a space around a mass in which another mass experiences a force due to gravitational attraction.
The gravitational field strength is defined as the gravitational force acting on unit mass.
This opposing force is the static friction F_s.
When the block is sliding, friction still exists. It is known as kinetic friction.
This constant velocity achieved by an object is called its terminal velocity.
When an object rolls over a surface, the friction produced is called rolling friction.
The momentum of a moving body is the product of its mass and velocity.
When a large force F acts on an object for a short interval of time, the impulse of the force is defined as the total change in momentum of the object.

definitions.term: Newton's second law in terms of momentum
definitions.text: The rate of change of momentum of a body is equal to the force acting on it.
If no external force acts on an isolated system, the final total momentum of the system is equal to the initial total momentum of the system.

explain.title: Parallel forces
explain.body: Your textbook defines them this way: “All those forces which act parallel to one another are known as parallel forces. The points of application of such forces may be different.” In other words, the forces act along parallel lines, but they do not have to start at the same point.

explain.title: Like parallel forces
explain.body: Your textbook states: “If the parallel forces are acting in the same direction, then they are called like parallel forces”. For example, two parallel upward forces are like parallel forces.

explain.title: Unlike parallel forces
explain.body: Your textbook states: “if their directions are opposite to one another, they are called unlike parallel forces.” For example, an upward force and a downward force along parallel lines are unlike parallel forces.

mistakes: Calling forces like or unlike without first checking that they are parallel.
