explain.title: Rigid body and axis of rotation
explain.body: If the distance between two points of the body remains the same under the action of a force, it is called a rigid body. During rotation, the body turns about an axis of rotation.

explain.title: Line of action and moment arm
explain.body: The line along which the force acts is called the line of action of the force. The perpendicular distance of the line of action of a force from the axis of rotation is known as moment arm of the force or simply moment arm.

explain.title: Moment of force or torque
explain.body: Moment of a force or torque is defined as the product of the force and the moment arm. Its magnitude is τ = F×ℓ, and its SI unit is newton metre (N m).

explain.title: Torque direction and couple
explain.body: Torque is positive if the force tends to produce an anticlockwise rotation and negative if it tends to produce a clockwise rotation. When two equal and opposite parallel forces act at two different points of the same body, they form a couple.

explain.title: Centre of gravity

explain.title: Centre of mass

explain.title: Equilibrium means no acceleration
explain.body: Your textbook defines it this way: “A body is said to be in equilibrium if it has no acceleration.” Forces may act on the body, but they must balance so their resultant is zero.

explain.title: Static equilibrium
explain.body: “A body at rest is in static equilibrium whereas a body moving with uniform velocity is in dynamic equilibrium.” A book lying on a table is a static example: its upward normal force balances its downward weight.

explain.title: Dynamic equilibrium
explain.body: A body can move and still be in equilibrium if its velocity is uniform. A paratrooper descending with uniform velocity is in dynamic equilibrium because air resistance balances gravity.

explain.title: Balanced forces can act
explain.body: Equilibrium does not mean that no forces act. It means the forces balance, so the body has no acceleration.

mistakes: Do not say a body in equilibrium must be at rest; uniform-velocity motion is dynamic equilibrium.
Do not say that no forces act on an object in equilibrium. Forces can act and balance each other.
Do not confuse uniform velocity with changing speed or direction; changing velocity means acceleration.

writtenQuestions.text: Why an accelerated body cannot be considered in equilibrium?
modelAnswer: By Newton’s second law of motion, F = ma.
For an accelerated body, a ≠ 0, therefore the net force F is not zero.
But the first condition of equilibrium requires ΣF = 0.
Therefore, an accelerated body cannot be considered in equilibrium.

explain.title: First condition: forces balance
explain.body: By Newton’s second law of motion, F = ma. If a body is in translational equilibrium, then a = 0, therefore, net force F should be 0 or ΣF = 0. A body is said to be in translational equilibrium only if the vector sum of all the external forces acting on it is equal to zero. For coplanar forces, ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0.

explain.title: Second condition: torques balance
explain.body: The second condition of equilibrium implies to the rotational equilibrium which means that the body should not rotate under the action of the forces. The vector sum of all the torques acting on a body about any point must be zero. Mathematically, Στ = 0.

explain.title: Complete equilibrium
explain.body: A body will be in complete equilibrium when ΣF_x = 0, ΣF_y = 0, and Στ = 0. The first two equations prevent a resultant force; the last prevents a resultant turning effect.

explain.title: A useful problem-solving order
explain.body: Treat each object separately, draw the forces acting on it, choose convenient axes, resolve forces when needed, and apply the force equations. If necessary, apply the torque equation and solve the equations together.

mistakes: Writing ΣF = 0 and assuming the body must be completely in equilibrium without checking Στ = 0.
Forgetting to split a slanting force into x- and y-components.
Including forces that the object exerts on its environment instead of showing only forces acting on the object.
Using a torque distance that is not the perpendicular distance from the selected point of rotation.
Dropping units or using inconsistent signs in the torque equation.

writtenQuestions.text: Discuss the concepts of stability and centre of gravity in relation to objects toppling over. Provide an example where an object’s centre of gravity affects its stability, and explain how altering its base of support can influence stability.
modelAnswer: An object is more stable when its centre of gravity is low and its base of support is wide.
It topples if the line of action of its weight falls outside its base.
For example, a cone on its base returns after a slight tilt while its centre of gravity remains above the base.
Widening the base makes toppling less likely.

explain.title: Equilibrium and support
explain.body: An object is balanced when its centre of mass and its point of support lie on the same vertical line. Then forces on each side are balanced, and the object is said to be in equilibrium.

explain.title: Stable equilibrium
explain.body: A body is said to be in a state of stable equilibrium, if after a slight tilt, it comes back to its original position. A cone on its circular base is stable: tilting raises its centre of gravity, and the resulting torque brings it back.

explain.title: Unstable equilibrium
explain.body: A body is said to be in a state of unstable equilibrium, if after a slight tilt, it tends to move on further away from its original position. A cone balanced on its tip is unstable because tilting makes it fall farther away.

explain.title: Neutral equilibrium
explain.body: A body is in neutral equilibrium, if it comes to rest in its new position after disturbance without any change in its centre of mass. A cylinder rolling on a horizontal surface is an example because the height of its centre of mass remains unchanged.

explain.title: The base of support and toppling
explain.body: A body remains in equilibrium as long as its centre of mass lies within the base. If the line of action of its weight no longer lies inside the base, the body can topple.

mistakes: Do not mix up stable and unstable: stable returns after a slight tilt; unstable moves farther away.
Do not call every object that moves unstable. A rolling cylinder can show neutral equilibrium if its centre of mass stays at the same height.
Do not say a body topples simply because it is tilted; explain whether the line of action of its weight lies outside its base.
Do not confuse the centre of mass with the base of support; both are needed when explaining toppling.

recap.answer: ΣF_x = 0, ΣF_y = 0, and Στ = 0

writtenQuestions.text: Two boxes of the same weight but different heights are lying on the floor of a truck. If the truck makes a sudden stop, which box is more likely to tumble over? Why?
modelAnswer: The taller box is more likely to tumble over.
It has a higher centre of gravity than the shorter box.
A higher centre of gravity makes a body less stable.
Therefore, when the truck stops suddenly, the taller box is more likely to topple.

solution: Stability depends on the position of the centre of gravity and the base of support.
An object with a high centre of gravity is more likely to topple; lowering the centre of gravity makes it more stable.
For example, a low armchair is more stable than a high chair because its centre of gravity is lower.
A bus carrying heavy loads on the floor has a lower centre of gravity than one carrying those loads on the top.
Widening the base also improves stability and makes toppling less likely.

writtenQuestions.text: A car travels at the same speed around two curves with different radii. For which radius the car experiences more centripetal force? Prove your answer.
modelAnswer: Centripetal force is given by F = mv²/r.
The mass and speed of the car are the same for both curves.
Therefore, F is inversely proportional to r.
So the car experiences more centripetal force on the curve with the smaller radius.

hints: At each point, the velocity follows the direction of the path at that point.

yourTurn.question: How can you prove that the centripetal force always acts perpendicular to velocity?
solution: The velocity at any point on a circular path is directed along the tangent.
If the force were not perpendicular to velocity, it would have a component in the direction of velocity.
This component would change the magnitude of velocity.
As the body moves with constant speed, this component is zero: F cos 90° = 0.
Therefore, the centripetal force acts perpendicular to velocity.
yourTurn.answer: The velocity of a body moving in a circle is along the tangent. If the force had a component along the velocity, it would change the magnitude of velocity. For constant speed, that component must be zero, so the force is perpendicular to velocity.

explain.title: How racing cars are made stable
explain.body: Racing cars move fast and take sharp turns, so they may topple. Their centre of mass is kept as low as possible. Their base area is increased by keeping the wheels outside the main body.

explain.title: Why balancing toys return
explain.body: In these toys, the centre of gravity remains below the pivot in the stable position. When disturbed, the centre of gravity rises. The toy returns to its original stable position by lowering its centre of gravity.

explain.title: Rotational motion and translational motion
explain.body: The section pairs velocity with angular velocity, acceleration with angular acceleration, force with torque, and momentum with angular momentum. Torque plays the role in rotational motion that force plays in translational motion.

explain.title: Velocity and force in circular motion
explain.body: The velocity of a body moving in a circle points along the tangent at each point. The direction of the tangent changes around the circle, so the velocity changes direction. A force perpendicular to velocity is needed to keep the body moving at constant speed in a circle.

mistakes: Do not say that a racing car is made more stable by raising its centre of mass; the section says it is kept as low as possible.
Do not confuse the tangent direction of velocity with the inward direction of the force in circular motion.
Do not say that a force along the velocity keeps the speed constant; a component along velocity changes the magnitude of velocity.
Do not forget the second racing-car design feature: increasing the base area by keeping the wheels outside the main body.

recap.question: How can you improve the stability of an object?
recap.answer: Lower its centre of gravity or widen its base.

recap.question: Which change generally makes a standing object more stable?
recap.answer: Lower its centre of gravity.

explain.title: Meaning of centripetal force
explain.body: The force that causes an object to move in a circle at constant speed is called the centripetal force. It points towards the centre of the circle.

explain.body: Centripetal force acts along the radius towards the centre. Velocity acts along the tangent to the circle. A radius and a tangent at the point of contact are perpendicular.

explain.title: Sources of centripetal force
explain.body: The force can come from different sources. String tension keeps a whirled stone in a circle; Earth's gravity keeps the Moon and satellites in orbit; friction between clothes and a dryer drum helps keep the clothes moving in a circle.

mistakes: Using the mass in grams instead of converting it to kilograms.
Using r² in the denominator or forgetting to square the speed; the relation is F_c = mv²/r.

explain.title: Vectors and components
explain.body: A force can be split into two perpendicular rectangular components. For a force F making angle θ with the x-axis, Fx = F cos θ and Fy = F sin θ. Like parallel forces act in the same direction; unlike parallel forces act in opposite directions.

explain.title: Moment and torque
explain.body: The moment of a force is its turning effect about a pivot. It is found by multiplying the force by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to its line of action: τ = rF sin θ. A force acting farther from the pivot has a greater turning effect.

explain.title: Equilibrium
explain.body: A body is in complete equilibrium when the resultant force is zero and the resultant torque is zero: ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0. For a balanced lever, clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments.

explain.title: Centre of gravity and stability
explain.body: A body is more stable when its centre of gravity is lower and its base of support is wider. It topples when the line of action of its weight falls outside its base.

explain.title: Circular motion
explain.body: Centripetal force keeps a body moving in a circular path and is given by Fc = mv²/r. It acts perpendicular to the velocity, changing the velocity's direction.

mistakes: Do not swap the sine and cosine components: for an angle measured from the x-axis, x uses cosine and y uses sine.
Use the perpendicular distance from the pivot when calculating a moment; do not automatically use the full distance if the force is inclined.
Do not confuse the moment arm (a distance) with the moment or torque (a turning effect).
For complete equilibrium, checking only the forces is not enough; the resultant torque must also be zero.
In a moments equation, measure both lever arms from the same pivot and keep units consistent.
Write the correct unit: force is measured in N, distance in m, and torque in N m.
For stability, remember that a high centre of gravity and a narrow base make toppling more likely.

recap.question: In circular motion, which way does centripetal force act compared with the object's velocity?
recap.answer: The force acts towards the centre; the velocity is along the tangent, so they are perpendicular.

recap.question: In uniform circular motion, what is the direction of centripetal force?
recap.answer: Towards the centre of the circle

solutions.question: Define like and unlike parallel forces.
steps: Like parallel forces are parallel forces that act in the same direction.
Unlike parallel forces are parallel forces that act in opposite directions.
solutions.answer: Like parallel forces act in the same direction; unlike parallel forces act in opposite directions.

solutions.question: What are rectangular components of a vector and their values?
steps: The components of a vector along two mutually perpendicular directions are called its rectangular components.
If a force F makes an angle θ with the x-axis, its rectangular components are:
Horizontal component: Fx = F cos θ.
Vertical component: Fy = F sin θ.
solutions.answer: Rectangular components are the mutually perpendicular components of a vector: Fx = F cos θ and Fy = F sin θ, when θ is measured from the x-axis.

solutions.question: What is the line of action of a force?
steps: The line of action of a force is the straight line along which the force acts.
solutions.answer: The line of action is the straight line along which a force acts.

solutions.question: Define moment of a force. Prove that τ = rF sinθ, where θ is angle between r and F.
steps: The moment of a force about a point is the product of the force and the perpendicular distance of its line of action from that point.
Let a force F act at a point whose position vector r makes an angle θ with F.
The perpendicular distance d from the point of rotation to the line of action of F is d = r sin θ.
Moment of force, τ = Fd.
Substituting d = r sin θ: τ = F(r sin θ) = rF sin θ.
solutions.answer: The moment of a force is τ = rF sin θ.

solutions.question: With the help of a diagram, show that the resultant force is zero but the resultant torque is not zero.

Identify the state of equilibrium in each case in the figure given below. [Figure: Three illustrations labelled (a), (b), and (c): (a) a cone resting on its circular base; (b) a ball on top of a dome; (c) a cylinder lying horizontally on its side.]
steps: (a) The cone resting on its circular base is in stable equilibrium.
(b) The ball on top of the dome is in unstable equilibrium.
(c) The cylinder lying on its side is in neutral equilibrium.
solutions.answer: (a) Stable equilibrium; (b) unstable equilibrium; (c) neutral equilibrium.
solutions.figure: (a) The cone on its circular base: stable equilibrium. (b) The ball on top of the dome: unstable equilibrium. (c) The cylinder lying on its side: neutral equilibrium.

solutions.question: Give an example of the body which is moving yet in equilibrium.
steps: A body moving with constant velocity in a straight line is in dynamic equilibrium because the resultant force acting on it is zero.
For example, a car moving along a straight road with constant velocity is in equilibrium.
solutions.answer: A car moving in a straight line with constant velocity is in dynamic equilibrium.

solutions.question: Define centre of mass and centre of gravity of a body.
steps: The centre of mass of a body is the point at which the whole mass of the body may be considered to be concentrated.
The centre of gravity of a body is the point through which the whole weight of the body acts.
solutions.answer: The centre of mass represents the body's whole mass, while the centre of gravity is the point through which its whole weight acts.

solutions.question: What are two basic principles of stability in physics which are applied in designing balancing toys and racing cars?
steps: A body is more stable when its centre of gravity is lower.
A body is more stable when it has a wider base.
Balancing toys are designed with a low centre of gravity, while racing cars are made low and broad to increase their stability.
solutions.answer: Stability is increased by lowering the centre of gravity and widening the base.

solutions.question: How can you prove that the centripetal force always acts perpendicular to velocity?
steps: In circular motion, the velocity of a body at any instant is along the tangent to its circular path.
The centripetal force is directed towards the centre of the circle, along the radius.
A tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
Therefore, the centripetal force is always perpendicular to the velocity.
solutions.answer: Centripetal force acts along the radius, while velocity acts along the tangent; hence they are perpendicular.

solutions.question: A car travels at the same speed around two curves with different radii. For which radius the car experiences more centripetal force? Prove your answer.
steps: The car experiences more centripetal force on the curve with the smaller radius.
For a body moving in a circle, centripetal force is given by F = mv²/r.
For the same car and the same speed, m and v are constant, so F is inversely proportional to r.
Thus, decreasing the radius increases the centripetal force. Therefore, the car experiences more force on the curve with the smaller radius.
solutions.answer: The car experiences more centripetal force on the curve with the smaller radius.

solutions.question: A ripe mango does not normally fall from the tree. But when the branch of the tree is shaken, the mango falls down easily. Can you tell the reason?
steps: A ripe mango tends to remain at rest because of inertia of rest.
When the branch is shaken, the branch moves suddenly but the mango tends to remain in its original position.
The stalk is unable to hold the mango, so it breaks and the mango falls down.
solutions.answer: Due to inertia of rest, the mango tends to remain in place when the branch is shaken, causing its stalk to break.

solutions.question: Discuss the concepts of stability and centre of gravity in relation to objects toppling over. Provide an example where an object’s centre of gravity affects its stability, and explain how altering its base of support can influence stability.
steps: The stability of an object depends on the position of its centre of gravity and the size of its base of support.
An object topples when the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside its base of support.
A lower centre of gravity makes an object more stable. For example, a low, broad racing car is less likely to topple than a tall, narrow one.
Widening the base of support makes an object more stable because the vertical line through its centre of gravity is more likely to remain within the base.
solutions.answer: An object is more stable with a lower centre of gravity and a wider base; it topples when the vertical through its centre of gravity falls outside its base.

solutions.question: Why an accelerated body cannot be considered in equilibrium?
steps: A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force acting on it is zero.
According to Newton’s second law, a non-zero resultant force produces acceleration.
Therefore, an accelerated body has a non-zero resultant force and cannot be in equilibrium.
solutions.answer: An accelerated body is not in equilibrium because the resultant force acting on it is not zero.

solutions.question: Two boxes of the same weight but different heights are lying on the floor of a truck. If the truck makes a sudden stop, which box is more likely to tumble over? Why?
steps: The taller box is more likely to tumble over.
When the truck stops suddenly, each box tends to continue moving due to inertia of motion.
The retarding force of the floor acts near the base and produces a turning effect on the box.
The taller box has a higher centre of gravity, so this turning effect is more likely to make the vertical line through its centre of gravity fall outside its base.
solutions.answer: The taller box is more likely to tumble because its higher centre of gravity makes it less stable.

solutions.question: Explain the principle of moments with an example.
steps: The turning effect of a force about a point or pivot is called its moment.
Moment of a force = force × perpendicular distance of the line of action of the force from the pivot.
The principle of moments states that, for a body in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about a pivot is equal to the sum of the anticlockwise moments about the same pivot.
For example, a balanced see-saw is in equilibrium when the clockwise moment of one person equals the anticlockwise moment of the other person.
solutions.answer: For a body in equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about a pivot equals the sum of anticlockwise moments.

solutions.question: Describe how could you determine the centre of gravity of an irregular shaped lamina experimentally.
steps: Suspend the irregular lamina freely from a small hole near its edge.
Hang a plumb line from the same point of suspension.
When the lamina comes to rest, draw a line on it along the plumb line.
Suspend the lamina from another point and again draw the line along the plumb line.
The point where the two lines intersect is the centre of gravity of the lamina.
solutions.answer: The intersection of the two plumb-line marks gives the centre of gravity of the irregular lamina.

solutions.question: State and explain two conditions of equilibrium.
steps: First condition: The resultant force acting on a body must be zero. In other words, the sum of the forces acting in one direction must be equal to the sum of the forces acting in the opposite direction. This condition prevents translational motion.

Second condition: The resultant torque acting on a body must be zero. In other words, the sum of the clockwise moments must be equal to the sum of the anticlockwise moments. This condition prevents rotational motion.
solutions.answer: For equilibrium, the resultant force and the resultant torque on a body must both be zero.

solutions.question: How the stability of an object can be improved? Give a few examples to support your answer.
steps: The stability of an object can be increased by lowering its centre of gravity.
The stability of an object can also be increased by increasing the area of its base.
An object is more stable when the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls within its base.
Racing cars are made low and broad to increase their stability.
Buildings and other heavy structures are given broad bases to make them more stable.
solutions.answer: An object can be made more stable by lowering its centre of gravity and increasing the area of its base.

solutions.question: A force of 200 N is acting on a cart at an angle of 30° with the horizontal direction. Find the x and y-components of the force.
steps: Given: F = 200 N, θ = 30°
Required: The x-component Fx and the y-component Fy of the force.
Formula: Fx = F cos θ; Fy = F sin θ
Substitution: Fx = 200 N × cos 30°; Fy = 200 N × sin 30°
Result: Fx = 173.2 N and Fy = 100 N

solutions.question: A force of 300 N is applied perpendicularly at the knob of a door to open it as shown in the given figure. If the knob is 1.2 m away from the hinge, what is the torque applied? Is it positive or negative torque? [Figure: A door with hinges along its left edge, a knob on the right edge, a dashed line from the hinge to the knob labelled 1.2 m, and a force arrow labelled F.]
steps: Given: F = 300 N, d = 1.2 m
Required: The torque and its sign.
Formula: Torque = F × d
Substitution: Torque = 300 N × 1.2 m
Working: Torque = 360 N m. The force turns the door anticlockwise about the hinge, so the torque is positive.
Result: Torque = 360 N m, positive
solutions.answer: 360 N m, positive torque

solutions.question: Two weights are hanging from a metre rule at the positions as shown in the given figure. If the metre rule is balanced at its centre of gravity (C. G), find the unknown weight w. [Figure: A metre rule balanced on a support labelled C.G, with a weight w hanging 40 cm to the left and a 4 N weight hanging 30 cm to the right.]
steps: Given: Left weight = w N, left distance = 40 cm = 0.40 m; right weight = 4 N, right distance = 30 cm = 0.30 m
Required: The unknown weight w.
Formula: For balance, clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment; moment = force × perpendicular distance
Substitution: w × 0.40 m = 4 N × 0.30 m
Working: w = (4 N × 0.30 m) ÷ 0.40 m = 3 N
Result: w = 3 N
solutions.answer: 3 N

solutions.question: A see-saw is balanced with two children sitting near either end. Child A weighs 30 kg and sits 2 metres away from the pivot, while child B weighs 40 kg and sits 1.5 metres from the pivot. Calculate the total moment on each side and determine if the sea-saw is in equilibrium.
steps: Given: m_A = 30 kg, d_A = 2 m; m_B = 40 kg, d_B = 1.5 m; take g = 10 N kg⁻¹.
Weight of A: W_A = m_Ag = 30 × 10 = 300 N.
Moment due to A = W_A d_A = 300 × 2 = 600 N m (anticlockwise).
Weight of B: W_B = m_Bg = 40 × 10 = 400 N.
Moment due to B = W_B d_B = 400 × 1.5 = 600 N m (clockwise).
The moments are equal and opposite, so the net moment is 600 − 600 = 0 N m.
solutions.answer: Each side produces a moment of 600 N m (equivalently 60 kgf m using kgf). The moments are equal and opposite, so the see-saw is in rotational equilibrium. The printed 60 corresponds to the kgf m convention.

solutions.question: A crowbar is used to lift a box as shown in the given figure. If the downward force of 250 N is applied at the end of the bar, how much weight does the other end bear? The crowbar itself has negligible weight. [Figure: A box rests at the left end of a crowbar angled upward to the right. The bar is supported near the box; the distances shown are 5 cm from the box to the support and 30 cm from the support to the downward force F at the right end.]
steps: Given: Applied force = 250 N, effort arm = 30 cm = 0.30 m, load arm = 5 cm = 0.05 m
Required: The weight lifted by the crowbar.
Formula: For balance, effort × effort arm = load × load arm
Substitution: 250 N × 0.30 m = W × 0.05 m
Result: The other end bears a weight of 1500 N

solutions.question: A 30 cm long spanner is used to open the nut of a car. If the torque required for it is 150 N m, how much force F should be applied on the spanner as shown in the figure given below. [Figure: A horizontal spanner with its head at the left and a nut at the right; a vertical force F is applied at the right end, with a horizontal dashed line extending to the right.]
steps: Given: Length of spanner, d = 30 cm = 0.30 m; torque, τ = 150 N m.
Required: Force, F.
Formula: τ = F d
Substitution: 150 N m = F × 0.30 m
Working: F = 150 N m ÷ 0.30 m = 500 N
Result: F = 500 N

solutions.question: A 5 N ball hanging from a rope is pulled to the right by a horizontal force F. The rope makes an angle of 60° with the ceiling, as shown in the given figure. Determine the magnitude of force F and tension T in the string. [Figure: A ball hangs from a slanting rope attached to a horizontal ceiling. The angle between the rope and ceiling is 60°. The rope is labelled T, and a horizontal arrow pointing right toward the ball is labelled F.]
steps: Given: Weight of ball, W = 5 N; angle between the rope and the ceiling, θ = 60°.
Required: Horizontal force, F, and tension in the string, T.
For equilibrium in the vertical direction: T sin θ = W
Substitution: T sin 60° = 5 N
Working: T = 5 N ÷ sin 60° = 5.8 N
For equilibrium in the horizontal direction: F = T cos θ
Substitution: F = 5.8 N × cos 60°
Working: F = 2.9 N
Result: F = 2.9 N and T = 5.8 N

solutions.question: A signboard is suspended by means of two steel wires as shown in the given figure. If the weight of the board is 200 N, what is the tension in the strings? [Figure: A signboard is suspended by two vertical wires labelled T_1 and T_2. The distances from the centre to the wires are marked 2 m on each side. The board is labelled “Signboard”, with a downward arrow labelled 200 N.]
steps: Given: Weight of signboard, W = 200 N; distance of each wire from the centre, d = 2 m.
Required: Tension in each wire, T₁ and T₂.
For rotational equilibrium about the centre: T₁ × 2 m = T₂ × 2 m
Working: T₁ = T₂
For vertical equilibrium: T₁ + T₂ = 200 N
Substitution: 2T₁ = 200 N
Result: T₁ = 100 N and T₂ = 100 N
solutions.answer: T₁ = 100 N, T₂ = 100 N

solutions.question: One girl of 30 kg mass sits 1.6 m from the axis of a see-saw. Another girl of mass 40 kg wants to sit on the other side, so that the see-saw may remain in equilibrium. How far away from the axis, the other girl may sit?
steps: Given: Mass of first girl, m₁ = 30 kg; distance from axis, d₁ = 1.6 m; mass of second girl, m₂ = 40 kg.
Required: Distance of the second girl from the axis, d₂.

steps: Given: Weight of block, W = 150 N; angle between the inclined string and the horizontal, θ = 60°.
Required: Tension in the horizontal string, T₁, and tension in the inclined string, T₂.
For equilibrium in the vertical direction: T₂ sin θ = W
Substitution: T₂ sin 60° = 150 N
Working: T₂ = 150 N ÷ sin 60° = 173.2 N
For equilibrium in the horizontal direction: T₁ = T₂ cos θ
Substitution: T₁ = 173.2 N × cos 60°
Working: T₁ = 86.6 N
Result: T₁ = 86.6 N and T₂ = 173.2 N

definitions.text: All those forces which act parallel to one another are known as parallel forces.
If the parallel forces are acting in the same direction, then they are called like parallel forces and if their directions are opposite to one another, they are called unlike parallel forces.
A force which is equal to the sum of all the forces is known as resultant force.
As forces are vectors, so forces can also be added by head-to-tail rule.
If the distance between two points of the body remains the same under the action of a force, it is called a rigid body.

definitions.term: Line of action of a force
definitions.text: The line along which the force acts is called the line of action of the force.
The perpendicular distance of the line of action of a force from the axis of rotation is known as moment arm of the force or simply moment arm.
Moment of a force or torque is defined as the product of the force and the moment arm.
When two equal and opposite parallel forces act at two different points of the same body, they form a couple.
A component of a vector is its effective value in a given direction.
When a body is in balanced position, the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about that point.
Centre of gravity is that point where total weight of the body appears to be acting.
The centre of mass of a body is that point where the whole mass of the body is assumed to be concentrated.
A body is said to be in equilibrium if it has no acceleration.
A body at rest is in static equilibrium whereas a body moving with uniform velocity is in dynamic equilibrium.
A body is said to be in translational equilibrium only if the vector sum of all the external forces acting on it is equal to zero.

definitions.term: First condition of equilibrium in components
definitions.text: The sum of all the components of forces along x-axis should be zero and the sum of all the components of forces along y-axis should also be zero.
The vector sum of all the torques acting on a body about any point must be zero.
A body is said to be in a state of stable equilibrium, if after a slight tilt, it comes back to its original position.
A body is said to be in a state of unstable equilibrium, if after a slight tilt, it tends to move on further away from its original position.
A body is in neutral equilibrium, if it comes to rest in its new position after disturbance without any change in its centre of mass.

definitions.term: Determining the centre of gravity of an irregular plane lamina
definitions.text: Each time the object is suspended, its centre of gravity lies on the vertical line drawn from the point of suspension with the help of a plumb line. The exact position of the centre of gravity is at the point where two such lines cross each other as shown in Fig 4.15(b).

Therefore, we are justified to predict that analogous to Newton's first law of motion, a rotating object will continue to do so with constant angular velocity unless acted upon by a resultant moment (torque).
The force that causes an object to move in a circle at constant speed is called the centripetal force.

shortTheory.question: Define like and unlike parallel forces.
shortTheory.answer: If the parallel forces are acting in the same direction, then they are called like parallel forces and if their directions are opposite to one another, they are called unlike parallel forces.

shortTheory.question: What are rectangular components of a vector and their values?
shortTheory.answer: Usually, a force is resolved into two components which are perpendicular to each other. These are called its perpendicular or rectangular components of the force. The x-component of force F is denoted as F_x and y-component as F_y. F_x = F cos θ; F_y = F sin θ.

shortTheory.question: What is the line of action of a force?
shortTheory.answer: The line along which the force acts is called the line of action of the force.

shortTheory.question: Give an example of the body which is moving yet in equilibrium.
shortTheory.answer: A good example of dynamic equilibrium is a paratrooper. In a few second after the free fall, the parachute opens and a little later, the paratrooper starts descending with a uniform velocity. In this state, the force of gravity acting vertically downward on the paratrooper is balanced by the resistance of air on the parachute acting upward.

shortTheory.question: Why an accelerated body cannot be considered in equilibrium?
shortTheory.answer: A body is said to be in equilibrium if it has no acceleration. If a body is accelerated, it has acceleration and therefore cannot be in equilibrium.

explain.title: When is work done?
explain.body: Work is said to be done when a force acts on an object and moves it through some distance. The textbook defines work as: “Work is defined as the product of magnitude of force and the distance covered in the direction of force.”

explain.title: Work in the same direction
explain.body: When force and distance are in the same direction, use W = F × S. If an object does not move, its displacement is zero and no work is done by the force.

explain.title: A force at an angle
explain.body: Only the component F cos θ acts along the motion. Therefore, W = FS cos θ. At 90°, cos 90° = 0, so a perpendicular force does no work.

explain.title: Work, graphs and units
explain.body: Work is a scalar quantity, so it has magnitude but no direction. The area under a force-distance graph represents work. The SI unit is the joule: 1 J = 1 N m.

explain.title: Energy
explain.body: Energy can be defined as the ability of a body to do work. Energy is a scalar quantity, and its SI unit is joule (J). When work is done, energy is transferred to the body on which the work is done.

explain.title: Kinetic energy
explain.body: The kinetic energy of a body is the energy that a body possesses by virtue of its motion. The work needed to stop a moving body equals its kinetic energy. For mass m and velocity v, Eₖ = ½mv².

explain.title: Potential energy
explain.body: Potential energy is defined as the energy that a body possesses by virtue of its position or deformation. A raised body has gravitational potential energy because work was done to lift it.

explain.title: Gravitational potential energy
explain.body: The work done to lift a body at constant velocity is its weight multiplied by the height: Eₚ = wh. Since w = mg, the relation becomes Eₚ = mgh.

explain.title: The law of conservation of energy
explain.body: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It may be transformed from one form to another, but the total amount of energy never changes.

explain.title: Energy during a fall
explain.body: At the top, a body at rest has potential energy mgh and no kinetic energy. As it falls, potential energy decreases while kinetic energy increases. At point B, their sum is mg(h − x) + mgx = mgh.

explain.title: Energy at the ground and waste energy
explain.body: Just before hitting the ground, the body's potential energy is zero and its kinetic energy is mgh. On impact, energy is dissipated as heat and sound. During energy transfers, some energy may become waste energy because work is done against friction; it is not available for useful work.

At the ground, potential energy is zero, but kinetic energy is not zero just before impact.

explain.title: Fossil fuel energy
explain.body: Fossil fuel energy comes out from burning of oil, coal and natural gas. These materials are known as fossil fuels. Their burning gives out heat, which is used to generate steam. The steam runs turbines to produce electricity.

explain.title: Hydroelectric generation
explain.body: Hydroelectric generation is the electricity generated from the power of falling water. Water in a high lake or reservoir possesses gravitational potential energy stored in it. When water is allowed to fall from height, the potential energy is changed into kinetic energy. Running water rotates a turbine, which runs the electric generator.

explain.title: Solar energy
explain.body: The energy obtained from sunlight is referred to as solar energy. Solar cells, also known as photo voltaic cells, transform sunlight directly into electricity. A single cell gives very low voltage, so many cells are connected in series to form a solar cell panel.

explain.title: Geothermal energy
explain.body: This energy is known as geothermal energy which can be extracted to run electric generators. Cold water is pumped down to hot rocks, where it heats up and boils. The steam comes out through another hole and runs the generator.

explain.title: Biofuel energy
explain.body: It is that energy which is obtained from the biomass. Biomass consists of organic materials such as plants, waste foods, animals dung, sewage, etc. In a digester, micro-organisms break down biomass in the absence of oxygen to produce methane-rich biogas.

mistakes: Do not confuse renewable with unlimited: explain that a renewable source is naturally replenished.
Do not call coal, oil or natural gas renewable; they are fossil fuels.
For hydroelectricity, do not skip the energy change from gravitational potential energy to kinetic energy.
Do not say a single solar cell provides high voltage; your textbook says many cells are connected in series for sufficient voltage.
Do not mix up the roles of a turbine, generator and transformer: running water or steam turns the turbine, the generator produces electricity, and a transformer changes voltage.

explain.title: What power means
explain.body: Power is defined as the time rate of doing work. It tells us how quickly work is done. Doing the same work in less time means greater power.

explain.title: The formula for power
explain.body: If W is the work done in time t, then P = W/t. Power of any agency can also be defined as energy transferred per unit time.

explain.title: The watt

explain.title: Larger units

explain.title: What efficiency means
explain.body: The ratio of useful output energy and the total input energy is called the efficiency of a working system. Input energy is the energy available for conversion; output energy is the energy converted into the required useful form.

explain.title: Percentage efficiency
explain.body: To express efficiency as a percentage, multiply the ratio of useful output energy to total input energy by 100. It can also be calculated using useful power output and total power input.

explain.title: Why efficiency is below 100%
explain.body: Energy output is always less than energy input because some energy is wasted as heat during conversion. The losses in a working machine are inevitable, so a real system cannot have 100% efficiency.

explain.title: Perpetual energy machines
explain.body: A perpetual machine is hypothetical: it would work indefinitely without an external source of energy. This is impossible because it would have to produce energy from nothing, while real machines lose energy as heat through friction and air resistance.

mistakes: Reversing the ratio: use useful output energy divided by total input energy.
Using the slope distance to calculate useful gravitational potential energy; use the vertical height for mgh or wh.
Forgetting to multiply by 100 when the question asks for percentage efficiency.
Leaving out the percentage sign or mixing energy units in one calculation.
Claiming that a real machine can have 100% efficiency; some energy is always wasted as heat.

recap.answer: Power = work done ÷ time taken; P = W/t.

explain.title: Work
explain.body: Work is done when a force causes displacement. For a force making angle θ with the displacement, W = Fd cos θ. Work is measured in joules.

explain.title: Kinetic energy
explain.body: Kinetic energy is the energy of a moving body. Use KE = ½mv²; because speed is squared, doubling the speed makes kinetic energy four times as large.

explain.title: Potential energy
explain.body: A body raised above a reference level gains gravitational potential energy: PE = mgh. Height is measured vertically.

explain.title: Power and efficiency
explain.body: Power is the rate of doing work: P = W/t. Efficiency compares useful output work or energy with input work or energy, expressed as a percentage.

explain.title: Energy sources and conservation
explain.body: Energy changes from one form to another; it is not lost overall. Renewable sources are naturally replenished, while non-renewable sources are finite.

mistakes: Using W = Fd without including cos θ when force and displacement are not in the same direction.
Forgetting to square the speed in KE = ½mv².
Using the distance along a ramp instead of the vertical height in PE = mgh.
Leaving mass in grams instead of converting it to kilograms.
Writing power in joules instead of watts, or omitting units.
Reversing the efficiency fraction: use useful output divided by input, then multiply by 100%.

recap.question: A machine has a total input energy of 500 J and useful output energy of 300 J. What is its percentage efficiency?
recap.answer: Efficiency = (useful output energy / total input energy) × 100 = (300 J / 500 J) × 100 = 60%.

recap.question: Which expression gives the efficiency of a working system?
recap.answer: The useful output energy divided by the total input energy

solutions.question: What is the work done on an object that remains at rest when a force is applied on it?
steps: Work is the product of force and displacement in the direction of the force: W = Fs.
When the object remains at rest, its displacement is zero.
Therefore, the work done is zero.
solutions.answer: The work done is zero because the object's displacement is zero.

solutions.question: A slow-moving car may have more kinetic energy than a fast-moving motorcycle. How is this possible?
steps: Kinetic energy depends on both the mass and the speed of an object: K.E. = ½mv².
A car has much greater mass than a motorcycle.
Therefore, even at a lower speed, the car may have more kinetic energy than the motorcycle.
solutions.answer: The car's much greater mass can give it more kinetic energy, even if it moves more slowly.

solutions.question: A force F₁ does 5 J of work in 10 s. Another force F₂ does 3 J of work in 5 s. Which force delivers greater power?
steps: Given: W₁ = 5 J, t₁ = 10 s; W₂ = 3 J, t₂ = 5 s
Required: Which force delivers greater power
Formula: P = W/t
Substitution: P₁ = 5 J/10 s = 0.5 W
Substitution: P₂ = 3 J/5 s = 0.6 W
Working: 0.6 W > 0.5 W
Therefore, force F₂ delivers greater power.
solutions.answer: F₂ delivers greater power: 0.6 W.

solutions.question: A woman runs up a flight of stairs. The gain in her gravitational potential energy is 4500 J. If she runs up the same stairs with twice the speed, what will be her gain in potential energy?
steps: Gravitational potential energy is given by P.E. = mgh.
The woman runs up the same stairs, so her mass and the height gained remain unchanged.
The speed does not affect the gain in gravitational potential energy.
Therefore, her gain in potential energy remains 4500 J.
solutions.answer: Her gain in potential energy is 4500 J.

solutions.question: Define work and its SI unit.
steps: Work is done when a force produces displacement in the direction of the force.
Work is the product of force and displacement in the direction of the force: W = Fs.
The SI unit of work is the joule (J).
One joule is the work done when a force of one newton displaces an object one metre in the direction of the force.
solutions.answer: Work is force multiplied by displacement in the direction of the force; its SI unit is the joule (J).

solutions.question: What is the potential energy of a body of mass m when it is raised through a height?
steps: The potential energy of a body is the work done in raising it against gravity.
For a body of mass m raised through a vertical height h, P.E. = mgh.
Here, g is the acceleration due to gravity.
solutions.answer: The potential energy of a body of mass m raised through height h is P.E. = mgh.

solutions.question: Find an expression for the kinetic energy of a moving body.
steps: Let a body of mass m be accelerated from rest to velocity v by a force F through displacement s.
The work done on the body is W = Fs.
Using F = ma, W = mas.
From v² = u² + 2as and u = 0, s = v²/(2a).
Substituting for s: W = ma × v²/(2a) = ½mv².
This work is stored in the body as kinetic energy.
Therefore, K.E. = ½mv².
solutions.answer: The kinetic energy of a moving body is K.E. = ½mv².

solutions.question: Define efficiency of a working system. Why a system cannot have 100% efficiency?
steps: Efficiency is the ratio of useful output energy to the total input energy of a working system.
Efficiency = (useful output energy / total input energy) × 100%.
A system cannot have 100% efficiency because some input energy is always wasted, for example as heat or sound due to friction.
solutions.answer: Efficiency is the percentage of input energy converted into useful output energy; it is always less than 100% because some energy is wasted.

solutions.question: What is power? Define the unit used for it.
steps: Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy.
Power = work done / time taken.
The SI unit of power is the watt (W).
A system has a power of one watt if it does one joule of work in one second.
solutions.answer: Power is the rate of doing work; its SI unit, the watt, is one joule per second.

solutions.question: Differentiate between renewable and non-renewable energy sources.
steps: Renewable energy sources are replenished naturally and can be used again and again; examples include solar and wind energy.
Non-renewable energy sources are limited and cannot be replaced within a short time after they are used; examples include coal, oil and natural gas.
solutions.answer: Renewable sources are naturally replenished, whereas non-renewable sources are limited and cannot be replaced quickly.

solutions.question: Can the kinetic energy of a body ever be negative?
steps: No. Kinetic energy cannot be negative.
Kinetic energy = ½mv².
Since mass is positive and the square of velocity is never negative, kinetic energy is zero or positive.
solutions.answer: No; kinetic energy cannot be negative because it depends on the square of velocity.

solutions.question: Which one has the greater kinetic energy: an object travelling with a velocity v or an object twice as heavy travelling with a velocity of 1/2 v?
steps: Kinetic energy of the first object = ½mv².
Kinetic energy of the second object = ½(2m)(v/2)² = ¼mv².
Therefore, the object travelling with velocity v has greater kinetic energy; it has twice the kinetic energy of the other object.
solutions.answer: The object travelling with velocity v has greater kinetic energy, twice that of the other object.

solutions.question: A car is moving along a curved road at constant speed. Does its kinetic energy change?
steps: No. Kinetic energy does not change.
Kinetic energy depends on the mass and speed of a body: K.E. = ½mv².
The car’s speed and mass remain constant, although its direction of motion changes.
solutions.answer: No; its kinetic energy remains constant because its speed remains constant.

solutions.question: Comment on the statement: “An object has one joule of potential energy.”
steps: Potential energy is measured with respect to a chosen reference level.
Therefore, the statement is incomplete unless the reference level is specified.
One joule of potential energy means the object can do one joule of work relative to that reference level.
solutions.answer: The statement is incomplete because potential energy is relative to a chosen reference level.

solutions.question: While driving on a motorway, tyre of a vehicle sometimes bursts. What may be its cause?
steps: Friction between the tyres and the road produces heat while the vehicle is moving.
At high speed, the tyres may become very hot and the air inside them expands, increasing the pressure.
The increased pressure may cause a tyre to burst.
solutions.answer: Friction heats the tyre and expands the air inside it, increasing the pressure until the tyre may burst.

solutions.question: While playing cricket on a street, the ball smashes a window pane. Describe the energy changes in this event.
steps: The chemical energy in the muscles of the player is converted into the kinetic energy of the moving ball.
When the ball hits the window pane, its kinetic energy is transferred to the pane, causing it to break.
Some energy is also changed into sound and heat energy.
solutions.answer: Chemical energy changes into kinetic energy, which is transferred to the window pane and changes partly into sound and heat energy.

solutions.question: A man rowing boat upstream is at rest with respect to the shore. Is he doing work?
steps: Work is done when a force produces displacement in the direction of the force.
The man and the boat are at rest with respect to the shore, so they have no displacement with respect to the shore.
Therefore, the man is not doing work on the boat with respect to the shore.
solutions.answer: No. Since there is no displacement with respect to the shore, no work is done on the boat.

solutions.question: A cyclist goes downhill from the top of a steep hill without pedalling and takes it to the top of the next hill. (i) Draw a diagram of what happened.
steps: Draw a steep hill rising to a high point on the left and sloping down to a valley.
Draw the next hill rising from the valley on the right.
Show the cyclist at the top of the first hill and the downhill path toward the next hill.
solutions.answer: A cyclist at the top of the first hill travelling downhill and then up the next hill.

solutions.question: A cyclist goes downhill from the top of a steep hill without pedalling and takes it to the top of the next hill. (ii) Analyse this event in terms of potential and kinetic energy. Label your diagram using these terms.
Is timber or wood renewable source of heat energy? Comment.
steps: Wood is a renewable source of heat energy if trees are replanted and allowed to grow.
It can be replenished, but it may become depleted if trees are cut down faster than they can grow.
solutions.answer: Wood is a renewable source of heat energy when trees are replanted and allowed to grow.

solutions.question: What is meant by kinetic energy? State its unit. Describe how it is determined.
steps: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion.
Its SI unit is the joule (J).
The kinetic energy of a body is determined by the work done to bring the body from rest to its velocity.
For a body of mass m moving with velocity v: KE = ½mv².
solutions.answer: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion; its SI unit is the joule, and it is given by KE = ½mv².

solutions.question: State the law of conservation of energy. Explain it with the help of an example of a body falling from certain height in terms of its potential energy and kinetic energy.
steps: The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be changed from one form to another.
The total energy of a system remains constant.
A body at a certain height has potential energy and, when released, begins to fall.
During the fall, its potential energy decreases while its kinetic energy increases.
Just before reaching the ground, its kinetic energy is greatest and its potential energy is least.
Neglecting air resistance, the sum of its potential and kinetic energies remains constant.
solutions.answer: As a falling body loses potential energy, it gains an equal amount of kinetic energy, so its total energy remains constant.

solutions.question: Differentiate between renewable and non renewable sources of energy. Give three examples for each.
steps: Renewable sources of energy are replenished naturally and can be used again.
Examples of renewable sources are solar energy, wind energy and water (hydel) energy.
Non-renewable sources of energy are available in limited amounts and cannot be replenished in a short time after use.
Examples of non-renewable sources are coal, petroleum and natural gas.
solutions.answer: Renewable energy sources are naturally replenished, whereas non-renewable sources are limited and cannot be replaced quickly; examples are solar, wind and water energy, and coal, petroleum and natural gas, respectively.

solutions.question: Explain what is meant by efficiency of a machine. How is it calculated? Why there is a limit for the efficiency of a machine?
steps: Efficiency is the ratio of useful work done by a machine to the work put into the machine.
Efficiency = (Useful work output / Work input) × 100%
The efficiency of a machine is always less than 100% because some of the input energy is wasted in overcoming friction and is transformed into heat and sound.
Therefore, the useful work output is always less than the work input.
solutions.answer: Efficiency is the percentage of the input work converted into useful output work; it is less than 100% because some energy is wasted, mainly due to friction.

solutions.question: Describe the process of electricity generation by drawing a block diagram of the process in the following cases: (i) Hydroelectric power generations
steps: Water stored at a height behind a dam has gravitational potential energy.
When released, the water flows down and its potential energy changes into kinetic energy.
The moving water turns the blades of a turbine.
The turbine drives a generator, which converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
Draw the blocks in this order, joining each block with an arrow: Reservoir (stored water) → Flowing water → Turbine → Generator → Electrical energy.
solutions.answer: The falling water turns a turbine, which drives a generator to produce electrical energy.
solutions.figure: Water stored behind a dam → water flows down through a penstock → water turns a turbine → the turbine drives a generator → electrical energy.

solutions.question: Describe the process of electricity generation by drawing a block diagram of the process in the following cases: (ii) Fossil fuels
steps: Fossil fuel is burned in a boiler to heat water.
The water changes into high-pressure steam.
The steam turns a turbine.
The turbine drives a generator, which converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
Draw the blocks in this order, joining each block with an arrow: Fossil fuel → Boiler (steam) → Turbine → Generator → Electrical energy.
solutions.answer: Burning fossil fuels produces steam that turns a turbine, which drives a generator to produce electrical energy.
solutions.figure: Fossil fuel → boiler (water heated to steam) → steam turns a turbine → the turbine drives a generator → electrical energy.

solutions.question: A force of 20 N acting at an angle of 60° to the horizontal is used to pull a box through a distance of 3 m across a floor. How much work is done?
steps: Given: F = 20 N, θ = 60°, s = 3 m
Required: Work done, W
Formula: W = Fs cos θ
Substitution: W = (20 N)(3 m) cos 60°
Working: W = 60 × 0.5 N m = 30 J
Result: W = 30 J

solutions.question: A body moves a distance of 5 metres in a straight line under the action of a force of 8 newtons. If the work done is 20 joules, find the angle which the force makes with the direction of motion of the body.
steps: Given: F = 8 N, s = 5 m, W = 20 J
Required: Angle θ between the force and the direction of motion
Formula: W = Fs cos θ
Substitution: 20 J = (8 N)(5 m) cos θ
Working: cos θ = 20 / 40 = 0.5; therefore, θ = 60°
Result: θ = 60°

solutions.question: An engine raises 100 kg of water through a height of 80 m in 25 s. What is the power of the engine?
steps: Given: m = 100 kg, h = 80 m, t = 25 s, g = 10 m/s²
Required: Power, P
Formula: P = Work done / time = mgh / t
Substitution: P = (100 kg)(10 m/s²)(80 m) / 25 s
Working: P = 80000 J / 25 s = 3200 W
Result: P = 3200 W

solutions.question: A body of mass 20 kg is at rest. A 40 N force acts on it for 5 seconds. What is the kinetic energy of the body at the end of this time?
steps: Given: m = 20 kg, u = 0 m/s, F = 40 N, t = 5 s
Required: Kinetic energy, KE
Formula: F = ma; v = u + at; KE = ½mv²
Substitution: a = 40 N / 20 kg = 2 m/s²; v = 0 m/s + (2 m/s²)(5 s)
Working: v = 10 m/s; KE = ½(20 kg)(10 m/s)² = 1000 J
Result: KE = 1000 J

solutions.question: A ball of mass 160 g is thrown vertically upward. The ball reaches a height of 20 m. Find the potential energy gained by the ball at this height.
steps: Given: m = 160 g = 0.160 kg, h = 20 m, g = 10 m/s²
Required: Potential energy gained, PE
Formula: PE = mgh
Substitution: PE = (0.160 kg)(10 m/s²)(20 m)
Working: PE = 32 kg m²/s² = 32 J
Result: PE = 32 J

solutions.question: A 0.14 kg ball is thrown vertically upward with an initial velocity of 35 m s⁻¹. Find the maximum height reached by the ball.
steps: Given: Initial velocity, u = 35 m s⁻¹; final velocity at maximum height, v = 0 m s⁻¹; acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻².
Required: Maximum height, h.
Formula: v² = u² + 2as; here a = −g, so h = (u² − v²)/(2g).
Substitution: h = [(35 m s⁻¹)² − (0 m s⁻¹)²]/[2 × 10 m s⁻²].
Working: h = 1225 m² s⁻² / 20 m s⁻² = 61.25 m.
Result: The maximum height reached by the ball is 61.25 m.

solutions.question: A girl is swinging on a swing. At the lowest point of her swing, she is 1.2 m from the ground, and at the highest point she is 2.0 m from the ground. What is her maximum velocity and where?
steps: Given: Height at the lowest point, h₁ = 1.2 m; height at the highest point, h₂ = 2.0 m; acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻²; velocity at the highest point, v₂ = 0 m s⁻¹.
Required: Maximum velocity and the position where it occurs.
Formula: By conservation of energy, mgh₁ + ½mv₁² = mgh₂ + ½mv₂².
Substitution: ½mv₁² = mg(h₂ − h₁), so v₁ = √[2g(h₂ − h₁)] = √[2 × 10 m s⁻² × (2.0 m − 1.2 m)].
Working: v₁ = √(16 m² s⁻²) = 4 m s⁻¹. The velocity is maximum at the lowest point.
Result: Her maximum velocity is 4 m s⁻¹ at the lowest position.
solutions.answer: 4 m s⁻¹, at the lowest position

solutions.question: A person pushes a lawn mower with a force of 50 N making an angle of 45° with the horizontal. If the mower is moved through a distance of 20 m, how much work is done?
steps: Given: Force, F = 50 N; angle with the horizontal, θ = 45°; displacement, s = 20 m.
Required: Work done, W.
Formula: W = Fs cos θ.
Substitution: W = 50 N × 20 m × cos 45°.
Working: W = 1000 J × 0.707 = 707 J (approximately).
Result: The work done is 707 J.

solutions.question: Calculate the work done in (i) Pushing a 5 kg box up a frictionless inclined plane 10 m long that makes an angle of 30° with the horizontal.
steps: Given: Mass of box, m = 5 kg; length of inclined plane, s = 10 m; angle with the horizontal, θ = 30°; acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻².
Required: Work done in pushing the box up the inclined plane, W.
Formula: W = Fs. For a frictionless inclined plane, F = mg sin θ; therefore W = mg s sin θ = mgh.
Substitution: W = 5 kg × 10 m s⁻² × 10 m × sin 30°.
Result: The work done is 250 J.

solutions.question: Calculate the work done in (ii) Lifting the box vertically up from the ground to the top of the inclined plane. The box is 5 kg and the inclined plane is 10 m long, making an angle of 30° with the horizontal.
steps: Given: Mass of box, m = 5 kg; length of inclined plane, s = 10 m; angle with the horizontal, θ = 30°; acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻².
Required: Work done in lifting the box vertically, W.
Formula: W = mgh.
Substitution: h = s sin θ = 10 m × sin 30° = 5 m; W = 5 kg × 10 m s⁻² × 5 m.
Working: W = 250 J.
Result: The work done is 250 J.

solutions.question: A box of mass 10 kg is pushed up along a ramp 15 m long with a force of 80 N. If the box rises up a height of 5 m, what is the efficiency of the system?
steps: Given: Mass of box, m = 10 kg; force applied, F = 80 N; distance moved along ramp, s = 15 m; vertical height, h = 5 m; acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻².
Required: Efficiency of the system.
Formula: Efficiency = (useful output work / input work) × 100%.
Substitution: Input work = Fs = 80 N × 15 m = 1200 J. Useful output work = mgh = 10 kg × 10 m s⁻² × 5 m = 500 J.
Working: Efficiency = (500 J / 1200 J) × 100% = 41.7%.
Result: The efficiency of the system is 41.7%.

solutions.question: A force of 600 N acts on a box to push it 5 m in 15 s. Calculate the power.
steps: Given: Force, F = 600 N; displacement, s = 5 m; time, t = 15 s.
Required: Power, P.
Formula: P = W/t and W = Fs; therefore P = Fs/t.
Substitution: P = (600 N × 5 m) / 15 s.
Working: P = 3000 J / 15 s = 200 W.
Result: The power is 200 W.

solutions.question: A 40 kg boy runs up-stair 10 m high in 8 s. What power he developed.
steps: Given: Mass of boy, m = 40 kg; vertical height, h = 10 m; time, t = 8 s; acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻².
Required: Power developed, P.
Formula: P = W/t and W = mgh; therefore P = mgh/t.
Substitution: P = (40 kg × 10 m s⁻² × 10 m) / 8 s.
Working: P = 4000 J / 8 s = 500 W.
Result: The power developed is 500 W.

definitions.text: Work is defined as the product of magnitude of force and the distance covered in the direction of force.
One joule work is done when a force of one newton acting on a body moves it through a distance of one metre in its own direction.
Energy can be defined as the ability of a body to do work.
The kinetic energy of a body is the energy that a body possesses by virtue of its motion.
Potential energy is defined as the energy that a body possesses by virtue of its position or deformation.
the energy possessed by an object by virtue of its position relative to the Earth is known as gravitational potential energy.
The energy stored in a compressed or stretched spring is called elastic potential energy
Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It may be transformed from one form to another, but the total amount of energy never changes.
Fossil fuel energy is the energy that is released by burning of oil, coal and natural gas.
Hydroelectric generation is the electricity generated by using the kinetic energy of the falling water.
Solar energy is the energy of the sunlight that can be converted into electricity.
The energy released by breaking the nucleus of an atom is known as nuclear energy.
Geothermal energy is the heat energy of the hot rocks present deep under the surface of the Earth.
Wind energy is the electrical energy produced by using the kinetic energy of the fast-blowing wind.
Biofuel energy is that energy which is obtained by fermentation of organic materials in the form of biogas or ethanol.
The resources of energy which are replaced by new ones after their use are called renewable energy source.
On the other hand, non-renewable sources are those, which are depleted with the continuous use.
Power is defined as the time rate of doing work.
One watt is the work done at the rate of one joule per second.
The ratio of useful output energy and the total input energy is called the efficiency of a working system.
It is a hypothetical machine that can do work indefinitely, without any external source of energy.

writtenQuestions.text:
A spring having spring constant k hangs vertically from a fixed point. A load of weight L, when hung from the spring, causes an extension x, the elastic limit of the spring is not exceeded. Some identical springs, each with spring constant k, are arranged as shown below: For each arrangement, complete the table by determining:
(i) the total extension in terms of x.
(ii) the spring constant in terms of k. | Arrangement | Total Extension x | Spring constant (k) of the arrangement |
|---|---|---|
| [FIGURE: Two springs arranged vertically in series, hanging from a fixed support, with a load labelled L at the bottom.] | | |
| [FIGURE: Two springs arranged in parallel between a fixed support and a horizontal bar, with a load labelled L hanging from the bar.] | | |
modelAnswer: For one spring, L = kx.
Series: each spring carries load L, so each extends by x.
Total extension in series = x + x = 2x.
Spring constant in series = L/(2x) = kx/(2x) = k/2.
Parallel: the identical springs share the load equally, so each carries L/2.
Extension of each spring = (L/2)/k = x/2; hence total extension = x/2.
Spring constant in parallel = L/(x/2) = 2L/x = 2k.

rubric.how: Use k arrangement = L/(2x) and L = kx, giving k/2.

rubric.description: Find the total extension for the parallel arrangement.
rubric.why: In parallel, the load is shared equally, so each spring extends by x/2 and the bar moves that distance.

rubric.description: Find the spring constant for the parallel arrangement.
rubric.why: Two parallel springs have the combined effect of both spring constants.
rubric.how: Add the constants k + k to obtain 2k.

explain.title: Deforming force
explain.body: Your textbook defines a deforming force as an external force applied on an object that can change its size or shape. Stretching a spring increases its length; compression reduces it.

explain.title: Elasticity
explain.body: Your textbook defines an elastic object as: “An object is said to be elastic, if after removal of the deforming force, it restores to its original size and shape.” The property of the material is called elasticity.

explain.title: Inelastic materials and elastic limit
explain.body: Some materials, such as clay dough or plasticine, do not return to their original shape after the deforming force is removed; your textbook calls them inelastic materials. Beyond the elastic limit, the change becomes permanent and the material does not regain its original shape or size.

explain.title: Spring constant
explain.body: For a spring, spring constant is force divided by extension: k = F/x. Use force in newtons and extension in metres to obtain k in N m⁻¹. A larger k means more force is needed for the same extension.

mistakes: Calling any changed shape elastic without checking whether the object returns to its original size and shape when the force is removed.

Reversing the spring-constant formula: use k = F/x, not x/F.
Giving a Hooke's law statement without specifying the range in which force and extension are proportional.

explain.title: Hooke’s law
explain.body: If a force F is applied on a spring to stretch or compress it, the extension or compression x has been found directly proportional to the applied force within the elastic limit. Thus, F ∝ x or F = kx or k = F/x.

explain.title: Spring constant and stiffness
explain.body: where k is the constant of proportionality and is known as spring constant. In fact, it is a measure of stiffness of the spring. The greater the value of spring constant, the greater will be the stiffness or strength of the spring. Its unit is N m⁻¹.

explain.title: Force-extension graph
explain.body: A graph of force against extension is a straight line passing through the origin. The gradient or slope of force-extension graph is a measure of spring constant k. If the load exceeds the elastic limit, the spring is permanently deformed and the graph will no longer remain linear.

explain.title: Applications
explain.body: Springs are used in spring scales, the balance wheel of mechanical clocks and galvanometers. A spring scale measures weight from extension or compression; a clock spring controls back-and-forth motion; and a galvanometer’s hair spring helps restore its pointer to zero.

explain.title: Why substances have different densities

explain.title: Meaning of pressure

explain.body: Pressure produces force at right angle to a surface. A force or its component that is parallel to the surface does not contribute to pressure.

explain.title: What atmospheric pressure means
explain.body: The Earth is surrounded by air called the atmosphere. Air molecules move and collide with objects. Your textbook defines it this way: “This force per unit area is the atmospheric pressure.”

explain.title: Pressure acts in all directions
explain.body: Air molecules move randomly and collide with objects from different directions. Your textbook states: “Since the molecules of air have random motion, therefore, atmospheric pressure acts equally in all directions.”

explain.title: Pressure at sea level
explain.body: At sea level, atmospheric pressure is about 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa. Your textbook calls this value standard atmospheric pressure.

explain.title: Atmospheric pressure changes with height
explain.body: Air density decreases with altitude, and atmospheric pressure decreases as we go higher. Your textbook gives about 55 kPa at 5 km and 1 kPa at 30 km. Lower atmospheric pressure means greater altitude.

explain.title: Evidence of atmospheric pressure
explain.body: In the tin-can activity, steam condenses as the can cools. The pressure inside falls, and the outside atmospheric pressure pushes the can inward.

mistakes: Do not say atmospheric pressure acts only downward; it acts equally in all directions.
Do not confuse pressure with force: pressure is force per unit area.
Do not say atmospheric pressure increases with altitude; it decreases as altitude increases.

explain.title: What a barometer measures
explain.body: “Atmospheric pressure is usually measured by the height of mercury column which it can support.” Instruments which measure the atmospheric pressure are called barometers.

explain.title: How the simple mercury barometer works
explain.body: A tube closed at one end is filled with mercury and inverted in a dish of mercury. The space above the mercury is completely empty, so its pressure is almost zero. A scale beside the tube measures the column height.

explain.title: Why the column represents atmospheric pressure
explain.body: Points A and B are at the same level in the mercury, so their pressures are equal. The pressure at the mercury surface in the dish is atmospheric pressure, and the liquid-column pressure is P = ρgh.

explain.title: Pressure and weather
explain.body: Atmospheric pressure changes with conditions. At high altitudes air is less dense and pressure falls. More water vapour also lowers air density, so low pressure in cloudy regions can warn that rain may follow.

steps.why: The gas must push harder to force mercury lower in its arm.
steps.text: Therefore, the unknown gas pressure is greater than atmospheric pressure.

explain.title: The manometer
explain.body: A simple manometer consists of a U-shaped glass tube which contains mercury. It compares an unknown gas pressure with atmospheric pressure.

explain.title: Equal starting levels
explain.body: In the beginning, atmospheric pressure at the two open ends of the tube is the same and hence, mercury level in the two arms remains same.

explain.title: Gas pressure greater than atmospheric pressure
explain.body: If the mercury level in the arm connected to the gas is lower than in the open arm, the unknown pressure is more than atmospheric pressure.

explain.title: Gas pressure less than atmospheric pressure
explain.body: If the mercury level in the arm connected to the gas is higher than in the open arm, the unknown pressure is less than atmospheric pressure.

mistakes: Do not confuse which arm is connected to the gas and which is open to the atmosphere.
Do not say gas pressure is greater when mercury is higher in the gas-connected arm; it is lower in that case.
Do not confuse the height difference between mercury levels with the length of the tube.
When explaining the starting levels, mention that atmospheric pressure acts equally at both open ends.

recap.question: What instrument measures atmospheric pressure?
recap.answer: Atmospheric pressure supports the mercury column; pressure at the same level in the mercury is equal.

recap.question: In a simple mercury barometer, atmospheric pressure is measured by the:
recap.answer: The height of the mercury column it can support

writtenQuestions.text: Example 6.4: The diameters of the pistons of a hydraulic press are 5 cm and 25 cm respectively. A normal force of 160 N is applied on the smaller piston, what will be the pressure exerted by this force on the bigger piston? How much weight can be lifted by the other piston?
modelAnswer: Let the areas of cross-sections of the pistons be A₁ and A₂ and their radii be r₁ and r₂ respectively.
A₁ = πr₁² and A₂ = πr₂²
F₁ = 160 N
According to Pascal's law, F₁/A₁ = w/A₂
w = F₁A₂/A₁ = F₁πr₂²/(πr₁²) = F₁ × r₂²/r₁²
Pressure transmitted = 8.15 × 10⁴ Pa; weight lifted = 4000 N = 4 kN.

explain.title: Pascal's law
explain.body: The textbook states: “When pressure is applied at one point in an enclosed fluid, it is transmitted equally to all parts of fluid without loss.” A fluid includes a liquid or a gas. This means pressure applied at one point is passed on throughout the enclosed fluid.

explain.title: Hydraulic press
explain.body: In a hydraulic press, a small piston pushes on an incompressible liquid. The liquid transmits the pressure to a larger piston. Since the larger piston has a greater area, the force on it is greater: F₂ = F₁A₂/A₁.

explain.title: Hydraulic brakes
explain.body: Pushing the brake pedal applies pressure to liquid in the master cylinder. Pascal's law transmits this pressure through the brake fluid to larger pistons at the wheels. Those pistons press brake pads towards the discs or drums, and friction slows the vehicle.

mistakes: Do not say pressure is transmitted only downwards; Pascal's law says it is transmitted equally to all parts of the enclosed fluid.
Do not reverse the piston-area ratio. From F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂, the output force is F₂ = F₁A₂/A₁.
Do not confuse force with pressure: pressure is force divided by area.
Convert areas to m² when the answer for pressure is required in N m⁻².
Include the unit in the final answer and show the equation and substitution.
