explain.title: Pressure
explain.body: Pressure is force per unit area: p = F/A. For the same force, a smaller area produces greater pressure. Pressure is measured in pascals (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻².

explain.title: Pressure in liquids and the atmosphere
explain.body: Liquid pressure is given by p = ρgh, so it depends on density, depth and gravity. Atmospheric pressure is caused by the weight of the air above us. A mercury barometer measures it by balancing atmospheric pressure against a mercury column.

explain.title: Pascal's law
explain.body: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted unchanged to every part of the fluid and the walls of its container. Hydraulic presses, lifts and brakes use this law.

explain.title: Elasticity and Hooke's law
explain.body: Elasticity is the ability of a solid to regain its original shape and size when the deforming force is removed. Hooke's law states that extension is directly proportional to applied force, provided the elastic limit is not exceeded: F = kx.

explain.title: Springs and pressure calculations
explain.body: Springs in series extend more under the same load; parallel springs share the load and have a greater combined spring constant. In calculations, convert measurements to SI units before substituting into a formula.

mistakes: Using area in cm² with a formula that requires m², or forgetting to convert litres and centimetres to SI units.
Confusing force with pressure: pressure is force divided by area.
Using the largest brick face for maximum pressure; maximum pressure comes from the smallest area.
Forgetting that liquid pressure depends on depth, density and gravity, not on the container's shape or the plate's area.
Applying Hooke's law beyond the elastic limit.
In hydraulic calculations, mixing up the small and large piston areas or pairing an area with the wrong force.
Leaving out units or giving an answer with the wrong unit.

recap.question: What happens to pressure applied at one point in an enclosed fluid?
recap.answer: The pressure is transmitted equally to every part of the enclosed fluid.

recap.question: According to Pascal's law, pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is:
recap.answer: It is transmitted equally to all parts of the enclosed fluid.

solutions.question: Why heavy animals like an elephant have a large area of the foot?
steps: Pressure is the force acting normally per unit area: P = F/A.
An elephant has a large area of the feet, so its weight acts over a large area.
Therefore, the pressure exerted on the ground is reduced.
solutions.answer: An elephant has large feet to reduce the pressure exerted on the ground.

solutions.question: Why animals like deer who run fast have a small area of the foot?
steps: Pressure is the force acting normally per unit area: P = F/A.
A deer has a small area of the feet, so its weight acts over a small area.
Therefore, greater pressure is exerted on the ground, helping the deer run fast.
solutions.answer: A deer’s small foot area produces greater pressure on the ground and helps it run fast.

solutions.question: Why is it painful to walk bare footed on pebbles?
steps: The area of contact between a bare foot and a pebble is very small.
Pressure is the force acting normally per unit area, P = F/A.
The body’s weight acting on this small area produces great pressure, so walking on pebbles is painful.
solutions.answer: Pebbles exert great pressure on the small area of contact with the bare foot, causing pain.

solutions.question: State Pascal's law. Give an application of Pascal's law.
steps: Pascal’s law states that pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally and undiminished in all directions and to the walls of the container.
An application of Pascal’s law is a hydraulic press.
solutions.answer: Pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally and undiminished in all directions; a hydraulic press is an application.

solutions.question: State what do you mean by elasticity of a solid.
steps: The property of a solid by virtue of which it regains its original shape and size when the deforming force is removed is called elasticity.
solutions.answer: Elasticity is the property of a solid to regain its original shape and size when the deforming force is removed.

solutions.question: What is Hooke's law? Does an object remain elastic beyond elastic limit? Give reason.
steps: Hooke’s law states that, within the elastic limit, the extension produced in a body is directly proportional to the applied force.
In symbols, F ∝ x, or F = kx, where x is the extension and k is a constant.
An object does not remain elastic when stretched beyond its elastic limit.
Beyond the elastic limit, it does not regain its original shape and size when the force is removed; it becomes permanently deformed.
solutions.answer: Within the elastic limit, extension is directly proportional to applied force; beyond the limit, an object is permanently deformed.

solutions.question: Distinguish between force and pressure.
steps: Force is a push or pull acting on a body; pressure is the force acting normally per unit area.
Force is measured in newtons (N); pressure is measured in pascals (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m².
Force is a vector quantity; pressure is a scalar quantity.
Pressure depends on the area over which the force acts: P = F/A.
solutions.answer: Force is a push or pull measured in newtons, while pressure is normal force per unit area measured in pascals.

solutions.question: What is the relationship between liquid pressure and the depth of the liquid?
steps: The pressure exerted by a liquid increases with the depth below its surface.
For a liquid of density ρ, the pressure at depth h is given by P = ρgh.
Thus, for the same liquid, liquid pressure is directly proportional to depth.
solutions.answer: Liquid pressure increases directly with depth.

solutions.question: What is the basic principle to measure the atmospheric pressure by a simple mercury barometer?
steps: Atmospheric pressure acting on the mercury in the reservoir supports a column of mercury in the tube.
The mercury column comes to rest when the pressure due to its weight balances the atmospheric pressure acting on the reservoir surface.
solutions.answer: A mercury barometer measures atmospheric pressure by balancing it against the pressure of a column of mercury.

solutions.question: State the basic principle used in the hydraulic brake system of the automobiles.
steps: The hydraulic brake system works on Pascal’s principle.
Pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally and undiminished in all directions.
The transmitted pressure acts on the brake pistons and applies the brakes.
solutions.answer: Hydraulic brakes work on Pascal’s principle.

solutions.question: A spring having spring constant k hangs vertically from a fixed point. A load of weight L, when hung from the spring, causes an extension x, the elastic limit of the spring is not exceeded. Some identical springs, each with spring constant k, are arranged as shown below: For each arrangement, complete the table by determining: (i) the total extension in terms of x. Arrangements: two springs arranged vertically in series, hanging from a fixed support, with a load labelled L at the bottom; two springs arranged in parallel between a fixed support and a horizontal bar, with a load labelled L hanging from the bar.
steps: For two identical springs in series, the load L acts on each spring, so each extends by x.
Total extension in series = x + x = 2x.
For two identical springs in parallel, the load is shared equally, so each spring carries L/2.
Since a load L produces extension x in one spring, a load L/2 produces extension x/2.
The two parallel springs have the same extension, so the total extension is x/2.
solutions.answer: Series: 2x; parallel: x/2.
solutions.figure: Completed table: two springs in series — total extension 2x; two springs in parallel — total extension x/2.

solutions.question: A spring having spring constant k hangs vertically from a fixed point. A load of weight L, when hung from the spring, causes an extension x, the elastic limit of the spring is not exceeded. Some identical springs, each with spring constant k, are arranged as shown below: For each arrangement, complete the table by determining: (ii) the spring constant in terms of k. Arrangements: two springs arranged vertically in series, hanging from a fixed support, with a load labelled L at the bottom; two springs arranged in parallel between a fixed support and a horizontal bar, with a load labelled L hanging from the bar.
steps: For two identical springs in series, the total extension under load L is 2x.
Using L = kx for one spring, the equivalent spring constant in series is L/(2x) = k/2.
For two identical springs in parallel, the total extension under load L is x/2.
The equivalent spring constant in parallel is L/(x/2) = 2k.
solutions.answer: Series: k/2; parallel: 2k.
solutions.figure: Completed table: two springs in series — spring constant k/2; two springs in parallel — spring constant 2k.

solutions.question: Springs are made of steel instead of iron. Why?
steps: Steel has a greater elastic limit than iron.
Therefore, a steel spring can be stretched or compressed more without being permanently deformed, and returns to its original shape when the force is removed.
solutions.answer: Steel is used for springs because it has a greater elastic limit than iron.

solutions.question: Which of the following material is more elastic? (a) Iron or rubber (b) Air or water
steps: (a) Iron is more elastic than rubber because iron has a greater Young’s modulus.
(b) Water is more elastic than air because water has a greater bulk modulus.
solutions.answer: (a) Iron  (b) Water

solutions.question: How does water pressure one metre below the surface of a swimming pool compare to water pressure one metre below the surface of a very large and deep lake?
steps: The water pressure at a depth h is given by P = ρgh.
At one metre below the surface, the depth and the liquid are the same in both cases.
Therefore, the water pressure is the same in the swimming pool and in the lake.
solutions.answer: The pressures are equal.

solutions.question: What will happen to the pressure in all parts of a confined liquid if pressure is increased in one part? Give an example from your daily life where such principle is applied.
steps: The pressure applied to any part of a confined liquid is transmitted equally and undiminished in all directions to every part of the liquid and to the walls of its container.
This is Pascal’s principle.
A hydraulic brake is a daily-life application: pressure applied to the brake fluid is transmitted to the brakes at the wheels.
solutions.answer: An increase in pressure in one part of a confined liquid is transmitted equally and undiminished throughout it; hydraulic brakes apply this principle.

solutions.question: If some air remains trapped within the top of the mercury column of the barometer which is supposed to be vacuum, how would it affect the height of the mercury column?
steps: The trapped air exerts pressure on the mercury at the top of the column.
This pressure adds to the pressure of the mercury column, so a smaller height of mercury is needed to balance atmospheric pressure.
Therefore, the mercury column becomes lower than it should be, giving an incorrect barometer reading.
solutions.answer: The mercury column would be lower than its correct height.

solutions.question: How does the long neck is not a problem to a giraffe while raising its neck suddenly?
steps: The giraffe’s heart produces high blood pressure to pump blood up its long neck to the brain.
Special valves in its blood vessels help regulate blood flow and pressure when it raises or lowers its neck suddenly.
Thus, the brain continues to receive blood without being exposed to a harmful change in pressure.
solutions.answer: High blood pressure from the heart and special valves help maintain safe blood flow to a giraffe’s brain when it raises its long neck.

solutions.question: The end of glass tube used in a simple barometer is not properly sealed, some leak is present. What will be its effect?
steps: Air enters through the leak and occupies the space above the mercury column, which should be a vacuum.
The air exerts pressure on the mercury at the top of the column.
The mercury column falls, so the barometer gives a reading lower than the true atmospheric pressure.
solutions.answer: Air entering through the leak lowers the mercury column and makes the barometer reading incorrect.

solutions.question: Comment on the statement. “Density is a property of a material not the property of an object made of that material.”
steps: Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance: density = mass ÷ volume.
For a given material, density is the same for different-sized objects made of that material, provided the conditions are the same.
Therefore, density is a property of the material, not of the size or shape of an individual object.
solutions.answer: Density is a property of a material because it does not depend on the size or shape of an object made from it.

solutions.question: How the load of a large structure is estimated by an engineer?
steps: An engineer estimates the volume of each material used in the structure.
The mass of each material is calculated using mass = density × volume.
The masses are added and multiplied by gravitational field strength to find the total weight (load) of the structure.
The engineer can then determine how this load is distributed over the supporting parts and foundation.
solutions.answer: An engineer estimates a structure’s load by using the density and volume of its materials to calculate their total weight.

solutions.question: What is Hooke’s law? Give three applications of this law.
steps: Hooke’s law states that the extension of an elastic body is directly proportional to the applied force, provided its elastic limit is not exceeded.
In symbols: F ∝ x, or F = kx, where F is the applied force, x is the extension and k is the spring constant.
A spring balance uses this law to measure force or weight.
Vehicle suspension and shock absorbers use springs that extend or compress under force.
Springs in devices such as clocks use this law to produce controlled motion.
solutions.answer: Within the elastic limit, extension is directly proportional to applied force; this principle is used in spring balances, vehicle suspension and clocks.

solutions.question: Describe the working and applications of a simple mercury barometer and a manometer.
steps: A simple mercury barometer consists of a long glass tube, closed at one end, filled with mercury and inverted in a mercury trough.
Some mercury flows out, leaving a space called the Torricellian vacuum above the mercury column.
Atmospheric pressure acting on the mercury in the trough supports the column; its height measures atmospheric pressure.
A barometer is used to measure atmospheric pressure and to help forecast changes in the weather.
A manometer is a U-shaped tube partly filled with a liquid, with one end connected to a gas container and the other usually open to the atmosphere.
The gas pressure causes the liquid levels in the two arms to differ. The difference in level is used to determine the gas pressure relative to atmospheric pressure.
A manometer is used to measure the pressure of a gas in a container or pipe.
solutions.answer: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure from the height of its mercury column, while a manometer measures gas pressure from the difference between liquid levels in its arms.

solutions.question: Describe Pascal’s Law. State its applications with examples.
steps: Pascal’s Law states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and to the walls of its container.
A hydraulic press applies this law: pressure applied to a small piston is transmitted through the fluid to a larger piston, producing a greater output force.
A hydraulic lift uses the pressure transmitted through oil to raise a heavy vehicle.
In hydraulic brakes, pressure applied at the brake pedal is transmitted by brake fluid to the wheel brakes.
solutions.answer: Pascal’s Law: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid and to the container walls. Its applications include hydraulic presses, hydraulic lifts and hydraulic brakes.

solutions.question: On what factors the pressure of a liquid in a container depend? How is it determined?
steps: The pressure of a liquid depends upon the depth below its surface and the density of the liquid.
It also depends upon the gravitational field strength, g.
The pressure at depth h is determined by the relation: P = ρgh, where ρ is the density of the liquid.
Thus, pressure increases with the depth and density of the liquid.
solutions.answer: Liquid pressure is determined by P = ρgh and depends on liquid density, depth, and gravitational field strength.

solutions.question: Explain that atmosphere exerts pressure. What are its applications? Give at least three examples.
steps: The air surrounding the Earth is called the atmosphere.
The atmosphere has weight and exerts pressure on the Earth and on all objects in it; this pressure is called atmospheric pressure.
Atmospheric pressure acts in all directions.
When we drink through a straw, air pressure on the liquid surface pushes the liquid up the straw when pressure inside the straw is reduced.
A syringe or dropper draws liquid in when the pressure inside it is reduced and atmospheric pressure pushes the liquid inside.
A suction cup sticks to a smooth surface because the pressure inside it is reduced and atmospheric pressure presses it against the surface.
A hand pump lifts water when the pressure inside the pump is reduced, allowing atmospheric pressure to push water up.
solutions.answer: Atmospheric pressure is exerted by the weight of the air and is used in straws, syringes or droppers, suction cups, and hand pumps.

solutions.question: A spring is stretched 20 mm by a load of 40 N. Calculate the value of spring constant. If an object causes an extension of 16 mm, what will be its weight?
steps: Given: Extension, x₁ = 20 mm = 0.020 m; load, F₁ = 40 N; extension, x₂ = 16 mm = 0.016 m.
Required: Spring constant, k; weight of the object, F₂.
Formula: F = kx, so k = F/x and F₂ = kx₂.
Substitution: k = 40 N / 0.020 m.
Working: k = 2000 N m⁻¹ = 2 kN m⁻¹.
Substitution: F₂ = (2000 N m⁻¹)(0.016 m).
Working: F₂ = 32 N.
Result: Spring constant = 2 kN m⁻¹; weight of the object = 32 N.
solutions.answer: 2 kN m⁻¹; 32 N

solutions.question: The mass of 5 litres of milk is 4.5 kg. Find its density in SI units.
steps: Given: Mass, m = 4.5 kg; volume, V = 5 L = 5 × 10⁻³ m³.
Required: Density, ρ.
Formula: ρ = m/V.
Substitution: ρ = 4.5 kg / (5 × 10⁻³ m³).
Working: ρ = 900 kg m⁻³ = 0.9 × 10³ kg m⁻³.
Result: Density of milk = 0.9 × 10³ kg m⁻³.
solutions.answer: 0.9 × 10³ kg m⁻³

solutions.question: When a solid of mass 60 g is lowered into a measuring cylinder, the level of water rises from 40 cm³ to 44 cm³. Calculate the density of the solid.
steps: Given: Mass, m = 60 g = 0.060 kg; initial water volume = 40 cm³; final water volume = 44 cm³.
Required: Density of the solid, ρ.
Volume of solid: V = 44 cm³ − 40 cm³ = 4 cm³ = 4 × 10⁻⁶ m³.
Formula: ρ = m/V.
Substitution: ρ = 0.060 kg / (4 × 10⁻⁶ m³).
Working: ρ = 15 000 kg m⁻³ = 15 × 10³ kg m⁻³.
Result: Density of the solid = 15 × 10³ kg m⁻³.
solutions.answer: 15 × 10³ kg m⁻³

solutions.question: A block of density 8 × 10³ kg m⁻³ has a volume 60 cm³. Find its mass.
steps: Given: Density, ρ = 8 × 10³ kg m⁻³; volume, V = 60 cm³ = 60 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 6 × 10⁻⁵ m³.
Required: Mass, m.
Formula: ρ = m/V, so m = ρV.
Substitution: m = (8 × 10³ kg m⁻³)(6 × 10⁻⁵ m³).
Working: m = 0.48 kg.
Result: Mass of the block = 0.48 kg.

solutions.question: A brick measures 5 cm × 10 cm × 20 cm. If its mass is 5 kg, calculate the maximum and minimum pressure which the brick can exert on a horizontal surface.
steps: Given: Length = 20 cm = 0.20 m; width = 10 cm = 0.10 m; height = 5 cm = 0.05 m; mass, m = 5 kg; take g = 10 N kg⁻¹.
Required: Maximum and minimum pressure exerted by the brick.
Weight of brick: W = mg = (5 kg)(10 N kg⁻¹) = 50 N.
Formula: P = F/A.
For maximum pressure, use the smallest face area: A = (0.10 m)(0.05 m) = 0.005 m².
Substitution and working: Pmax = 50 N / 0.005 m² = 10 000 Pa = 1 × 10⁴ Pa.
For minimum pressure, use the largest face area: A = (0.20 m)(0.10 m) = 0.020 m².
Substitution and working: Pmin = 50 N / 0.020 m² = 2500 Pa = 25 × 10² Pa.
Result: Maximum pressure = 1 × 10⁴ Pa; minimum pressure = 25 × 10² Pa.
solutions.answer: Maximum pressure = 1 × 10⁴ Pa; minimum pressure = 25 × 10² Pa

solutions.question: What will be the height of the column in barometer at sea level if mercury is replaced by water of density 1000 kg m⁻³, where density of mercury is 13.6 × 10³ kg m⁻³
steps: Given: Height of mercury column, hₘ = 0.76 m; density of mercury, ρₘ = 13.6 × 10³ kg m⁻³; density of water, ρw = 1000 kg m⁻³.
Required: Height of water column, hw.
At sea level, pressure due to the mercury column equals pressure due to the water column: ρₘ g hₘ = ρw g hw.
Therefore, hw = (ρₘ hₘ) / ρw.
Substitution: hw = (13.6 × 10³ kg m⁻³ × 0.76 m) / (1000 kg m⁻³).
Working: hw = 10.336 m ≈ 10.3 m.
Result: The height of the water column is 10.3 m.

solutions.question: Suppose in the hydraulic brake system of a car, the force exerted normally on its piston of cross-sectional area of 5 cm² is 500 N. What will be the pressure transferred to the brake oil? What will be the force on the second piston of area of cross-section 20 cm²?
steps: Given: Force on the first piston, F₁ = 500 N; area of the first piston, A₁ = 5 cm² = 5 × 10⁻⁴ m²; area of the second piston, A₂ = 20 cm² = 2 × 10⁻³ m².
Required: Pressure transferred to the brake oil, P; force on the second piston, F₂.
Pressure, P = Force / Area.
Substitution: P = 500 N / (5 × 10⁻⁴ m²).
Working: P = 1.0 × 10⁶ N m⁻².
By Pascal’s principle, the pressure is transmitted equally throughout the brake oil. Therefore, F₂ = P A₂.
Substitution: F₂ = 1.0 × 10⁶ N m⁻² × 2 × 10⁻³ m².
Working: F₂ = 2000 N.
Result: The pressure transferred is 1.0 × 10⁶ N m⁻² and the force on the second piston is 2000 N.

solutions.question: Find the water pressure on a deep-sea diver at a depth of 10 m, where the density of sea water is 1030 kg m⁻³.
steps: Given: Density of sea water, ρ = 1030 kg m⁻³; depth, h = 10 m; acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻².
Required: Water pressure on the diver, P.
Pressure in a liquid, P = ρgh.
Substitution: P = 1030 kg m⁻³ × 10 m s⁻² × 10 m.
Working: P = 103000 N m⁻² = 1.03 × 10⁵ N m⁻².
Result: The water pressure on the diver is 1.03 × 10⁵ N m⁻².

solutions.question: The area of cross-section of the small and large pistons of a hydraulic press is respectively 10 cm² and 100 cm². What force should be exerted on the small piston in order to lift a car of weight 4000 N?
steps: Given: Area of the small piston, A₁ = 10 cm²; area of the large piston, A₂ = 100 cm²; weight of the car, F₂ = 4000 N.
Required: Force on the small piston, F₁.
According to Pascal’s principle, pressure is transmitted equally through the liquid: F₁ / A₁ = F₂ / A₂.
Therefore, F₁ = (F₂ A₁) / A₂.
Substitution: F₁ = (4000 N × 10 cm²) / 100 cm².
Working: F₁ = 400 N.
Result: A force of 400 N should be exerted on the small piston.

solutions.question: In a hot air balloon, the following data was recorded. Draw a graph between the altitude and pressure and find out: (a) What would the air pressure have been at sea level? Altitude (m), Pressure (kPa): 150, 99.5; 500, 95.7; 800, 92.4; 1140, 88.9; 1300, 87.2; 1500, 85.3.
steps: Given: Altitude = 150 m, 500 m, 800 m, 1140 m, 1300 m and 1500 m; pressure = 99.5 kPa, 95.7 kPa, 92.4 kPa, 88.9 kPa, 87.2 kPa and 85.3 kPa, respectively.
Required: Air pressure at sea level (altitude = 0 m), in Pa.
Plot altitude on the x-axis and pressure on the y-axis; plot the given data points and draw a best-fit straight line.
Extend the line to altitude 0 m. From the graph, the pressure intercept is approximately 101 kPa.
Convert to SI units: 101 kPa = 101 × 10³ Pa.
Result: Air pressure at sea level ≈ 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa.

solutions.question: In a hot air balloon, the following data was recorded. Draw a graph between the altitude and pressure and find out: (b) At what height the air pressure would have been 90 kPa? Altitude (m), Pressure (kPa): 150, 99.5; 500, 95.7; 800, 92.4; 1140, 88.9; 1300, 87.2; 1500, 85.3.

solutions.question: If the pressure in a hydraulic press is increased by an additional 10 N cm⁻², how much extra load will the output platform support if its cross-sectional area is 50 cm²?
steps: Given: Increase in pressure, P = 10 N cm⁻²; area of the output platform, A = 50 cm².
Required: Extra load supported, F.
Pressure = Force / Area; therefore, F = PA.
Substitution: F = 10 N cm⁻² × 50 cm².
Working: F = 500 N.
Result: The output platform will support an extra load of 500 N.

solutions.question: The force exerted normally on the hydraulic brake system of a car, with its piston of cross sectional area 5 cm² is 500 N. What will be the: (a) pressure transferred to the brake oil?
steps: Given: Force on the piston, F = 500 N; area of the piston, A = 5 cm² = 5 × 10⁻⁴ m².
Required: Pressure transferred to the brake oil, P.
Pressure, P = Force / Area.
Substitution: P = 500 N / (5 × 10⁻⁴ m²).
Working: P = 1.0 × 10⁶ N m⁻².
Result: The pressure transferred to the brake oil is 1.0 × 10⁶ N m⁻².

solutions.question: The force exerted normally on the hydraulic brake system of a car, with its piston of cross sectional area 5 cm² is 500 N. What will be the: (b) force on the brake piston of area of cross section 20 cm²?
steps: Given: F₁ = 500 N, A₁ = 5 cm² = 5 × 10⁻⁴ m², A₂ = 20 cm² = 2 × 10⁻³ m².
Required: Force on the brake piston, F₂.
By Pascal’s principle, pressure is transmitted equally throughout the liquid: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.
Substitution: 500 N/(5 × 10⁻⁴ m²) = F₂/(2 × 10⁻³ m²).

definitions.text: Such a force is known as deforming force.
An object is said to be elastic, if after removal of the deforming force, it restores to its original size and shape.
This property of the material is known as elasticity.
Some materials such as clay dough or plasticine do not return to their original shape after the removal of the deforming force. They are known as inelastic materials.
Most of the materials are elastic up to a certain limit known as elastic limit.
If a force F is applied on a spring to stretch or compress it, the extension or compression x has been found directly proportional to the applied force within the elastic limit.
Density of a substance is defined as its mass per unit volume.
Pressure is defined as the force exerted normally on unit area of an object.
This force per unit area is the atmospheric pressure.
Instruments which measure the atmospheric pressure are called barometers.
When pressure is applied at one point in an enclosed fluid, it is transmitted equally to all parts of fluid without loss.

important.why: A direct application of pressure and contact area, likely for a short-answer question.
A standard everyday example of pressure increasing when contact area decreases.
A key law with a common two-part short-answer format.

fullMarks: For a definition or law, write the complete statement clearly; for Pascal’s law include both “enclosed fluid” and “equally … without loss.”
For a numerical, write the given quantities first and convert them to SI units before substituting: cm to m, cm² to m², litres to m³, and g to kg.
Show the formula, substitution with units, calculation, and final answer with its SI unit. Keep suitable significant figures.
For spring questions, use extension x (not the spring’s full length) and show that the force–extension relationship applies only within the elastic limit.
For pressure questions, identify the area actually in contact and use the area perpendicular to the normal force. For maximum and minimum pressure, use the smallest and largest faces respectively.
For liquid pressure, state that it depends on liquid density and depth, then use P = ρgh. Do not include atmospheric pressure unless the question asks for total pressure.
For hydraulic systems, show equal pressure at both pistons before calculating the unknown force; label the small and large piston areas correctly.
In an explanation of hydraulic brakes, describe the pressure transfer through the brake fluid and how the pistons press the brake pads against the discs or drums.
mistakes: Using the spring’s total length instead of its extension. Fix: calculate extension as the change in length, then use k = F ÷ x.
Leaving extensions, dimensions, or areas in cm or cm² in an SI calculation. Fix: convert lengths to m and areas to m² before substituting.
Using mass in place of force when finding pressure. Fix: first find weight using F = mg, then use P = F ÷ A.
Choosing the wrong face of a brick for maximum or minimum pressure. Fix: the smallest contact area gives maximum pressure; the largest gives minimum pressure.
Thinking liquid pressure depends on the container’s shape or the area of its base. Fix: for pressure at a depth, use P = ρgh; it depends on density, depth, and g.
Swapping the small and large piston areas in a hydraulic calculation. Fix: label A₁ and A₂ carefully and use F₁ ÷ A₁ = F₂ ÷ A₂.

Writing that pressure is transmitted equally by any fluid without mentioning confinement. Fix: state that pressure applied at one point in an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally to all parts without loss.

shortTheory.question: Why is it painful to walk bare footed on pebbles?
shortTheory.answer: But when we walk on pebbles, the contact area is reduced. Then the pressure due to reaction force becomes so high that it becomes painful.

shortTheory.question: What is the relationship between liquid pressure and the depth of the liquid?
shortTheory.answer: Equation 6.4 shows that pressure in a liquid increases with depth. The value of pressure depends on the depth and density of the liquid.

modelAnswer: Gas molecules are relatively far away from one another.
They move freely, so a gas has neither a definite volume nor a definite shape.

Constructed-response questions may ask you to describe plasma or explain why it is called a conducting fourth state of matter.
In comparison questions, earn marks by giving both the particle arrangement or motion and the resulting property of each state.
Use precise terms from your textbook: intermolecular force, fixed positions, vibrational motion, slide over one another, and relatively far apart.

Explain how the spacing and motion of the molecules relate to shape and volume.
yourTurn.question: What are the reasons that gases have neither a fixed volume nor a fixed shape?
solution: Gas molecules are relatively far away from one another.
They move freely and spread out.
Therefore, a gas has neither a definite volume nor a definite shape.
yourTurn.answer: Gas molecules are relatively far apart and move freely, so a gas has neither a definite volume nor a definite shape.

steps.why: The strength of the attraction between solid molecules explains why they stay in place.
steps.text: The intermolecular forces in a solid are so strong that they hold the molecules at fixed positions.

steps.why: Molecules in a solid still move, but their motion is limited to vibration about fixed points.
steps.text: The molecules vibrate about their fixed positions.

steps.why: Fixed positions explain why the solid keeps both its shape and its volume.
steps.text: Therefore, a solid has a definite shape and a definite volume.

example.question: Why solids have a fixed volume and shape according to particle theory of matter?
example.answer: Strong intermolecular forces hold solid molecules at fixed positions; they vibrate about those positions, giving a solid a definite shape and volume.

explain.title: Particles are always moving
explain.body: According to this theory, matter is composed of very small particles called molecules which are always in motion. Their motion may be vibrational, rotational or linear. Molecules have kinetic energy due to their motion.

explain.title: Forces act between molecules
explain.body: There exists a mutual force of attraction between the molecules known as intermolecular force. This force depends upon the distance between the molecules. It decreases with increasing distance between them. Molecules also possess potential energy due to this force of attraction.

explain.title: Heating makes molecular motion more vigorous
explain.body: When a substance is heated, its temperature rises and its molecular motion becomes more vigorous which increases the kinetic energy of the molecules. Thus, the temperature of the substance depends upon the average kinetic energy of its molecules.

explain.title: Solids, liquids and gases
explain.body: In solids, strong intermolecular forces hold molecules at fixed positions, but the molecules vibrate about those positions. Liquids have weaker intermolecular forces, so molecules can slide over one another and the liquid flows. Gas molecules are relatively far away from one another, so a gas has neither a definite volume nor a definite shape.

explain.title: Plasma
explain.body: The plasma is a gas in which most of the atoms are ionized containing positive ions and electrons. These particles move freely. Their presence makes plasma a conducting state of matter, which is why plasma is known as the fourth state of matter.

mistakes: Do not say that molecules in a solid are motionless; they vibrate about fixed positions.
Do not say that a liquid has a definite shape. It has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container.
Do not say that a gas has a definite volume. It has neither a definite volume nor a definite shape.
Do not say that intermolecular force increases as molecules get farther apart; it decreases with increasing distance.
Do not describe plasma as an ordinary gas: it contains positive ions and free electrons and conducts electricity.

steps.why: The activity asks whether the spoon heats up when placed in hotter water.
steps.text: Put the spoon in the hot water and stir it.

steps.why: A spoon becoming hotter shows that energy has transferred to it.
steps.text: The spoon gets hotter, including its other end.

steps.why: The water is at a higher temperature than the spoon, so energy transfers from the water to the spoon.
steps.text: Heat is transferred from the hot water to the spoon because the temperature of the water was higher than that of the spoon.

example.question: Does the other end of the spoon also become hot?
example.answer: Yes. The spoon gets hotter because heat is transferred from the hotter water to the spoon.

explain.title: Temperature
explain.body: Temperature of a body is defined as degree of its hotness or coldness. Temperature also determines the direction in which thermal energy flows.

explain.title: Heat
explain.body: Heat is the energy which is transferred from one object to another due to difference of temperature between the two bodies. It is energy in transit, not something a body contains.

explain.title: Internal energy
explain.body: The sum of kinetic and potential energies of the molecules of an object is called its internal energy. Molecules have kinetic energy because they move and potential energy because attractive forces act between them.

explain.title: Heating a substance
explain.body: When a substance is heated, its molecular motion becomes more vigorous and its internal energy increases. As a result, its temperature rises.

explain.title: Why a thermometer is needed
explain.body: Our sense of touch can tell us whether something feels hot or cold, but it cannot measure the exact temperature. A thermometer is an instrument used to measure temperature. Thermometers use some property of a substance, which changes appreciably with the change of temperature.

explain.title: Choosing a thermometric material
explain.body: Some basic thermometric properties for a material suitable to construct a thermometer are the following: It is a good conductor of heat; it gives quick response to temperature changes; it has uniform thermal expansion; it has high boiling point; it has low freezing point; it has large expansivity (low specific heat capacity); it does not wet glass; it does not vapourize; it is visible.

explain.title: Liquid-in-glass thermometers
explain.body: Liquids expand on heating, so the expansion in the volume of a liquid can be used to measure temperature. A liquid-in-glass thermometer has a glass bulb filled with liquid and a narrow capillary tube. As the temperature rises, the liquid expands and moves up the tube. The position of the end of the liquid thread gives the temperature. Mercury is opaque and easy to see; alcohol must be coloured to make it visible.

explain.title: Fixed points and temperature scales
explain.body: A temperature scale is constructed using two reference temperatures called fixed points. The steam point is the upper fixed point and the melting point of pure ice is the lower fixed point. Celsius assigns 0 and 100 to these points; Fahrenheit assigns 32 and 212; Kelvin assigns 273 and 373. Kelvin is also called the absolute temperature scale.

explain.title: Converting temperatures
explain.body: For Celsius to Fahrenheit use T_f = 9/5 × T_c + 32. For Fahrenheit to Celsius use T_c = 5/9 (T_f − 32). For Celsius to Kelvin use T_k = T_c + 273. Substitute the given value into the appropriate formula and include the correct unit in your answer.

explain.title: Thermocouple thermometers
explain.body: A thermocouple has two wires made of different materials joined to form two junctions. When the junctions are at different temperatures, a small current and potential difference are produced. A greater temperature difference produces a greater potential difference. Thermocouples are useful for very high temperatures and rapidly changing temperatures.

mistakes: Do not confuse the lower fixed point with the upper fixed point: the ice point is lower and the steam point is upper.
Do not use the Celsius-to-Fahrenheit formula when converting Fahrenheit to Celsius; use T_c = 5/9 (T_f − 32).
Do not forget the +273 when converting Celsius to Kelvin, or the temperature unit in the final answer.
Do not say that touch measures exact temperature; it only gives an idea of hotness or coldness.
Do not describe the liquid level as the temperature without explaining that the position of the end of the thread is read against the scale.
For thermometer-length problems, do not treat the length above the lower mark as the full fixed-point interval.

recap.question: Which way does thermal energy flow when two bodies have different temperatures?
recap.answer: Thermal energy flows from the body at higher temperature to the body at lower temperature.

recap.answer: The degree of hotness or coldness

explain.title: Sensitivity
explain.body: Sensitivity of a thermometer refers to its ability to detect small changes in the temperature of an object. For example, a thermometer marked every 0.1°C is more sensitive than one marked every 1°C.

explain.title: Range
explain.body: This refers to the span of temperature, from low to high, over which the thermometer can measure accurately. A clinical thermometer has a short range, about 35°C to 45°C, while a laboratory thermometer may have a longer range.

explain.title: The liquid affects range
explain.body: The choice of liquid for thermometers puts a lower and upper limit for the range of a thermometer. Mercury freezes at −39°C and boils at 357°C; alcohol freezes at about −112°C and boils at 78°C.

explain.title: Linearity
explain.body: This refers to a direct proportional relationship between the temperature and scale reading across entire range of measurement. A good linear thermometer has evenly spaced markings, so equal scale increments correspond to equal temperature changes.

mistakes: Do not confuse sensitivity with range: sensitivity is about detecting small changes, while range is the span of temperatures measured.
Do not define linearity only as having evenly spaced marks; explain that equal temperature changes correspond to equal scale changes.
Do not say that a narrow range makes a thermometer more sensitive; these are different properties.
When comparing scale divisions, remember that smaller divisions indicate greater sensitivity.
Give the correct example for each property: small divisions for sensitivity, low-to-high temperature span for range, and equal increments for linearity.

explain.title: Particles in the three states
explain.body: Matter is made of particles. In a solid, particles are closely packed and vibrate about mean positions. In a liquid, particles remain close but can move past one another. In a gas, particles are far apart and move freely in random directions.

explain.title: Temperature and heat
explain.body: Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body. Heat is energy in transit from a body at higher temperature to one at lower temperature. A body contains internal energy, not heat.

explain.title: Thermometers and their properties
explain.body: A thermometer uses a thermometric property that changes with temperature. Sensitivity describes the change in reading for a temperature change; range is the interval it can measure; linearity means equal temperature changes give equal scale changes.

explain.title: Temperature scales
explain.body: The Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin scales use different fixed-point readings. For ice and steam points they are 0°C and 100°C, 32°F and 212°F, and approximately 273 K and 373 K. Kelvin starts at absolute zero.

explain.title: Liquid-in-glass thermometers

solutions.question: Why solids have a fixed volume and shape according to particle theory of matter?
steps: The molecules of a solid are closely packed and have strong forces of attraction between them.
They vibrate about their fixed positions and cannot move freely from place to place.
Therefore, a solid has a fixed shape and a fixed volume.
solutions.answer: Closely packed molecules vibrate about fixed positions, so a solid has a fixed shape and volume.

solutions.question: What are the reasons that gases have neither a fixed volume nor a fixed shape?
steps: The molecules of a gas are far apart and the forces of attraction between them are very weak.
They move freely and randomly in all directions.
Therefore, gas molecules spread out to fill their container and gases have neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume.
solutions.answer: Gas molecules move freely and spread out to fill their container, so a gas has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume.

solutions.question: Compare the spacing of molecules in the solid, liquid and gaseous state.
steps: In a solid, molecules are very closely packed together.
In a liquid, molecules are less closely packed than in a solid, but remain close to one another.
In a gas, molecules are very far apart.
solutions.answer: Molecules are closest in solids, farther apart in liquids, and very far apart in gases.

solutions.question: What is the effect of raising the temperature of a liquid?
steps: When the temperature of a liquid is raised, its molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster.
The increased motion causes the liquid to expand.
solutions.answer: Raising a liquid’s temperature makes its molecules move faster and causes the liquid to expand.

solutions.question: What is meant by temperature of a body?
steps: The temperature of a body is the measure of its degree of hotness or coldness.
solutions.answer: Temperature is the measure of the degree of hotness or coldness of a body.

solutions.question: Define heat as ‘energy in transit’.
steps: Heat is energy in transit from a body at a higher temperature to a body at a lower temperature because of the temperature difference between them.
solutions.answer: Heat is energy transferred from a hotter body to a colder body due to a temperature difference.

solutions.question: What is meant by thermometric property of a substance? Enlist some thermometric properties.
steps: A thermometric property is a property of a substance that changes with temperature and can be used to measure temperature.
Examples include the volume of a liquid, the pressure of a gas at constant volume, the electrical resistance of a conductor, and the electromotive force of a thermocouple.
solutions.answer: A thermometric property changes with temperature and is used to measure it; examples include liquid volume, gas pressure, electrical resistance, and thermocouple emf.

solutions.question: State the main scales used for the measurement of temperature.
steps: The main temperature scales are the Celsius scale, the Fahrenheit scale and the Kelvin scale.
solutions.answer: Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin are the main scales used to measure temperature.

solutions.question: What is meant by sensitivity of a thermometer?
steps: The sensitivity of a thermometer is its ability to detect small changes in temperature.
A thermometer is more sensitive when a small change in temperature produces a large change in its thermometric property.
solutions.answer: Sensitivity is the ability of a thermometer to detect small changes in temperature.

solutions.question: What do you mean by the linearity of a thermometer?
steps: The linearity of a thermometer is the property by which equal changes in temperature produce equal changes in its thermometric property.
solutions.answer: Linearity means equal temperature changes produce equal changes in the thermometer’s thermometric property.

solutions.question: What makes the scale reading of a thermometer accurate?
steps: A thermometer should be read with the eye level with the top of the liquid column.
This avoids parallax error and makes the scale reading accurate.
solutions.answer: Read the thermometer at eye level with the top of the liquid column to avoid parallax error.

solutions.question: What does determine the direction of heat flow?
steps: The temperature difference between two bodies determines the direction of heat flow.
Heat flows from the body at higher temperature to the body at lower temperature.
solutions.answer: Heat flows from a higher-temperature body to a lower-temperature body.

solutions.question: Distinguish between the heat and internal energy.
steps: Heat is energy transferred from one body to another because of a temperature difference.
Internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of the molecules of a body.
Heat is energy in transit, whereas internal energy is the energy possessed by a body.
solutions.answer: Heat is energy transferred due to a temperature difference; internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of a body’s molecules.

solutions.question: When you touch a cold surface, does cold travel from the surface to your hand or does energy travel from your hand to cold surface?
steps: Cold does not travel from the surface to your hand.
Energy flows from your warmer hand to the colder surface.
solutions.answer: Energy travels from your hand to the cold surface; cold does not travel.

solutions.question: Can you feel your fever by touching your own forehead? Explain.
steps: No. Touching your own forehead does not reliably tell you whether you have a fever.
The sensation of warmth depends on the temperature difference between your hand and forehead, so a thermometer is needed to measure your temperature accurately.
solutions.answer: No. Touch alone cannot reliably detect a fever; use a thermometer to measure temperature.

solutions.question: Is kinetic molecular theory of matter applicable to the plasma state of matter? Describe briefly.
steps: Yes. Plasma consists of charged particles moving randomly at high speeds, so the kinetic molecular theory can be applied to it.
However, plasma differs from an ordinary gas because it contains ions and free electrons.
solutions.answer: The kinetic molecular theory applies to plasma, which is an ionised state of matter.

solutions.question: Why is mercury usually preferred to alcohol as a thermometric liquid?
steps: Mercury remains liquid over a wide range of temperatures because it has a low freezing point and a high boiling point.
It expands uniformly with temperature.
It does not wet the glass, and its shiny surface is easy to see in a glass tube.
solutions.answer: Mercury is preferred because it expands uniformly, is easy to see, does not wet glass, and works over a wide temperature range.

solutions.question: Why is water not suitable for use in thermometers? Without calculations, guess what is equivalent temperature of 373 K on Celsius and Fahrenheit scales?
steps: Water is not suitable for thermometers because it expands irregularly, especially between 0°C and 4°C.
It wets the glass and is difficult to see in a narrow tube.
373 K is approximately 100°C, which is approximately 212°F.
solutions.answer: Water expands irregularly and wets glass; 373 K is about 100°C or 212°F.

solutions.question: Mention two ways in which the design of a liquid-in-glass thermometer may be altered to increase its sensitivity.
steps: Use a larger bulb so that a small temperature change produces a greater expansion of the liquid.
Use a narrower capillary tube so that the expanded liquid rises farther for the same temperature change.
solutions.answer: A larger bulb and a narrower capillary tube increase the thermometer’s sensitivity.

solutions.question: One litre of water is heated by a stove and its temperature rises by 2°C. If two litres of water is heated on the same stove for the same time, what will be then rise in temperature?
steps: For the same stove and heating time, approximately the same amount of heat is supplied.
Twice the mass of water requires twice as much heat for the same temperature rise.
Therefore, the temperature rise is halved: 2°C ÷ 2 = 1°C.
solutions.answer: The temperature rises by 1°C.

solutions.question: Why are there no negative numbers on the Kelvin scale?
steps: The Kelvin scale begins at absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature.
A temperature lower than absolute zero is not possible, so there are no negative numbers on the Kelvin scale.
solutions.answer: There are no negative Kelvin temperatures because the Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero.

solutions.question: Comment on the statement. "A thermometer measures its own temperature."
steps: The statement is correct: a thermometer measures its own temperature.
When it is placed in contact with an object, heat flows between them until they reach thermal equilibrium.
At thermal equilibrium, the thermometer and the object have the same temperature; the thermometer’s reading is therefore the object’s temperature.
solutions.answer: A thermometer measures its own temperature, which equals the object’s temperature at thermal equilibrium.

solutions.question: There are various objects made of cotton, wood, plastic, metals, etc. In a winter night, compare their temperatures with the air temperature by touching them with your hand.
steps: After being in the same room for a long time, the objects and the surrounding air are at approximately the same temperature.
Metals feel colder than cotton, wood or plastic because metals conduct heat away from the hand more quickly.
Cotton, wood and plastic feel warmer because they are poor conductors of heat.
solutions.answer: The objects are approximately at the air temperature, but metals feel colder because they conduct heat away from the hand faster.

solutions.question: Which is greater; an increase in temperature 1°C or one 1°F?
steps: An increase in temperature of 1°C is greater than an increase of 1°F.
A change of 1°C is equal to a change of 1.8°F.
solutions.answer: An increase of 1°C is greater.

solutions.question: Why would not you expect all the molecules in a gas to have the same speed?
steps: The molecules of a gas are in continuous random motion.
They have different kinetic energies and therefore different speeds.
Molecules also collide with one another, continually changing their speeds.
solutions.answer: Gas molecules have different speeds because they have different kinetic energies and continually collide.

solutions.question: Does it make sense to talk about the temperature of a vacuum?
steps: Temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of the particles of a substance.
A vacuum has no particles, so it does not have a temperature in this sense.
solutions.answer: No; a vacuum has no particles whose average kinetic energy could define its temperature.

solutions.question: Comment on the statement: “A hot body does not contain heat”.
steps: The statement is correct because heat is energy transferred from one body to another due to a difference in temperature.
A body does not contain heat; it contains internal energy.
When a hot body transfers energy to a colder body, that transferred energy is called heat.
solutions.answer: A hot body contains internal energy; heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference.

solutions.question: Discuss whether the Sun is matter.
steps: The Sun is matter because it has mass and occupies space.
It consists of hot gases, mainly hydrogen and helium.
solutions.answer: Yes. The Sun is matter because it has mass, occupies space and consists mainly of gases.

solutions.question: Describe the main points of particle theory of matter which differentiate solids, liquids and gases.
steps: Matter consists of tiny particles which are in continuous motion.
In a solid, particles are very close together and the forces between them are strong.
Solid particles vibrate about fixed positions; a solid has a definite shape and volume.
In a liquid, particles are close together but the forces between them are weaker than in a solid.
Liquid particles can move past one another; a liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape.
In a gas, particles are far apart and the forces between them are very weak.
Gas particles move freely and rapidly in all directions; a gas has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume.
solutions.answer: Solids have closely packed particles vibrating in fixed positions, liquids have close particles that slide past one another, and gases have far-apart particles moving freely and rapidly.

solutions.question: What is temperature? How is it measured? Describe briefly the construction of a mercury-in-glass thermometer.
steps: Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body.
It is measured with a thermometer.
A mercury-in-glass thermometer consists of a glass bulb connected to a narrow glass capillary tube.
The bulb and part of the capillary contain mercury, and the other end of the tube is sealed.
The tube is marked with a temperature scale.
When the temperature changes, the mercury expands or contracts and its level moves in the capillary; the temperature is read from the scale.
solutions.answer: Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body and is measured with a thermometer. In a mercury-in-glass thermometer, mercury in a bulb and narrow capillary expands or contracts, and its level is read against a marked scale.

solutions.question: Compare the three scales used for measuring temperature.
steps: The three commonly used temperature scales are Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin.
On the Celsius scale, the ice point is 0°C and the steam point is 100°C; there are 100 equal divisions between them.
On the Fahrenheit scale, the ice point is 32°F and the steam point is 212°F; there are 180 equal divisions between them.
On the Kelvin scale, the ice point is 273 K and the steam point is 373 K; there are 100 equal divisions between them.
The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero; 0 K is equal to −273°C.
The relation between the scales is: C/5 = (F − 32)/9 = (K − 273)/5.
solutions.answer: Celsius and Kelvin have 100 divisions between the ice and steam points, while Fahrenheit has 180; their fixed points and relation are given above.

solutions.question: What is meant by sensitive, range and linearity of thermometers? Explain with examples.
steps: Sensitivity: The sensitivity of a thermometer is its ability to detect a small change in temperature. A thermometer is more sensitive if a small change in temperature produces a large change in the length of its liquid column.
Example: A narrow capillary tube makes a thermometer more sensitive because the liquid column rises farther for the same temperature change.
Range: The range of a thermometer is the difference between the highest and lowest temperatures it can measure.
Example: A clinical thermometer has a small range, about 35°C to 42°C, while a laboratory thermometer has a wider range.
Linearity: A thermometer is linear if equal changes in temperature produce equal changes in the thermometric property, such as the length of the liquid column.
Example: In a linear thermometer, the liquid column rises by equal lengths for equal temperature intervals.
solutions.answer: Sensitivity is the ability to detect small temperature changes; range is the span of measurable temperatures; linearity means equal temperature changes produce equal changes in the thermometric property.

solutions.question: Explain, how the parameters mentioned in question 7.4 are improved in the structure of liquid-in-glass thermometer.
steps: Sensitivity is increased by using a large bulb and a narrow capillary tube. A small temperature change then produces a large rise in the liquid column.
The range is increased by using a smaller bulb, a wider capillary tube and a longer tube, so that a greater volume of liquid can expand within the tube.
Linearity is improved by using a capillary tube of uniform bore and a thermometric liquid that expands uniformly with temperature.
solutions.answer: A large bulb and narrow capillary improve sensitivity; a smaller bulb, wider and longer tube improve range; a uniform capillary bore and uniformly expanding liquid improve linearity.

solutions.question: The temperature of a normal human body on Fahrenheit scale is 98.6°F. Convert it into Celsius scale and Kelvin scale.
steps: Given: Temperature on Fahrenheit scale, F = 98.6°F.
Required: Temperature on Celsius scale and Kelvin scale.
Substitution: C = (98.6 − 32) × 5/9 °C.
Result: The temperature is 37°C and 310 K.

solutions.question: At what temperature Celsius and Fahrenheit thermometer reading would be the same?
steps: Let the temperature at which both thermometers show the same reading be x.
Formula: F = (9/5)C + 32.
At the same reading, F = C = x.
Substitution: x = (9/5)x + 32.
Result: Both thermometers read −40°.

solutions.question: Convert 5°F to Celsius and Kelvin scale.
steps: Given: Temperature on Fahrenheit scale, F = 5°F.
Required: Temperature on Celsius scale and Kelvin scale.
Substitution: C = (5 − 32) × 5/9 °C.
Result: The temperature is −15°C and 258 K.

solutions.question: What is equivalent temperature of 25°C on Fahrenheit and Kelvin scales?
steps: Given: Temperature on Celsius scale, C = 25°C.
Required: Temperature on Fahrenheit scale and Kelvin scale.
Substitution: F = (9/5)(25) + 32 °F; K = 25 + 273 K.
Result: The temperature is 77°F and 298 K.

solutions.question: The ice and steam points on an ungraduated thermometer are found to be 192 mm apart. What temperature will be on Celsius scale if the length of mercury thread is at 67.2 mm above the ice point mark?
steps: Given: Distance between the ice point and steam point = 192 mm; length of mercury thread above the ice point = 67.2 mm.
Required: Temperature on the Celsius scale.
Formula: C/100 = length above ice point / distance between fixed points.
Substitution: C/100 = 67.2 mm / 192 mm.
Result: The temperature is 35°C.

solutions.question: The length between the fixed point of liquid-in-glass thermometer is 20 cm. If the mercury level is 4.5 cm above the lower mark, what is the temperature on the Fahrenheit scale?
steps: Given: Distance between the fixed points = 20 cm; mercury level above the lower mark = 4.5 cm.
Required: Temperature on the Fahrenheit scale.
Formula: C/100 = length above lower fixed point / distance between fixed points; F = (9/5)C + 32.
Substitution: C/100 = 4.5 cm / 20 cm; F = (9/5)C + 32.
Result: The temperature is 72.5°F.

definitions.text: According to this theory, matter is composed of very small particles called molecules which are always in motion.
The plasma is a gas in which most of the atoms are ionized containing positive ions and electrons (Fig. 7.3-a).
Temperature of a body is defined as degree of its hotness or coldness.

definitions.term: Temperature and direction of thermal energy flow
definitions.text: Temperature can be defined as a physical quantity which determines the direction of flow of thermal energy.
Heat is the energy which is transferred from one object to another due to difference of temperature between the two bodies.
The sum of kinetic and potential energies of the molecules of an object is called its internal energy.
For the exact measurement of the hotness of a substance, we require an instrument called a thermometer.
Thermometers use some property of a substance, which changes appreciably with the change of temperature.

One is the steam point slightly above the boiling of water at standard atmospheric pressure. This corresponds to upper fixed point of the scale. The second fixed point is the melting point of pure ice or simply ice point. It is called the lower fixed point.
Sensitivity of a thermometer refers to its ability to detect small changes in the temperature of an object.
This refers to the span of temperature, from low to high, over which the thermometer can measure accurately.
This refers to a direct proportional relationship between the temperature and scale reading across entire range of measurement.
Thermocouple thermometer is based on the flow of electric current between two junctions of two wires of different materials due to difference of temperatures at the junctions.

fullMarks: For a definition, write the complete sentence clearly; do not replace key terms such as “energy in transit” with informal wording.

When distinguishing heat from internal energy, state that heat is energy being transferred because of a temperature difference, while internal energy is the sum of molecular kinetic and potential energies.
For thermometer questions, name the thermometric property being used and explain how it changes with temperature.

For temperature-scale comparisons, include the fixed-point readings: Celsius 0 and 100, Fahrenheit 32 and 212, and Kelvin 273 and 373. State that the steam point is the upper fixed point and the ice point is the lower fixed point.
For a conversion numerical, write the given temperature, choose the correct conversion formula, show substitution, and include the correct temperature unit in the final answer.
When converting between Celsius and Kelvin, use the chapter’s calculation value 273. Keep the scale units clear: °C, °F and K.

For questions about thermometers, explain the reason as well as the fact—for example, mercury is visible and has a wider useful range than alcohol because of its high boiling point and low freezing point.
mistakes: Mistake: Saying a body “contains heat.” Fix: Say it contains internal energy; heat is energy transferred from one object to another because of a temperature difference.
Mistake: Confusing temperature with the total internal energy of a body. Fix: Temperature describes hotness or coldness and is related to the average kinetic energy of its molecules.
Mistake: Using T_F = 9/5 × T_C + 32 when converting Fahrenheit to Celsius. Fix: Use T_C = 5/9 × (T_F − 32) for that direction.
Mistake: Writing the Kelvin unit as °K or adding 273 to Fahrenheit. Fix: Write K without a degree sign, and convert Fahrenheit to Celsius first if needed.
Mistake: Giving only one reason why mercury is preferred to alcohol. Fix: Include useful points such as mercury’s visibility, high boiling point and low freezing point.

Mistake: Listing Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin without their fixed-point readings in a comparison answer. Fix: Add each scale’s ice-point and steam-point values and the number of divisions between them.

shortTheory.question: What is meant by temperature of a body?
shortTheory.answer: Temperature of a body is defined as degree of its hotness or coldness.

shortTheory.question: What determines the direction of heat flow?
shortTheory.answer: Temperature can be defined as a physical quantity which determines the direction of flow of thermal energy.

shortTheory.question: What is meant by thermometric property? Enlist some thermometric properties.
shortTheory.answer: Thermometers use some property of a substance, which changes appreciably with the change of temperature. Some basic thermometric properties for a material suitable to construct a thermometer are the following: it is a good conductor of heat; it gives quick response to temperature changes; it has uniform thermal expansion; it has high boiling point; it has low freezing point; it has large expansivity (low specific heat capacity); it does not wet glass; it does not vapourize; it is visible.

shortTheory.question: State the main scales used for the measurement of temperature.
shortTheory.answer: Three different scales are: (i) Celsius or centigrade scale (ii) Fahrenheit scale (iii) Kelvin scale

shortTheory.question: Distinguish between heat and internal energy.
shortTheory.answer: The sum of kinetic and potential energies of the molecules of an object is called its internal energy. Heat is the energy which is transferred from one object to another due to difference of temperature between the two bodies.

shortTheory.question: What is the effect of raising the temperature of a liquid?
shortTheory.answer: When a substance is heated, its temperature rises and its molecular motion becomes more vigorous which increases the kinetic energy of the molecules.

modelAnswer: Bring the object close to a known magnet.
If the object repels the magnet, the object is a magnet.
If the object is attracted but does not repel, it is a magnetic material, not a magnet.

writtenQuestions.text: How can you identify whether an object is a magnet or a magnetic material?
modelAnswer: Bring one end of the object close to any pole of a suspended bar magnet.
If it is attracted, it may be the opposite pole of a magnet or a magnetic material.
Bring the same end of the object close to the other pole of the suspended magnet.
If it is attracted again, the object is a magnetic material, not a magnet.
If it is repelled by the other end, the object is a magnet.
Repulsion between like poles is the real test for identifying a magnet.

explain.title: A suspended magnet points north–south
explain.body: If a bar magnet is suspended horizontally through a string and allowed to come to rest, it will point in north-south direction. The end of the magnet that points north is called the north magnetic pole (N) and the end that points south is the south magnetic pole (S).

explain.title: How poles interact
explain.body: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Two north poles repel; two south poles repel; a north pole and a south pole attract.

explain.title: How to identify a magnet
explain.body: If the same end of an unknown object is attracted by both ends of a suspended magnet, it is a magnetic material. If it is repelled by the other end, it is a magnet. The repulsion between the like poles is a real test to identify a magnet.

explain.title: A magnet always has two poles
explain.body: Breaking a bar magnet does not give separate north and south poles. Each piece will have its two poles, i.e., N-pole and S-pole. Even if a magnet is divided into thousands pieces, each piece will be a complete magnet with its N, and S-poles.

explain.title: Temporary magnets

explain.title: What is an electromagnet?
explain.body: An iron nail or a rod becomes a magnet when an electric current passes through a coil of wire around it. It is called an electromagnet. The current in the coil produces a magnetic field that magnetizes the iron.

explain.title: An electromagnet is temporary
explain.body: The iron object remains a magnet as long as electric current passes through the coil. When the current is stopped, it no longer remains a magnet.

explain.title: How to make it stronger

explain.title: Devices that use electromagnets
explain.body: A magnetic relay uses a low-current input circuit to activate a high-current circuit. A circuit breaker switches off a circuit if current becomes excessive. explain.title: Cranes and maglev trains

writtenQuestions.text: Differentiate between paramagnetic and diamagnetic materials.
modelAnswer: In paramagnetic materials, the orbital and spin axes of the electrons are so oriented that their fields support one another, and the atom behaves like a tiny magnet.

writtenQuestions.text: Differentiate between paramagnetic, diamagnetic and ferromagnetic materials with reference to the domain theory.
modelAnswer: In paramagnetic materials, the orbital and spin fields support one another, so each atom has a resultant magnetic field and behaves like a tiny magnet.
Examples are aluminium and lithium.
In diamagnetic materials, the orbital and spin fields add up to zero, so each atom has no resultant field.
Examples are copper, bismuth and water.
In ferromagnetic materials, electron spins in large groups of neighbouring atoms are naturally aligned parallel to each other.
These groups form highly magnetized domains, each of which behaves as a small magnet with its own north and south poles.

explain.title: Electrons can produce magnetism
explain.body: An electron revolves about the nucleus and also spins about an axis through it. Both motions give rise to a magnetic field. If the fields do not cancel, the atom behaves like a tiny magnet called a magnetic dipole.

explain.title: Paramagnetic and diamagnetic materials
explain.body: In paramagnetic materials, electron fields support one another, so atoms behave like tiny magnets; aluminium and lithium are examples. In diamagnetic materials, orbital and spin fields add up to zero; copper, bismuth and water are examples.

explain.title: Ferromagnetic materials contain domains
explain.body: Large groups of neighbouring atoms in ferromagnetic materials have electron spins naturally aligned parallel. Each domain is a highly magnetized region of about 0.1 mm size and acts as a small magnet with its own north and south poles.

explain.title: Alignment magnetizes iron
explain.body: Domains in unmagnetized iron point randomly, so their fields cancel. An external field makes suitably oriented domains grow and causes other domains to rotate towards the field. The iron then acts like a magnet.

explain.title: Soft iron and steel behave differently
explain.body: Soft-iron domains are easily oriented and return to random positions when the field is removed, which is useful in electromagnets and transformers. Steel is harder to align but retains its alignment, so it is used for permanent magnets.

mistakes: Do not say that a domain is a single electron; it is a region containing a large group of atoms.
Do not confuse a magnetic dipole (an atom with a resultant magnetic field) with a magnetic domain (a highly magnetized region in a ferromagnetic material).
Do not say that domains in unmagnetized iron are absent; they are present but randomly oriented.
Do not swap the behaviours of soft iron and steel: soft iron readily loses alignment, while steel retains it.
Do not describe diamagnetic atoms as having a resultant magnetic field; their orbital and spin fields add up to zero.

explain.title: Single-touch stroking
explain.body: A steel bar is stroked several times from one end to the other in the same direction using the same pole of a permanent magnet. Lift the magnet sufficiently high after each stroke.

explain.title: Double-touch stroking
explain.body: Stroke outwards from the centre of the steel bar using the unlike poles of two permanent magnets at the same time. This method is more efficient than single-touch.

explain.title: Magnetising with a solenoid
explain.body: Place the steel bar inside a solenoid with several hundred turns of insulated copper wire. Passing direct current through the solenoid makes the bar a magnet. Use the right-hand grip rule to find its polarity.

explain.title: Demagnetising a magnet
explain.body: Strong heating or hammering disturbs the order or alignment of the domains. A magnet can also be demagnetised by slowly moving it out from inside a solenoid carrying alternating current.

mistakes: Do not mix up the currents: direct current in a solenoid magnetises the steel bar; alternating current is used to demagnetise a magnet as it is slowly withdrawn.
Do not forget to lift the magnet at the end of each single-touch stroke before returning it to the start.
In double-touch stroking, use unlike poles and stroke outwards from the centre.
Do not assign the same polarity to an end as the stroking pole; the produced pole is opposite to the stroking pole.

steps.text: The curved part of the magnetic field called as fringe field penetrates magnetic coating on the moving tape and induces magnetism in the coating.

steps.why: This is how the tape keeps the recorded information after it moves away from the head.
steps.text: This induced magnetism is retained when the tape leaves the vicinity of the recording head.

example.question: Describe how a varying sound or picture signal is recorded on a magnetic tape.
example.answer: Varying currents make the recording head an electromagnet. Its fringe field penetrates the moving tape’s magnetic coating and induces magnetism, which the tape retains after leaving the head.

explain.title: What magnetic recording does
explain.body: Your textbook says, “Electromagnets have widely used in recording technology of sound, video and data in the form of electrical signals through magnetization of a magnetic material.” In simple terms, electrical signals create changing magnetism in a material so the information can be stored.

explain.title: How tape recording works
explain.body: “Induced magnetism is used in the process of magnetic tape recording.” The recording head is a coil of wire wrapped around an iron core. Varying currents make it an electromagnet, and its fringe field magnetises the coating on the moving tape.

explain.title: How information stays on tape
explain.body: “This induced magnetism is retained when the tape leaves the vicinity of the recording head.” During playback, the reverse process changes the varying induced magnetism into varying current, which is converted into sound or picture.

explain.title: How a hard disk records data
explain.body: A hard disk is a circular flat plate coated on both sides with iron oxide. Its small magnetic head writes a binary digit (1 or 0) by magnetising tiny spots in different directions, and reads the digit by detecting the direction of magnetisation.

explain.title: Why disks are useful
explain.body: A disk unit can read or write a recording instantly. Locating desired information on tape may take many minutes.

explain.title: Protecting electronic devices
explain.body: Your textbook says electronic devices can be protected from strong magnetic effects by enclosing them in boxes made of soft iron.

mistakes: Do not say the whole recording head is a permanent magnet; it becomes an electromagnet when varying current passes through its coil.
Do not confuse the fringe field with the magnetic coating: the fringe field penetrates the coating.
Do not say the tape loses its magnetism as soon as it leaves the head; it retains the induced magnetism.
For a hard disk, do not say the head writes digits by cutting grooves; it magnetises tiny spots in different directions.
Do not mix up the tape’s plastic backing with its magnetic coating; the coating records the information.

example.question: Explain how a soft iron casing shields a sensitive magnetic device from an external magnetic field.
example.answer: The soft iron casing has higher permeability than air, so magnetic flux is established in the casing rather than in the device. Thus, the device is shielded from the external magnetic field.

explain.title: What permeability means
explain.body: Permeability is the ability of a material to allow the magnetic flux or lines of force through it when the material is placed inside a magnetic field.

explain.title: How soft iron shields a device
explain.body: Soft iron has higher magnetic permeability than air. When a sensitive magnetic device is enclosed in a soft iron casing, magnetic flux is established in the soft iron rather than the device. The device is therefore shielded from the external magnetic field.

explain.title: Why casing corners are rounded
explain.body: Soft iron casings are usually made with rounded corners to facilitate the magnetic field lines lining up easily.

explain.title: Other uses of soft iron
explain.body: Soft iron is used in transformer and electromagnet cores because of its high permeability. An electromagnet's soft iron core is easily magnetised when current is passed around it and quickly loses its magnetism when current stops. A soft iron core also increases the sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer.

mistakes: Do not say soft iron completely destroys or blocks the external magnetic field; explain that flux is established in the casing rather than the device.
Do not confuse high permeability with permanent magnetism; soft iron can be magnetised easily and quickly lose its magnetism when current stops.
Do not say a soft iron casing shields a device because it is an insulator; its relevant property is high magnetic permeability.
When explaining an electromagnet core, include what happens both when current is switched on and when it is stopped.
