You must have seen the iron filings following the movement of the magnet. Magnetic force accounts for these movements. This activity also shows that magnets can attract objects containing iron, etc. even if they are not in direct contact with them.
procedure: Scatter some iron filings on top of a card paper, a sheet of glass, or a plastic sheet.
Move a magnet beneath the sheet.
Observe the movement of the iron filings and describe what happens.
practicals.aim: To observe the effect of a magnet on iron filings through a sheet.

viva.question: What happens to the iron filings when the magnet is moved beneath the sheet?
viva.answer: The filings are attracted and follow the movement of the magnet.

viva.question: Why do the iron filings move?
viva.answer: The magnet exerts a magnetic force on them.

viva.question: Do the magnet and iron filings need to touch for attraction to occur?
viva.answer: No, magnetic force can act without direct contact.

viva.question: What material in the filings is attracted by the magnet?
viva.answer: Iron.

apparatus: Card paper, a sheet of glass, or a plastic sheet
practicals.diagram: Draw iron filings scattered on a sheet in one sketch and gathered above a magnet held beneath the sheet in another; label the iron filings, sheet, magnet, and direction of magnet movement.
practicals.title: Attraction of Iron Filings by a Magnet
precautions: Keep the magnet beneath the sheet and do not let it touch the iron filings.
Move the magnet slowly so the filings can be observed clearly.
Keep iron filings away from the eyes and avoid inhaling them.
Collect the iron filings carefully after the activity.
practicals.result: The iron filings are attracted to the magnet and follow its movement, even though the magnet is not in direct contact with them.

practicals.label: Activity 8.3
practicals.bookText:
The teacher should facilitate each group to perform this activity as per instructions.
1. Take a magnetic compass. Put it on a table and see which end of its needle points north. The N-pole of the needle is usually coloured red.
2. Place a bar magnet on the table. Bring the compass near to its N-pole. In which direction does the N-pole of the needle stay?

3. Put the compass near to the S-pole of the bar magnet. In which direction does the N-pole of the needle stay this time?
4. Now place an iron nail having its head in contact with any pole of the bar magnet.

5. Put the compass near to the pointed end of an iron nail. Observe the direction in which N-pole of the needle settles. Has the nail become a magnet? Has magnetism been induced in it?
6. Take the bar magnet away from the nail. Again check the behaviour of the nail by bringing compass near to its ends. Does the magnetism vanish?
From the above activity, we conclude that the S-pole of the true magnet induces N-pole in the near end of the piece of iron (nail) while the far end of the iron piece becomes S-pole as shown in the figure.
It should be noted that the induced magnetism vanishes as the true magnet is removed.
procedure: Take a magnetic compass. Put it on a table and see which end of its needle points north. The N-pole of the needle is usually coloured red.
Place a bar magnet on the table. Bring the compass near to its N-pole. Observe the direction in which the N-pole of the needle stays.
Put the compass near to the S-pole of the bar magnet. Observe the direction in which the N-pole of the needle stays this time.
Place the head of an iron nail in contact with the S-pole of the bar magnet.

Put the compass near to the pointed end of the iron nail. Observe the direction in which the N-pole of the needle settles. Note whether the nail has become a magnet and whether magnetism has been induced in it.
Take the bar magnet away from the nail. Again check the behaviour of the nail by bringing the compass near to its ends. Observe whether the magnetism vanishes.
practicals.aim: To observe the direction of a compass needle near a bar magnet and demonstrate induced magnetism in an iron nail.

viva.question: Which end of a compass needle points north?
viva.answer: The N-pole of the needle.

viva.question: What happens to the compass N-pole near the bar magnet’s N-pole?
viva.answer: It points away from the magnet’s N-pole.

viva.question: What happens to the compass N-pole near the bar magnet’s S-pole?
viva.answer: It points towards the magnet’s S-pole.

viva.question: Which pole is induced at the nail’s head when it touches the magnet’s S-pole?
viva.answer: An N-pole is induced at the nail’s head.

viva.question: Which pole is induced at the nail’s pointed end?
viva.answer: An S-pole is induced at the pointed end.

viva.question: What happens to the nail’s induced magnetism when the bar magnet is removed?
viva.answer: It vanishes.

rows: Near nail’s pointed end while its head touches the magnet’s S-pole
Pointed end acts as an S-pole
Near the nail after removing the bar magnet
No clear attraction to either end

practicals.diagram: Draw two labelled sketches: a bar magnet with N and S poles and a compass near each pole, showing the compass N-pole pointing away from N and towards S; then draw the magnet’s S-pole touching the nail’s head, label the nail end at the head N and its pointed end S, and show a nearby compass with its N-pole pointing towards the nail’s pointed end.
practicals.title: Induced magnetism in an iron nail
precautions: Keep the compass on a level table and allow its needle to settle before observing.
Keep the compass close to the magnet or nail, but do not let it touch them.
Ensure that the nail’s head remains in contact with the magnet’s S-pole during the observation.
Keep other magnets and magnetic objects away from the compass during the activity.
practicals.result: The S-pole of the bar magnet induces an N-pole at the nail’s head and an S-pole at its pointed end. The nail’s induced magnetism vanishes when the bar magnet is removed.

practicals.label: Activity 8.4
practicals.bookText:
The teacher should facilitate the groups to provide each a bar magnet, a stand with clamp, some small nails made of iron and also some nails of steel. He should further supervise them to perform the activity as per instructions.

1. Clamp the bar magnet horizontally on the stand.
2. Touch the head of an iron nail to anyone end of the magnet. It will be attracted and stick to the magnet. Touch another iron nail to the lower end of the first one, does it stick to it?
Yes, it will, because the upper nail has become a magnet itself. Go on hanging iron nail one by one to make a chain until no more nails stay attached to the chain.
3. Try to hang steel nails at the other end of the bar magnet to form a similar chain.
4. Remove the chain of iron nails by pulling the topmost nail. Does the chain collapse?
5. Remove the chain of steel nails in the same way. Does this collapse?
You will observe that the chain of iron nails immediately collapses but the steel nails remain attached to each other for some time. This shows that the magnetism induced in the iron nails is temporary while that in the steel nails is permanent.
procedure: Clamp the bar magnet horizontally on the stand.
Touch the head of an iron nail to one end of the magnet. Touch another iron nail to the lower end of the first one and observe whether it sticks.
Go on hanging iron nails one by one to make a chain until no more nails stay attached to the chain.
Try to hang steel nails at the other end of the bar magnet to form a similar chain.
Remove the chain of iron nails by pulling the topmost nail. Observe whether the chain collapses.
Remove the chain of steel nails in the same way. Observe whether it collapses.
practicals.aim: To compare the temporary magnetism induced in iron nails with the permanent magnetism induced in steel nails.

viva.question: What happens when an iron nail touches a bar magnet?
viva.answer: It is attracted and becomes temporarily magnetised.

viva.question: Why can one iron nail hold another?
viva.answer: The first nail becomes a temporary magnet by induction.

viva.question: What happens to the chain of iron nails when the top nail is removed?
viva.answer: The chain immediately collapses.

viva.question: What happens to the chain of steel nails when the top nail is removed?
viva.answer: The nails remain attached to each other for some time.

viva.question: Which material shows temporary induced magnetism in this activity?
viva.answer: Iron.

viva.question: Which material retains magnetism for longer?
viva.answer: Steel.

rows: Nails remain attached for some time

practicals.diagram: Draw a bar magnet clamped horizontally on a stand, labelled S at the left end and N at the right end, with chains of nails hanging from both ends; label the bar magnet, stand, clamp, iron-nail chain, and steel-nail chain.
practicals.title: Temporary and permanent magnetism in nails
precautions: Clamp the bar magnet firmly in a horizontal position.
Touch each nail gently to the magnet and avoid disturbing the stand.
Use separate chains for iron and steel nails.
Pull the topmost nail carefully when removing each chain.
practicals.result: The iron-nail chain collapses immediately, showing that the induced magnetism in iron is temporary. The steel nails remain attached for some time, showing that steel retains induced magnetism longer.

practicals.label: Activity 8.5
practicals.bookText:
The teacher should divide the students into groups and facilitate them to perform this activity.
Take a battery of two cells, a switch, an iron nail, cotton (or plastic) covered copper wire, thread and a few paper clips.
Wind the wire over the iron nail to form a coil. Suspend the coil by means of thread tied to its centre. Connect ends of the wire to the battery through the switch as shown in the figure.

Keeping the switch OFF, bring some paper clips near to one end of the nail. Do they stick to the nail? Now turn the switch ON and again bring the paper clips near to the end of the nail. Do they stick this time? Does the nail behave like a magnet? Yes, the nail has become a magnet. Turn the switch OFF and see what happens to the clips. Do they fall down? What do you conclude from this activity?
An iron nail or a rod becomes a magnet when an electric current passes through a coil of wire around it. It is called an electromagnet.
When an electric current passes through the coil of wire, magnetic field is produced inside the coil that magnetizes the iron nail. As we have observed that the magnetic properties of an electromagnet are temporary, therefore, iron object remains a magnet as long as the electric current passes through the coil. When the current is stopped, it no longer remains a magnet.
If we increase the number of cells in the battery or increase the number of turns of the coil, we will observe that the strength of the magnetic field in each case increases. This will be indicated by the more number of clips held by the nail in these cases.
procedure: Wind the wire over the iron nail to form a coil.
Suspend the coil by means of thread tied to its centre.
Connect the ends of the wire to the battery through the switch.
Keeping the switch OFF, bring some paper clips near to one end of the nail and observe whether they stick to the nail.
Turn the switch ON and again bring the paper clips near to the end of the nail. Observe whether they stick.
Turn the switch OFF and observe what happens to the clips.
practicals.aim: To show that an iron nail becomes a temporary magnet when electric current passes through a coil wound around it.

viva.question: What is an electromagnet?
viva.answer: A magnet produced when electric current passes through a coil of wire around an iron object.

viva.question: What happens to the iron nail when the switch is turned ON?
viva.answer: It becomes magnetized and can attract paper clips.

viva.question: What happens to the nail’s magnetism when the switch is turned OFF?
viva.answer: The nail no longer remains a magnet, so the clips fall.

viva.question: What is the role of the iron nail?
viva.answer: It acts as the iron core that becomes magnetized by the coil’s magnetic field.

viva.question: How can the strength of the electromagnet be increased?
viva.answer: By increasing the number of cells or the number of turns in the coil.

practicals.diagram: Draw a coil wound around an iron nail, suspended by a thread and connected through a switch to a battery, with paper clips near one end of the nail; label Thread, Coil, Iron Nail, Clips, Switch and Battery.
practicals.title: Making an electromagnet
precautions: Keep the switch OFF while setting up the circuit.
Ensure the wire is wound securely around the nail.
Make firm connections between the wire, switch and battery.
Turn the switch OFF when observations are complete to avoid unnecessary heating of the wire.
practicals.result: The iron nail attracts paper clips when current passes through the coil, showing that it becomes a temporary magnet. When the current is stopped, it no longer remains a magnet.

notes.title: Physical and Non-Physical Quantities
notes.answer: A physical quantity can be measured; a non-physical quantity cannot be measured with tools and instruments.
notes.explanation: A physical quantity can be measured with tools or instruments. A non-physical quantity cannot be measured with tools and instruments; it may be described or compared using agreed criteria or surveys.
notes.simple: If you can measure it with an instrument and give its result as a number with a unit, it is a physical quantity. If you cannot, it is non-physical.
examples: Length is a physical quantity because it can be measured with a ruler.
Fear is a non-physical quantity because it cannot be measured with a measuring instrument.
steps: Ask whether the quantity can be measured with a tool or instrument.
If it can be measured, classify it as a physical quantity.
If it cannot be measured, classify it as a non-physical quantity.
For a physical measurement, state its numerical value and unit.
notes.checkQuestion: Does a non-physical quantity have dimensions?
notes.checkAnswer: No. A non-physical quantity cannot be measured with tools and instruments, so it has no measurable magnitude and unit.

notes.title: Base and Derived Quantities
notes.answer: Base quantities are chosen quantities used as a starting point. Derived quantities are described in terms of one or more base quantities. A measurement is a comparison with a standard and consists of a number and a unit.
notes.explanation: Base quantities are the chosen starting quantities. A derived quantity is described using one or more base quantities. Measurements compare an unknown quantity with a standard, and every measurement needs both a number and a unit.
notes.simple: Base quantities are the starting quantities. Derived quantities are made from them. A measurement needs a number and a unit.
examples: Distance and time are base quantities; speed depends on distance and time, so speed is derived.
Density is described in terms of mass and volume, so density is derived.
steps: Identify the quantity being described.
Check whether it is one of the chosen base quantities or is described using base quantities.
If it depends on one or more base quantities, call it a derived quantity.
For any measurement, include both the number and the unit.
notes.checkQuestion: Why is speed a derived quantity?
notes.checkAnswer: Speed is derived because it depends on distance and time, which are base quantities.

notes.title: SI units and prefixes
notes.answer: The SI unit of mass is the kilogram (kg).
notes.explanation: SI units give people around the world a common way to measure. Base units are the starting units; derived units are made from them. Prefixes show powers of ten, making very large or very small measurements easier to write.
notes.simple: Think of base units as the basic building blocks. Derived units combine those blocks, and prefixes tell you how many powers of ten a unit represents.
examples: Area = length × breadth = metre × metre = square metre = m².
steps: Name the physical quantity and identify its unit.
For a derived unit, write how the quantity is made from other quantities.
Replace each quantity with its SI base unit.
For a prefix, replace it with its power of ten and convert.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the SI unit and symbol for mass?
notes.checkAnswer: The unit of area is the square metre, m².

notes.title: Writing numbers in scientific notation
notes.answer: A number written as a number from 1 to 9 multiplied by a power of 10.
notes.explanation: Scientific notation writes a number as a value from 1 to 9 multiplied by a power of 10. The power shows how far, and in which direction, the decimal point moved.
notes.simple: Move the decimal point until one non-zero digit is left of it. Moving left gives a positive power; moving right gives a negative power.
steps: Move the decimal point until one non-zero digit remains on the left.
Count the places the decimal point moved.
Use that count as the exponent of 10: positive if the decimal moved left, negative if it moved right.
notes.checkQuestion: Write 0.00052 in scientific notation.

notes.title: Measuring length accurately
notes.answer: 0.1 mm
notes.explanation: To measure length accurately, choose an instrument with a suitable least count, line it up correctly with the object, and read the scale with your eye directly above it. For smaller objects, Vernier Callipers and a micrometer screw gauge give more precise readings than a metre rule.
notes.simple: Least count tells you the smallest length an instrument can measure accurately. Keep your eye straight above the scale so the reading does not look different.
examples: For the Vernier Callipers example: 4.3 cm + (0.01 cm × 4) = 4.34 cm.
For the screw gauge example: 6.5 mm + (25 × 0.01 mm) = 6.75 mm.
steps: Choose the instrument that suits the size of the object.
Place the object correctly and make sure the scale starts from the object's edge.
Read the scale with your eye directly above it to avoid parallax error.
For Vernier Callipers or a screw gauge, combine the main scale reading with the smaller scale reading multiplied by the least count.
Check for zero error and correct the observed reading as required.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the least count of the Vernier Callipers described in this section?
notes.checkAnswer: The least count is the smallest measurement that can be taken accurately with an instrument.

notes.title: Measuring Mass with a Physical Balance
notes.answer: The total of the standard masses on the right pan gives the mass of the object on the left pan.
notes.explanation: A physical balance measures mass by comparing an object with known standard masses. Put the object on the left pan and standard masses on the right pan. When the pointer stays at zero or oscillates equally on both sides of zero, add the standard masses to find the object's mass.
notes.simple: A physical balance finds mass by balancing an object against known masses.
examples: If the balance is level when a 20 g mass and a 5 g mass are on the right pan, the object on the left pan has a mass of 25 g.
A spring balance measures weight, which is a force; a physical balance is used to compare masses.
steps: Level the base using the levelling screws until the plumb line is exactly above the pointed mark.
Raise the pans and make sure the beam is horizontal and the pointer is at the centre of the scale. Adjust the balancing screws if needed.
Place the object on the left pan.
Use forceps to place known masses from the weight box on the right pan.
Adjust the masses until the pointer stays on zero or oscillates equally on both sides of zero.
Add the standard masses on the right pan. Their total is the mass of the object.
notes.checkQuestion: When the pointer is balanced, how do you find the object's mass?
notes.checkAnswer: The total of the standard masses on the right pan is the mass of the object on the left pan.

notes.title: Measuring time with a stopwatch
notes.answer: A mechanical stopwatch measures an event's duration, and its least count is one tenth of a second.
notes.explanation: A stopwatch measures how long an event lasts. A mechanical stopwatch in this section has a least count of one tenth of a second. A digital stopwatch can measure one hundredth of a second.
notes.simple: Use a stopwatch to measure how long something takes. Its least count tells you the smallest time interval it can measure.
steps: Press the knob to start the stopwatch.
Press the same knob to stop it when the event ends.
Read the time shown by the needles.
Press the knob again to return the needles to zero.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the least count of the mechanical stopwatch described in this section?
notes.checkAnswer: One tenth of a second (0.1 s).

notes.title: Measuring the volume of liquids and solids
notes.answer: For water, read the volume at the bottom edge of the meniscus, with your eye level with it.
notes.explanation: To measure liquid volume, place the measuring cylinder on a horizontal surface and read the meniscus at eye level. For water, read the bottom edge of the meniscus. To find the volume of a solid that does not dissolve, compare the liquid reading before and after immersing it. If the solid is too large for the cylinder, use a displacement can and measure the overflow.
notes.simple: Read the water level straight on, at the bottom of its curved surface. A solid’s volume is the amount of water it displaces.
examples: If the water level rises from 20 mL to 32 mL after a solid is immersed, the solid’s volume is 32 mL − 20 mL = 12 mL.
If a solid does not fit in a measuring cylinder, collect the overflow from a displacement can and measure it with a measuring cylinder.
steps: Place the measuring cylinder on a horizontal surface.
Bring your eye level with the water meniscus.
Read the scale at the bottom edge of the water meniscus.
To find a solid’s volume, subtract the initial liquid reading from the reading after the solid is immersed.
If the solid does not fit in the cylinder, collect the overflow from a displacement can and measure it in a measuring cylinder.
notes.checkQuestion: When reading the volume of water in a measuring cylinder, which edge of the meniscus should you read?
notes.checkAnswer: Read the bottom edge of the water meniscus with your eye level with it.

notes.title: Errors in Measurements
notes.answer: The three types of experimental errors are human errors, systematic errors and random errors.
notes.explanation: Measurements can be affected by human, systematic and random errors. Human errors come from the person taking the measurement; systematic errors affect readings consistently; random errors make repeated readings differ unpredictably.
notes.simple: Errors are differences between measured values and the true values. We identify the type of error by asking what caused it and how it affects the readings.
examples: A balance that is not properly calibrated causes a systematic error.
Air current making a balance fluctuate causes a random error.
steps: Look for the cause of the error.
If it comes from the person reading or handling the instrument, identify it as human error.
If a definite cause affects readings consistently, identify it as systematic error.
If repeated readings vary unpredictably, identify it as random error.
notes.checkQuestion: A balance has not been properly calibrated. What type of error can it cause?
notes.checkAnswer: A systematic error.

notes.title: Uncertainty in a Measurement
notes.answer: For a metre rule with 0.1 cm smallest divisions, the maximum uncertainty is ±0.05 cm.
notes.explanation: Every measurement has some uncertainty, because an instrument cannot measure beyond the precision allowed by its smallest division. For an analogue scale, the maximum uncertainty is usually half the smallest division. Repeated readings and an average can reduce uncertainty.
notes.simple: A measurement is not perfectly exact. The instrument limits how certain the reading can be.
examples: A metre rule has a smallest division of 0.1 cm, so the maximum uncertainty is ±0.05 cm.
If a digital instrument's last digit fluctuates, that fluctuation shows uncertainty in the reading.
steps: Find the instrument's smallest division.
For the metre-rule example, divide 0.1 cm by 2.
State the maximum uncertainty as ±0.05 cm.
notes.checkQuestion: A scale has a smallest division of 0.1 cm. What is the maximum uncertainty?
notes.checkAnswer: The maximum uncertainty is ±0.05 cm.

notes.title: Counting Significant Figures
notes.answer: Significant figures are the reliably known digits in a measurement, including the first doubtful digit.
notes.explanation: Significant figures show which digits in a measurement are reliably known, including the first doubtful digit. Count all digits from 1 to 9. A zero between non-zero digits counts, a zero at the left does not, and a zero at the right of a decimal does. In scientific notation, count the digits before the exponent.
notes.simple: Significant figures are the measurement digits we can rely on, plus the first estimated digit. Count carefully: some zeros count and some do not.
examples: 5.06 m has 3 significant figures.
0.0034 m has 2 significant figures.
steps: Count all digits from 1 to 9.
Count a zero between two digits.
Do not count zeros on the left side of a measured value.
Count zeros on the right side of a decimal.
In scientific notation, count all digits before the exponent.
notes.checkQuestion: How many significant figures are there in 0.0034 m?
notes.checkAnswer: 2 significant figures

notes.title: Precision and Accuracy
notes.answer: They are precise, but not accurate.
notes.explanation: Precision tells us how close repeated measurements are to one another. Accuracy tells us how close a measured value is to the accepted or true value. A measurement can be precise without being accurate, accurate without being precise, both, or neither.
notes.simple: Precision is about measurements agreeing with each other. Accuracy is about a measurement agreeing with the true value.
examples: Arrows clustered together but away from the bullseye are precise, but not accurate.
A measurement of 2.00 cm is more precise than 2 cm because it is recorded to a smaller scale division; whether it is accurate depends on the true value.
steps: Compare repeated readings with one another to judge precision.
Compare the measured value with the accepted or true value to judge accuracy.
Remember: a smaller least count gives a more precise measurement.
A larger number of significant figures reflects higher accuracy.
notes.checkQuestion: A group of readings are very close to one another but all far from the true value. Are they precise, accurate, both, or neither?
notes.checkAnswer: Precision: repeated measurements are close together. Accuracy: a measurement is close to the accepted or true value.

notes.title: Rounding off to significant figures
notes.explanation: To round a number to a given number of significant figures, keep the required digits and use the next digit to decide whether to change the last kept digit. If the next digit is 5, use the rule in your textbook: an odd last kept digit goes up by one, while an even one stays the same.
notes.simple: Keep the digits you need. Look at the next digit to decide what happens to the last digit you keep.
examples: 3.4567 × 10⁴ kg rounded to 3 significant figures is 3.46 × 10⁴ kg.
4.45 × 10² m rounded to 2 significant figures is 4.4 × 10² m.
steps: Choose how many significant figures to keep.
Look at the first digit that will be left out.
If it is greater than 5, increase the last kept digit by 1; if it is less than 5, keep it unchanged.
If the digit is exactly 5, use the odd/even rule given in your textbook.
Write the rounded number with its original power of ten and unit.
notes.checkQuestion: Round off to 2 significant figures: 4.55 × 10² m.

notes.title: Measuring physical quantities
notes.answer: A measurement consists of a numerical value and a unit.
notes.explanation: Measurements use numbers and units. This chapter explains how to choose units and instruments, record readings carefully, use prefixes and scientific notation, and handle errors and significant digits.
notes.simple: A measurement tells how much of something there is. It needs a number and a unit.
examples: A desk height may be measured in metres (m).
A thickness may be measured with a micrometer screw gauge.
steps: Choose the quantity to measure.
Choose an appropriate instrument and unit.
Read the instrument carefully, avoiding viewing errors.
Record the number with its unit.
Use prefixes or scientific notation when useful.
notes.checkQuestion: Why do we need a standard unit for measurements?
notes.checkAnswer: A standard unit lets different people compare measurements consistently.

notes.title: Scalars, vectors and their representation
notes.answer: A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has magnitude and direction.
notes.explanation: Scalars are fully described by magnitude only. Vectors need both magnitude and direction. A vector can be shown by a straight line with an arrow: its length shows magnitude according to a scale, and the arrow shows direction.
notes.simple: A scalar tells you how much. A vector tells you how much and which way.
examples: 5 kg of mass is a scalar: the magnitude and unit describe it completely.
A velocity of 25 m s⁻¹ towards north is a vector: it has magnitude and direction.
steps: Identify whether the quantity needs direction as well as magnitude.
For a scalar, give its magnitude and unit.
For a vector, give its magnitude, unit and direction.
To draw a vector, choose a scale and draw a line with an arrow in the required direction.
notes.checkQuestion: What two things are needed to describe a vector completely?
notes.checkAnswer: A vector has magnitude and direction.

notes.title: Rest and motion depend on the observer
notes.answer: Rest or motion is decided by comparing an object's position with its surroundings.
notes.explanation: Rest and motion describe whether an object's position changes compared with its surroundings. The same object can be at rest compared with one observer and in motion compared with another.
notes.simple: Ask: “Is the object's position changing compared with this observer and these surroundings?” The answer may change when the observer changes.
examples: A parked motorcycle is at rest compared with a nearby tree.
A passenger sitting in a moving train is at rest compared with other passengers, but in motion compared with someone standing on the platform.
steps: Choose the object and the observer.
Compare the object's position with its surroundings.
If its position does not change, it is at rest with respect to those surroundings.
If its position continuously changes, it is in motion with respect to those surroundings.
notes.checkQuestion: A passenger is sitting in a moving train. Is the passenger at rest or in motion compared with someone standing on the platform?
notes.checkAnswer: The passenger is at rest with respect to the other passengers, but in motion with respect to the observer on the platform.

notes.title: Recognising types of motion
notes.answer: The three general types are translatory, rotatory, and vibratory motion.
notes.explanation: Motion is classified by how a body moves: it may move as a whole, turn around an axis, or move to and fro around a fixed position.
notes.simple: Look at the path or movement: straight, irregular, circular, turning around an axis, or to and fro.
steps: Notice how the body moves.
If every particle moves in the same direction, identify translatory motion and then check whether its path is straight, irregular, or circular.
If points of the body move around a fixed axis, identify rotatory motion.
If the body repeats a to-and-fro movement about a fixed position, identify vibratory motion.
notes.checkQuestion: What type of motion does an electric fan show?
notes.checkAnswer: A fan shows rotatory motion.

notes.title: Distance and Displacement
notes.answer: Distance is the length of actual path of the motion. Displacement is the shortest distance from the initial to the final position, with direction from the initial position to the final position.
notes.explanation: Distance tells how much actual path an object travels. Displacement tells how far and in what direction it is from its starting position to its final position.
notes.simple: Distance is the route taken. Displacement is the straight way from where you started to where you ended, including its direction.
examples: A car may travel 320 km along roads from Lahore to Multan; that is its distance travelled.
If the car’s starting and ending points are A and B, the straight, directed line from A to B represents its displacement.
steps: Identify the actual path travelled: its length is the distance.
Identify the initial and final positions.
Join these positions with a straight line and show its direction from initial to final: this is the displacement.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the difference between distance and displacement?
notes.checkAnswer: Distance is the length of the actual path; displacement is the shortest directed distance from the initial position to the final position.

notes.title: Speed and Velocity
notes.answer: Average speed is total distance divided by total time. Average velocity is displacement divided by time and has a direction.
notes.explanation: Speed tells how much distance is covered per unit time. Velocity also tells the direction of motion, so it depends on displacement rather than distance. For example, a car moving north at 70 km h⁻¹ has speed 70 km h⁻¹ and velocity 70 km h⁻¹ north.
notes.simple: Speed tells how fast something moves. Velocity tells how fast it moves and in which direction.
steps: For average speed, divide total distance by total time.
For average velocity, divide displacement by time.
Give the direction when stating velocity.
notes.checkQuestion: What extra information does velocity give that speed does not?
notes.checkAnswer: Direction

notes.title: Acceleration
notes.answer: 2 m s⁻²
notes.explanation: Acceleration tells us how quickly velocity changes. A change in velocity may be a change in speed, direction, or both.
notes.simple: Acceleration is how quickly velocity changes. If velocity gets smaller, acceleration is negative.
examples: A car speeds up from rest: its velocity increases, so it has positive acceleration.
A moving car brakes and slows down: its velocity decreases, so it has negative acceleration.
steps: Find the change in velocity: v_f − v_i.
Divide the change in velocity by the time taken: a_av = (v_f − v_i)/t.
Write the answer in m s⁻².
notes.checkQuestion: A body changes velocity from 4 m s⁻¹ to 10 m s⁻¹ in 3 s. What is its average acceleration?
notes.checkAnswer: Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken: a_av = (v_f − v_i)/t.

notes.title: Reading distance-time graphs
notes.answer: A distance-time graph shows the relation between distance S and time t taken by a moving body.
notes.explanation: A distance-time graph shows how distance changes with time. Its slope tells us the speed: a straight rising line means uniform speed, a curved line can show changing speed, and a horizontal line means the body is at rest.
notes.simple: Look at how the graph changes as you move to the right. If distance rises evenly, speed is uniform. If distance does not change, the body is not moving.
examples: If a car travels 1.2 km each minute, its distance-time graph is a straight rising line.
If distance stays at 1.2 km as time passes, the graph is horizontal and the car is at rest.
steps: Put time t on the x-axis and distance S on the y-axis.
Choose a suitable scale for each axis.
Plot each time-distance pair.
Join the plotted points and interpret the graph shape.
notes.checkQuestion: What does a horizontal distance-time graph show?
notes.checkAnswer: The body is at rest.

notes.title: Gradient of a Distance-Time Graph
notes.answer: The gradient of a distance-time graph is equal to the average speed of the body.
notes.explanation: The gradient of a distance-time graph tells you the average speed during a time interval. Find it by dividing the change in distance by the change in time.
notes.simple: Gradient tells you how much distance changes for each unit of time.
examples: If distance changes by 12 m in 3 s, gradient = 12/3 = 4 m s⁻¹.
A horizontal distance-time line has gradient 0, so the body is at rest.
steps: Find the change in distance: S₂ − S₁.
Find the change in time: t₂ − t₁.
Divide the change in distance by the change in time.
Write the result with suitable units.
notes.checkQuestion: A body covers 15 m in 3 s. What is the gradient of its distance-time graph?
notes.checkAnswer: Average speed is 5 m s⁻¹.

notes.title: Reading a speed-time graph
notes.answer: A speed-time graph is a graph between speed v and time t. A straight line rising upward shows uniform acceleration; a horizontal line shows constant speed.
notes.explanation: A speed-time graph shows how an object's speed changes with time. The shape of the line helps us describe the motion.
notes.simple: Look at the line: rising means speed is increasing; horizontal means speed is unchanged.
examples: A straight line rising from the origin shows speed increasing by the same amount in equal time intervals.
A horizontal line shows that speed stays the same as time passes.
steps: Put time t on the x-axis and speed v on the y-axis.
Mark the speed at each time.
Join the points and observe the shape of the line.
notes.checkQuestion: What kind of motion is shown by a straight line rising upward on a speed-time graph when speed increases equally every second?
notes.checkAnswer: A horizontal line parallel to the time axis represents constant speed.

notes.title: Gradient of a Speed-Time Graph
notes.answer: The gradient is 3 m s⁻².
notes.explanation: The gradient of a speed-time graph tells us the average acceleration. Find it by dividing the change in speed by the time taken.
notes.simple: A steeper speed-time graph means speed is changing more quickly. A flat graph means speed is not changing.
examples: If speed changes from 4 m s⁻¹ to 10 m s⁻¹ in 3 s, the gradient is (10 − 4)/3 = 2 m s⁻².
If speed stays constant, the speed-time graph is horizontal and its gradient is zero.
steps: Find the change in speed: 18 − 6 = 12 m s⁻¹.
Divide the change in speed by the time: 12/4 = 3 m s⁻².
State the gradient as 3 m s⁻².
notes.checkQuestion: A body's speed changes from 6 m s⁻¹ to 18 m s⁻¹ in 4 s. What is the gradient?
notes.checkAnswer: The average acceleration is 2 m s⁻².

notes.title: Finding Distance from a Speed-Time Graph
notes.answer: The area under a speed-time graph up to the time axis is numerically equal to the distance covered by the object.
notes.explanation: A speed-time graph shows how an object's speed changes with time. The area between the graph and the time axis gives the distance covered. For constant speed, this area is a rectangle; for speed increasing uniformly from zero, it is a triangle.
notes.simple: Think of the area under a speed-time graph as the distance travelled. Find the area of the shape below the graph and above the time axis.
examples: At a constant speed of 5 m/s for 4 s, the distance is the rectangular area: 5 × 4 = 20 m.
If speed increases uniformly from 0 to 6 m/s in 3 s, the distance is the triangular area: 1/2 × 6 × 3 = 9 m.
steps: Identify the shape under the speed-time graph.
Find its area using the correct formula.
The area is numerically equal to the distance covered.
notes.checkQuestion: An object moves at a constant speed of 4 m/s for 3 s. What distance does it cover?

notes.title: Solving problems for motion under gravity
notes.answer: Use the equations of motion with acceleration due to gravity and a consistent choice of signs.
notes.explanation: For motion under gravity, use the equations of motion with acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻², as used for the answers in your textbook. Choose positive and negative directions consistently, then substitute the known quantities.
notes.simple: Gravity changes an object's velocity as it falls or rises. Use the motion equations and give quantities the correct signs.
steps: Write down the known quantities and the quantity to find.
Choose a positive direction and assign signs to the other quantities.
Select the equation containing the known quantities and the unknown.
Substitute the values, calculate, and write the answer with its unit.
notes.checkQuestion: A stone is dropped from rest and falls for 3 s. Take g = 10 m s⁻². What is its final velocity?
notes.checkAnswer: t = 3 s; v_f = 30 m s⁻¹ downward.

notes.title: Using equations for free fall
notes.answer: For a freely falling object released from rest, vᵢ = 0 and g = +10 m s⁻² when downward is positive.
notes.explanation: For free fall, use the equations of motion with acceleration replaced by g. Take g = 10 m s⁻² downward as positive. If an object is thrown upward, take g = −10 m s⁻².
notes.simple: A freely falling object speeds up because Earth’s gravity pulls it downward. Use g = 10 m s⁻², and choose signs to match the direction of motion.
examples: A body dropped from rest for 3 s falls 45 m: S = 0 × 3 + ½ × 10 × 3² = 45 m.
An arrow thrown upward at 30 m s⁻¹ takes 3 s to reach its highest point: 0 = 30 − 10t, so t = 3 s.
steps: Write down the known values, including the direction of motion.
Use vᵢ = 0 if the object is released from rest.
Take g as positive downward; for an object thrown upward, take g as negative.
Choose the equation of motion that contains the unknown you need.
Substitute the values and give the answer with its unit.
notes.checkQuestion: A stone is dropped from rest. What is its initial velocity, and which way is g positive?
notes.checkAnswer: For a body dropped from rest, vᵢ = 0 and g = 10 m s⁻² downward.

notes.title: Describing motion
notes.answer: Kinematics describes motion using distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration.
notes.explanation: Kinematics describes motion and how position, speed, velocity and acceleration change with time. Graphs and equations of motion help us describe and calculate these changes.
notes.simple: Kinematics is the study of motion. It tells us how far and in which direction something moves, how fast it moves, and how its motion changes.
examples: A car travelling at constant speed in a straight line has constant velocity.
A ball thrown vertically upward has zero velocity for an instant at its highest point, but its acceleration is still downward.
steps: Choose a positive direction and keep it consistent.
Use distance for the total path covered and displacement for the change in position.
Use speed or velocity to describe how quickly position changes.
Use acceleration to describe how quickly velocity changes.
For calculations, choose an equation of motion that includes the known quantities and the quantity required.
notes.checkQuestion: What does the gradient of a speed–time graph represent?
notes.checkAnswer: Speed is the gradient of a distance–time graph; acceleration is the gradient of a speed–time graph.

notes.title: Understanding force
notes.answer: A force is a push or pull that can start, stop or change an object's motion.
notes.explanation: A force is a push or pull. It can change how an object moves, and forces are either contact or non-contact forces.
notes.simple: A force is a push or pull that can change an object's motion. Some forces need objects to touch; others act from a distance.
examples: A hand pushing a door applies a contact force.
Earth attracts a falling apple by a non-contact force.
steps: Look for a push or pull acting on an object.
Decide whether the objects touch where the force acts.
If they touch, it is a contact force; if not, it is a non-contact force.
Identify the force by its effect or source, such as friction or gravity.
notes.checkQuestion: Name one non-contact force.
notes.checkAnswer: Electrostatic force.

notes.title: The four fundamental forces
notes.answer: The four fundamental forces are gravitational, electromagnetic, strong nuclear and weak nuclear forces.
notes.explanation: The four fundamental forces are gravitational, electromagnetic, strong nuclear and weak nuclear. They explain the basic interactions in nature.
notes.simple: Nature has four basic kinds of force. Each force has a different job and range.
steps: Name the four forces: gravitational, electromagnetic, strong nuclear and weak nuclear.
Link gravity with attraction over long distances.
Link electromagnetic force with interactions between charged particles.
Link strong nuclear force with holding the nucleus together.
Link weak nuclear force with radioactive decay such as beta decay.
notes.checkQuestion: Which force holds protons and neutrons together in a nucleus?
notes.checkAnswer: Strong nuclear force holds the nucleus together.

notes.title: Drawing a Free-Body Diagram
notes.answer: A free-body diagram is used to show the relative magnitudes and directions of all the forces acting on an object in a given situation.
notes.explanation: A free-body diagram shows the forces acting on one object. It uses arrows to show the direction and relative magnitude of each force, and labels to name each force.
notes.simple: Draw the object as a box. Add an arrow for every force acting on it, point each arrow in the force's direction, and label it.
examples: A book pushed to the right across a table has an applied force to the right and friction to the left.
The table exerts a normal force upward on the book, while the book's weight acts downward.
steps: Represent the object by a box.
Draw each force arrow outward from the centre of the box.
Point each arrow in the direction of the force.
Use arrow length to show the force's relative magnitude.
Label each arrow with the exact type of force.
notes.checkQuestion: A book is pushed to the right across a table. Name the four forces shown in its free-body diagram and give their directions.
notes.checkAnswer: The book has an applied force to the right, friction to the left, a normal force upward, and weight downward.

notes.title: Newton’s Laws of Motion
notes.answer: Newton’s first law describes inertia; the second law is F = ma; the third law says that every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
notes.explanation: Newton’s laws explain how forces affect motion. The first law describes how an object resists a change in its motion, the second law links force to mass and acceleration, and the third law says forces between two interacting bodies are equal and opposite.
notes.simple: A force can change motion. Objects resist changes to their motion, and when two objects interact, each pushes or pulls the other.
examples: When a bus stops suddenly, passengers tend to move forward because their bodies tend to keep moving.
When a gun fires a bullet forward, the gun recoils backward.
steps: Use the first law to describe what happens when no net external force acts.
Use F = ma when a question gives mass and acceleration, or asks for force.
For the third law, identify the two interacting bodies and state the equal, opposite forces acting on them.
notes.checkQuestion: Why do action and reaction forces not balance each other?
notes.checkAnswer: The forces are equal and opposite, but they act on different bodies, so they do not balance each other.

notes.title: Limitations of Newton’s Laws
notes.answer: Relativistic mechanics is applicable to elementary particles having velocities close to the speed of light.
notes.explanation: Newton’s laws describe everyday motion very accurately, but they are not exact for every situation. For very small particles or objects moving close to the speed of light, relativistic mechanics is needed.
notes.simple: Newton’s laws work very well for ordinary things we see and use. For tiny particles or extremely fast objects, Einstein’s relativistic mechanics is more suitable.
examples: A car moving at an ordinary road speed is well described by Newton’s laws.
An elementary particle moving close to the speed of light needs relativistic mechanics.
steps: Use Newton’s laws for objects and speeds we meet in everyday life.
Recognise that they are not exact for all types of motion.
For elementary particles moving close to the speed of light, use relativistic mechanics.
notes.checkQuestion: When is relativistic mechanics applicable?
notes.checkAnswer: Newton’s laws are a good approximation for everyday motion, but are not exact for very small objects or objects moving close to the speed of light.
checkAccept: close to the speed of light

notes.title: Mass and Weight
notes.answer: Weight is the gravitational force acting on an object: w = mg.
notes.explanation: Mass tells us how much matter an object contains and stays the same everywhere. Weight is the gravitational force on the object, so it can change when gravitational field strength changes.
notes.simple: Mass is how much matter is in something. Weight is the pull of gravity on it.
examples: A person with a mass of 80 kg has a weight of 800 N on Earth when g = 10 N kg⁻¹.
The same person has a weight of 128 N on the Moon when g = 1.6 m s⁻².
steps: Write the relation: w = mg.
Put in the mass and the value of g.
Multiply to find the weight, and give the answer in newtons.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the weight of a 2 kg object where g = 10 N kg⁻¹?
notes.checkAnswer: Mass is measured in kilograms and stays the same; weight is a gravitational force measured in newtons and can change with g.

notes.title: Balances and force meters
notes.answer: A force meter, also called a newton meter or spring balance, measures force directly in newtons (N).
notes.explanation: Mechanical and electronic balances measure mass. A force meter measures force directly in newtons. An electronic balance needs a power supply or, in some models, dry-cell batteries; it does not need standard weights.
notes.simple: Balances measure mass; a force meter measures force.
examples: A mechanical balance compares an object with standard weights.
A force meter can show the weight of an object in newtons.
steps: Use a mechanical balance with standard weights to compare masses.
Use a mechanical platform balance for heavy items; its calibrated small weights are used instead of separate standard weights.
Connect an electronic balance to a power supply, or use a model that operates on dry-cell batteries.
Use a force meter to measure force in newtons; if a spring balance scale shows mass in kilograms, multiply by g = 10 m s⁻² to find the weight in newtons.
notes.checkQuestion: Which instrument measures force directly in newtons?
notes.checkAnswer: A force meter measures force directly in newtons (N).

notes.title: Friction and its effects
notes.answer: Friction opposes motion. Static friction acts before surfaces start sliding; kinetic friction acts while they slide; rolling friction acts while an object rolls. Air resistance can balance gravity and produce terminal velocity.
notes.explanation: Friction is a force that opposes motion between surfaces. It can slow moving objects and change some of their energy into heat. The main types in this section are static friction, kinetic friction and rolling friction.
notes.simple: Friction is a force that resists motion. It can slow things down, warm surfaces, and make it harder for objects to slide.
examples: A cricket ball slows down on the ground because friction acts opposite to its motion.
A wheel rolls more easily than an object slides because rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction.
steps: Identify the surfaces or fluid involved.
Decide whether the object is at rest, sliding, rolling or falling through air.
Name the friction or resistance acting on it.
State how that force affects the object's motion.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the constant velocity reached when air resistance balances gravity called?
notes.checkAnswer: Terminal velocity

notes.title: Momentum and Impulse
notes.answer: Impulse is the total change in momentum of an object when a large force acts on it for a short time.
notes.explanation: Impulse measures the change in an object's momentum when a force acts on it. A force acting for a longer time can produce the same change in momentum with a smaller average force.
notes.simple: Impulse tells us how much an object's momentum changes during a force. More time for the change means less average force.
examples: A cricketer draws his hands back while catching a ball to increase the time of impact and reduce the force on his hands.
Packing materials increase the time over which a fragile object slows down, reducing the force on it.
steps: Find the object's mass and velocity.
Calculate momentum using p = mv.
For a force acting over time, use F = Δp/Δt.
For an impact, calculate the change in momentum as final momentum minus initial momentum.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens to the average force if the same change in momentum takes place over a longer time?
notes.checkAnswer: Impulse is the total change in momentum of an object when a large force acts on it for a short time.

notes.title: Conservation of Momentum
notes.answer: If no external force acts on an isolated system, the final total momentum of the system is equal to the initial total momentum of the system.
notes.explanation: In an isolated system, the total momentum before an interaction stays equal to the total momentum after it. Use signs to show direction: if an object moves in the opposite direction, its velocity is negative.
notes.simple: Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity. When no external force acts on a system, its total momentum does not change.
examples: A gun and bullet start at rest, so their total momentum is zero. After firing, the bullet's forward momentum is balanced by the gun's backward momentum.
When two balls stick together after a collision, add their masses to find the moving mass after collision.
steps: Write the law: total momentum before = total momentum after.
Choose a positive direction and give opposite velocities negative signs.
Substitute each object's mass and velocity before and after the interaction.
Solve for the unknown and include its direction in the answer.
notes.checkQuestion: What stays equal before and after a collision in an isolated system?
notes.checkAnswer: The total momentum before and after the collision is equal.

notes.title: Dynamics: forces, motion and momentum
notes.answer: Dynamics studies forces and their effects on motion.
notes.explanation: A force can change an object's motion. Newton's laws explain how forces affect motion, while momentum and impulse help us study collisions and recoil. Friction opposes motion between surfaces.
notes.simple: A force is a push or pull that can change motion. Momentum depends on mass and velocity.
examples: A 10 kg block pushed by a 5 N force has acceleration 0.5 m s⁻².
When a gun fires a bullet forward, the gun recoils backward.
steps: Find the resultant force acting on the object.
Use F = ma to find acceleration, or use momentum change where appropriate.
For collisions in an isolated system, equate total momentum before and after.
Include units and direction in the final answer.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the acceleration of a 10 kg block when a 5 N force acts on it?
notes.checkAnswer: The block accelerates at 0.5 m s⁻².

notes.title: Like and Unlike Parallel Forces
notes.answer: Parallel forces act parallel to one another. Same-direction parallel forces are like; opposite-direction parallel forces are unlike.
notes.explanation: Parallel forces act along parallel lines, though they may act at different points. If they point in the same direction, they are like parallel forces; if they point in opposite directions, they are unlike parallel forces.
notes.simple: Check two things: are the forces parallel, and do they point the same way or opposite ways?
examples: Two upward forces acting at different points on a body are like parallel forces.
An upward force and a downward force acting along parallel lines are unlike parallel forces.
steps: Check that the forces act along parallel lines.
If their directions are the same, call them like parallel forces.
If their directions are opposite, call them unlike parallel forces.
notes.checkQuestion: In Fig. 4.1, which pair is unlike parallel forces?
notes.checkAnswer: F₁ and F₂ are like parallel forces; F₂ and F₃ are unlike parallel forces.

notes.title: Adding forces by the head-to-tail rule
notes.answer: The resultant is the single force that has the same effect as the forces acting together.
notes.explanation: A force is a vector, so it has both magnitude and direction. To add forces graphically, draw them head-to-tail. The resultant goes from the tail of the first force to the head of the last force.
notes.simple: Put each force arrowhead-to-tail. The resultant is one arrow from where you started to where you finish.
examples: Forces of 4 N and 3 N placed at right angles have a resultant of 5 N.
In Example 4.1, the measured resultant is 7.1 cm. With the scale 100 N = 1 cm, its magnitude is 710 N.
steps: Choose a suitable scale, such as 100 N = 1 cm.
Draw each force as an arrow using the scale and the given direction.
Place the tail of each new arrow at the head of the previous arrow.
Draw the resultant from the tail of the first arrow to the head of the last arrow.
Measure the resultant and use the scale to find its magnitude; read its direction from the diagram.
notes.checkQuestion: In Example 4.1, what force does a measured resultant length of 7.1 cm represent at the scale 100 N = 1 cm?

notes.title: Torque and the moment arm
notes.answer: Torque is the product of the force and the moment arm: τ = F × ℓ.
notes.explanation: Torque tells us how strongly a force tends to turn an object. It depends on both the size of the force and its moment arm. For example, a door is easier to open when you push at its handle rather than near its hinge. A spanner turns a nut more easily when you apply force farther from the nut.
notes.simple: Torque is the turning effect of a force. A bigger force or a longer moment arm gives a greater turning effect.
examples: A door handle is placed far from the hinge so a smaller force can turn the door.
A force of 400 N applied at the end of a 0.25 m spanner produces a torque of 100 N m.
steps: Identify the force and its perpendicular distance from the axis.
Use τ = F × ℓ.
Multiply the force by the moment arm.
Give the torque in newton metres (N m).
notes.checkQuestion: A force of 20 N acts perpendicularly at a moment arm of 0.4 m. What is the moment arm?
notes.checkAnswer: The moment arm is 0.4 m.

notes.title: Resolving a Force into Components
notes.answer: The x-component is found using cosine, and the y-component is found using sine.
notes.explanation: A force can be split into perpendicular x- and y-components. If the force F makes an angle θ with the x-axis, use cosine for the x-component and sine for the y-component.
notes.simple: Think of the force as the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle. Its horizontal part uses cosine, and its vertical part uses sine.
examples: For F = 200 N at 30° to the x-axis: F_x = 200 cos 30° = 173.2 N.
For the same force: F_y = 200 sin 30° = 100 N.
steps: Identify F and the angle θ it makes with the x-axis.
Use F_x = F cos θ.
Use F_y = F sin θ.
Substitute the values and calculate each component.
notes.checkQuestion: A force of 10 N makes an angle of 30° with the x-axis. What are its x- and y-components?
notes.checkAnswer: F_x = F cos θ; F_y = F sin θ. For 200 N at 30°: F_x = 173.2 N and F_y = 100 N.

notes.title: Finding a Force from Its Perpendicular Components
notes.answer: F = √(F_x² + F_y²), and θ = tan⁻¹(F_y/F_x).
notes.explanation: A force can be split into two perpendicular components: one along the x-axis and one along the y-axis. If these components are known, use Pythagoras to find the force’s magnitude and the tangent ratio to find its direction.
notes.simple: The x- and y-components are the horizontal and vertical parts of a force. Join them at a right angle: Pythagoras gives the force’s size, and tan⁻¹ gives its angle.
examples: If F_x = 3 N and F_y = 4 N, then F = √(3² + 4²) = 5 N.
For the same components, θ = tan⁻¹(4/3) ≈ 53.1°.
steps: Use F = √(F_x² + F_y²) to find the magnitude.
Use θ = tan⁻¹(F_y/F_x) to find the direction.
State the magnitude in newtons and the angle with its reference direction.
notes.checkQuestion: If F_x = 3 N and F_y = 4 N, what are the magnitude and direction of the force measured from the positive x-axis?

notes.title: Principle of Moments
notes.answer: When a body is in balanced position, the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about that point.
notes.explanation: A body is balanced when the total clockwise moment about a point equals the total anticlockwise moment about that point. A moment is calculated by multiplying the force by its perpendicular distance from the pivot.
notes.simple: Think of a seesaw: a smaller force can balance a larger one if it acts farther from the pivot.
examples: A 10 N force acting 0.2 m from a pivot makes a moment of 10 × 0.2 = 2 N m.
If a 30 N force acts 0.4 m from a pivot, its moment is 30 × 0.4 = 12 N m.
steps: Choose the pivot or point about which the body turns.
Work out each moment using force × perpendicular distance from the pivot.
Separate the moments that turn clockwise from those that turn anticlockwise.
For balance, set total clockwise moments equal to total anticlockwise moments.
Solve the equation and include the correct unit.
notes.checkQuestion: What must be equal for a body to balance about a point?
notes.checkAnswer: The clockwise and anticlockwise moments are equal.

notes.title: Centre of Gravity and Centre of Mass
notes.answer: For an irregular plane lamina, the centre of gravity is at the intersection of the vertical lines drawn when the lamina is suspended from different points.
notes.explanation: An object's weight acts as if it is concentrated at one point called its centre of gravity. Its mass can also be treated as concentrated at one point called its centre of mass. In a uniform gravitational field, these points coincide. For an irregular plane lamina, suspend it from two different points and draw the vertical line each time; their intersection gives its centre of gravity.
notes.simple: Think of the centre of gravity as the point where an object's weight seems to act. For an irregular flat shape, hang it from two places: the crossing of the two vertical lines shows that point.
examples: A rectangle's centre of gravity is at the intersection of its diagonals.
A cup's centre of gravity can lie outside the material of the cup.
steps: Make a small hole near the edge of the lamina and suspend it freely from that point.
Hang a plumb line from the same point of suspension.
When the lamina stops moving, draw the vertical line along the plumb line.
Suspend the lamina from a different point and draw a second vertical line.
Mark the point where the two lines cross; this is the centre of gravity.
notes.checkQuestion: When an irregular plane lamina is suspended from two different points, where is its centre of gravity?
notes.checkAnswer: The point where the two vertical lines cross.

notes.title: Equilibrium: balanced forces, no acceleration
notes.answer: A body is in equilibrium if it has no acceleration. It can be at rest in static equilibrium or move with uniform velocity in dynamic equilibrium.
notes.explanation: A body is in equilibrium when it has no acceleration. It may be at rest (static equilibrium) or move with uniform velocity (dynamic equilibrium). Forces balance when their resultant is zero.
notes.simple: Equilibrium means there is no change in the body's motion: it stays at rest or keeps moving at the same velocity.
examples: A book resting on a table is in static equilibrium: the table’s upward normal force balances the book’s downward weight.
A paratrooper descending with uniform velocity is in dynamic equilibrium: air resistance balances gravity.
steps: Check whether the body has acceleration.
If it has no acceleration, it is in equilibrium.
If it is at rest, it is in static equilibrium.
If it moves with uniform velocity, it is in dynamic equilibrium.
Forces acting on it balance when their resultant is zero.
notes.checkQuestion: What type of equilibrium describes a body moving with uniform velocity?
notes.checkAnswer: A body moving with uniform velocity is in dynamic equilibrium.

notes.title: Conditions of Equilibrium
notes.answer: ΣF_x = 0, ΣF_y = 0, and Στ = 0.
notes.explanation: For complete equilibrium, the forces must balance in both directions and the turning effects must balance too. This means the object has no acceleration and no rotation.
notes.simple: An object is completely in equilibrium when it neither speeds up or slows down nor starts turning.
examples: A picture hanging still has balanced upward tensions and downward weight.
Two equal and opposite forces along different lines can have zero resultant force but still turn a body.
steps: Choose the object you are studying and show the forces acting on it.
Choose x- and y-axes that make resolving forces as easy as possible.
Resolve forces into components if needed.
Use ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0.
If needed, use Στ = 0 and solve the equations.
notes.checkQuestion: What three sums must be zero for a body to be in complete equilibrium?
notes.checkAnswer: The vector sum of all external forces is zero, and the vector sum of all torques about any point is zero.

notes.title: States of Equilibrium
notes.answer: The three states are stable, unstable and neutral equilibrium.
notes.explanation: A body's equilibrium state depends on what happens when it is tilted or disturbed. A stable body returns to its starting position; an unstable body moves farther away; a neutral body rests in its new position. The centre of mass and the base of support help explain whether a body topples.
notes.simple: Ask what the body does after a small push: return means stable, move farther away means unstable, and stay in its new position means neutral.
examples: A cone standing on its circular base is stable: a slight tilt raises its centre of gravity, and the resulting torque brings it back.
A cylinder rolling on a flat surface is neutral: its centre of mass stays at the same height as it moves.
steps: Imagine the body has been disturbed slightly.
Check whether it returns, moves farther away, or stays in its new position.
Use the body's centre of mass and base of support to explain why.
notes.checkQuestion: What state of equilibrium does a cone standing on its circular base show?
notes.checkAnswer: A cone on its circular base is in stable equilibrium.

notes.title: Improving stability
notes.answer: Improve stability by lowering the centre of gravity or widening the base.
notes.explanation: Stability depends on where an object's centre of gravity is and how wide its base is. A low centre of gravity and a wide base make toppling less likely.
notes.simple: An object is harder to tip over when its weight is low down or spread over a wider base.
examples: A low armchair is more stable than a high chair because its centre of gravity is lower.
A bus carrying heavy loads on its floor has a lower centre of gravity than one carrying those loads on its roof.
steps: Put heavy parts or loads as low as possible.
Make the base wider if the design allows.
If an object tilts, consider whether its weight and the ground's reaction form a turning couple that will topple it.
notes.checkQuestion: How can you improve the stability of an object?
notes.checkAnswer: Lower its centre of gravity or widen its base.

notes.title: Stability and motion in a circle
notes.answer: A racing car is made more stable by keeping its centre of mass low and increasing its base area. A balancing toy returns to its stable position by lowering its centre of gravity. A body moving in a circle has velocity along the tangent and needs a force perpendicular to its velocity to keep moving in the circle.
notes.explanation: Racing cars and balancing toys are designed using ideas about stability. A low centre of mass and a wide base help a car resist toppling. In a balancing toy, the centre of gravity is below the pivot, so disturbing the toy raises its centre of gravity; it returns to its stable position by lowering it. In circular motion, the velocity points along the tangent, while the force needed to keep the body moving in a circle acts perpendicular to the velocity.
notes.simple: A low, wide object is harder to tip over. A balancing toy returns to its resting position by lowering its centre of gravity. In circular motion, the force points inward and the velocity points along the circle’s tangent.
examples: A racing car is made more stable by keeping its centre of mass low and its wheels outside the main body, which increases its base area.
A balancing toy returns to its original position after it is disturbed because it lowers its centre of gravity.
steps: Keep the centre of mass as low as possible.
Increase the base area, for example by keeping the wheels outside the main body.
For a balancing toy, identify the pivot and check that its centre of gravity is below it.
For circular motion, draw the velocity along the tangent and the force towards the centre; these directions are perpendicular.
notes.checkQuestion: What two design features improve the stability of a racing car?
notes.checkAnswer: A low centre of mass and a wide base area.

notes.title: Centripetal Force
notes.answer: Centripetal force is the force that keeps an object moving in a circle at constant speed. It acts towards the centre and is perpendicular to the object's velocity.
notes.explanation: Centripetal force keeps an object moving in a circular path at constant speed. Its direction is towards the centre of the circle, while the object's velocity is along the tangent. For example, tension in a string keeps a whirled stone moving in a circle, and Earth's gravity keeps a satellite in orbit.
notes.simple: Centripetal force is the inward pull that keeps an object going around a circle instead of flying off in a straight line.
examples: A string provides the centripetal force for a stone being whirled in a circle.
Earth's gravitational pull provides the centripetal force for a satellite orbiting Earth.
steps: Write the relation: F_c = mv²/r.
Convert mass to kilograms and identify the speed and radius.
Substitute the values into the relation.
Calculate the force and write its unit, newtons (N).
notes.checkQuestion: In circular motion, which way does centripetal force act compared with the object's velocity?
notes.checkAnswer: The force acts towards the centre; the velocity is along the tangent, so they are perpendicular.

notes.title: Turning Effects of Force
notes.answer: Complete equilibrium requires zero resultant force and zero resultant torque.
notes.explanation: For a force to turn a body, its turning effect (torque) depends on the force and its perpendicular distance from the pivot. A body is in complete equilibrium when both the resultant force and the resultant torque are zero.
notes.simple: A force can push or pull an object, and it can also make the object turn. How strongly it turns depends on how big the force is and how far from the pivot it acts.
examples: A 10 N force acting 0.5 m from a pivot at right angles produces torque 10 × 0.5 = 5 N m.
A 200 N force at 30° to the horizontal has components Fx = 200 cos 30° = 173.2 N and Fy = 200 sin 30° = 100 N.
steps: Resolve a force into components using Fx = F cos θ and Fy = F sin θ when θ is measured from the x-axis.
For torque, use τ = rF sin θ, where r is the distance from the pivot to the point of application of force.
For a balanced body, clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments.
For complete equilibrium, ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0.
For circular motion, centripetal force is Fc = mv²/r and acts perpendicular to the velocity.
notes.checkQuestion: What two conditions must be satisfied for complete equilibrium?
notes.checkAnswer: Both the resultant force and the resultant torque must be zero.

notes.title: Work done by a force
notes.answer: Work is the product of the magnitude of force and the distance covered in the direction of force.
notes.explanation: In physics, work is done when a force moves an object through a distance. Only the part of the force in the direction of the object's motion does work. Work is measured in joules.
notes.simple: A force does work only when it moves something in the force's direction. A force sideways to the motion, or no movement at all, means no work by that force.
examples: A force of 10 N moves an object 3 m in the same direction: W = FS = 10 × 3 = 30 J.
A person carries a bag horizontally at a steady height. The supporting force is vertical and the displacement is horizontal, so the work done by that force is zero.
steps: Identify the force, the distance moved and the angle between them.
Use W = FS when the force and displacement are in the same direction.
Use W = FS cos θ when the force makes an angle θ with the direction of motion.
Give the answer in joules (J).
notes.checkQuestion: A force holds a bag upward while the bag moves horizontally. How much work does this force do?
notes.checkAnswer: Zero joules; the force and displacement are perpendicular.

notes.title: Kinetic and potential energy
notes.answer: Energy is the ability of a body to do work. Kinetic energy is due to motion; potential energy is due to position or deformation.
notes.explanation: Kinetic energy is the energy a body has because it is moving. Potential energy is stored energy due to a body's position or deformation. Near the Earth, a raised body's gravitational potential energy is found using Eₚ = mgh.
notes.simple: Energy is the ability to do work. Motion gives a body kinetic energy; height or deformation can give it potential energy.
examples: A moving truck has kinetic energy.
A block held above the ground has gravitational potential energy.
steps: Choose the correct relation: Eₖ = ½mv² for motion, or Eₚ = mgh for a raised body.
Write the given values in SI units.
Substitute the values into the relation.
Calculate the answer and write the unit joule (J).
notes.checkQuestion: What is the gravitational potential energy of a 2 kg body raised 3 m? Take g = 10 m s⁻².
notes.checkAnswer: The body's gravitational potential energy is 60 J.

notes.title: Conservation of Energy
notes.answer: The total energy remains mgh while the body falls, assuming air resistance is negligible.
notes.explanation: As a body falls, its potential energy changes into kinetic energy. If air resistance is negligible, the total energy stays the same.
notes.simple: Energy changes form, but the total amount does not disappear. A falling object changes potential energy into kinetic energy.
examples: At point B, the body has potential energy mg(h − x) and kinetic energy mgx.
Just before the body reaches the ground, its potential energy is zero and its kinetic energy is mgh.
steps: At A, the body is at rest and has potential energy mgh.
As it falls to B, it loses potential energy and gains kinetic energy.
At B, E_p = mg(h − x) and E_k = mgx.
Add the two forms: E = mg(h − x) + mgx = mgh.
Just before reaching the ground, E_p = 0 and E_k = mgh.
notes.checkQuestion: At point B, what are the body's potential energy, kinetic energy, and total energy?
notes.checkAnswer: At B, E_p = mg(h − x), E_k = mgx, and total energy = mgh.

notes.title: Renewable and non-renewable energy
notes.answer: Renewable sources are naturally replenished; non-renewable sources are limited and can run out.
notes.explanation: Renewable sources are naturally replenished, while non-renewable sources are limited and can run out. Your textbook describes several sources of energy, including fossil fuels, water, sunlight, wind, tides, waves, biomass, nuclear fuels and heat from rocks inside Earth.
notes.simple: Renewable energy sources are replaced naturally. Non-renewable sources are used up faster than nature can replace them.
examples: Solar energy comes from sunlight and is renewable.
Fossil fuels such as coal, oil and natural gas are non-renewable.
steps: Decide whether nature can replace the source in a relatively short time.
If it is naturally replenished, call it renewable.
If it is limited and can run out, call it non-renewable.
Give examples to support your answer.
notes.checkQuestion: Is wind energy renewable or non-renewable? Give one reason.
notes.checkAnswer: Wind energy is renewable because wind is naturally replenished.

notes.title: Renewable and Non-Renewable Energy Sources
notes.answer: Renewable sources are replaced by new ones after use; non-renewable sources are depleted with continuous use and are not easily replaced.
notes.explanation: Renewable energy sources are replaced by new ones after use. Your textbook gives hydroelectricity, solar, wind, tidal, wave and geothermal energy as examples. Non-renewable sources are depleted with continuous use and are not easily replaced once they run out. Fossil fuels and nuclear energy are non-renewable. For example, rain and snowfall replenish water supplies, while fossil fuels take millions of years to form.
notes.simple: Renewable sources are replaced after we use them. Non-renewable sources can run out and are not quickly replaced.
examples: Solar energy is renewable because it will remain available.
Fossil fuels are non-renewable because they are limited and take millions of years to form.
steps: Check whether the source is replaced after it is used.
If it is replaced, classify it as renewable.
If continuous use depletes it and it is not easily replaced, classify it as non-renewable.
Give examples to support your classification.
notes.checkQuestion: Is tidal energy renewable or non-renewable?
notes.checkAnswer: Tidal energy is renewable.

notes.title: Comparing methods of energy production
notes.answer: Hydroelectric power is economical and pollution free, while burning fossil fuels pollutes the environment.
notes.explanation: Energy sources can be compared by whether they can be replaced, their cost, and the pollution or other problems they cause.
notes.simple: Some energy sources can be replaced and cause little pollution. Others run out or create pollution and other risks.
examples: Hydroelectric power is economical and pollution free.
Burning fossil fuels releases smoke, carbon dioxide and heat.
steps: Identify the energy source.
Check whether it is renewable or non-renewable.
Compare its cost and pollution or other disadvantages.
notes.checkQuestion: Name one problem caused by burning fossil fuels.
notes.checkAnswer: Fossil fuels are non-renewable and burning them causes pollution.

notes.title: Finding power
notes.explanation: Power tells us how quickly work is done or energy is transferred. To find power, divide the work done by the time taken.
notes.simple: Power is how fast work is done.
examples: If 100 J of work is done in 5 s, the power is 100/5 = 20 W.
A machine that transfers 600 J of energy in 3 s has power 600/3 = 200 W.
steps: Write the formula: P = W/t.
Put the work done, W, and time taken, t, into the formula.
Divide work by time.
Write the answer in watts (W), unless another unit is requested.
notes.checkQuestion: A machine does 120 J of work in 6 s. What is its power?
notes.checkAnswer: Power = work done ÷ time taken; P = W/t.

notes.title: Efficiency of a working system
notes.answer: Percentage efficiency = (Useful output energy / Total input energy) × 100.
