This is incorrect because the section says relativistic mechanics applies to elementary particles moving close to light speed.
This is incorrect because Newton’s laws are a good approximation in everyday situations, not only at near-light speeds.

quiz.stem: When does the section say that relativistic mechanics is applicable?
options: When dealing with elementary particles having velocities close to that of light
Only when an object is at rest
rationales: This is incorrect because ordinary motion can be described accurately by Newton’s laws.
This is correct: the section names elementary particles with velocities close to light speed.
This is incorrect because being at rest is not the stated condition for using relativistic mechanics.
This is incorrect because friction is not the condition given for relativistic mechanics.

quiz.stem: The section identifies whose work as the basis of relativistic mechanics?
rationales: This is correct: the section names relativistic mechanics developed by Albert Einstein.
This is incorrect because Newton is associated with the laws being discussed, not the development named here.
This is incorrect because Galileo is not named in this section as the developer of relativistic mechanics.
This is incorrect because Faraday is not named in this section as the developer of relativistic mechanics.

quiz.stem: Which statement best summarises the limitation described in this section?
options: Newton’s laws are a good approximation for everyday motion.
Newton’s laws are exact for every type of motion.
Newton’s laws apply only to objects that are small.
Newton’s laws apply only to objects moving at light speed.
rationales: This is correct: the section calls Newton’s laws a good approximation except in particular extreme cases.
This is incorrect because the section explicitly says Newton’s laws are not exact for all types of motion.
This is incorrect because the section says being small enough is a limitation, not the only situation in which the laws apply.
This is incorrect because the section refers to velocities close to the speed of light, not only light speed.

quiz.stem: According to the final statement in the section, when may Newton’s laws stop being a good approximation?
options: A very small object or an object moving close to the speed of light
Any object moving at a constant everyday speed
rationales: This is correct: the section gives small size and speeds close to light speed as the exceptions.
This is incorrect because everyday motion is where Newton’s laws work with very high accuracy.
This is incorrect because zero mass is not mentioned in the section.
This is incorrect because being on Earth is not given as the limitation in this section.

quiz.stem: Which statement is consistent with the section’s conclusion?
options: Newton’s laws provide a good approximation, but are not exact for all types of motion.
Newton’s laws are useless for everyday objects.
Newton’s laws are exact only for elementary particles.
Newton’s laws and relativistic mechanics are the same theory.
rationales: This is correct: it restates the section’s conclusion about approximation and limits.
This is incorrect because the section says Newton’s laws work with very high accuracy in everyday life.
This is incorrect because the section associates elementary particles near light speed with relativistic mechanics.
This is incorrect because the section presents relativistic mechanics as applicable for a different range of motion.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes the mass of a body?
options: The quantity of matter in a body
The gravitational force on a body
The space occupied by a body
rationales: This is the simplest definition of mass given in your textbook.
This describes weight, not mass.
This describes volume, not mass.
Speed describes motion and is not mass.

quiz.stem: What is the SI unit of mass?
rationales: A newton is the SI unit of force and weight.
The kilogram is the SI unit of mass.
A metre is the SI unit of length.
A joule is the SI unit of energy.

quiz.stem: Which statement about mass is correct?
options: A scalar quantity that remains the same everywhere
A vector quantity that always has the same value everywhere
A scalar quantity that changes with altitude
rationales: Mass is scalar and remains the same everywhere.
Mass is not a vector, and weight—not mass—varies with location.
Mass does not change with altitude.
Kilogram is the unit of mass, but mass is not a force.

quiz.stem: What is the weight of an object?
options: The force with which Earth attracts a body towards its centre
The quantity of matter in a body
The force acting on unit area
rationales: This is the textbook definition of the weight of an object.
This describes mass.
This describes pressure, not weight.
Acceleration is not weight.

quiz.stem: Which equation gives the weight w of a body of mass m in a gravitational field of strength g?
rationales: Dividing mass by g does not give the weight relation.
Weight is the product of mass and gravitational field strength.
This is not the weight relation.
Weight is not found by adding mass and field strength.

quiz.stem: Which instrument can be used to measure weight?
rationales: An ordinary balance is used to measure mass.
A spring balance can be used to measure weight.
A metre rule measures length.
A stopwatch measures time.

quiz.stem: Which feature distinguishes weight from mass?
options: It is the quantity of matter in a body.
It is directed towards the centre of Earth.
rationales: Mass is scalar; weight is a vector.
This describes mass.
Weight is a vector directed downward, towards Earth's centre.
Kilogram is the unit of mass, not weight.

quiz.stem: Why can an object's weight change from one place to another?
options: It varies because gravitational field strength varies from place to place.
It varies because the amount of matter in the object changes.
It remains the same because it is measured in newtons.
It varies because mass is a vector.
rationales: Weight depends on g, and g varies from place to place and with altitude.
The object's mass does not change just because it moves to another place.
Being measured in newtons does not make weight constant.
Mass is a scalar, not a vector.

quiz.stem: Which feature describes a mechanical balance?
options: It has a rigid horizontal beam that oscillates on a central knife edge.
It measures force directly in newtons.
It displays the total price of an object.
It uses a spring to measure mass.
rationales: This is the textbook description of the beam and its central fulcrum.
A force meter, not a mechanical balance, measures force directly in newtons.
Some electronic balances can display a total price when the rate per kg is entered.
An ordinary force meter has a spring; this is not how the section describes a mechanical balance.

quiz.stem: Why can a mechanical platform balance use smaller weights instead of separate standard weights?
options: They are already calibrated to standard weights.
They are made from standard weights.
They remove the need for a fulcrum.
rationales: The small weights have already been calibrated to the standard weights.
The text says the weights are calibrated, not made from standard weights.
A force meter measures force in newtons; this is not the stated function of the platform balance weights.
The platform balance still has a beam and a fulcrum.

quiz.stem: Which statement about an electronic balance is correct?
options: It needs no standard weights and displays mass on a screen.
It uses two pans and a central knife edge.
It measures force directly in newtons.
It works only when dry-cell batteries are used.
rationales: The section says no standard weights are needed and the mass is displayed on the screen.
These are features of the mechanical balance described in the section.
A force meter measures force directly in newtons.
Some models can use dry-cell batteries, but the section does not say all electronic balances work only that way.

quiz.stem: What does a force meter measure?
options: It measures force directly in newtons.
It compares masses using two pans.
It displays the total price per kilogram.
It measures mass only in kilograms.
rationales: A force meter measures force directly in newtons (N).
A mechanical balance uses pans to compare masses.
An electronic balance may display total price when a rate per kg is entered.
Balances measure mass; a force meter measures force.

quiz.stem: In an ordinary force meter, what should the pointer indicate when nothing is hung from the hook?
options: The pointer coincides with zero when nothing is hung from the hook.
The pointer shows zero only when the heaviest object is hung.
The scale is marked in kilograms in every force meter.
The spring is detached from the handle.
rationales: The scale is arranged so the pointer coincides with zero when the hook is unloaded.
The pointer is set to zero when nothing is hung, not when the heaviest object is attached.
The section says the scale is provided in newtons, although some spring balances measure mass.
The upper end of the spring is attached to the handle.

quiz.stem: How can a mass reading in kilograms on some spring balances be converted into weight in newtons?
options: Multiply the mass in kg by g = 10 m s⁻².
Divide the mass in kg by 10.
Multiply the mass in kg by 100.
Add 10 to the mass in kg.
rationales: The section gives weight in newtons as mass in kilograms multiplied by g = 10 m s⁻².
Dividing by 10 is not the conversion stated in the section.
Multiplying by 100 does not convert the mass to weight in newtons.
Adding 10 does not convert mass to weight.

quiz.stem: A ball rolling across the ground eventually stops. What is the main reason?
options: It acts in the direction of motion
It opposes the motion of the ball
It makes the ball's mass decrease
It causes the ball to move in a circle
rationales: This is wrong because friction acts against, not along, the ball's motion.
This is right because friction between the ball and ground opposes its motion.
This is wrong because friction does not make the ball lose mass.
This is wrong because friction does not necessarily make the ball move in a circle.

quiz.stem: A block is at rest while a pull is applied to it, but it has not started sliding. Which friction opposes the pull?
rationales: This is right because static friction acts before the surfaces start sliding.
This is wrong because kinetic friction acts when surfaces are sliding.
This is wrong because rolling friction acts when an object rolls over a surface.
This is wrong because air resistance is not the friction holding the block at rest on the table.

quiz.stem: What happens when the applied pull on a stationary block exceeds the limit of static friction?
options: The block stops experiencing any force
rationales: This is right because the block begins to slide once the limiting static friction is overcome.
This is wrong because exceeding static friction does not by itself make the block roll.
This is wrong because forces, including kinetic friction, still act on the block.
This is wrong because the applied pull does not change the block's weight.

quiz.stem: What happens when a falling object reaches terminal velocity?
options: Air resistance balances gravity and the object falls at constant velocity
Gravity stops acting on the object
rationales: This is wrong because the object stops accelerating when the forces balance.
This is right because balanced air resistance and gravity leave the object falling at constant velocity.
This is wrong because gravity continues to act downward.
This is wrong because balanced forces do not make the object reverse direction.

quiz.stem: How does rolling friction compare with sliding friction, according to this section?
options: Rolling friction is greater than sliding friction
Rolling friction is about one hundred times smaller than sliding friction
Rolling friction and sliding friction are always equal
Rolling friction exists only in liquids
rationales: This is wrong because the section says rolling friction is smaller.
This is right because the section states that rolling friction is about one hundred times smaller.
This is wrong because the two types of friction are not stated to be equal.
This is wrong because rolling friction is associated with an object rolling over a surface, not only with liquids.

quiz.stem: Which method does the section recommend to reduce friction between moving machine parts?
options: Apply oil or grease between moving parts
Make the front of a vehicle flat
rationales: This is right because oil or grease is applied between moving parts to reduce friction.
This is wrong because rougher surfaces do not follow the section's methods for reducing friction.
This is wrong because converting rolling motion to sliding would increase friction.
This is wrong because a flat front faces more air or water resistance than a streamlined front.

quiz.stem: What is the SI unit of momentum?
rationales: This is the SI unit of momentum.
This is equivalent to a newton, the unit of force.
This is not the SI unit of momentum.
This is the unit of work or energy, not momentum.

quiz.stem: Which expression gives the momentum of a moving body?
rationales: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity.
Dividing mass by velocity does not give momentum.
Force multiplied by distance is work, not momentum.
Velocity divided by time gives acceleration.

quiz.stem: According to the momentum form of Newton's second law, force is equal to what?
options: The rate of change of momentum
The product of mass and time
The rate of change of velocity only
The product of force and distance
rationales: Force equals the change in momentum per unit time.
Mass multiplied by time is not the definition of force.
Change in velocity per unit time is acceleration, not force by itself.
Force multiplied by distance is work.

quiz.stem: Which expression represents the impulse of a force acting for time Δt?
rationales: Impulse is the product of force and the time interval.
Dividing force by time does not give impulse.
Mass divided by time is not impulse.
Dividing time by force is not impulse.

quiz.stem: In what direction is the change in momentum of a body?
options: Momentum changes in the direction of the force.
Momentum changes opposite to the force.
Momentum changes at right angles to the force.
rationales: The direction of change in momentum is that of the force.
The change in momentum is not opposite to the force.
A force produces a change in momentum.
The textbook states that the change in momentum is in the force's direction, not at right angles.

quiz.stem: Why does a cricketer draw his hands back when catching a fast ball?
options: Increase the time of impact and reduce the average force
Decrease the time of impact and reduce the average force
Increase the ball's momentum without applying a force
Make the ball's momentum zero before it is caught
rationales: Increasing the time for the momentum change reduces the average force.
A shorter impact time would increase the average force for the same momentum change.
The ball's momentum changes because a force acts on it.
The ball's momentum becomes zero only after it has been brought to rest.

quiz.stem: How does soft packing help protect fragile objects during an impact?
options: The mass is converted to velocity.
The momentum change takes place over a longer time, reducing the force.
The packing material makes the object heavier.
The packing material prevents all changes in momentum.
rationales: Mass is not converted to velocity by packing.
Soft packing increases the time of the momentum change, so the force is reduced.
Making an object heavier is not how packing protects it.
Packing reduces the effect of a quick momentum change; it does not prevent every change.

quiz.stem: Which equation gives the average force in terms of change in momentum?
options: The force is equal to the object's momentum.
The force is equal to change in momentum divided by time.
The force is equal to time divided by change in momentum.
The force is equal to mass divided by velocity.
rationales: Momentum alone is not equal to force.
The average force is the change in momentum per unit time.
This reverses the relationship and is not the force equation.
Mass divided by velocity is not the force equation.

quiz.stem: In an isolated system, two objects collide. Which statement follows from conservation of momentum?
options: Momentum before the collision equals momentum after it.
The heavier object always stops after collision.
The system's total mass becomes zero.
rationales: Correct: the system's total momentum before collision equals its total momentum after collision.
Incorrect: conservation of momentum does not say that the heavier object stops.
Incorrect: momentum may transfer between objects, even though the system total stays the same.
Incorrect: a collision does not make the system's mass zero.

quiz.stem: A gun of mass m₂ and a bullet of mass m₁ are initially at rest. The bullet moves forward with velocity v₁ after firing. What is the gun's velocity v₂?
rationales: Correct: zero initial momentum gives 0 = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂, so v₂ = −m₁v₁/m₂.
Incorrect: this omits the negative sign that shows the gun moves opposite to the bullet.
Incorrect: the masses are in the wrong positions in the ratio.
Incorrect: the gun recoils, so its velocity is not zero after the bullet is fired.

quiz.stem: Two identical balls collide. The first moves at 5 m s⁻¹ and the second is initially at rest. If the first ball stops after collision, what does conservation of momentum predict for the second ball?
options: The first ball stops and the second moves at 5 m s⁻¹.
Both balls move at 2.5 m s⁻¹.
The first ball moves at 5 m s⁻¹ and the second stays at rest.
rationales: Correct: the second ball takes the first ball's momentum and, being identical, moves at the same speed.
Incorrect: this would not conserve the initial total momentum if both balls moved at this speed.
Incorrect: this describes the initial situation rather than the stated collision result.
Incorrect: stopping both balls would remove the initial system momentum.

quiz.stem: Why does a gun recoil when it fires a bullet?
options: The gun moves forward faster than the bullet.
The gun and bullet move forward together.
rationales: Correct: the gun moves backward so the total momentum of the gun-bullet system is conserved.
Incorrect: the gun moves in the direction opposite to the bullet.
Incorrect: the gun acquires momentum after firing.
Incorrect: the gun and bullet move in opposite directions just after firing.

quiz.stem: A car stops suddenly, but its passengers tend to move forward. Which principle helps explain why a seatbelt is needed?
options: The total momentum of the system remains the same.
Each passenger's momentum becomes zero instantly.
The car's mass increases during braking.
The seatbelt makes the car stop more slowly.
rationales: Correct: passengers in motion tend to keep moving, and the belt restrains them as the car stops.
Incorrect: a passenger's momentum does not become zero without a force acting over time.
Incorrect: braking does not increase the car's mass.
Incorrect: the seatbelt restrains the passenger; it does not make the car stop more slowly.

quiz.stem: A 0.5 kg ball's velocity changes from 2 m s⁻¹ to 10 m s⁻¹ in the same direction. What is the change in its momentum?
rationales: Incorrect: the velocity changed, so its momentum did not stay unchanged.
Correct: Δp = mΔv = 0.5(10 − 2) = 4 N s.
Incorrect: this does not equal mass multiplied by the change in velocity.
Incorrect: the velocity change is positive in the stated direction, so the change in momentum is positive.

quiz.stem: A 0.2 kg ball moves right at 20 m s⁻¹ while a 0.4 kg ball moves left at 5 m s⁻¹. Taking right as positive, what is their total momentum before collision?
options: The total momentum before collision is 2 kg m s⁻¹.
The total momentum before collision is 6 kg m s⁻¹.
The total momentum before collision is 10 kg m s⁻¹.
The total momentum before collision is 14 kg m s⁻¹.
rationales: Incorrect: this adds the momentum magnitudes without accounting for opposite directions.
Incorrect: this is not the signed sum of the two momenta.
Incorrect: this does not follow from adding the two signed momenta.

quiz.stem: A particle is simultaneously acted upon by two forces of 4 and 3 newtons. The net force on the particle is:
rationales: A net force of 1 N occurs only when the forces act in opposite directions, so it is not the only possible value.
Depending on the angle between the forces, the resultant can range from 1 N to 7 N.
A resultant of 5 N is possible for a particular angle, but it is not the only possible value.
A resultant of 7 N occurs only when the forces act in the same direction, so it is not the only possible value.

quiz.stem: A force F is making an angle of 60° with x-axis. Its y-component is equal to:
rationales: The x-component, not the y-component, is F cos 60°.
The y-component is F sin 60° when the angle is measured from the x-axis.
F cos 60° gives the x-component for an angle measured from the x-axis.
F tan 60° is not the component of F along the y-axis.

quiz.stem: Moment of force is called:
rationales: The moment arm is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force’s line of action, not the moment itself.
A couple is a pair of equal and opposite forces that produces a turning effect.
The couple arm is the perpendicular distance between the forces in a couple.
Torque is another name for the moment of a force.

quiz.stem: If F_1 and F_2 are the forces acting on a body and τ is the torque produced in it, the body will be completely in equilibrium, when:
rationales: Complete equilibrium requires both zero net force and zero net torque.
A nonzero net torque causes rotational acceleration, so the body is not in complete equilibrium.
A nonzero net force causes translational acceleration, so the body is not in complete equilibrium.
Nonzero net force and nonzero net torque mean the body is not in equilibrium.

quiz.stem: A Shopkeeper sells his articles by a balance having unequal arms of the pans. If he puts the weights in the pan having shorter arm, then the customer.
rationales: The customer loses because weights on the shorter arm balance a smaller load on the longer arm, so the customer receives less than the stated weight.
The customer does not gain because the arrangement gives the seller an advantage.
The customer does not receive an equal weight because the unequal arms make the balance unfair.
The customer loses whenever the weights are placed on the shorter arm and the goods on the longer arm.

quiz.stem: A man walks on a tight rope. He balances himself by holding a bamboo stick horizontally. It is an application of:
rationales: Conservation of momentum does not explain how the stick helps the man balance against rotation.
Newton’s second law relates net force to acceleration but does not specifically describe this balancing technique.
Holding the stick horizontally helps the man control his turning effect by using the principle of moments.
Newton’s third law concerns action-reaction force pairs, not the balancing effect of the stick.

quiz.stem: In stable equilibrium, the centre of gravity of the body lies:
rationales: A body whose centre of gravity is at its highest position is generally in unstable, not stable, equilibrium.
In stable equilibrium, a small displacement raises the centre of gravity, so its equilibrium position is at the lowest attainable height.
The centre of gravity is not at an arbitrary position in stable equilibrium; it is at a minimum-height position.
The centre of gravity need not lie outside the body, and its location outside does not define stable equilibrium.

quiz.stem: The centre of mass of a body:
options: lies always on the surface of the body
may lie within , outside or on the surface
rationales: The centre of mass can lie outside a body, as for a ring, so it is not always inside.
The centre of mass can lie inside a body, so it is not always outside.
The centre of mass can lie inside or outside a body, so it is not always on its surface.
Depending on the body’s shape and mass distribution, its centre of mass may be within, outside, or on its surface.

quiz.stem: A cylinder resting on its circular base is in:
rationales: A cylinder resting on its circular base is in stable equilibrium because a small tilt raises its centre of gravity.
The cylinder does not move farther from equilibrium after a small displacement, so its equilibrium is not unstable.
The centre of gravity rises when the cylinder is slightly tilted, so its equilibrium is not neutral.
The cylinder is in stable equilibrium, making this option incorrect.

quiz.stem: Centripetal force is given by:
rationales: The expression rF has units of torque and is not the general formula for centripetal force.
The expression rF cos θ is not the formula for centripetal force.
Centripetal force is mass times centripetal acceleration, giving F = mv²/r.
The expression mv/r² has the wrong dimensions for force and is not the centripetal-force formula.

quiz.stem: Which description matches parallel forces?
options: Forces acting at the same point only
Forces that must have equal magnitudes
rationales: Correct: parallel forces act parallel to one another, and their points of application may differ.
Incorrect: perpendicular forces meet at right angles, so they are not parallel.
Incorrect: parallel forces may act at different points.
Incorrect: the definition does not require parallel forces to have equal magnitudes.

quiz.stem: What makes parallel forces like parallel forces?
options: They act in the same direction
They act at the same point
rationales: Correct: parallel forces pointing in the same direction are called like parallel forces.
Incorrect: opposite directions make them unlike parallel forces.
Incorrect: the points of application do not determine whether forces are like.
Incorrect: equal magnitude is not part of the definition of like parallel forces.

quiz.stem: When are parallel forces called unlike parallel forces?
options: They act in the same direction
They act on the same point
rationales: Correct: parallel forces with opposite directions are unlike parallel forces.
Incorrect: forces in the same direction are like parallel forces.
Incorrect: the points of application do not define unlike forces.
Incorrect: unequal magnitudes do not by themselves make forces unlike.

quiz.stem: Which statement about the points of application of parallel forces is correct?
options: They may act at different points
They must act at one point
They must point in opposite directions
rationales: Correct: parallel forces may have different points of application.
Incorrect: parallel forces do not have to act at one point.
Incorrect: their magnitudes need not be equal.
Incorrect: parallel forces may point in the same or opposite directions.

quiz.stem: Two forces act along parallel lines and both point upward. What kind of forces are they?
rationales: Correct: they are parallel and point in the same direction, so they are like parallel forces.
Incorrect: unlike parallel forces point in opposite directions.
Incorrect: the forces are parallel, not perpendicular.
Incorrect: the question states that the forces act along parallel lines.

quiz.stem: Two forces act along parallel lines, one upward and one downward. What kind of forces are they?
rationales: Correct: their directions are opposite, so they are unlike parallel forces.
Incorrect: like parallel forces point in the same direction.
Incorrect: their points of application are not specified and do not determine the classification.
Incorrect: this description does not classify the forces and is not a property of parallel forces.

quiz.stem: Which arrangement follows the head-to-tail rule for adding force vectors?
options: Place the tail of each new vector at the head of the previous vector
Place all vector tails at the same point
Place each vector head at the same point
Draw the vectors without showing their directions
rationales: This is the head-to-tail arrangement used to add vectors.
This is a common-origin diagram, not the head-to-tail construction.
Joining all the heads does not follow the head-to-tail rule.
A force vector must show its direction to be added graphically.

quiz.stem: What happens to the resultant when the same force vectors are added in a different order?
options: The resultant changes whenever the order changes
The resultant is the same for any order of addition
The resultant always points along the x-axis
rationales: Changing the order does not change the resultant of the vectors.
The resultant is the same for any order of addition of vectors.
The resultant is zero only in special cases, not always.
The resultant can point in different directions, not just along the x-axis.

quiz.stem: A force of 400 N is drawn using the scale 100 N = 1 cm. How long should its arrow be?
rationales: At this scale, 2 cm represents 200 N, not 400 N.
At this scale, 3 cm represents 300 N, not 400 N.
At this scale, 4 cm represents 400 N.
At this scale, 5 cm represents 500 N, not 400 N.

quiz.stem: After arranging several vectors head-to-tail, how is the resultant drawn?
options: The first arrow's tail to the last arrow's head
The first arrow's head to the last arrow's tail
The head of the first arrow to the head of the last arrow
The tail of the first arrow to the tail of the last arrow
rationales: The resultant joins the starting tail to the final head.
This reverses the start and finish of the resultant.
This does not start at the beginning of the vector chain.
This does not end at the final head of the vector chain.

quiz.stem: How can the magnitude of a resultant be found from a scaled head-to-tail diagram?
options: Measure the length of the resultant arrow and apply the drawing scale
Add the lengths of all the arrows and call that the resultant
Use the length of the longest force arrow
Multiply the angle by the drawing scale
rationales: The measured resultant length is converted to force using the chosen scale.
The sum of arrow lengths is not generally the resultant length.
The longest individual arrow does not determine the resultant.
An angle is not multiplied by the force-per-length scale to find magnitude.

quiz.stem: A resultant measures 7.1 cm on a diagram drawn at 100 N = 1 cm. What is its magnitude?
rationales: Multiplying 7.1 cm by 100 N per centimetre gives 710 N.
This does not apply the stated scale correctly.
This treats the measured centimetres as newtons without using the scale.
This makes the result ten times too large.

quiz.stem: What does the resultant force represent?
options: A single vector representing the combined effect of the forces
The longest force in the group
The angle between the first two forces only
The force with the smallest magnitude
rationales: The resultant is the single vector that represents the combined effect of the forces.
The resultant need not be the longest individual force.
An angle alone is not a resultant force.
The smallest force alone does not represent all the forces together.

quiz.stem: In a force-addition diagram, what does the measured angle of the resultant tell you?
options: It shows the direction of the resultant relative to the x-axis
It gives the scale used to draw the arrows
It gives the magnitude of every individual force
It shows that the resultant must be zero
rationales: The angle states the resultant's direction relative to the chosen axis.
The scale is chosen separately and is not given by the resultant angle.
One resultant angle does not give the magnitudes of every individual force.
A direction angle does not mean that the resultant has zero magnitude.

quiz.stem: What is the magnitude of the torque when a force acts perpendicularly to its moment arm?
rationales: This is correct because torque is the product of force and moment arm.
This is incorrect because torque is not found by dividing force by moment arm.
This is incorrect because the moment arm is not divided by force.
This is incorrect because force multiplied by time is not the definition of torque.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes the moment arm of a force?
options: The distance from the axis to the point where the force is applied
The perpendicular distance from the line of action of the force to the axis of rotation
The length of the rotating object
The distance travelled by the object
rationales: This is not always the moment arm because the distance must be perpendicular to the line of action.
This is correct because the moment arm is the perpendicular distance from the force’s line of action to the axis.
This is incorrect because the object's full length need not be the perpendicular distance.
This is incorrect because the moment arm is a distance from the axis, not the distance travelled.

quiz.stem: According to the sign convention in this section, which torque is positive?
rationales: This is incorrect because clockwise torque is taken as negative.
This is correct because a force tending to produce anticlockwise rotation gives positive torque.
This is incorrect because a particular torque is assigned a direction according to the rotation it tends to produce.
This is incorrect because a force can produce a turning effect in either rotational direction.

quiz.stem: Which pair of forces forms a couple?
options: Two equal and opposite parallel forces acting at different points
Two equal forces acting at the same point in the same direction
One force acting through the axis of rotation
Two unequal forces acting along the same line
rationales: This is correct because equal and opposite parallel forces at different points form a couple.
This is incorrect because forces at the same point in the same direction do not form a couple.
This is incorrect because one force through the axis is not a pair of forces forming a couple.
This is incorrect because a couple consists of equal and opposite parallel forces.

quiz.stem: What is the SI unit of torque?
rationales: This is incorrect because the newton is the unit of force, not torque.
This is correct because torque is force multiplied by distance, so its SI unit is newton metre.
This is incorrect because metre per second is a unit of speed.
This is incorrect because kilogram metre is not the SI unit of torque.

quiz.stem: A force of 10 N makes an angle of 37° with the x-axis. Using cos 37° = 0.8, what is its x-component?
rationales: This is incorrect because the x-component is not 6 N for the given cosine value.
This is correct because F_x = F cos θ = 10 × 0.8 = 8 N.
This is incorrect because 10 N is the magnitude of the full force, not its x-component at 37°.
This is incorrect because the component cannot be greater than the force magnitude in this case.

quiz.stem: A force F makes an angle θ with the x-axis. Which expression gives its y-component?
rationales: This is incorrect because F cos θ gives the x-component when θ is measured from the x-axis.
This is correct because F_y = F sin θ.
This is incorrect because tangent gives the ratio of the perpendicular to the base, not the component directly.
This is incorrect because dividing by sin θ does not give the y-component.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes a component of a vector?
options: A component is the effective value of a vector in a given direction.
A component is always larger than the original vector.
A component is the angle between two vectors.
A component is the point where a vector begins.
rationales: This is correct because a component gives the effective value of a vector in a chosen direction.
This is incorrect because a component is not larger than the original vector.
This is incorrect because an angle is not a vector component.
This is incorrect because the starting point of a vector is not its component.

quiz.stem: What is the relationship between the rectangular components of a vector?
options: F_x is always equal to F_y.
F_x and F_y point in the same direction.
rationales: This is incorrect because rectangular components act along perpendicular axes.
This is correct because the x- and y-components are perpendicular to each other.
This is incorrect because their magnitudes depend on the force and its angle.
This is incorrect because the components act in different, perpendicular directions.

quiz.stem: A 20 N force acts at 90° to the x-axis. What is its x-component?
rationales: This is correct because F_x = 20 cos 90° = 0 N.
This is incorrect because the x-component is zero when the force is perpendicular to the x-axis.
This is incorrect because 10 N is not obtained from the cosine of 90°.
This is incorrect because the whole force points along the y-axis, not the x-axis.

quiz.stem: In a right-angled triangle, which ratio represents sin θ?
rationales: This is incorrect because base/hypotenuse represents cosine θ.
This is correct because sin θ is perpendicular/hypotenuse.
This is incorrect because it reverses the sine ratio.
This is incorrect because perpendicular/base represents tan θ.

quiz.stem: A force F points straight along the positive y-axis. What are its rectangular components?
rationales: This is incorrect because the force has no x-direction component.
This is correct because the full force lies along the y-axis and its x-component is zero.
This is incorrect because the force is not at an angle that divides it equally between the axes.
This is incorrect because the component magnitudes cannot both equal the full force in this direction.

quiz.stem: A force makes an angle of 45° with the x-axis. How do the magnitudes of its x- and y-components compare?
options: The x-component is greater than the y-component.
The y-component is greater than the x-component.
rationales: This is incorrect because sine and cosine have equal values at 45°.
This is incorrect because sine and cosine have equal values at 45°.
This is correct because F cos 45° = F sin 45°.
This is incorrect because a non-zero force at 45° has non-zero components.

quiz.stem: Two perpendicular components of a force are 3 N and 4 N. What is the magnitude of the force?
rationales: Correct: F = √(3² + 4²) = 5 N.
Incorrect: 7 N is the sum of the component magnitudes, not their perpendicular resultant.
Incorrect: 12 N is not obtained by applying Pythagoras to the components.
Incorrect: 25 is the squared magnitude, not the magnitude in newtons.

quiz.stem: A force F makes an angle θ with the horizontal x-axis. Which expression gives its x-component?
rationales: Incorrect: F sin θ gives the y-component for an angle measured from the x-axis.
Correct: The x-component is F_x = F cos θ.
Incorrect: F tan θ is not the expression for either component.
Incorrect: Dividing by cos θ does not give the x-component.

quiz.stem: A force F makes an angle θ with the horizontal x-axis. Which expression gives its y-component?
rationales: Correct: The y-component is F_y = F sin θ.
Incorrect: F cos θ gives the x-component for an angle measured from the x-axis.
Incorrect: F tan θ is not the expression for the y-component.
Incorrect: Dividing by sin θ does not give the y-component.

quiz.stem: Which equation gives the magnitude of a force from its perpendicular components?
rationales: Incorrect: Adding the magnitudes directly does not apply the Pythagorean theorem.
Correct: The magnitude is F = √(F_x² + F_y²).
Incorrect: This is the square of the magnitude, not the magnitude itself.
Incorrect: This ratio is not a formula for the magnitude.

quiz.stem: Which equation gives the angle θ of a force from its perpendicular components?
rationales: Incorrect: This reverses the component ratio and gives the wrong angle.
Incorrect: The section gives the direction using the tangent ratio, not this sine ratio.
Correct: The direction is θ = tan⁻¹(F_y/F_x).
Incorrect: The section does not use this cosine ratio to determine the direction.

quiz.stem: A 160 N force acts at 60° to the horizontal. What is its x-component? Use cos 60° = 0.5.
rationales: Incorrect: 100 N is not 160 × cos 60°.
Incorrect: 138.6 N is the y-component, found using sin 60°.
Incorrect: 160 N is the whole force, not its x-component.
Correct: F_x = F cos θ = 160 × 0.5 = 80 N.

quiz.stem: A 4 N force acts perpendicular to a bar at a distance of 3 m from its pivot. What is the magnitude of its moment?
rationales: This is correct because moment = force × perpendicular distance = 4 × 3 = 12 N m; the force's turning direction is clockwise in the stated arrangement.
The magnitude is 12 N m, but the stated arrangement turns clockwise, not anticlockwise.
This is incorrect because it does not equal 4 × 3.
This is incorrect because it does not equal 4 × 3 and gives the wrong direction.

quiz.stem: A beam is in rotational balance about a pivot. Which statement must be true?
options: The total clockwise and anticlockwise moments are equal
rationales: This would make the beam turn clockwise rather than remain balanced.
This would make the beam turn anticlockwise rather than remain balanced.
This is correct: in a balanced position, total clockwise and anticlockwise moments are equal.
A beam can have moments acting on it while still being balanced.

quiz.stem: A force of 2 N acts perpendicular to a lever at a distance of 3 m from the pivot. What is the moment?
rationales: This is incorrect because the force and distance must be multiplied.
This is correct because 2 × 3 = 6 N m.
This is incorrect because it is not the product of 2 N and 3 m.
This is incorrect because it doubles the correct product.

quiz.stem: A 12 N force balances a 6 N force acting 2 m from a pivot on the opposite side. How far from the pivot should the 12 N force act?
rationales: This distance would give a 3 N m moment, which is too small.
This distance would give a 6 N m moment, which is too small.
This is correct because 12 × d = 6 × 2, so d = 1 m.
This distance would give a 24 N m moment, which is too large.

quiz.stem: Which force produces zero moment about a pivot?
options: A force acting through the pivot
A force acting 0.5 m from the pivot
A force acting 1 m from the pivot
A force acting 2 m from the pivot
rationales: This is correct because the perpendicular distance from the pivot is zero.
This force has a non-zero perpendicular distance and can produce a moment.
This force has a non-zero perpendicular distance and can produce a moment.
This force has a non-zero perpendicular distance and can produce a moment.

quiz.stem: A 5 N force acts perpendicular to a rod 2 m from its pivot. What is the moment of the force?
rationales: This is incorrect because 5 × 2 is not 2.
This is incorrect because 5 × 2 is not 6.
This is correct because moment = force × distance = 5 × 2 = 10 N m.
This is incorrect because it is twice the correct product.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes the centre of gravity of a body?
options: The point where the body's total weight appears to act
The point where the body's speed is greatest
The point where the body touches the ground
The point where the body's volume is greatest
rationales: This is correct: the body's total weight appears to act at its centre of gravity.
This is incorrect because speed does not define the centre of gravity.
This is incorrect because the contact point with the ground need not be the centre of gravity.
This is incorrect because the centre of gravity is not defined by the body's volume.

quiz.stem: Where is the centre of gravity of a uniform round plate?
rationales: This is correct: the centre of gravity of a round plate is at the centre of the plate.
This is incorrect because diagonals are used to locate the centre of a square or rectangle.
This is incorrect because the medians locate the centre of gravity of a triangle.
This is incorrect because a corner is not the geometrical centre of a round plate.

quiz.stem: How can the centre of gravity of an irregular plane lamina be found experimentally?
options: At the intersection of two vertical lines drawn from suspension points
At the lowest point of the lamina
At the point where the lamina is thickest
At the first point from which it was suspended
rationales: This is correct: each vertical line passes through the centre of gravity, so their intersection locates it.
This is incorrect because the lowest point changes with the way the lamina is suspended.
This is incorrect because thickness does not determine the centre of gravity by this method.
This is incorrect because one suspension point gives only one vertical line, not the exact position.

quiz.stem: Where may the centre of gravity of an object lie?
options: It must always lie inside the material
It must always lie outside the material
It may lie inside or outside the material
It must always lie on the edge
rationales: This is incorrect because the centre of gravity of a cup can lie outside its material.
This is incorrect because many solid, regular objects have their centre of gravity inside them.
This is correct: the centre of gravity may be inside a body or outside it.
This is incorrect because the centre of gravity does not have to be on the object's edge.

quiz.stem: What is meant by the centre of mass of a body?
options: The whole mass of the body is assumed to be concentrated there
The whole weight of the body disappears there
The body has no acceleration there
The body must be supported there
rationales: This is correct: the centre of mass is the point where the body's whole mass is assumed to be concentrated.
This is incorrect because the body's weight does not disappear at the centre of mass.
This is incorrect because the definition of centre of mass does not mean acceleration is zero.
This is incorrect because a body need not be supported at its centre of mass.

quiz.stem: On Earth's surface, where gravitational acceleration is almost uniform, how are the centre of mass and centre of gravity related?
options: They are always at opposite ends
The centre of mass is always above the centre of gravity
rationales: This is correct: in an almost uniform gravitational field, the centre of mass coincides with the centre of gravity.
This is incorrect because the two points do not have to be at opposite ends.
This is incorrect because there is no general rule that one point is above the other.
This is incorrect because the textbook states that the two points coincide where g is almost uniform.

quiz.stem: Where is the centre of gravity of a uniform triangular lamina?
options: At the intersection of the diagonals
At the intersection of the medians
At the centre of the axis
At the centre of the sphere
rationales: This is incorrect because the intersection of the diagonals gives the centre for a square or rectangle.
This is correct: the centre of gravity of a triangle is at the intersection of its medians.
This is incorrect because the centre of the axis is listed for a cylinder.
This is incorrect because the centre of a sphere is its centre of gravity.

quiz.stem: A rotating wrench slides along a frictionless floor with no resultant force on it. What does its centre of mass do?
options: It follows a straight-line path at constant speed
It moves in a circle because the wrench rotates
It remains fixed because there is no resultant force
It accelerates in the direction of the wrench's rotation
rationales: This is correct: with no resultant force, the centre of mass follows a linear path with constant speed.
This is incorrect because the wrench's rotation does not make the centre of mass move in a circle.
This is incorrect because no resultant force does not mean the centre of mass must remain fixed.
This is incorrect because the wrench's rotation does not make its centre of mass accelerate.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes a body in equilibrium?
options: It must have zero forces acting on it.
It must be moving with uniform velocity.
rationales: This is correct because the textbook defines equilibrium as having no acceleration.
This is wrong because a body moving with uniform velocity can also be in equilibrium.
This is wrong because forces may act but balance each other.
This is wrong because a body at rest can also be in equilibrium.

quiz.stem: A book lies motionless on a table. What is its state of equilibrium?
rationales: This is wrong because dynamic equilibrium describes motion with uniform velocity.
This is correct because a body at rest is in static equilibrium.
This is wrong because the book has no acceleration and its forces balance.
This is wrong because the book is supported by the table rather than falling freely.

quiz.stem: A body moves in a straight line with uniform velocity and has no acceleration. What kind of equilibrium is this?
rationales: This is wrong because static equilibrium describes a body at rest.
This is correct because a body moving with uniform velocity is in dynamic equilibrium.
This is wrong because no acceleration means the body is in equilibrium.
This is wrong because equilibrium requires no acceleration.

quiz.stem: When the resultant force on a body is zero, what can happen to it?
options: The body remains at rest or continues with uniform velocity.
rationales: This is correct: it can remain at rest or continue moving with uniform velocity.
This is wrong because a zero resultant force does not cause the body to speed up.
This is wrong because a zero resultant force does not cause a change in velocity.
This is wrong because a zero resultant force does not make a moving body stop.

quiz.stem: A book rests on a table. Which statement explains why it remains in equilibrium?
options: The book’s weight is greater than the normal force.
The normal force balances the book’s weight.
The book has no forces acting on it.
The table pulls the book downward.
rationales: This is wrong because unequal forces would give the book a resultant force.
This is correct because the upward normal force equals the downward weight.
This is wrong because both the weight and normal force act on the book.
This is wrong because the normal force from the table acts upward.

quiz.stem: A paratrooper descends with uniform velocity. Which forces are balanced?
options: The paratrooper has no forces acting on them.
Air resistance acts downward and is greater than gravity.
rationales: This is correct because upward air resistance balances downward gravity.
This is wrong because gravity acts downward on the paratrooper.
This is wrong because gravity and air resistance both act on the paratrooper.
This is wrong because air resistance acts upward and balances gravity.

quiz.stem: Which statement about forces on a body in equilibrium is correct?
options: Forces can act on a body without accelerating it if they balance.
Any force makes a body accelerate.
Only bodies at rest can have forces acting on them.
A body in equilibrium has no weight.
rationales: This is correct because balanced forces can act without accelerating the body.
This is wrong because a body's acceleration depends on the resultant force, not merely the presence of a force.
This is wrong because forces can act on moving bodies too.
This is wrong because a body can have weight while in equilibrium.

quiz.stem: Which set of conditions must be satisfied for a body to be in complete equilibrium?
rationales: These two force conditions alone do not rule out a turning effect.
Zero net torque alone does not rule out a non-zero resultant force.
All force components and the net torque must be zero for complete equilibrium.
A non-zero net torque means the body can rotate, so it is not in complete equilibrium.

quiz.stem: According to the first condition of equilibrium, what must be zero?
options: Only the weight of the body
The vector sum of all external forces
The largest force acting on the body
The force acting through its centre
rationales: The weight need not be zero; it can be balanced by other forces.
The first condition requires the vector sum of all external forces to be zero.
The largest individual force need not be zero or cancelled by one force alone.
A force through the centre is not the general statement of the first condition.

quiz.stem: Which equation expresses the second condition of equilibrium?
rationales: This is the force-balance condition along the x-axis.
This is the force-balance condition along the y-axis.
The second condition requires the vector sum of torques to be zero.
These two equations express the first condition, not the second.

quiz.stem: When applying the conditions of equilibrium, how should each selected object be treated?
options: It must be treated together with every other object
Only its weight should be shown
The forces it exerts on its environment must be included
rationales: The textbook method selects objects and treats each one separately.
This is the stated method: each object should be treated separately.
The diagram should show all forces acting on the object, not just its weight.
The diagram includes forces acting on the object, not forces it exerts on its environment.

quiz.stem: How should axes be chosen to simplify an equilibrium problem?
options: Choose axes that make as many forces as possible lie along the axes
Always choose the axes horizontally and vertically
Choose axes so that every force is diagonal
Choose axes only after solving the equations
rationales: This reduces the number of forces that need to be resolved into components.
Horizontal and vertical axes are not always the most convenient choice.
Making every force diagonal would usually increase the number of components needed.
Axes are chosen before resolving forces and applying the equations.

quiz.stem: Two equal and opposite forces can have zero resultant force but still turn a body when:
options: The forces have equal magnitudes and opposite directions
The forces act along the same line of action
rationales: Different magnitudes generally give a non-zero resultant force.
With separated lines of action, equal and opposite forces can form a couple and produce torque.
Forces along the same line of action do not form the separated-force couple described.
A body's weight does not determine whether the pair of forces produces torque.

quiz.stem: A body has ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0, but Στ is not zero. What is true?
rationales: The resultant force is zero, so the first condition is satisfied.
A non-zero sum of torques means rotational equilibrium is not satisfied.
Complete equilibrium requires the torque sum to be zero as well.
The force conditions are satisfied, so it is not correct to say there is no force equilibrium.

quiz.stem: A picture hangs at rest from two strings. Which statement describes its equilibrium?
options: The centre of gravity is at the highest position
The upward forces equal the downward forces and the torque sum is zero
Every force on the body is zero
rationales: This is not a condition for equilibrium.
At rest, its forces and torques balance; these are the equilibrium conditions.
Individual forces can be non-zero while their vector sum is zero.
A hanging picture has mass; its weight is balanced by the strings.

quiz.stem: What happens to a body in stable equilibrium after a slight tilt?
options: It returns to its original position
It moves farther away from its original position
It stays in its new position
rationales: This is the defining behaviour of stable equilibrium.
Moving farther away describes unstable equilibrium.
Remaining in the new position describes neutral equilibrium.
Stable equilibrium does not mean that the body must topple.

quiz.stem: What happens to the centre of mass when a cone standing on its base is tilted slightly?
options: Its centre of mass is lowered on tilting
Its centre of mass is raised on tilting
Its centre of mass stays at the same height
rationales: The centre of mass is lowered in the unstable case, such as a cone balanced on its tip.
Tilting a cone on its base raises its centre of mass, helping produce a restoring effect.
Unchanged height is associated with neutral equilibrium.
Tilting does not make the cone's weight zero.

quiz.stem: A cone balanced on its tip falls farther away from its original position after a slight tilt. What state is this?
rationales: A stable body would return to its starting position.
Moving farther away after a slight tilt is unstable equilibrium.
A neutral body would rest in its new position without moving farther away.
The cone is momentarily balanced before the tilt, so this is not the best description.

quiz.stem: Why does a cylinder rolling on a horizontal surface show neutral equilibrium?
options: Its centre of mass remains at the same height
Its centre of mass rises continuously
Its centre of mass falls continuously
rationales: The height of the cylinder's centre of mass remains unchanged as it rolls.
A continuous rise in centre-of-mass height is not the reason for neutral equilibrium.
A continuous fall would cause the body to move farther away, not describe the stated neutral case.
The cylinder's base does not disappear; this is unrelated to equilibrium.

quiz.stem: Why can a body topple when its centre of mass is no longer above its base of support?
options: The weight's line of action lies outside the base of support
The floor stops exerting a reaction
rationales: The body topples when the line of action of its weight no longer lies within the base of support.
Toppling does not require the body's weight to become larger.
The floor can still exert a reaction while the body topples.
The centre of mass does not disappear when the body is tilted.

quiz.stem: Which object is an example of stable equilibrium?
options: A ball resting on a horizontal surface
A cone standing on its circular base
A cone balanced on its tip
A body that returns after a slight tilt
rationales: A ball rolling on a horizontal surface is given as an example of neutral equilibrium.
A cone on its circular base returns after a slight tilt and is stable.
A cone balanced on its tip is unstable.
Returning after a slight tilt describes stable equilibrium, but this option is a description rather than an object.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes neutral equilibrium?
options: The height of its centre of mass changes
It comes to rest in its new position without a change in its centre of mass
It always returns to its original position
It moves farther away from its original position
rationales: A change in centre-of-mass height is not the defining feature of neutral equilibrium.
This gives the defining behaviour of neutral equilibrium.
Returning to the original position describes stable equilibrium.
Moving farther away describes unstable equilibrium.

quiz.stem: For a balanced body to remain supported without toppling, which condition is important?
options: The body's centre of mass is always outside its body
The body's centre of mass lies above the base of support
The body has no point of support
rationales: The centre of mass is not always outside the body, and this is not the support condition.
The section explains that a body remains in equilibrium as long as its centre of mass lies within its base.
The weight acts downward, not horizontally.
A balanced supported body has a point of support.

quiz.stem: Which change generally makes a standing object more stable?
options: Place all its load at the top.
rationales: Raising the centre of gravity generally makes toppling easier, not harder.
A lower centre of gravity makes the object more stable.
A narrower base generally makes the object less stable.
A load at the top raises the centre of gravity and reduces stability.

quiz.stem: Why does placing heavy loads on the floor of a bus improve its stability?
options: It lowers the bus's centre of gravity.
It raises the bus's centre of gravity.
It makes the bus's base narrower.
rationales: Loads low down lower the bus's centre of gravity, improving stability.
Loads on the floor do not raise the centre of gravity; they lower it.
Placing loads on the floor does not make the bus's base narrower.
The loads still have weight; moving them does not remove it.

quiz.stem: Which design change can improve the stability of a system?
options: Place its heaviest parts as high as possible.
rationales: A wider base makes toppling less likely.
A higher centre of gravity makes toppling more likely.
A narrower base generally reduces stability.
Putting heavy parts high raises the centre of gravity and reduces stability.

quiz.stem: Which combination is most helpful for improving stability?
options: A low centre of gravity and a wide base.
A high centre of gravity and a narrow base.
A high centre of gravity and a wide base only.
A low centre of gravity and a narrow base only.
rationales: Both a low centre of gravity and a wide base improve stability.
Both a high centre of gravity and a narrow base tend to reduce stability.
A high centre of gravity is not helpful for stability.
A narrow base is not helpful for stability.

quiz.stem: A bus loaded with heavy steel sheets on its top is less stable mainly because:
options: Its centre of gravity is raised.
Its centre of gravity is lowered.
rationales: Putting heavy loads high raises the bus's centre of gravity.
The centre of gravity is raised, not lowered.
The loading described does not make the base wider.
The bus's weight does not disappear when it is loaded.

quiz.stem: In the tilted-chair illustration, what does the couple formed by the chair's weight and the ground's reaction tend to do?
options: It forms a clockwise couple that tends to overturn the chair backward.
It lowers the chair's centre of gravity and restores it upright.
It makes the chair's base wider.
It removes the reaction force from the ground.
rationales: The textbook describes this clockwise couple as tending to overturn the chair backward.
The described couple tends to overturn the chair, not restore it upright.
Tilting the chair does not make its base wider.
The ground's reaction force is shown; it is not removed.

quiz.stem: A body in stable equilibrium is generally in a position where its centre of gravity is:
options: It is stable because its centre of gravity is at its lowest position.
It is unstable because its centre of gravity is at its lowest position.
It is stable only if it has a narrow base.
It cannot be affected by a turning couple.
rationales: A stable position corresponds to a low position of the centre of gravity.
A low centre of gravity is associated with stability, not instability.
A narrow base generally does not improve stability.
A turning couple can affect a body, so it is not immune to one.

quiz.stem: Which loading and design choice would best help a double-decker bus resist overturning?
options: Loads low down and a broad base.
Loads high up and a broad base.
Loads low down and a narrow base.
Loads high up and a narrow base.
rationales: Low loads lower the centre of gravity, and a broad base improves stability.
A broad base helps, but high loads raise the centre of gravity.
Low loads help, but a narrow base is less stable.
Both high loads and a narrow base tend to reduce stability.

quiz.stem: Which design change best improves the stability of a racing car?
options: Keep the centre of mass high and make the base narrow.
Keep the centre of mass low and increase the base area.
Keep the centre of mass low and make the base narrow.
Keep the centre of mass high and increase the base area.
rationales: A high centre of mass and narrow base make toppling easier.
Correct: a low centre of mass and a wider base make toppling less likely.
A narrow base reduces stability even if the centre of mass is low.
A high centre of mass makes toppling more likely despite the wider base.

quiz.stem: Where does the centre of gravity of a balancing toy remain in its stable state?
options: At the edge of the toy.
At any position, because its position does not matter.
rationales: A centre of gravity above the pivot would not describe the stable arrangement given in the section.
Correct: in these toys the centre of gravity remains below the pivot point.
The section does not say that it remains at the edge of the toy.
The position matters; the section states that it remains below the pivot.

quiz.stem: What happens to a balancing toy when it is disturbed from its stable position?
options: It becomes lower, so the toy moves farther from its initial position.
It is raised, and the toy returns by lowering it.
It stays at the same height, so the toy remains disturbed.
It moves above the pivot and stays there.
rationales: The section says the centre of gravity is raised when the toy is disturbed.
Correct: it is raised momentarily, then lowered as the toy returns to its stable position.
The centre of gravity is raised when the toy is disturbed, not kept at the same height.
The section says the centre of gravity is below the pivot in the stable state; it does not say the toy stays above the pivot.

quiz.stem: Which rotational-motion quantity plays the same role as force does in translational motion?
rationales: Angular velocity is paired with velocity, not force.
Angular acceleration is paired with acceleration, not force.
Correct: moment of force (torque) is the counterpart of force.
Angular momentum is paired with momentum, not force.

quiz.stem: In which direction is the velocity of a body moving along a circular path at any point?
options: Along the radius, away from the centre.
Along the tangent to the circular path.
Towards the centre of the circle.
At right angles to the plane of the circle.
rationales: The section states that velocity is directed along the tangent, not the radius.
Correct: the velocity at each point is along the tangent to the circle.
The inward direction is the direction of the required force, not the velocity.
The section identifies the tangent direction in the plane of the circular path.

quiz.stem: For uniform-speed motion in a circular path, how is the required force directed relative to velocity?
options: It acts in the same direction as velocity.
It has no relation to velocity.
rationales: A force along the velocity would change the magnitude of velocity.
Correct: the force is perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes direction without changing speed.
A force opposite to velocity would change the speed.
The section states that the force is essentially perpendicular to velocity.

quiz.stem: Why must the force in uniform circular motion be perpendicular to the velocity?
options: It would have a component along the velocity and change the magnitude of velocity.
It would make the centre of gravity lower.
It would increase the base area of the object.
It would change the tangent into a radius.
rationales: Correct: a component of force along the velocity changes the magnitude of velocity, so the speed would not remain constant.
The direction of force does not determine the height of the centre of gravity in this explanation.
The direction of force cannot change the object's base area.
A force does not change the tangent direction into a radius; velocity remains tangent to the path.

quiz.stem: In uniform circular motion, what is the direction of centripetal force?
options: Towards the centre of the circle
Along the tangent to the circle
Away from the centre of the circle
In the direction of the object's velocity
rationales: This is correct: centripetal force is always directed towards the centre.
The tangent gives the direction of velocity, not centripetal force.
Centripetal force points inward, not away from the centre.
Velocity is along the tangent and is perpendicular to centripetal force.

quiz.stem: Which relation gives the magnitude of centripetal force?
rationales: This is correct: the textbook relation is F_c = mv²/r.
This is not the centripetal-force relation; the speed and radius are placed incorrectly.
This is not the textbook relation; the powers of speed and radius are incorrect.
This is not the textbook relation; radius is multiplied rather than divided.

quiz.stem: At any point on a circular path, in which direction does the object's velocity act?
options: The velocity is along the radius
The velocity is along the tangent to the circle
The velocity points towards the centre
The velocity points away from the centre
rationales: The radius points towards the centre and is not the direction of velocity.
This is correct: velocity acts along the tangent to the circular path.
This describes the direction of centripetal force, not velocity.
Velocity is tangent to the path, not directed away from its centre.

quiz.stem: What provides the centripetal force when a stone is whirled in a circle on a string?
rationales: This is correct: tension in the string pulls the stone towards the centre.
The textbook example identifies string tension as the centripetal force; gravity is neglected there.
Speed is a property of the motion, not the force supplying the inward pull.
The tangent indicates the velocity direction and does not provide the inward force.

quiz.stem: What supplies the centripetal force that keeps the Moon in orbit around Earth?
options: The Moon's distance from Earth alone
The Moon's velocity along its orbit
rationales: Speed alone does not provide the force needed to keep the Moon in its orbit.
This is correct: Earth's gravitational pull supplies the necessary centripetal force.
Distance alone is not a force and cannot supply centripetal force.
Velocity describes the Moon's motion; Earth's gravity supplies the inward force.

quiz.stem: In a rapidly rotating washing-machine dryer, what provides centripetal force to the clothes?
options: Friction between the clothes and drum wall
rationales: This is correct: friction between the clothes and drum walls provides the needed centripetal force.
The textbook explanation identifies friction with the drum wall, not weight, as the source.
The holes let water escape but do not provide the clothes' centripetal force.
The textbook explanation does not identify the air as the source of the centripetal force.

quiz.stem: For an object of fixed mass moving in a circle of fixed radius, what happens to centripetal force if its speed increases?
options: Increasing the radius increases centripetal force
Increasing the speed increases centripetal force
Centripetal force is independent of mass
Centripetal force is always zero at constant speed
rationales: At fixed mass and speed, a greater radius gives a smaller force because F_c = mv²/r.
This is correct: centripetal force is proportional to the square of speed.
The relation includes mass, so centripetal force depends on mass.
A constant speed in a circular path still requires centripetal force to change the direction of motion.

quiz.stem: Why can water escape through the holes of a rapidly rotating dryer drum?
options: The water molecules receive a larger centripetal force than the clothes
The water molecules cannot get the required centripetal force to move in circular paths
The drum stops rotating when the water reaches the holes
The water molecules move towards the centre of the drum
rationales: The textbook explanation says the free water molecules cannot get the required centripetal force.
This is correct: without the required inward force, the water molecules escape through the holes.
The drum continues rotating; its rotation is what helps separate water from the clothes.
The water escapes through the holes rather than gathering at the centre.

quiz.stem: Work done is maximum when the angle between the force F and the displacement d is:
rationales: Correct: work is W = Fd cos θ, which is greatest when cos θ = 1 at 0°.
Incorrect: at 30°, cos θ is less than 1, so the work is less than its maximum.
Incorrect: at 60°, cos θ is less than 1, so the work is less than its maximum.
Incorrect: at 90°, cos θ = 0, so the work done is zero.

quiz.stem: A joule can also be written as:
rationales: Incorrect: kg m s⁻² is the unit of force, a newton.
Incorrect: kg m s⁻¹ is the unit of momentum.
Incorrect: kg m² s⁻³ is the unit of power, a watt.
Correct: a joule is a newton-metre, equivalent to kg m² s⁻².

quiz.stem: The SI unit of power is:
rationales: Incorrect: a joule is the SI unit of energy, not power.
Incorrect: a newton is the SI unit of force.
Correct: the watt is the SI unit of power.
Incorrect: a second is the SI unit of time.

quiz.stem: The power of a water pump is 2 kW. The amount of water it can raise in one minute to a height of 5 metres is:
rationales: Incorrect: 1000 litres would require only about 49 kJ to raise 5 m, less than the pump supplies in one minute.
Incorrect: 1200 litres would require about 59 kJ, less than the pump supplies in one minute.
Incorrect: 2000 litres would require about 98 kJ, less than the pump supplies in one minute.
Correct: the pump supplies 120,000 J in one minute, enough to raise about 2400 kg (approximately 2400 litres) by 5 m using g ≈ 10 m s⁻².

quiz.stem: A bullet of mass 0.05 kg has a speed of 300 m s⁻¹. Its kinetic energy will be:
rationales: Correct: kinetic energy is ½mv² = ½ × 0.05 × 300² = 2250 J.
Incorrect: 4500 J is twice the kinetic energy calculated from ½mv².
Incorrect: 1500 J is below the value given by ½mv² for this mass and speed.
Incorrect: 1125 J is half the kinetic energy calculated from ½mv².

quiz.stem: If a car doubles its speed, its kinetic energy will be:
rationales: Incorrect: kinetic energy changes when speed changes.
Incorrect: because kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared, doubling speed does not merely double the energy.
Incorrect: doubling speed multiplies kinetic energy by four, not three.
Correct: kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared, so doubling speed increases it fourfold.

quiz.stem: The energy possessed by a body by virtue of its position is:
rationales: Incorrect: kinetic energy is energy due to motion, not position.
Correct: potential energy is energy a body has by virtue of its position.
Incorrect: chemical energy is stored in chemical bonds, not defined by position.
Incorrect: solar energy comes from the Sun and is not the energy defined by an object's position.

quiz.stem: The magnitude of momentum of an object is doubled, the kinetic energy of the object will:
rationales: Incorrect: at fixed mass, kinetic energy is proportional to momentum squared, so doubling momentum does not merely double the energy.
Correct: using K = p²/(2m), doubling momentum increases kinetic energy to four times its original value.
Incorrect: doubling momentum increases, rather than reduces, kinetic energy.
Incorrect: kinetic energy changes when momentum doubles.

quiz.stem: Which of the following is not renewable energy source?
rationales: Incorrect: hydroelectric energy is renewable because it is replenished by the water cycle.
Correct: fossil fuels are finite resources and are not renewable on human timescales.
Incorrect: wind energy is renewable because wind is continually replenished by atmospheric processes.
Incorrect: solar energy is renewable because sunlight is continually supplied by the Sun.

quiz.stem: A force of 4 N moves an object 3 m in the direction of the force. How much work is done?
rationales: This is correct because W = FS = 4 × 3 = 12 J.
This is incorrect because it does not equal the product of force and distance.
This is incorrect because the object moves in the direction of the applied force.
This is incorrect because it multiplies by an extra factor of 4.

quiz.stem: A force acts on an object, but the object does not move. What is the work done by that force?
options: The object has a large mass
The force acts for a long time
rationales: This is incorrect because a force can be non-zero even when no work is done.
This is correct because W = FS, and zero displacement makes the work zero.
This is incorrect because mass alone does not determine work.
This is incorrect because time alone does not determine work in this definition.

quiz.stem: A force F acts at an angle θ to the direction of motion over distance S. Which expression gives the work done?
rationales: This is incorrect unless the force is entirely along the direction of motion.
This is incorrect because the component along the motion is F cos θ.
This is correct because only the force component F cos θ acts along the displacement.
This is incorrect because force divided by distance is not work.

quiz.stem: A force acts perpendicular to an object's displacement. What is the work done by this force?
rationales: This is correct because cos 90° = 0 in W = FS cos θ.
This is incorrect because it would apply if force and displacement were in the same direction.
This is incorrect because work is not the sum of force and distance.
This is incorrect because force divided by distance is not work.

quiz.stem: What is the SI unit of work?
rationales: This is incorrect because a newton is the SI unit of force.
This is correct because the SI unit of work is the joule (J).
This is incorrect because a metre is a unit of distance.
This is incorrect because a watt is a unit of power.

quiz.stem: For a force-distance graph, what represents the work done by the force?
options: The slope of a force-distance graph
The area under a force-distance graph
The highest force shown on the graph
rationales: This is incorrect because the slope does not generally give the work.
This is correct because the area under the force-distance curve represents work done.
This is incorrect because force alone does not include the distance moved.
This is incorrect because distance alone does not include the force.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes kinetic energy?
options: The energy a body possesses by virtue of its motion
The energy a body possesses by virtue of its position
The force acting on a body
rationales: This is the definition of kinetic energy in your textbook.
This describes potential energy, not kinetic energy.
This describes power.
Force is not a form of energy.

quiz.stem: What is the SI unit of energy?
rationales: This is the unit of momentum.
Energy is measured in joules (J).
A newton is the SI unit of force.
A watt is the SI unit of power.

quiz.stem: Which expression gives the kinetic energy of a body of mass m moving with velocity v?
rationales: This expression is missing the square on velocity and the factor ½.
This expression is missing the factor ½.
This is the kinetic-energy relation derived in your textbook.
This gives gravitational potential energy for a body at height h.

quiz.stem: A body of mass m is raised through height h. Which expression gives its gravitational potential energy?
rationales: This is the expression for kinetic energy.
The work done in lifting the body is mgh, stored as potential energy.
This is not the relation for potential energy.
This gives the body's weight, not its energy.

quiz.stem: If the speed of a moving body is doubled while its mass stays the same, what happens to its kinetic energy?
options: It becomes four times as great.
rationales: Kinetic energy depends on the square of speed, so it does not merely double.
Since Eₖ = ½mv², doubling v multiplies Eₖ by 2² = 4.
Doubling speed increases, rather than reduces, kinetic energy.
The kinetic energy changes when the speed changes.

quiz.stem: Which statement about energy is correct?
rationales: Your textbook states that energy is scalar, not vector.
Energy, like work, is a scalar quantity.
Energy has the SI unit joule.
Energy is measured in joules; newtons measure force.

quiz.stem: What form of energy is stored in a compressed spring?
rationales: Chemical energy is stored in chemicals, such as those in a battery.
A compressed or stretched spring stores elastic potential energy.
Kinetic energy is the energy of motion.
Gravitational potential energy is associated with position relative to the Earth.

quiz.stem: When work is done on a body, what happens to energy?
options: The energy transferred to an object when work is done on it
The distance travelled by an object
The force needed to stop an object
The time taken to do work
