rationales: Energy is transferred to the body on which work is done.
Distance is not energy.
A stopping force may be used to determine kinetic energy, but it is not what energy means.
Time is not energy.

quiz.stem: A body falls freely from a height. Which statement best describes its energy transformation?
options: Potential energy changes into kinetic energy, while total energy stays constant.
Kinetic energy changes into potential energy, while total energy becomes zero.
Potential energy is destroyed as the body falls.
The body gains energy from the ground while falling.
rationales: Correct: as the body falls, potential energy changes into kinetic energy and the total remains constant.
Incorrect: a falling body generally loses potential energy and gains kinetic energy.
Incorrect: the conservation principle says energy is not destroyed.
Incorrect: the body's energy transformation occurs during the fall, not because the ground supplies energy.

quiz.stem: A body of mass m is at rest at height h above the ground. What is its total energy?
rationales: Correct: at rest its kinetic energy is zero, so its total energy is its potential energy mgh.
Incorrect: mgx is the kinetic energy at point B in the section's falling-body example.
Incorrect: mg(h − x) is the potential energy at point B, not the initial total energy.
Incorrect: the body has gravitational potential energy because it is raised above the ground.

quiz.stem: Just before a falling body reaches the ground, what is its kinetic energy if air resistance is negligible?
rationales: Correct: just before impact, all of its initial potential energy mgh has changed into kinetic energy.
Incorrect: this is the potential energy at point B, not the kinetic energy just before impact.
Incorrect: this is the kinetic energy at point B, not at ground level.
Incorrect: the body is moving just before impact, so its kinetic energy is not zero.

quiz.stem: According to the section, what happens to the body's energy when it hits the ground?
options: It is dissipated as heat and sound in the environment.
It becomes potential energy again while the body is still falling.
It remains stored as kinetic energy after the body has stopped.
rationales: Correct: the section says the energy is dissipated as heat and sound in the environment.
Incorrect: energy is not destroyed; it is transformed into other forms.
Incorrect: the section describes the energy as being dissipated on hitting the ground.
Incorrect: once the body has stopped, its energy is no longer retained as kinetic energy.

quiz.stem: In a fossil-fuel power station, what first uses the heat released by burning the fuel?
options: The burning fuel heats water to produce steam
The fuel directly turns the generator
The transformer changes fuel into steam
rationales: Correct: the heat is used to produce steam, which runs the turbine.
Incorrect: the steam turns the turbine, and the turbine runs the generator.
Incorrect: a condenser cools steam; it does not burn fuel.
Incorrect: a transformer changes voltage, not fuel into steam.

quiz.stem: What energy change occurs when water falls from a high reservoir in hydroelectric generation?
options: Chemical energy changes directly into electrical energy
Gravitational potential energy changes into kinetic energy as water falls
Nuclear energy changes into sound energy
Solar energy changes into gravitational potential energy
rationales: Incorrect: this is not the energy change described for falling reservoir water.
Correct: stored gravitational potential energy changes into kinetic energy as the water falls.
Incorrect: nuclear energy is not involved in this process.
Incorrect: the reservoir water's stored energy is gravitational potential energy, not solar energy.

quiz.stem: Which statement about solar cells agrees with your textbook?
options: Solar cells are also called photovoltaic cells
Solar cells work only by boiling water
A single solar cell gives a very high voltage
Solar cells are connected in parallel to make voltage sufficient
rationales: Correct: solar cells are also known as photovoltaic cells.
Incorrect: sunlight is transformed directly into electricity by solar cells; boiling water is another solar-energy method.
Incorrect: the voltage from a single voltaic cell is very low.
Incorrect: your textbook says many cells are connected in series to obtain sufficient voltage.

quiz.stem: Which material is named in your textbook as a nuclear fuel?
rationales: Incorrect: coal is a fossil fuel.
Correct: uranium is a nuclear fuel; plutonium is another example in the text.
Incorrect: wind is used to run wind generators, not as nuclear fuel.
Incorrect: sunlight is the source of solar energy.

quiz.stem: How is geothermal energy used to produce electricity in the method described in your textbook?
options: Cold water is pumped underground, heated by hot rocks and returned as steam
Hot rocks are burned at the surface to make fuel
Wind drives water through the hot rocks
A dam traps water above the hot rocks
rationales: Correct: cold water is heated by underground hot rocks, and the resulting steam runs a generator.
Incorrect: the rocks provide heat underground; they are not burned as fuel at the surface.
Incorrect: wind is not the mechanism used in the geothermal process described.
Incorrect: the described method pumps water down a drilled hole; it does not require a dam above the rocks.

quiz.stem: What does your textbook say may be needed for large-scale wind power generation?
options: A single windmill is always sufficient for large-scale generation
A wind farm with a hundred or more windmills may be needed for large-scale generation
Windmills generate electricity by burning biomass
Wind generators need falling water to turn their turbines
rationales: Incorrect: the text says a large wind farm may be needed.
Correct: a wind farm with a hundred or more windmills is given as the large-scale arrangement.
Incorrect: burning biomass is a separate energy method.
Incorrect: falling water is used in hydroelectric generation, not wind generation.

quiz.stem: According to your textbook, what gives rise to tides in the seas?
options: The Moon's gravitational force gives rise to tides
The Sun's heat makes the sea rise twice a day
Tides are caused by hot rocks beneath the sea
Tides are made by burning fossil fuels
rationales: Correct: the textbook attributes tides to the gravitational force of the Moon.
Incorrect: the text does not say that the Sun's heat causes the tides.
Incorrect: hot rocks are associated with geothermal energy.
Incorrect: burning fossil fuels does not cause tides.

quiz.stem: How is methane-rich biogas produced in a digester?
options: Micro-organisms break down biomass in the absence of oxygen
Biomass is frozen in a tank until it becomes methane
Biomass is mixed with steam in a turbine to make oxygen
Biomass is exposed to sunlight to produce coal
rationales: Correct: micro-organisms break down biomass in the absence of oxygen in the digester.
Incorrect: freezing biomass is not the method described.
Incorrect: the text describes breakdown without oxygen, not mixing biomass with steam to make oxygen.
Incorrect: sunlight does not turn biomass into coal in the described process.

quiz.stem: Which source is renewable according to the section?
rationales: Geothermal energy is listed as a renewable source.
Coal is a fossil fuel and is non-renewable.
The section identifies fuels for nuclear energy as limited.
Petroleum is a fossil fuel and is non-renewable.

quiz.stem: What is the defining feature of a renewable energy source?
options: They are replaced by new ones after use.
They are stored only in reservoirs.
They are made from buried plants and animals.
They are depleted with continuous use.
rationales: Renewable sources are replaced by new ones after use.
Being stored in reservoirs is not the definition of renewable energy.
Buried plants and animals form fossil fuels, which are non-renewable.
Depletion with continuous use describes non-renewable sources.

quiz.stem: Which of these sources is depleted with continuous use?
rationales: Wind energy is renewable.
Wave energy is renewable.
Fossil fuels are limited and are non-renewable.
Tidal energy is renewable.

quiz.stem: According to the section, how long did it take for buried plant and animal remains to change into fossil fuels?
rationales: The section says fossil fuels did not form in just a few days.
The section says their formation took much longer than a few months.
The section states that fossil fuels took millions of years to form.
The section says their formation took much longer than one year.

quiz.stem: Which source is identified as non-renewable in this section?
rationales: Solar energy is renewable.
Hydroelectricity is renewable.
Nuclear energy is listed among non-renewable sources.
Geothermal energy is renewable.

quiz.stem: Which continuous natural processes help replenish water supplies for hydroelectric power?
rationales: The section names snowfall and rainfall as continuous processes that supply water to dam reservoirs.
Burning fossil fuels does not replenish water supplies.
Using nuclear fuel does not replenish water supplies.
Mining coal does not replenish water supplies.

quiz.stem: Why does the section describe solar energy as renewable?
options: They are available only in dams.
They are not going to run out in future.
They take millions of years to form.
They are all made from plants and animals.
rationales: Solar energy is not available only in dams.

This is incorrect because the section says air is less dense, not denser, at high altitudes.
This is incorrect because the explanation concerns air density, not a change in mercury density.
This is incorrect because the section does not say gravity becomes zero at high altitude.

quiz.stem: Approximately how tall would a water column need to be to balance atmospheric pressure at sea level?
rationales: This is correct because water is much less dense than mercury, so the section's barometer calculation gives about 10.3 m.
This is incorrect because 0.76 m is the approximate height of mercury, not water.
This is incorrect because a 1.0 m water column would not balance sea-level atmospheric pressure.
This is incorrect because 13.6 m is not the result of the section's water-barometer calculation.

quiz.stem: How can observing atmospheric pressure help meteorologists?
options: It can indicate changes that help forecast weather
It directly measures the amount of rain in a cloud
It measures the temperature of the atmosphere
rationales: This is correct because meteorologists observe pressure variations to forecast weather conditions.
This is incorrect because a barometer measures pressure, not the amount of rain inside a cloud.
This is incorrect because atmospheric pressure measurement does not directly measure wind speed.
This is incorrect because a barometer measures pressure, not atmospheric temperature.

quiz.stem: Before a gas cylinder is connected, what happens to the mercury levels in a simple manometer?
options: The mercury levels in both arms are equal.
Mercury is lower in the open arm.
Mercury is lower in the arm connected to the gas.
rationales: This is correct because atmospheric pressure acts equally at both open ends.
This is wrong because equal atmospheric pressures do not create this level difference.
This is wrong because no gas pressure is acting in one arm yet.
This is wrong because equal pressure keeps the mercury in the tube.

quiz.stem: Mercury is lower in the arm connected to a gas cylinder than in the open arm. What does this indicate?
options: The gas pressure is greater than atmospheric pressure.
The gas pressure is less than atmospheric pressure.
The gas pressure equals atmospheric pressure.
The manometer cannot compare the pressures.
rationales: This is correct: the gas pushes the mercury down in its arm, showing greater pressure.
This is wrong because a lower mercury level in the gas-connected arm indicates greater, not less, gas pressure.
This is wrong because equal pressures would leave the mercury levels at the same height.
This is wrong because the level difference is used to compare the pressures.

quiz.stem: Mercury is higher in the arm connected to the gas than in the open arm. What does this indicate?
options: The gas pressure is greater than atmospheric pressure.
The gas pressure is less than atmospheric pressure.
rationales: This is wrong because greater gas pressure would push mercury lower in the connected arm.
This is correct: the gas pressure is less than atmospheric pressure.
This is wrong because the mercury level difference does not mean the gas pressure is zero.
This is wrong because the open arm is still subject to atmospheric pressure.

quiz.stem: Which apparatus is described as a simple manometer?
options: A U-shaped glass tube containing mercury
rationales: This is correct: the section describes a mercury-filled U-shaped glass tube.
This is wrong because the described manometer contains mercury in a U-shaped tube.
This is wrong because a sealed metal box is not the described apparatus.
This is wrong because a spring and pointer are not part of the described manometer.

quiz.stem: Why are the mercury levels equal in the two arms before a gas cylinder is connected?
options: Atmospheric pressure is the same at both open ends.
The two arms contain different liquids.
The tube is connected to a gas cylinder.
rationales: This is correct because equal atmospheric pressures act at the two open ends.
This is wrong because mercury has weight, and its levels balance under the equal pressures.
This is wrong because the section describes mercury in both arms.
This is wrong because the equal levels occur before a gas cylinder is connected.

quiz.stem: In the manometer diagrams, what does the label h indicate?
options: The vertical distance between the mercury levels
The length of the glass tube
The width of the gas cylinder
The depth of the tube below the table
rationales: This is correct: h marks the height difference between the two mercury levels.
This is wrong because h is shown between the mercury levels, not along the tube.
This is wrong because h is not a measurement of the cylinder.
This is wrong because h indicates the level difference, not the tube's position.

quiz.stem: According to Pascal's law, pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is:
options: It is transmitted equally to all parts of the enclosed fluid.
It is transmitted only towards the bottom of the container.
It becomes greater at every point in the fluid.
It is absorbed completely by the fluid.
rationales: This is the statement of Pascal's law.
Pascal's law applies in all directions, not only downwards.
The applied pressure is transmitted unchanged, not increased.
The fluid transmits the pressure rather than absorbing it.

quiz.stem: Which device works on Pascal's law?
rationales: A hydraulic press uses pressure transmitted through an enclosed liquid.
A simple pendulum works through oscillation under gravity.
A mercury thermometer works through expansion of mercury.
A spring balance works through extension of a spring.

quiz.stem: Why can a hydraulic press produce a force greater than the force applied to its small piston?
options: The larger piston has a greater area.
The larger piston has a smaller area.
The liquid increases the applied pressure.
rationales: The same pressure acts on the larger area, producing a greater force.
A smaller area would produce a smaller force at the same pressure.
Pascal's law transmits pressure without loss; it does not increase pressure.
The speed of the piston does not explain the force multiplication.

quiz.stem: Which property of the liquid helps a hydraulic system transmit pressure effectively?
rationales: The textbook identifies incompressibility as a reason liquids can move heavy loads and provide great forces.
A highly compressible fluid would not transmit the applied effect in the intended way.
Low density is not the stated reason hydraulic systems work.
Elasticity is not the property on which the hydraulic system is based.

quiz.stem: When a vehicle's brake pedal is pushed, what does the transmitted pressure cause?
options: The brake pads press towards the brake discs or drums.
The brake pads move away from the wheels.
The brake fluid is compressed and absorbs all pressure.
rationales: The pressure moves the larger pistons outward, pressing the pads towards the discs or drums.
The pads are pressed towards the discs or drums when the pedal is pushed.
The system uses liquid to transmit pressure; it does not absorb all of it.
Friction from the pads slows the vehicle rather than making the wheels turn faster.

quiz.stem: Which expression gives the pressure produced by a force F on a piston of area A?
rationales: Pressure is force acting normally per unit area.
Multiplying force by area does not give pressure.
Area divided by force is not the pressure definition.
Adding force and area does not give pressure.

quiz.stem: A hydraulic press has small-piston area A₁ and large-piston area A₂. Which equation follows from equal pressure at both pistons?
rationales: Equating F₁/A₁ and F₂/A₂ gives F₂ = F₁A₂/A₁.
This reverses the area ratio and does not follow from equal pressure.
This does not follow from the pressure equation.
Force and area cannot be combined by addition to obtain the output force.

quiz.stem: What is the basic Pascal's-law process in a hydraulic brake system?
options: The pressure applied at the master cylinder is transmitted through the brake fluid.
The brake fluid changes into a gas.
The brake pedal directly touches every brake pad.
The wheels stop because the liquid pressure disappears.
rationales: Pressure applied at the master cylinder is transmitted equally through the liquid to the wheel cylinders.
The system is filled with oil and relies on transmitted pressure, not a liquid-to-gas change.
The pedal acts on the master cylinder; it does not directly touch every brake pad.
The pressure moves the pistons and creates friction; it does not disappear as the cause of stopping.

quiz.stem: How do the molecules in a solid behave?
options: Rotate and vibrate randomly at their own positions
Move in a straight line from hot to cold ends.
rationales: Solids do not move randomly from place to place; their particles remain in fixed positions.
Solid molecules vibrate about their mean positions.
Rotational motion is not the characteristic motion of molecules in a solid.
Molecules in a solid do not travel from the hot end to the cold end.

quiz.stem: What type of motion is of the molecules in a gas?
rationales: Gas molecules do not move only in one straight line; they change direction in collisions.
Gas molecules move randomly, traveling in different directions between collisions.
Gas molecules are not limited to vibratory motion about fixed positions.
Gas molecules are not limited to rotational motion.

quiz.stem: Temperature of a substance is:
options: the total amount of heat contained in it
the total number of molecules in it
rationales: Temperature is not the total amount of heat in a substance.
Temperature does not measure how many molecules a substance contains.
Temperature indicates the degree of hotness or coldness of a substance.
Temperature is not defined by the distance between molecules.

quiz.stem: Heat is the:
options: total kinetic energy of the molecules
rationales: Heat is not the total kinetic energy of the molecules; that is related to a substance’s internal energy.
Heat is not simply the internal energy stored in a substance.
Work done by molecules is not the definition of heat.
Heat is energy transferred from one body to another because of a temperature difference.

quiz.stem: In Kelvin scale, the temperature corresponding to melting point of ice is:
rationales: Zero kelvin is absolute zero, not the melting point of ice.
32 is the melting point of ice in degrees Fahrenheit, not kelvins.
−273°C is approximately absolute zero, not the melting point of ice.
The melting point of ice is approximately +273 K.

quiz.stem: The temperature which has the same value on Celsius and Fahrenheit scale is:
rationales: −40 has the same numerical value on the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales.
+40°C and +40°F are different temperatures.
+45°C and +45°F are different temperatures.
−45°C and −45°F are different temperatures.

quiz.stem: Which one is a better choice for a liquid-in-glass thermometer?
rationales: Being colourless makes a liquid harder to see in the thermometer tube.
Being a bad conductor is not the key property that ensures accurate liquid expansion readings.
A suitable thermometric liquid should expand uniformly, or nearly linearly, with temperature.
A liquid that wets the glass can leave a film and make the reading less reliable.

quiz.stem: One disadvantage of using alcohol in a liquid-in-glass thermometer:
rationales: Alcohol’s large expansivity is generally an advantage because it makes temperature changes easier to detect.
Alcohol’s low freezing point is an advantage for measuring low temperatures.
Alcohol wets the glass, which can make the thermometer reading less reliable.
Alcohol’s approximately linear expansion is an advantage for a thermometric liquid.

quiz.stem: Water is not used as a thermometric liquid mainly due to:
rationales: Water’s lack of colour is inconvenient but is not the main reason it is unsuitable.
Water’s relatively poor thermal conductivity is not the main limitation cited for its use in thermometers.
Water expands non-linearly over a range of temperatures, making its scale unreliable.
A boiling point of 100°C limits the range but is not the main reason given here.

quiz.stem: A thermometer has a narrow capillary tube so that it:
options: gives a large change for a given temperature rise
can measure a large range of temperature
rationales: A narrow capillary does not by itself make the thermometer respond more quickly to temperature changes.
A narrow capillary does not allow a thermometer to record the maximum temperature.
A narrow capillary makes a small volume expansion produce a larger visible movement of the liquid column.
A narrow capillary does not increase the thermometer’s measurable temperature range.

quiz.stem: Which thermometer is most suitable for recording rapidly varying temperature?
rationales: A thermocouple thermometer responds quickly and is well suited to rapidly varying temperatures.
A mercury-in-glass laboratory thermometer responds more slowly than a thermocouple.
An alcohol-in-glass thermometer is not as suitable as a thermocouple for rapidly changing temperatures.
A clinical thermometer is designed for body-temperature measurement, not rapid temperature variations.

quiz.stem: According to the kinetic molecular theory, how do molecules in a solid move?
options: They move freely from place to place.
rationales: Solids do not have molecules moving freely from place to place.
Correct: solid molecules remain at fixed positions but vibrate about them.
Solid molecules are not motionless; they vibrate.
Particles far apart are characteristic of gases, not solids.

quiz.stem: Which feature of liquid molecules helps a liquid take the shape of its container?
options: Their molecules are fixed in position.
Their molecules can slide over one another.
Their molecules are spread throughout the whole container.
rationales: The section says liquids have intermolecular forces, though these are too weak to hold molecules fixed.
Fixed positions are characteristic of molecules in a solid.
Correct: liquid molecules can slide over one another in random directions, allowing the liquid to flow.
Particles spread throughout a container describe a gas.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes a gas according to the particle model in this section?
options: It has a definite shape and volume.
It has a definite volume but no definite shape.
It has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume.
It has a definite shape but no definite volume.
rationales: A gas does not have a definite shape or volume.
This describes a liquid.
Correct: gas molecules are far apart, so a gas has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume.
This is not a property of a gas in the section.

quiz.stem: What happens to intermolecular force when the distance between molecules increases?
options: Intermolecular force increases as distance increases.
Intermolecular force decreases as distance increases.
Intermolecular force does not depend on distance.
rationales: This reverses the relationship stated in the section.
Correct: intermolecular force decreases with increasing distance between molecules.
The section describes a mutual force of attraction, not a force that is always zero.
The section states that intermolecular force depends on distance.

quiz.stem: According to the section, what happens to a substance's molecular motion when it is heated?
options: The average kinetic energy of its molecules increases.
Its molecules' potential energy becomes zero.
Its molecules become fixed in place.
rationales: Correct: heating makes molecular motion more vigorous, increasing the molecules' kinetic energy.
Heating does not stop molecular motion.
The section does not say that heating makes potential energy zero.
Heating does not make all molecules fixed in place.

quiz.stem: Which description best identifies plasma?
options: A gas in which most atoms are ionized, containing positive ions and electrons.
A solid made only of neutral atoms.
A liquid in which molecules are fixed in position.
A gas whose particles cannot conduct electricity.
rationales: Correct: the section describes plasma as a gas with most atoms ionized and containing positive ions and electrons.
Plasma is not described as a solid made only of neutral atoms.
This does not describe plasma or a liquid.
Plasma conducts electricity because it contains positive ions and free electrons.

quiz.stem: Which property is specifically linked to the presence of positive ions and free electrons in plasma?
options: A liquid takes the shape of its container.
A solid has a definite volume.
A gas has no definite volume.
Plasma allows electric current to pass through it.
rationales: This happens because liquid molecules flow; it is not specifically due to ions and electrons.
A solid's definite volume is explained by its closely bound molecules.
A gas's lack of definite volume is explained by its widely spaced molecules.
Correct: positive ions and free electrons make plasma a conducting state of matter.

quiz.stem: What does the temperature of a body describe?
options: A measure of the total number of molecules
The degree of hotness or coldness
Energy stored only in a solid
The amount of matter in a body
rationales: Temperature does not count the molecules in a body.
This is the definition of temperature given in the section.
Internal energy is not energy stored only in a solid.
The amount of matter is not the definition of temperature.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes heat?
options: Energy transferred due to a temperature difference
The sum of all molecular masses
The temperature of the colder object
Energy that remains at rest inside a body
rationales: Heat is energy transferred between objects because their temperatures differ.
Molecular mass is not heat.
Temperature difference causes heat transfer, but heat is not the colder object's temperature.
The section uses heat for energy in transit, not energy at rest inside a body.

quiz.stem: Two bodies have different temperatures. In which direction does thermal energy transfer?
options: From the colder body to the hotter body
From the body at higher temperature to the body at lower temperature
In both directions only when the bodies are identical
Only from a solid to a liquid
rationales: This reverses the direction of heat transfer described in the section.
Thermal energy transfers from higher temperature to lower temperature.
The direction depends on the temperature difference, not whether the bodies are identical.
Heat transfer is not restricted to solids and liquids.

quiz.stem: What is the internal energy of an object?
options: The sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its molecules
The energy transferred to it during the last minute
rationales: Internal energy includes molecular potential energy as well as kinetic energy.
Internal energy includes molecular kinetic energy as well as potential energy.
This is the definition of internal energy in the section.
Energy transferred is called heat; internal energy is the sum of molecular kinetic and potential energies.

quiz.stem: According to the section, what happens when a substance is heated?
options: Its molecules move more vigorously and its internal energy increases
Its molecules become fixed in place
rationales: Heating makes molecular motion more vigorous, not stopped.
Heating increases molecular motion and internal energy, so the temperature rises.
The section does not say that potential energy disappears.
Molecules do not become fixed in place when a substance is heated.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes heat from internal energy?
options: A substance contains internal energy; heat refers to energy in transit
Heat and internal energy are exactly the same thing
Only hot substances have internal energy
rationales: The section says it is not true to say that a substance contains heat.
This matches the section's distinction between internal energy in a body and heat in transit.
The section distinguishes heat from internal energy rather than treating them as identical.
Molecules in matter possess kinetic and potential energies; the section does not limit internal energy to hot substances.

quiz.stem: What is a thermometric property?
options: It is a property that remains unchanged when temperature changes.
It is a property that changes appreciably when temperature changes.
It is the amount of heat stored in a body.
It is the fixed point used only on the Celsius scale.
rationales: This is incorrect because a thermometer needs a property that changes with temperature.
This is correct because thermometers use a property that changes appreciably with temperature.
This is incorrect because heat is energy in transit, not a thermometric property.
This is incorrect because thermometric properties are not limited to one temperature scale.

quiz.stem: Which fixed point is the upper fixed point on a temperature scale?
rationales: This is correct because the steam point is the upper fixed point.
This is incorrect because the ice point is the lower fixed point.
This is incorrect because absolute zero is not the upper fixed point used to construct the scales described here.
This is incorrect because room temperature is not one of the two fixed points.

quiz.stem: Into how many equal parts is the interval between the ice and steam points divided on the Fahrenheit scale?
rationales: This is incorrect because 100 equal parts are used on the Celsius and Kelvin scales.
This is correct because the Fahrenheit fixed-point values differ by 212 − 32 = 180.
This is incorrect because 273 is the Kelvin value assigned to the ice point in the textbook.
This is incorrect because 212 is the Fahrenheit value of the steam point, not the number of divisions.

quiz.stem: Which formula converts a Celsius temperature to Fahrenheit?
rationales: This is incorrect because the factor 5/9 is used when converting Fahrenheit to Celsius.
This is correct because T_f = 9/5 × T_c + 32 is the Celsius-to-Fahrenheit formula.
This is incorrect because this formula converts Celsius to Kelvin.
This is incorrect because the Fahrenheit-to-Celsius formula uses T_f − 32, not T_c − 32.

quiz.stem: What is the Kelvin temperature of the steam point according to the textbook scale values?
rationales: This is incorrect because 273 K is the lower fixed point, the ice point.
This is correct because the upper fixed point is labelled 373 K.
This is incorrect because 0 K is not the steam point.
This is incorrect because the interval between the Kelvin fixed points is 100 K.

quiz.stem: Which is a reason water is not suitable as a thermometric liquid?
options: It freezes at a high temperature.
It does not expand when heated.
It is opaque and easy to see.
rationales: This is incorrect because this is not the stated reason for water's unsuitability.
This is incorrect because a thermometric liquid must expand with temperature; water does expand.
This is correct because water has non-linear expansion, making it unsuitable for thermometer readings.
This is incorrect because visibility is a useful property, not the stated problem with water.

quiz.stem: Which pair of fixed-point values belongs to the Kelvin scale?
options: The lower fixed point is 32 and the upper fixed point is 212.
The lower fixed point is 0 and the upper fixed point is 100.
The lower fixed point is 273 and the upper fixed point is 373.
The lower fixed point is −273 and the upper fixed point is 0.
rationales: This is incorrect because these values belong to the Fahrenheit scale.
This is incorrect because these values belong to the Celsius scale.
This is correct because the Kelvin fixed points are 273 and 373.
This is incorrect because these are not the Kelvin fixed-point values given in the textbook.

quiz.stem: How does the potential difference across the junctions of a thermocouple change when their temperature difference increases?
options: The greater the temperature difference, the smaller the potential difference.
The temperature difference has no effect on the potential difference.
The greater the temperature difference, the greater the potential difference.
A thermocouple works only when both junctions are at the same temperature.
rationales: This is incorrect because the potential difference increases, rather than decreases.
This is incorrect because the potential difference depends on the temperature difference.
This is correct because a greater temperature difference produces a greater potential difference.
This is incorrect because the thermocouple produces a current when the junctions are at different temperatures.

quiz.stem: What does the sensitivity of a thermometer describe?
options: It detects large temperature changes only.
It measures only very high temperatures.
rationales: This is incorrect because sensitivity is about detecting small changes, not only large ones.
This is correct because sensitivity is the ability to detect small temperature changes.
This is incorrect because the temperatures a thermometer can measure describe its range.
This is incorrect because evenly spaced markings describe linearity.

quiz.stem: What is the range of a thermometer?
options: The span from the lowest to the highest temperature it can measure
The smallest division marked on its scale
The speed at which its liquid expands
The distance between its bulb and the top of the tube
rationales: This is correct because range is the span of temperatures over which the thermometer measures accurately.
This is incorrect because the smallest scale division is associated with sensitivity.
This is incorrect because liquid expansion alone does not define thermometer range.
This is incorrect because that distance does not define the temperature span measured.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes a linear thermometer?
options: Equal temperature changes correspond to equal scale changes.
The thermometer has a very short range.
The thermometer detects only whole-degree changes.
Its liquid has a low freezing point.
rationales: This is correct because linearity means equal temperature increments correspond to equal scale increments.
This is incorrect because a short range does not define linearity.
This is incorrect because whole-degree divisions do not determine whether the scale is linear.
This is incorrect because the freezing point of the liquid affects the possible range, not linearity.

quiz.stem: Which thermometer is more sensitive, assuming the markings show the smallest divisions?
options: A thermometer with a long tube
A thermometer with a high upper limit
rationales: This is incorrect because 1°C divisions cannot show changes as small as 0.1°C divisions.
This is correct because smaller divisions allow smaller temperature changes to be detected.
This is incorrect because tube length alone does not tell us the size of the scale divisions.
This is incorrect because a high upper limit concerns range, not sensitivity.

quiz.stem: Which statement about thermometer range is correct?
options: A clinical thermometer is designed for a narrow temperature range.
A clinical thermometer must measure from −10°C to 110°C.
rationales: This is correct because the section gives a clinical thermometer range of about 35°C to 45°C.
This is incorrect because −10°C to 110°C is given as an example of a long-range laboratory thermometer.
This is incorrect because 357°C is the boiling point stated for mercury, not alcohol.
This is incorrect because −112°C is the approximate freezing point stated for alcohol.

quiz.stem: What feature is expected of a good linear thermometer?
options: The scale markings are evenly spaced over the whole range.
The thermometer has the lowest possible freezing point.
The thermometer has a narrow capillary.
The thermometer measures only body temperature.
rationales: This is correct because evenly spaced markings correspond to equal temperature changes throughout the range.
This is incorrect because a low freezing point affects range, not linearity.
This is incorrect because a narrow capillary can increase sensitivity but does not itself define linearity.
This is incorrect because measuring body temperature describes a use, not linearity.

quiz.stem: Why is the bore of a liquid-in-glass thermometer made narrow and uniform?
options: It makes the thermometer measure a wider temperature range.
It allows the liquid to show an even expansion on a linear scale.
It prevents the liquid from expanding.
It makes the glass conduct heat more slowly.
rationales: A narrow, uniform bore does not itself determine the thermometer’s full temperature range.
Correct: the section explains that a uniform narrow bore ensures even expansion needed for a linear measuring scale.
The liquid must expand for the thermometer to work.
The thin bulb wall is intended to allow quick conduction to the liquid, not slow it.

quiz.stem: What is the main purpose of the thin glass wall of the thermometer bulb?
options: It allows heat to pass quickly from the object to the liquid.
It stops the liquid from changing temperature.
It raises the liquid’s boiling point.
rationales: Correct: the thin wall allows quick conduction through the glass to the liquid.
The liquid needs to change temperature so that it can respond to the object.
Even expansion in the uniform bore makes the scale linear, not the thin bulb wall.
The bulb wall does not change the liquid’s boiling point.

quiz.stem: Why is mercury suitable for normal liquid-in-glass thermometer measurements?
options: It is a metal and a good conductor, so it responds quickly to temperature change.
It has a lower boiling point than alcohol.
It expands six times more than alcohol.
It wets the glass and climbs the tube.
rationales: Correct: the section says mercury is a good conductor and responds quickly to temperature changes.
The section gives alcohol’s low boiling point as a limitation, not mercury’s.
The section says alcohol has six times more expansivity than mercury.
Wetting the glass is not given as a reason for choosing mercury.

quiz.stem: What limits the use of alcohol for measuring higher temperatures?
options: Alcohol has a lower expansivity than mercury.
Alcohol has a low boiling point, limiting measurements at higher temperatures.
Alcohol freezes at a higher temperature than mercury.
rationales: The section says alcohol’s expansivity is six times greater than mercury’s.
Correct: alcohol’s low boiling point of 78°C limits its use at higher temperatures.
This is not the limitation stated in the section.
Alcohol can expand, and its greater expansivity can help with accuracy.

quiz.stem: Which combination matches the described structure of a liquid-in-glass thermometer?
options: A thick-walled bulb and a wide tube
A thin-walled bulb and a fine, uniform bore
A large bulb and an uneven bore
A narrow tube with no liquid in the bulb
rationales: A thick wall and wide tube do not match the described thermometer structure.
Correct: the section describes a thin-walled bulb and a narrow, uniform capillary tube.
An uneven bore would not provide the even expansion needed for a linear scale.
The bulb must contain a thermometric liquid.

quiz.stem: What property of mercury helps a thermometer measure temperatures over a long range?
options: A low freezing point and a high boiling point
A high freezing point and a low boiling point
rationales: Correct: mercury’s low freezing point and high boiling point allow a fairly long measurement range.
These properties would restrict, rather than extend, the usable range.
A low boiling point would restrict high-temperature measurements.
A high freezing point would restrict low-temperature measurements.

quiz.stem: What makes the reading easier to notice in a fine-bore thermometer?
options: A larger change in liquid level for a temperature change
A smaller change in liquid level for a temperature change
A liquid level that moves unpredictably
rationales: Correct: in a fine bore, expansion is visible as movement along the narrow tube.
A smaller movement would be harder to read.
The liquid must move as it expands.
A uniform bore is intended to make expansion even, not unpredictable.

quiz.stem: According to the section, why does a small amount of thermometer liquid help?
options: The bulb contains a small amount of liquid, which responds more quickly to a temperature change.
The tube has a wide, uneven bore.
The thermometer is made without a scale.
rationales: Correct: the section states that a small amount of liquid responds more quickly to a temperature change.
Without liquid, the thermometer cannot show a liquid level.
An uneven bore does not ensure even expansion for a linear scale.
A scale is needed to read the temperature.

quiz.stem: Which one of the following is not a magnetic material?
rationales: Cobalt is a magnetic material and is attracted to a magnet.
Iron is a magnetic material and is strongly attracted to a magnet.
Aluminium is not classed as a magnetic material in the usual school-level classification.
Nickel is a magnetic material and is attracted to a magnet.

quiz.stem: Magnetic lines of force:
options: are always directed in a straight line
rationales: Magnetic field lines curve rather than always following straight paths.
Magnetic field lines never cross because the field has only one direction at any point.
Outside a magnet, field lines emerge from the north pole rather than enter it.
Outside a magnet, field lines enter the south pole.

quiz.stem: Permanent magnets cannot be made by:
rationales: Soft iron loses its magnetism readily, so it is unsuitable for making permanent magnets.
Steel retains magnetism and can be used to make permanent magnets.
Neodymium is used to make strong permanent magnets.
Alnico is an alloy used to make permanent magnets.

quiz.stem: Permanent magnets are used in:
rationales: Circuit breakers commonly use electromagnets to operate their mechanisms, not permanent magnets.
Loudspeakers commonly use a permanent magnet to provide a steady magnetic field.
Electric cranes use powerful electromagnets that can be switched on and off.
Magnetic recording typically uses electromagnets in the recording head.

quiz.stem: A common method used to magnetise a material is:
options: placing inside a solenoid having A.C
rationales: Stroking a material with a magnet in a consistent direction is a common way to magnetise it.
Hitting a material does not reliably magnetise it and can demagnetise it.
Heating generally weakens or destroys magnetisation rather than producing it.
An alternating-current solenoid repeatedly reverses the field and is commonly used to demagnetise a material.

quiz.stem: A magnetic compass is placed around a bar magnet at four points as shown in figure below. Which diagram would indicate the correct directions of the field?
options: Diagram (a): horizontal bar magnet with N on the left and S on the right; arrows point right above, left at the left, right at the right and left below.
Diagram (b): horizontal bar magnet with N on the left and S on the right; arrows point left above, left at the left, left at the right and right below.
Diagram (c): horizontal bar magnet with N on the left and S on the right; arrows point right above, left at the left, left at the right and right below.
Diagram (d): horizontal bar magnet with N on the left and S on the right; arrows point left above, left at the left, right at the right and left below.
rationales: In diagram (a), the field direction to the right of the south pole and below the magnet is incorrect.

quiz.stem: An S-pole is brought into contact with one end of an iron nail. Which statement describes the induced poles?

It increases the current inside the magnet.
rationales: This is correct: the section says that beating a magnet makes its domains lose their alignment.
This is incorrect because hammering disrupts domain alignment rather than strengthening it.
This is incorrect because hammering does not turn a magnet into a coil of wire.
This is incorrect because a permanent magnet does not have an electric current inside it in this explanation.

quiz.stem: How is a magnet demagnetised using a solenoid carrying alternating current?
options: Move the magnet out slowly from inside the solenoid.
Move the magnet into the solenoid quickly and leave it there.
Pass direct current through the solenoid and keep the magnet inside.
Heat the solenoid while the magnet is inside it.
rationales: This is correct: the section describes slowly moving a magnet out from inside an A.C.-carrying solenoid.
This is incorrect because the described method requires slowly moving the magnet out, not quickly moving it in.
This is incorrect because direct current in a solenoid is used to magnetise steel.
This is incorrect because heating the solenoid is not the stated A.C. demagnetisation method.

quiz.stem: What is a magnetic tape recording head made of, according to this section?
options: A coil of wire wrapped around an iron core
A permanent magnet with no coil
A plastic block with a metal coating
rationales: This is correct: the recording and playing head is a coil of wire wrapped around an iron core.
This is wrong: the section describes an electromagnet, not a permanent magnet alone.
This is wrong: the head has an iron core and coil, not a plastic block with a metal coating.
This is wrong: a compass needle is not the recording head described.

quiz.stem: Which part of the recording head’s magnetic field penetrates the tape coating?
options: The straight field lines outside the head
The curved part of the magnetic field in the gap
The current flowing through the tape
The plastic backing of the tape
rationales: This is wrong: the section identifies the curved part of the field in the gap.
This is correct: the curved part is called the fringe field and penetrates the magnetic coating.
This is wrong: current is sent to the head, not through the tape.
This is wrong: the plastic backing supports the tape but does not record the signal.

quiz.stem: What happens to the tape’s magnetic coating after it leaves the recording head?
options: It retains induced magnetism after leaving the recording head
It turns into an electrical signal immediately
Its plastic backing stores the magnetic pattern
rationales: This is wrong: the section says the induced magnetism is retained.
This is correct: the induced magnetism remains when the tape leaves the vicinity of the head.
This is wrong: the stored magnetic pattern is later converted back into varying current during playback.
This is wrong: the magnetic coating, not the plastic backing, stores the pattern.

quiz.stem: How does a hard-disk magnetic head write a binary digit?
options: By magnetising tiny spots in different directions
By cutting grooves into the disk
rationales: This is correct: the head writes 1 or 0 by magnetising tiny spots in different directions.
This is wrong: the section describes magnetic recording, not grooves cut into the disk.
This is wrong: the information is stored magnetically, not as heat.
This is wrong: changing the disk’s size is not how the head records a digit.

quiz.stem: What coating does the section say is used on hard disks?
options: The disk is coated on both sides with iron oxide
The disk is made only of iron
The disk is coated with plastic backing
The disk contains a moving tape
rationales: This is correct: hard disks are coated on both sides with iron oxide.
This is wrong: the disk may be made of aluminium, glass or plastic, with an iron oxide coating.
This is wrong: plastic backing is described as part of a tape, not a hard-disk coating.
This is wrong: a hard disk is a circular plate and does not contain a moving tape.

quiz.stem: What advantage of magnetic disks over tape recorders is given in this section?
options: A disk can read or write a recording instantly
A disk needs many minutes to locate information
A tape can store only binary digits
A disk does not need a magnetic head
rationales: This is correct: a disk unit can read or write a recording instantly.
This is wrong: the section says locating information on tape may take many minutes.
This is wrong: the section does not say that tape stores only binary digits.
This is wrong: the section describes a magnetic head for reading and writing a disk.

quiz.stem: Which material does the section recommend for boxes that protect electronic devices from strong magnetic effects?
rationales: This is correct: the section says to enclose devices in boxes made of soft iron.
This is wrong: wood is not the material recommended in the section.
This is wrong: plastic is not the material recommended in the section.
This is wrong: glass is not the material recommended in the section.

quiz.stem: Why does a soft iron casing help shield a sensitive magnetic device from an external magnetic field?
options: Because soft iron has higher magnetic permeability than air
Because soft iron blocks every magnetic field completely
Because soft iron is a permanent magnet
Because the device inside produces no magnetic field
rationales: Correct: magnetic flux is established more readily in the high-permeability soft iron than in air or the device.
Incorrect: the textbook explains that flux is established in the soft iron, not that the field is completely blocked.
Incorrect: the shielding explanation depends on permeability, not on soft iron acting as a permanent magnet.
Incorrect: shielding works because of the casing's effect on magnetic flux, not because the device produces no field.

quiz.stem: When a sensitive device is enclosed in a soft iron casing, where is the magnetic flux established mainly?
options: Magnetic flux is established mainly in the soft iron casing
Magnetic flux is forced to pass through the sensitive device
The casing changes the external field into an electric current
The soft iron casing removes the magnetic poles of the external magnets
rationales: Correct: the flux is established in the soft iron rather than in the device.
Incorrect: the casing helps keep the flux from being established in the sensitive device.
Incorrect: the section describes magnetic flux and shielding, not conversion into electric current.
Incorrect: the casing does not remove the poles of the magnets producing the external field.

quiz.stem: Which property of soft iron is most important for its use as a magnetic shield?
rationales: Correct: high permeability allows magnetic flux to pass through the soft iron readily.
Incorrect: electrical resistance is not the property described as causing magnetic shielding.
Incorrect: soft iron is used for its permeability, not because it has a permanent north pole.
Incorrect: melting point is not given as the reason for its shielding use.

quiz.stem: Why is a soft iron shielding casing usually made with rounded corners?
options: Rounded corners help magnetic field lines line up easily
Rounded corners increase the electrical current in the device
Rounded corners make soft iron a permanent magnet
Rounded corners stop all magnetic flux from entering the casing
rationales: Correct: rounded corners facilitate the magnetic field lines lining up easily.
Incorrect: the shape of the casing is not described as increasing current in the device.
Incorrect: rounded corners do not make soft iron a permanent magnet.
Incorrect: the casing provides an easier path for flux; it does not stop all flux from entering it.

quiz.stem: Why is soft iron suitable for the core of an electromagnet?
options: It is easily magnetised when current flows and quickly loses magnetism when current stops
It remains permanently magnetised after current stops
It has lower permeability than air
It cannot be magnetised by a magnetic field
rationales: Correct: soft iron is easily magnetised by the current and quickly loses its magnetism when the current stops.
Incorrect: a core that stays magnetised permanently would not match the temporary action described for an electromagnet.
Incorrect: soft iron has high permeability, not lower permeability than air.
Incorrect: soft iron can be magnetised when current passes around it.

quiz.stem: What is one effect of placing a soft iron core inside a moving coil galvanometer?
options: The sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer is increased
The galvanometer becomes a permanent magnet
The external magnetic field is eliminated
The coil no longer carries current
rationales: Correct: the section states that a soft iron core increases the galvanometer's sensitivity.
Incorrect: the stated effect is increased sensitivity, not making the galvanometer a permanent magnet.
Incorrect: the core does not eliminate every external magnetic field.
Incorrect: adding a core does not stop the coil from carrying current.

quiz.stem: Which use of soft iron is stated in this section?
options: It is used in the core of an electromagnet
It is used to make an electromagnet retain magnetism forever
It prevents current from flowing in the coil
It is used because its permeability is lower than air
rationales: Correct: the section says soft iron is generally used in the cores of electromagnets.
Incorrect: soft iron quickly loses magnetism when the current is stopped, rather than retaining it forever.
Incorrect: the core does not prevent current from flowing in the surrounding coil.
Incorrect: soft iron has higher, not lower, permeability than air.

quiz.stem: Which arrangement is described as protecting a sensitive magnetic device from an external magnetic field?
options: A sensitive magnetic device enclosed in a soft iron casing
A permanent magnet placed beside the device
A wooden casing around the device
A steel bar placed far from the device
rationales: Correct: the section describes enclosing the sensitive device in a soft iron casing.
Incorrect: placing a permanent magnet beside the device is not the shielding method described.
Incorrect: the section identifies soft iron, not wood, as the shielding material.
Incorrect: a steel bar placed far away is not the stated shielding arrangement.

quiz.stem: Physics is a branch of:
rationales: Social science studies human society and behavior, not physical phenomena.
Life science focuses on living organisms rather than the physical world.
Physics is a physical science that studies matter, energy, and their interactions.

quiz.stem: Which branch of science plays vital role in technology and engineering?
rationales: Biology contributes to fields such as medicine but is not the central science underlying most technology and engineering.
Chemistry supports many technologies but is not the branch most directly associated with the foundations of engineering.
Geology informs earth-related engineering but is not the general scientific foundation of technology and engineering.
Physics provides principles widely used in technology and engineering, such as mechanics, electricity, and energy.

quiz.stem: Automobile technology is based on:
rationales: Acoustics concerns sound and is not the main basis of automobile operation.
Electromagnetism is involved in some automobile components but does not explain the vehicle’s overall operation.
Optics concerns light and is not the main basis of automobile technology.
Thermodynamics explains engines and the conversion of heat into mechanical work in automobiles.

quiz.stem: A user friendly software application of smart phone use:
rationales: Laser technology is not what makes a smartphone application user-friendly.
Information technology includes software applications and their use on smartphones.
Medical technology concerns health-related tools and is not the general category for smartphone applications.
Electronic technology describes electronic devices and components, rather than the software application itself.

quiz.stem: The working of refrigeration and air conditioning involves:
rationales: Electromagnetism may be used in components but does not describe the main principle of cooling.
Mechanics describes motion and forces, not the heat-transfer cycle central to refrigeration and air conditioning.
Climate science studies climate and does not explain how these appliances operate.
Thermodynamics explains the transfer of heat and the refrigeration cycle used in these systems.

quiz.stem: What is the ultimate truth of a scientific method?
rationales: A hypothesis is a tentative proposed explanation, not the final result of scientific investigation.
Experimentation tests ideas but is a method rather than a conclusion.
A theory is a well-supported explanation, but the textbook-style answer identifying the most established scientific statement is a law.
A scientific law expresses a consistently observed relationship and is the expected answer for the most established statement among these options.

quiz.stem: The statement "If I do not study for this test, then I will not get good grade" is an example of:
rationales: A theory is a well-supported explanation, not a specific statement about an expected outcome.
An observation is something noticed or recorded, rather than an outcome stated in advance.
The sentence predicts an expected result if the person does not study.
A law describes a consistently observed relationship and is not this conditional expectation.

quiz.stem: Which of the following are methods of investigation?
rationales: Observation is one method used to investigate questions.
Experimentation is one method used to investigate questions.
Research is a method used to investigate questions and gather information.
All three listed activities are methods of investigation.

quiz.stem: A hypothesis:
options: may or may not be testable
is a possible answer to a question
rationales: A scientific hypothesis should be testable, so it is not accurately described as possibly untestable.
Evidence can support a hypothesis, but being supported by evidence is not what defines a hypothesis in this question.
A hypothesis is a proposed or possible answer to a question.
This is not correct because a scientific hypothesis must be testable, making the first statement false.

quiz.stem: A graph of an organized data is an example of:
rationales: Collecting data means gathering observations or measurements, not organizing them into a graph.
Forming a hypothesis means proposing a possible explanation or answer.
Asking a question is an earlier step and does not itself produce a graph of data.
A graph organizes and displays data so that patterns can be examined, which is analyzing data.

quiz.stem: The colour of a door is brown. It is an example of:
rationales: The door’s brown colour is a directly noticed feature, so it is an observation.
A hypothesis is a proposed answer or explanation, not simply a recorded colour.
A prediction states an expected future result, not a present feature of the door.
A law expresses a consistently observed relationship and is not a description of one door.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes the scope of physics?
options: The study of living things only
The study of matter, energy, space, time, and their interactions
The study of human societies only
rationales: This is not the book's definition of physics; living things are the focus of biological sciences.
This matches the textbook's description of physics and its subject matter.

quiz.stem: In the textbook's description, what is space?

quiz.stem: What is the main idea of interdisciplinary research?

This is incorrect because this is not the example discussed in the section.

This is incorrect because these are not the fields listed for artificial intelligence.

options: It prevents scientists from sharing findings.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes the scientific method?
options: A systematic approach to investigate problems in the natural and physical world

quiz.stem: A student suggests that a plant grows faster in sunlight. What is this suggested explanation called?

quiz.stem: Which choice describes an experiment?
options: An organized repeatable process used to test a hypothesis
A final statement that can never change
A prediction that has not been tested
A list of observations without a question
rationales: This is correct because an experiment is an organized repeatable process used to test the truth of a hypothesis.
This is wrong because scientific theories and laws can be disproved or modified as new evidence appears.
This is wrong because a prediction is not itself an experiment.
This is wrong because an experiment is designed to test an idea, not merely list observations.

quiz.stem: According to this section, when is a theory called a law?

A hypothesis has been suggested once
A prediction has not yet been checked
An observation has been written down
rationales: This is correct because the section says a theory tested many times and generally accepted as true is called a law.
This is wrong because a newly suggested hypothesis has not yet undergone repeated testing.
This is wrong because an unchecked prediction does not establish a law.

quiz.stem: What does falsifiability require of a scientific theory?
options: It makes the theory impossible to change
It requires predictions that can be tested and potentially shown to be false
It proves a theory true after one experiment
It prevents scientists from making predictions
rationales: This is wrong because scientific theories may be modified or disproved with new evidence.
This is correct because a falsifiable theory makes predictions that can be tested and potentially proven false.
This is wrong because one experiment does not prove a theory true forever.

quiz.stem: What should happen if experimental results do not agree with a prediction?

This is wrong because recording and analysing evidence is part of the scientific method.

Scientific knowledge is used only in laboratories.
rationales: This is correct because the section explains that discoveries lead to technologies and engineers rely on scientific knowledge.
This is incorrect because the section says engineering relies on scientific knowledge rather than replacing it.
This is incorrect because the section says these fields often work together.
This is incorrect because the section describes scientific knowledge being applied in everyday technologies and engineering.

readiness.stem: The instrument that is most suitable for measuring the thickness of a few sheets of cardboard is:
rationales: A metre rule is too coarse to measure the small thickness accurately.
A measuring tape is intended for longer lengths and is not precise enough here.
Vernier Callipers are less suitable than a micrometer for measuring the very small thickness of a few sheets.
A micrometer screw gauge is designed to measure small thicknesses with high precision.

readiness.stem: The numerical ratio of displacement to distance is:
options: equal to or less than one
rationales: The ratio cannot always be less than one because displacement and distance are equal for straight-line motion without reversing direction.
The ratio is not always one because a change in direction can make the distance greater than the displacement.
The magnitude of displacement can never exceed the distance traveled, so this ratio cannot be greater than one.
The magnitude of displacement is at most the distance traveled, making the ratio equal to or less than one.

readiness.stem: When we kick a stone, we get hurt. This is due to:
rationales: Inertia resists changes in motion but does not explain the force that causes the pain.
Velocity describes motion and is not the cause of the stone’s force on the foot.
Momentum describes the stone’s motion but does not identify the interaction responsible for the injury.
The stone exerts an equal and opposite force on the foot, producing the pain.

readiness.stem: A particle is simultaneously acted upon by two forces of 4 and 3 newtons. The net force on the particle is:
rationales: A net force of 1 N occurs only when the forces act in opposite directions, so it is not the only possible value.
Depending on the angle between the forces, the resultant can range from 1 N to 7 N.
A resultant of 5 N is possible for a particular angle, but it is not the only possible value.
A resultant of 7 N occurs only when the forces act in the same direction, so it is not the only possible value.

readiness.stem: Work done is maximum when the angle between the force F and the displacement d is:
rationales: Correct: work is W = Fd cos θ, which is greatest when cos θ = 1 at 0°.
Incorrect: at 30°, cos θ is less than 1, so the work is less than its maximum.
Incorrect: at 60°, cos θ is less than 1, so the work is less than its maximum.
Incorrect: at 90°, cos θ = 0, so the work done is zero.

readiness.stem: A wire is stretched by a weight w. If the diameter of the wire is reduced to half of its previous value, the extension will become:
rationales: This is incorrect because reducing the diameter does not halve the extension; extension varies inversely with cross-sectional area.
This is incorrect because halving the diameter reduces the area to one quarter and therefore increases the extension fourfold.
This is incorrect because the extension increases when the wire’s cross-sectional area decreases.
This is correct because extension is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area, and halving the diameter reduces the area to one quarter.

readiness.stem: How do the molecules in a solid behave?
options: Rotate and vibrate randomly at their own positions
Move in a straight line from hot to cold ends.
rationales: Solids do not move randomly from place to place; their particles remain in fixed positions.
Solid molecules vibrate about their mean positions.
Rotational motion is not the characteristic motion of molecules in a solid.
Molecules in a solid do not travel from the hot end to the cold end.

readiness.stem: Which one of the following is not a magnetic material?
rationales: Cobalt is a magnetic material and is attracted to a magnet.
Iron is a magnetic material and is strongly attracted to a magnet.
Aluminium is not classed as a magnetic material in the usual school-level classification.
Nickel is a magnetic material and is attracted to a magnet.
Social science studies human society and behavior, not physical phenomena.
Life science focuses on living organisms rather than the physical world.
Physics is a physical science that studies matter, energy, and their interactions.
Biological science studies living things, so it is not the broad branch that includes physics.

mcqs.stem: One femtometre is equal to:
rationales: 10⁻⁹ m is one nanometre, not one femtometre.
The prefix femto means 10⁻¹⁵, so one femtometre is 10⁻¹⁵ m.
10⁹ m is an extremely large length and is not a femtometre.
10¹⁵ m is an extremely large length and is not a femtometre.

mcqs.stem: A light year is a unit of:
rationales: A light year is not a unit of light itself; it is the distance light travels in a year.
A light year is not a unit of time, despite containing the word “year.”
A light year is a unit of distance equal to the distance light travels in one year.
A light year measures distance, not speed.

mcqs.stem: Which one is a non-physical quantity?
rationales: Distance is a physical quantity that can be measured.
Density is a physical quantity that can be measured.
Colour is treated here as a non-physical quantity rather than a measurable physical quantity.
Temperature is a physical quantity that can be measured.

mcqs.stem: When using a measuring cylinder, one precaution to take is to:
options: look at the meniscus from below the level of the water surface
take several readings by looking from more than one direction
position the eye in line with the bottom of the meniscus
rationales: Checking for zero error is not the key precaution specified for reading a measuring cylinder.
Looking from below the water surface causes parallax error rather than preventing it.
Taking readings from different directions does not ensure an accurate meniscus reading.
The eye should be level with the bottom of the meniscus to avoid parallax error.

mcqs.stem: Volume of water consumed by you per day is estimated in:
rationales: A millilitre is a possible volume unit, but daily water consumption is conventionally estimated in litres.
A litre is a suitable unit for estimating a person’s daily water consumption.
A kilogram is a unit of mass, not volume.
A cubic metre is far too large and is not a convenient unit for daily personal water consumption.

mcqs.stem: A displacement can is used to measure:
rationales: A displacement can measures volume, not mass, so it cannot directly measure the mass of a liquid.
A displacement can measures volume, not mass, so it cannot directly measure the mass of a solid.
It is not used to measure the volume of a liquid, which can be measured directly in a graduated vessel.
A displacement can determines the volume of an irregular solid by measuring the displaced liquid.

mcqs.stem: Two rods with lengths 12.321 cm and 10.3 cm are placed side by side, the difference in their lengths is:
rationales: 2.02 cm reports more decimal places than justified by the less precise measurement, 10.3 cm.
The difference is 2.021 cm before rounding, and it should be rounded to one decimal place to give 2.0 cm.
2 cm does not retain the tenths place justified by the measurement 10.3 cm.
2.021 cm is the unrounded difference, but it gives unjustified precision relative to 10.3 cm.

mcqs.stem: Four students measure the diameter of a cylinder with Vernier Callipers. Which of the following readings is correct?
rationales: 3.4 cm is less precise than a Vernier Callipers reading normally allows.
3.475 cm gives more precision than the stated instrument reading typically supports.
3.47 cm is a suitably precise reading for Vernier Callipers.
3.5 cm is too rounded to represent a typical Vernier Callipers reading accurately.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following measures are likely to represent the thickness of a sheet of this book?
rationales: 6 × 10⁻²⁵ m is vastly smaller than the thickness of a book sheet.
A thickness of 1 × 10⁻⁴ m, or 0.1 mm, is plausible for a sheet of paper.
1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m is far smaller than atomic dimensions and cannot represent a sheet thickness.
4 × 10⁻² m is 4 cm thick, far too thick for a sheet.

mcqs.stem: In a Vernier Callipers ten smallest divisions of the Vernier scale are equal to nine smallest divisions of the main scale. If the smallest division of the main scale is half millimetre, the Vernier constant is equal to:
rationales: 0.5 mm is the main-scale division, not the Vernier constant.
0.1 mm is not the difference between one main-scale division and one Vernier division in this setup.
Each Vernier division is 9/10 × 0.5 mm = 0.45 mm, so the Vernier constant is 0.5 − 0.45 = 0.05 mm.
0.001 mm is much smaller than the calculated Vernier constant of 0.05 mm.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following is a physical quantity?
rationales: Length can be measured using an instrument, so it is physical.
Beauty cannot be measured with a measuring instrument, so it is non-physical.
Wisdom cannot be measured with a measuring instrument, so it is non-physical.
Affection cannot be measured with a measuring instrument, so it is non-physical.

mcqs.stem: The numerical ratio of displacement to distance is:
options: equal to or less than one
rationales: The ratio cannot always be less than one because displacement and distance are equal for straight-line motion without reversing direction.
The ratio is not always one because a change in direction can make the distance greater than the displacement.
The magnitude of displacement can never exceed the distance traveled, so this ratio cannot be greater than one.
The magnitude of displacement is at most the distance traveled, making the ratio equal to or less than one.

mcqs.stem: If a body does not change its position with respect to some fixed point, then it will be in a state of:
rationales: A body whose position does not change relative to a fixed point is at rest.
Motion means a change in position relative to a reference point, which is absent here.
Uniform motion involves continued movement at constant velocity, not an unchanged position.
Variable motion involves a change in velocity and therefore movement, not an unchanged position.

mcqs.stem: A ball is dropped from the top of a tower, the distance covered by it in the first second is:
rationales: In free fall from rest, the first-second distance is approximately ½ × 9.8 × 1² = 4.9 m, or 5 m.
The body falls about 5 m, not 10 m, in the first second.
The body falls about 5 m, not 50 m, in the first second.
The body falls about 5 m, not 100 m, in the first second.

mcqs.stem: A body accelerates from rest to a velocity of 144 km h⁻¹ in 20 seconds. The distance covered by it is:
rationales: The final speed is 40 m/s, so the average speed is 20 m/s and the distance in 20 s is 400 m, not 100 m.
With uniform acceleration from rest to 40 m/s, the average speed is 20 m/s and the distance is 20 × 20 = 400 m.
The distance is 400 m, not 1400 m.
The distance is 400 m, not 1440 m.

mcqs.stem: A body is moving with constant acceleration starting from rest. It covers a distance S in 4 seconds. How much time does it take to cover one-fourth of this distance?
rationales: For motion from rest with constant acceleration, distance is proportional to time squared, so one-fourth the distance takes 2 s, not 1 s.
Since S ∝ t², covering S/4 takes half of 4 s, which is 2 s.
Four seconds is the time to cover the full distance S, not one-fourth of it.
Sixteen seconds is not consistent with the fact that distance grows as the square of time.

mcqs.stem: The displacement time graphs of two objects A and B are shown in the figure. Point out the true statement from the following:
options: The velocity of A is greater than B.
The velocity of A is less than B.
The velocity of A is equal to that of B.
The graph gives no information in this regard.
rationales: The graph indicates that A has the steeper displacement-time slope, and slope represents velocity.
This is false because A's displacement-time slope is steeper than B's.
The velocities would be equal only if the two graph slopes were equal.
A displacement-time graph conveys velocity through its slope, so it does provide information about the velocities.

mcqs.stem: The area under the speed-time graph is numerically equal to:
rationales: The area under a speed-time graph represents distance, not velocity.
Uniform velocity is represented by a horizontal speed-time line, not by its area.
Acceleration is represented by the graph's gradient, not its area.
Speed multiplied by time gives distance, so the area under the speed-time graph is distance covered.

mcqs.stem: Gradient of the speed-time graph is equal to:
rationales: The vertical value on a speed-time graph is speed; its gradient is not speed.
The gradient of a speed-time graph gives acceleration, not velocity as the requested graph quantity.
The change in speed per unit time is acceleration, which is the graph's gradient.
The area under a speed-time graph gives distance, while its gradient gives acceleration.

mcqs.stem: Gradient of the distance-time graph is equal to the:
rationales: The gradient of a distance-time graph is change in distance per unit time, which is speed.
Velocity is the gradient of a displacement-time graph; this graph is specified as distance-time.
The graph's gradient is a rate of change, not the distance covered itself.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity and is not the gradient of a distance-time graph.

mcqs.stem: A car accelerates uniformly from 80.5 km h⁻¹ at t = 0 to 113 km h⁻¹ at t = 9 s. Which graph best describes the motion of the car?
options: a rising curve that starts above the origin and bends upward
a straight rising line from the origin
a straight rising line that starts above the origin
a straight falling line that starts above the origin and reaches the horizontal axis
rationales: Uniform acceleration produces a straight velocity-time line, not a curve.
The line must start above the origin because the initial speed is 80.5 km h⁻¹, not zero.
The speed increases uniformly from a nonzero initial value, so the graph is a straight rising line starting above the origin.
The speed increases rather than decreases, and it remains above zero throughout the stated interval.

mcqs.stem: Which quantity is a scalar?
rationales: Mass is a scalar because it is described by magnitude only.
Displacement is a vector because it has magnitude and direction.
Force is a vector because it has magnitude and direction.
Velocity is a vector because it has magnitude and direction.

Weight is a vector because it is a force with a direction.
Acceleration is a vector because its direction is needed.
