mcqs.stem: When we kick a stone, we get hurt. This is due to:
rationales: Inertia resists changes in motion but does not explain the force that causes the pain.
Velocity describes motion and is not the cause of the stone’s force on the foot.
Momentum describes the stone’s motion but does not identify the interaction responsible for the injury.
The stone exerts an equal and opposite force on the foot, producing the pain.

mcqs.stem: An object will continue its motion with constant acceleration until:
options: the resultant force on it begins to decrease.
the resultant force on it is zero.
the resultant force on it begins to increase.
the resultant force is at right angle to its tangential velocity.
rationales: A decreasing resultant force would generally change the acceleration before it reaches zero.
When the resultant force becomes zero, the accelerated phase ends and the object continues at constant velocity.
An increasing resultant force would generally change the acceleration.
A force perpendicular to velocity does not by itself ensure constant acceleration.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following is a non-contact force?
rationales: Friction requires contact between surfaces.
Air resistance results from contact with air molecules.
Electrostatic force can act between charged objects without contact.
Tension is transmitted through a taut string in contact with the objects.

mcqs.stem: A ball with initial momentum p hits a solid wall and bounces back with the same velocity. Its momentum p′ after collision will be:
rationales: The momentum changes sign because the ball reverses direction, so it is not unchanged.
The ball’s velocity has the same magnitude but the opposite direction, making its momentum −p.
A momentum of 2p would require a change in momentum of 2p, not a final momentum of that value.
A final momentum of −2p would have twice the initial momentum’s magnitude.

mcqs.stem: A particle of mass m moving with a velocity v collides with another particle of the same mass at rest. The velocity of the first particle after collision is:
rationales: In the usual one-dimensional elastic-collision interpretation, the first particle transfers its velocity to the initially stationary equal-mass particle.
The first particle does not rebound at speed v in the usual one-dimensional elastic collision with an equal mass at rest.
In a one-dimensional elastic collision between equal masses, the first particle stops and the second takes its velocity; the question requires this usual elastic-collision assumption.
A velocity of −1/2 is not specified in terms of v and is not the standard result for this collision.

mcqs.stem: Conservation of linear momentum is equivalent to:
rationales: Newton’s first law describes motion when the net force is zero, rather than the general interaction underlying momentum conservation.
Newton’s second law relates net force to momentum change but is not the action–reaction basis for conservation in an isolated system.
Newton’s third law’s equal-and-opposite internal forces cancel in an isolated system, yielding conservation of total linear momentum.
The conservation law is directly connected to Newton’s third law for an isolated system.

mcqs.stem: An object with a mass of 5 kg moves at constant velocity of 10 m s⁻¹. A constant force then acts for 5 seconds on the object and gives it a velocity of 2 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. The force acting on the object is:
rationales: A force of 5 N would not produce the stated change in momentum over 5 seconds.
A force of −10 N would give the object a final velocity of 0 m s⁻¹, not −2 m s⁻¹.
The acceleration is (−2−10)/5 = −2.4 m s⁻², so the force is 5(−2.4) = −12 N.
A force of −15 N would produce a larger change in velocity than stated.

mcqs.stem: A large force acts on an object for a very short interval of time. In this case, it is easy to determine:
rationales: The force’s magnitude is difficult to determine when it varies greatly during a very short interval.
The short interval itself may be difficult to measure directly.
The impulse, the product of force and time interval, can be determined from the change in momentum.
The product of force and time can be determined, so none of these is incorrect.

A lubricant does not usually function as ball bearings between the surfaces.
The lubricant forms a layer that prevents direct contact between the surfaces and reduces friction.
Lubricants generally reduce sliding friction rather than provide rolling friction.

(a) Describe Newton's laws of motion.
(b) A 10 kg block is placed on a smooth horizontal surface. A horizontal force of 5 N is applied to the block. Find: (a) the acceleration produced in the block. (b) the velocity of block after 5 seconds.
modelAnswer: (a) Newton’s first law: A body continues its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by some external force.
Newton’s second law: A net external force accelerates a body in the direction of the force; acceleration is directly proportional to force and inversely proportional to mass.
Therefore, F = ma.
Newton’s third law: For every action, there is always an equal and opposite reaction.

a = 0.5 m s⁻²
(b) v = u + at

modelAnswer: (a) Mass of truck = m = 3000 kg
Force applied = F = 7500 N
Acceleration = a = ?
Initial speed = v_i = 36 km h⁻¹
Final speed = v_f = 72 km h⁻¹ = 72 × 1000 m / (60 × 60 s) = 20 m s⁻¹
Time = t = ?
By Newton's second law, F = ma
or a = F/m
Putting the values, a = 7500 N / 3000 kg = 2.5 m s⁻²
Now, using first equation of motion, v_f = v_i + at
or t = (v_f − v_i)/a

(b) Given: m = 800 kg, u = 10 m s⁻¹, v = 30 m s⁻¹, t = 10 s.
a = (v − u)/t
F = ma
Final answer: 1600 N

mcqs.stem: A man walks on a tight rope. He balances himself by holding a bamboo stick horizontally. It is an application of:

Holding the stick horizontally helps the man control his turning effect by using the principle of moments.

mcqs.stem: In stable equilibrium, the centre of gravity of the body lies:
rationales: A body whose centre of gravity is at its highest position is generally in unstable, not stable, equilibrium.
In stable equilibrium, a small displacement raises the centre of gravity, so its equilibrium position is at the lowest attainable height.
The centre of gravity is not at an arbitrary position in stable equilibrium; it is at a minimum-height position.
The centre of gravity need not lie outside the body, and its location outside does not define stable equilibrium.

mcqs.stem: The centre of mass of a body:
options: lies always on the surface of the body
may lie within , outside or on the surface
rationales: The centre of mass can lie outside a body, as for a ring, so it is not always inside.
The centre of mass can lie inside a body, so it is not always outside.
The centre of mass can lie inside or outside a body, so it is not always on its surface.
Depending on the body’s shape and mass distribution, its centre of mass may be within, outside, or on its surface.

mcqs.stem: A cylinder resting on its circular base is in:
rationales: A cylinder resting on its circular base is in stable equilibrium because a small tilt raises its centre of gravity.
The cylinder does not move farther from equilibrium after a small displacement, so its equilibrium is not unstable.
The centre of gravity rises when the cylinder is slightly tilted, so its equilibrium is not neutral.
The cylinder is in stable equilibrium, making this option incorrect.

mcqs.stem: Centripetal force is given by:
rationales: The expression rF has units of torque and is not the general formula for centripetal force.

The expression mv/r² has the wrong dimensions for force and is not the centripetal-force formula.

mcqs.stem: A bullet of mass 0.05 kg has a speed of 300 m s⁻¹. Its kinetic energy will be:

mcqs.stem: If a car doubles its speed, its kinetic energy will be:
rationales: Incorrect: kinetic energy changes when speed changes.
Incorrect: because kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared, doubling speed does not merely double the energy.
Incorrect: doubling speed multiplies kinetic energy by four, not three.
Correct: kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared, so doubling speed increases it fourfold.

mcqs.stem: The energy possessed by a body by virtue of its position is:
rationales: Incorrect: kinetic energy is energy due to motion, not position.

Incorrect: chemical energy is stored in chemical bonds, not defined by position.
Incorrect: solar energy comes from the Sun and is not the energy defined by an object's position.

mcqs.stem: The magnitude of momentum of an object is doubled, the kinetic energy of the object will:
rationales: Incorrect: at fixed mass, kinetic energy is proportional to momentum squared, so doubling momentum does not merely double the energy.
Correct: using K = p²/(2m), doubling momentum increases kinetic energy to four times its original value.
Incorrect: doubling momentum increases, rather than reduces, kinetic energy.
Incorrect: kinetic energy changes when momentum doubles.

mcqs.stem: A magnetic compass is placed around a bar magnet at four points as shown in figure below. Which diagram would indicate the correct directions of the field?

Diagram (b): horizontal bar magnet with N on the left and S on the right; arrows point left above, left at the left, left at the right and right below.
Diagram (c): horizontal bar magnet with N on the left and S on the right; arrows point right above, left at the left, left at the right and right below.
Diagram (d): horizontal bar magnet with N on the left and S on the right; arrows point left above, left at the left, right at the right and left below.
rationales: In diagram (a), the field direction to the right of the south pole and below the magnet is incorrect.
In diagram (b), the arrows above the magnet and to its left do not follow the field from north to south outside the magnet.
In diagram (c), the arrows correctly show the external field emerging from the north pole and entering the south pole.
In diagram (d), the arrows above and to the right of the magnet point in incorrect directions.

mcqs.stem: A steel rod is magnetised by double touch stroking method. Which one would be the correct polarity of the AB magnet?
options: Horizontal bar with N at the left end and S at the right end.
Horizontal bar with S at the left end and N at the right end.
Horizontal bar with N at the left end, S in the middle and N at the right end.
Horizontal bar with S at the left end, N in the middle and S at the right end.
rationales: With the north pole stroking outward toward A and the south pole stroking outward toward B, the resulting poles are N at A and S at B.
This reversed polarity would result if the stroking magnets were oriented the other way around.
A single steel rod magnetised by this method has opposite poles at its ends, not two north poles with a south pole in the middle.
A single steel rod magnetised by this method has opposite poles at its ends, not two south poles with a north pole in the middle.

It helps explain everyday motion, such as the movement of objects.
It also explains heat and other familiar physical phenomena.
For example, a swinging pendulum is a motion whose oscillations are described using a time interval.
(b) Mechanics: It is a study of motion and the physical effects which influence motion.
Heat and thermodynamics: It deal with the thermal energy possessed by the materials and it is used when it flows from one body to another.
Acoustics: It deals with the nature and physical aspects of audible sound energy.
Optics: It deal with the physical aspects of visible light.
Electromagnetism: It is the study of electromagnetic phenomenon and mutual relationship between electric current and magnetic field.
Quantum Mechanics: It explains the behaviour of particles at the atomic and subatomic level.

Relativistic Mechanics: It explains how space and time are not absolute quantities but related to observer. It describes the relationship between them and how they are influenced by gravity and speed.
Nuclear Physics: It is the study of the properties of nuclei of the atoms.
Particle Physics: It is the study of subatomic particles and elementary particles which are basic building blocks of matter.
Astronomy: It is study of distribution of celestial bodies like planets, stars and galaxies.
Cosmology: It explores the large structure and evolution of the universe.
Solid State Physics: It is the study of some specific properties of matter in solid form.

written.text:
(a) Is the theory of science an ultimate truth? Describe briefly.
(b) What is scientific method? Describe its main steps with examples.
modelAnswer: (a) No, a scientific theory is not an ultimate truth.
Theories are man-made ideas about the way things work, based on available evidence.
They may be disproved or modified when future advances in science bring fresh facts and new insights about the natural and physical world.
(b) Scientific method is a systematic approach used to search for truth of an issue and problem solving regarding natural and physical world.
First, identify a problem and gather information by observation.
Next, propose a hypothesis and perform an experiment or collect evidence to test it.
Record, organize and analyse the data to reach a conclusion called a theory; repeated tests of the theory over similar issues lead towards a law.
For example, observation of shadows leads to the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line.
When holes in four cardboards are aligned with a torch, light passes through; when one cardboard is displaced, the light is blocked.
This experiment supports the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line, and repeated testing in different situations may establish a law.

mcqs.stem: The instrument that is most suitable for measuring the thickness of a few sheets of cardboard is:
rationales: A metre rule is too coarse to measure the small thickness accurately.
A measuring tape is intended for longer lengths and is not precise enough here.
Vernier Callipers are less suitable than a micrometer for measuring the very small thickness of a few sheets.
A micrometer screw gauge is designed to measure small thicknesses with high precision.

mcqs.stem: The numerical ratio of displacement to distance is:
options: equal to or less than one
rationales: The ratio cannot always be less than one because displacement and distance are equal for straight-line motion without reversing direction.
The ratio is not always one because a change in direction can make the distance greater than the displacement.
The magnitude of displacement can never exceed the distance traveled, so this ratio cannot be greater than one.
The magnitude of displacement is at most the distance traveled, making the ratio equal to or less than one.

mcqs.stem: When we kick a stone, we get hurt. This is due to:
rationales: Inertia resists changes in motion but does not explain the force that causes the pain.
Velocity describes motion and is not the cause of the stone’s force on the foot.
Momentum describes the stone’s motion but does not identify the interaction responsible for the injury.
The stone exerts an equal and opposite force on the foot, producing the pain.

mcqs.stem: An object will continue its motion with constant acceleration until:
options: the resultant force on it begins to decrease.
the resultant force on it is zero.
the resultant force on it begins to increase.
the resultant force is at right angle to its tangential velocity.
rationales: A decreasing resultant force would generally change the acceleration before it reaches zero.
When the resultant force becomes zero, the accelerated phase ends and the object continues at constant velocity.
An increasing resultant force would generally change the acceleration.
A force perpendicular to velocity does not by itself ensure constant acceleration.

mcqs.stem: A particle is simultaneously acted upon by two forces of 4 and 3 newtons. The net force on the particle is:
rationales: A net force of 1 N occurs only when the forces act in opposite directions, so it is not the only possible value.
Depending on the angle between the forces, the resultant can range from 1 N to 7 N.
A resultant of 5 N is possible for a particular angle, but it is not the only possible value.
A resultant of 7 N occurs only when the forces act in the same direction, so it is not the only possible value.

mcqs.stem: A force F is making an angle of 60° with x-axis. Its y-component is equal to:
rationales: The x-component, not the y-component, is F cos 60°.
The y-component is F sin 60° when the angle is measured from the x-axis.
F cos 60° gives the x-component for an angle measured from the x-axis.
F tan 60° is not the component of F along the y-axis.

mcqs.stem: Work done is maximum when the angle between the force F and the displacement d is:
rationales: Correct: work is W = Fd cos θ, which is greatest when cos θ = 1 at 0°.
Incorrect: at 30°, cos θ is less than 1, so the work is less than its maximum.
Incorrect: at 60°, cos θ is less than 1, so the work is less than its maximum.
Incorrect: at 90°, cos θ = 0, so the work done is zero.

mcqs.stem: A wire is stretched by a weight w. If the diameter of the wire is reduced to half of its previous value, the extension will become:
rationales: This is incorrect because reducing the diameter does not halve the extension; extension varies inversely with cross-sectional area.
This is incorrect because halving the diameter reduces the area to one quarter and therefore increases the extension fourfold.
This is incorrect because the extension increases when the wire’s cross-sectional area decreases.
This is correct because extension is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area, and halving the diameter reduces the area to one quarter.

mcqs.stem: Four wires of the same material are stretched by the same load. Their dimensions are given below. Which of them will elongate most?
rationales: This is incorrect because its length-to-area ratio is smaller than that of the fourth wire.
This is incorrect because its length-to-area ratio is smaller than that of the fourth wire.
This is incorrect because its length-to-area ratio is smaller than that of the fourth wire.
This is correct because elongation is proportional to length divided by cross-sectional area, and this wire has the greatest such ratio.

mcqs.stem: How do the molecules in a solid behave?
options: Rotate and vibrate randomly at their own positions
Move in a straight line from hot to cold ends.
rationales: Solids do not move randomly from place to place; their particles remain in fixed positions.
Solid molecules vibrate about their mean positions.
Rotational motion is not the characteristic motion of molecules in a solid.
Molecules in a solid do not travel from the hot end to the cold end.

mcqs.stem: Which one of the following is not a magnetic material?
rationales: Cobalt is a magnetic material and is attracted to a magnet.
Iron is a magnetic material and is strongly attracted to a magnet.
Aluminium is not classed as a magnetic material in the usual school-level classification.
Nickel is a magnetic material and is attracted to a magnet.

mcqs.stem: Physics is a branch of:
rationales: Social science studies human society and behavior, not physical phenomena.
Life science focuses on living organisms rather than the physical world.
Physics is a physical science that studies matter, energy, and their interactions.
Biological science studies living things, so it is not the broad branch that includes physics.

written.text: Identify and explain the reasons for human errors, random errors and systematic errors in experiments.
modelAnswer: Human errors occur due to personal performance, such as difficulty estimating a pointer's position or reaction time when starting or stopping a clock.
Random errors occur when repeated measurements give different values under the same conditions because of unknown, unpredictable causes, such as changes in temperature or air pressure.
Systematic errors arise from a definite cause and produce a consistent difference in readings; examples include zero error, poor calibration or incorrect marking.

written.text: Describe different types of motion. Also give examples.
modelAnswer: There are three general types of motion: translatory, rotatory and vibratory.
If every particle of a body moves uniformly in the same direction, it is called translatory motion; the motion of a train or a car is an example.
Translatory motion can be linear, random or circular: a freely falling body is linear, a bee moving along an irregular path is random, and a Ferris wheel is circular.
If each point of a body moves around a fixed point (axis), the motion is called rotatory motion; an electric fan or a top is an example.
When a body repeats its to and fro motion about a fixed position, the motion is called vibratory motion; a swing is an example.

written.text: A car travels 10 km with an average velocity of 20 m s⁻¹. Then it travels in the same direction through a diversion at an average velocity of 4 m s⁻¹ for the next 0.8 km. Determine the average velocity of the car for the total journey.
modelAnswer: First distance = 10 km = 10000 m
First average velocity = 20 m s⁻¹
Time for first part = 10000/20 = 500 s
Second distance = 0.8 km = 800 m
Second average velocity = 4 m s⁻¹
Time for second part = 800/4 = 200 s
Total displacement = 10000 m + 800 m = 10800 m
Total time = 500 s + 200 s = 700 s
Average velocity = total displacement/total time
Average velocity = 10800/700 = 15.4 m s⁻¹

written.text: The figure given below shows the distance - time graph for the travel of a cyclist. Find the velocities for the segments a, b and c. [FIGURE: Distance - time graph with vertical axis labelled “Distance → S (km)” and horizontal axis labelled “Time → t (min)”. The vertical scale is 0 to 2.0 in increments of 0.2; the horizontal scale is 0 to 20 in increments of 2. Segment a rises from (0, 0) to (6, 2.0), segment b is horizontal from (6, 2.0) to (10, 2.0), and segment c falls from (10, 2.0) to (20, 0).]

For segment c: (0 − 2.0)/(20 − 10) = −0.2 km min⁻¹ = −12 km h⁻¹

written.text: Is it possible for a body to have acceleration? When moving with: (i) constant velocity (ii) constant speed

written.text: Distance and displacement may or may not be equal in magnitude. Explain this statement.
modelAnswer: Distance is the total length of the path travelled, while displacement is the change in position in a specified direction.
If an object moves along a straight line in one direction, distance and displacement are equal in magnitude.
If the object changes direction or follows a curved path, the distance is greater than the magnitude of the displacement.

written.text: When a bullet is fired, its velocity with which it leaves the barrel is called the muzzle velocity of the gun. modelAnswer: For a bullet starting from rest, v² = u² + 2as and u = 0, so a = v²/(2s).
The question states that the longer-barrel gun has the smaller muzzle velocity; the acceleration comparison depends on both v² and barrel length.

With the usual textbook assumption that the compared muzzle velocities and barrel lengths give the shorter-barrel case the larger value of v²/(2s), the bullet's acceleration is larger in the shorter-barrel gun.

modelAnswer: For constant speed, the area under the speed–time graph is the area of a rectangle.

For changing speed, the areas of the portions of the graph are added; their total is the total distance covered.

Average velocity = total displacement / total time = 10800/700 = 15.4 m s⁻¹.

written.text:
(a) Describe Newton's laws of motion.
(b) A 10 kg block is placed on a smooth horizontal surface. A horizontal force of 5 N is applied to the block. Find: (a) the acceleration produced in the block. (b) the velocity of block after 5 seconds.
modelAnswer: (a) Newton’s first law: A body continues its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by some external force.
Newton’s second law: A net external force accelerates a body in the direction of the force; acceleration is directly proportional to force and inversely proportional to mass.
Therefore, F = ma.
Newton’s third law: For every action, there is always an equal and opposite reaction.
Final answer: Newton’s laws are the law of inertia, F = ma for a net force, and the law of equal and opposite action and reaction.
(b) Given: m = 10 kg, F = 5 N, u = 0, t = 5 s.
(a) F = ma
a = 0.5 m s⁻²
(b) v = u + at
v = 2.5 m s⁻¹

written.text:

modelAnswer: (a) Mass of truck = m = 3000 kg
Force applied = F = 7500 N
Acceleration = a = ?
Initial speed = v_i = 36 km h⁻¹
Final speed = v_f = 72 km h⁻¹ = 72 × 1000 m / (60 × 60 s) = 20 m s⁻¹
Time = t = ?
By Newton's second law, F = ma
or a = F/m
Putting the values, a = 7500 N / 3000 kg = 2.5 m s⁻²
Now, using first equation of motion, v_f = v_i + at
or t = (v_f − v_i)/a
Putting the values, t = (20 m s⁻¹ − 10 m s⁻¹) / 2.5 m s⁻² = 4 s
(b) Given: m = 800 kg, u = 10 m s⁻¹, v = 30 m s⁻¹, t = 10 s.
a = (v − u)/t
F = ma
Final answer: 1600 N

It has a higher centre of gravity than the shorter box.
A higher centre of gravity makes a body less stable.
Therefore, when the truck stops suddenly, the taller box is more likely to topple.

written.text: A car travels at the same speed around two curves with different radii. For which radius the car experiences more centripetal force? Prove your answer.
modelAnswer: Centripetal force is given by F = mv²/r.
The mass and speed of the car are the same for both curves.
Therefore, F is inversely proportional to r.
So the car experiences more centripetal force on the curve with the smaller radius.

written.text: How can you prove that the centripetal force always acts perpendicular to velocity?
modelAnswer: The velocity at any point on a circular path is directed along the tangent.
If the force were not perpendicular to velocity, it would have a component in the direction of velocity.
This component would change the magnitude of velocity.
As the body moves with constant speed, this component is zero: F cos 90° = 0.
Therefore, the centripetal force acts perpendicular to velocity.

written.text:
A spring having spring constant k hangs vertically from a fixed point. A load of weight L, when hung from the spring, causes an extension x, the elastic limit of the spring is not exceeded. Some identical springs, each with spring constant k, are arranged as shown below: For each arrangement, complete the table by determining:
(i) the total extension in terms of x.
(ii) the spring constant in terms of k. | Arrangement | Total Extension x | Spring constant (k) of the arrangement |
|---|---|---|
| [FIGURE: Two springs arranged vertically in series, hanging from a fixed support, with a load labelled L at the bottom.] | | |
| [FIGURE: Two springs arranged in parallel between a fixed support and a horizontal bar, with a load labelled L hanging from the bar.] | | |
modelAnswer: For one spring, L = kx.
Series: each spring carries load L, so each extends by x.
Total extension in series = x + x = 2x.
Spring constant in series = L/(2x) = kx/(2x) = k/2.
Parallel: the identical springs share the load equally, so each carries L/2.
Extension of each spring = (L/2)/k = x/2; hence total extension = x/2.
Spring constant in parallel = L/(x/2) = 2L/x = 2k.

rubric.how: Use k arrangement = L/(2x) and L = kx, giving k/2.

written.text: For each arrangement, complete the table by determining: (i) the total extension in terms of x. (ii) the spring constant in terms of k. Arrangement: Two springs arranged vertically in series, hanging from a fixed support, with a load labelled L at the bottom; two springs arranged in parallel between a fixed support and a horizontal bar, with a load labelled L hanging from the bar.
modelAnswer: For one spring, L = kx.
Series: each spring carries L, so each extends by x.
Total extension in series = x + x = 2x.
k_series = L/(2x) = k/2.
Parallel: the two identical springs share the load equally, so each carries L/2.
Extension in parallel = (L/2)/k = x/2.
k_parallel = L/(x/2) = 2k.

written.text: Example 6.4: The diameters of the pistons of a hydraulic press are 5 cm and 25 cm respectively. A normal force of 160 N is applied on the smaller piston, what will be the pressure exerted by this force on the bigger piston? How much weight can be lifted by the other piston?
modelAnswer: Let the areas of cross-sections of the pistons be A₁ and A₂ and their radii be r₁ and r₂ respectively.
A₁ = πr₁² and A₂ = πr₂²
F₁ = 160 N
According to Pascal's law, F₁/A₁ = w/A₂
w = F₁A₂/A₁ = F₁πr₂²/(πr₁²) = F₁ × r₂²/r₁²
Pressure transmitted = 8.15 × 10⁴ Pa; weight lifted = 4000 N = 4 kN.

written.text:
A spring having spring constant k hangs vertically from a fixed point. A load of weight L, when hung from the spring, causes an extension x, the elastic limit of the spring is not exceeded. Some identical springs, each with spring constant k, are arranged as shown below: For each arrangement, complete the table by determining:
(i) the total extension in terms of x.
(ii) the spring constant in terms of k. | Arrangement | Total Extension x | Spring constant (k) of the arrangement |
|---|---|---|
| [FIGURE: Two springs arranged vertically in series, hanging from a fixed support, with a load labelled L at the bottom.] | | |
| [FIGURE: Two springs arranged in parallel between a fixed support and a horizontal bar, with a load labelled L hanging from the bar.] | | |
modelAnswer: One spring under load L extends by x, so L = kx.
Series: the same load acts on each spring, so each extends by x.
Series total extension = x + x = 2x; equivalent k = L/(2x) = k/2.
Parallel: the load is shared equally, so each spring supports L/2.
Extension of each spring = (L/2)/k = x/2; both have the same total extension x/2.
Parallel equivalent spring constant = L/(x/2) = 2k.

written.text: Describe the main points of particle theory of matter which differentiate solids, liquids and gases.
modelAnswer: In solids, strong intermolecular forces hold the molecules at fixed positions, where they vibrate.
Therefore, a solid has a definite shape and a definite volume.
In liquids, the intermolecular force is too weak to hold the molecules at fixed positions; they slide over one another.
Therefore, a liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape and takes the shape of its container.
Gas molecules are relatively far apart, so a gas has neither a definite volume nor a definite shape.

written.text: What is temperature? How is it measured? Describe briefly the construction of a mercury-in-glass thermometer.

A mercury-in-glass thermometer is made of glass and has a bulb at one end filled with mercury.
The bulb is connected to a narrow capillary tube, and a scale is marked on the glass stem.
When the temperature rises, the mercury expands and moves up through the capillary tube; the position of the end of the thread reads the temperature.

written.text: Compare the three scales used for measuring temperature.
modelAnswer: In Celsius scale, the lower and upper fixed points are 0°C and 100°C; the space between them is divided into 100 equal parts.
In Fahrenheit scale, the lower and upper fixed points are 32°F and 212°F; the space between them is divided into 180 equal parts.
In Kelvin scale, the lower and upper fixed points are 273 K and 373 K; the space between them is divided into 100 equal parts.
The width of 1 K is the same as that of 1°C.
Kelvin is also known as the absolute temperature scale and is used in scientific measurements.

written.text: Describe the main points of particle theory of matter which differentiate solids, liquids and gases.
modelAnswer: Matter consists of tiny particles.
In a solid, particles are very closely packed, strongly attracted and vibrate about fixed mean positions; a solid has fixed shape and volume.
In a liquid, particles are close together but can move past one another; a liquid has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container.
In a gas, particles are far apart, weakly attracted and move freely in random directions; a gas has neither fixed shape nor fixed volume.
Thus, particle spacing, motion and intermolecular forces differentiate solids, liquids and gases.

written.text:
(a) Why is mercury usually preferred to alcohol as a thermometric liquid?
(b) Compare the three scales used for measuring temperature.
modelAnswer: (a) Mercury is opaque and can be easily seen due to its silvery colour.
It does not wet glass and has uniform thermal expansion.
Alcohol is also a choice for the thermometric liquid, but it must be coloured to make it visible.
(b) In Celsius scale, the lower and upper fixed points are 0°C and 100°C; the space between them is divided into 100 equal parts.
In Fahrenheit scale, the lower and upper fixed points are 32°F and 212°F; the space between them is divided into 180 equal parts.
In Kelvin scale, the lower and upper fixed points are 273 K and 373 K; the space between them is divided into 100 equal parts.
The width of 1 K is the same as that of 1°C.
Kelvin is also known as the absolute temperature scale and is used in scientific measurements.

written.text: Differentiate between paramagnetic, diamagnetic and ferromagnetic materials with reference to the domain theory.
modelAnswer: In paramagnetic materials, the orbital and spin fields support one another, so each atom has a resultant magnetic field and behaves like a tiny magnet.
Examples are aluminium and lithium.
In diamagnetic materials, the orbital and spin fields add up to zero, so each atom has no resultant field.
Examples are copper, bismuth and water.
In ferromagnetic materials, electron spins in large groups of neighbouring atoms are naturally aligned parallel to each other.
These groups form highly magnetized domains, each of which behaves as a small magnet with its own north and south poles.

written.text: What are the main branches of Physics? State briefly.
modelAnswer: Mechanics: It is a study of motion and the physical effects which influence motion.
Heat and thermodynamics: It deal with the thermal energy possessed by the materials and it is used when it flows from one body to another.
Acoustics: It deals with the nature and physical aspects of audible sound energy.
Optics: It deal with the physical aspects of visible light.
Electromagnetism: It is the study of electromagnetic phenomenon and mutual relationship between electric current and magnetic field.
Quantum Mechanics: It explains the behaviour of particles at the atomic and subatomic level.

Relativistic Mechanics: It explains how space and time are not absolute quantities but related to observer. It describes the relationship between them and how they are influenced by gravity and speed.
Nuclear Physics: It is the study of the properties of nuclei of the atoms.
Particle Physics: It is the study of subatomic particles and elementary particles which are basic building blocks of matter.
Astronomy: It is study of distribution of celestial bodies like planets, stars and galaxies.
Cosmology: It explores the large structure and evolution of the universe.
Solid State Physics: It is the study of some specific properties of matter in solid form.

Nuclear Physics: It is the study of the properties of nuclei of the atoms.
Particle Physics: It is the study of subatomic particles and elementary particles which are basic building blocks of matter.
Astronomy: It is study of distribution of celestial bodies like planets, stars and galaxies.
Cosmology: It explores the large structure and evolution of the universe.
Solid State Physics: It is the study of some specific properties of matter in solid form.

First, identify a problem and gather information by observation.
Next, propose a hypothesis and perform an experiment or collect evidence to test it.
Record, organize and analyse the data to reach a conclusion called a theory; repeated tests of the theory over similar issues lead towards a law.
For example, observation of shadows leads to the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line.
When holes in four cardboards are aligned with a torch, light passes through; when one cardboard is displaced, the light is blocked.
This experiment supports the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line, and repeated testing in different situations may establish a law.

(b) Q4.2. A force of 300 N is applied perpendicularly at the knob of a door to open it as shown in the given figure. If the knob is 1.2 m away from the hinge, what is the torque applied? Is it positive or negative torque?

Velocity v = 54 km h⁻¹ = 15 m s⁻¹

written.text:
(a) How can you identify whether an object is a magnet or a magnetic material?
(b) The ice and steam points on an ungraduated thermometer are found to be 192 mm apart. What temperature will be on Celsius scale if the length of mercury thread is at 67.2 mm above the ice point mark?
modelAnswer: (a) Bring one end of the object close to any pole of a suspended bar magnet.
If it is attracted, it may be the opposite pole of a magnet or a magnetic material.
Bring the same end of the object close to the other pole of the suspended magnet.
If it is attracted again, the object is a magnetic material, not a magnet.
If it is repelled by the other end, the object is a magnet.
Repulsion between like poles is the real test for identifying a magnet.
(b) 192 mm corresponds to 100°C
67.2 mm corresponds to T_c

written.text:
(a) A 10 kg block is placed on a smooth horizontal surface. A horizontal force of 5 N is applied to the block. Find: (a) the acceleration produced in the block. (b) the velocity of block after 5 seconds.
(b) How equations of motion can be applied to the bodies moving under the action of gravity?
modelAnswer: (a) Mass of block = m = 10 kg
Force applied = F = 5 N
By Newton's second law, F = ma
a = F/m = 5 N / 10 kg = 0.5 m s⁻²
Initial velocity = u = 0 m s⁻¹
Time = t = 5 s
Using first equation of motion, v = u + at
(b) Use the equations of motion: v_f = v_i + at.
S = v_i t + 1/2 at².
2aS = v_f² − v_i².
For motion under gravity, put a = g, with its sign set by the direction of acceleration.
Take the direction of initial velocity as positive; quantities in the opposite direction are negative.

(a) EXAMPLE 6.3: A cylindrical water tank 2 m deep has been built on the top of a building 20 m high. What will be the pressure of water at the ground floor when the tank is full? Density of water is 1000 kg m⁻³. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
(b) A 0.14 kg ball is thrown vertically upward with an initial velocity of 35 m s⁻¹. Find the maximum height reached by the ball.
modelAnswer: (a) Height h = 2 + 20 = 22m
Density ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³
g =10 m s⁻²
P = ρgh = 22 m ×1000 kg m⁻³ ×10 m s⁻²
(b) At maximum height, kinetic energy changes into potential energy.
½mv² = mgh
h = v²/(2g)
